## Author’s Preface

The research and writing for this book ‘Chaurasi-kosa Vraja Mandala Parikrama' took many years to complete. The detailing of over 600 holy places was a great endeavor, and travelling to each of these holy places while gathering the relevant information and mapping the area took considerable time. I actually began work on this book in 2008, and by Kartika 2011, at the request of many devotees, I extracted from the manuscript a special ISKCON version of Vraja Mandala Parikrama that starts from Vrindavana and visits eighty-four of the most important holy places. That version was entitled ‘The Complete Guide to ISKCON's Vraja Mandala Parikrama' and it became extremely popular among the devotees. Due to demand it was reprinted in 2016. The parikrama undertaken by ISKCON devotees has been named as the Chaurasi-tirtha Parikrama, as it visits eighty-four of the most prominent holy places of Vraja Mandala.

This new edition catalogues every holy tirtha within the 168-mile 'chaurasi-kosa' area of Vraja Mandala and for the first time the inner core region of the dhama containing all the sites of Krishna's pastimes has been accurately mapped. Located near the Vraja Mandala Parikrama route are many isolated holy places that are rarely visited but are important tirthas where Lord Krishna performed His pastimes. Therefore, visiting these holy places is presented in the form of excursions from the main parikrama route. This enables devotees to visit any of the isolated tirthas from any point on the parikrama route that they choose.

The history and exact location of the various pastime places in the holy dhama is sometimes difficult to ascertain, because many of them have been forgotten over time, or their history has been somewhat distorted. Regardless, it has always been my endeavor to document the places of Lord Krishna's pastimes based upon the three forms of evidence, or pramana, established by Shrila Rupa Goswami, in his own research and excavation of Vraja Mandala. The first is shastra-pramana - evidence based upon the revealed Vedic scriptures. The second is sadhu-pramana - evidence revealed through the writings of Vaishnava saints. The third is loka-pramana - evidence handed down by oral tradition by generations of local Vrajavasis.

Just as the Gaudiya Goswamis, Rupa and Sanatana, relied on the revealed Vedic scriptures during their excavation of Vraja, while writing this edition, we have also relied on the same scriptures. Some controversy created by neophytes has arisen surrounding the authenticity of the Garga Samhita, one of the most important reference books on Vraja Mandala. In response I may quote from the Dig-darshini commentary on Brihad-bhagavatamrita (1.1.21-23) by Shrila Sanatana Goswami where he says, "The confidential science of pure devotional service is taught explicitly only in a few Vedic scriptures. Among these rare texts are Gopala-tapani Upanishad, the Narada Pancharatra, the Garga Samhita, the Vishnu Purana, the Hari-vamsa Upapurana, the Padma Purana (Uttara khanda), and the Bhagavata Maha-purana." Thus, it is of utmost importance that when visiting the holy tirthas of Vraja, devotees are in possession of authoritative information as they take delight in seeing the various holy places of Lord Krishna's transcendental pastimes.

Rajasekhara Dasa Brahmachari Vrindavana Dhama, Kartika, 2018.

## Instructions on Performing Parikrama

Adapted From Vraja-bhakti Vilasa

It is accepted by all Vaishnava authorities that Vraja Mandala Parikrama can start from any point on the parikrama route, and at any time of the year according to practical convenience. Although there are a number of specific dates in the Vedic calendar that are recommended for starting Vraja Mandala Parikrama, one can perform the parikrama according to preference. Once Vraja Mandala Parikrama has been started, it should be completed and should finish at the same place where the parikrama began in order for it to be considered as a complete parikrama. In Vrindavana Dhama the results of devotional activities are magnified one hundred times and during the holy month of Kartika over one thousand times, thus a devotee can make rapid advancement while visiting the holy dhama. Concomitantly, one's offences are also similarly magnified and therefore one should strictly not commit any offence in the holy dhama in order to avoid unwanted karmic reactions.

**The Ten Offences to Be Avoided In the Holy Dhama**

1\.    To have disrespect or contempt for the acharya, or guru who is the revealer of the holy dhama.

2\.    To think that the holy dhama is temporary.

3\.    To commit violence towards anyone in the holy dhama and to think that the residents or pilgrims visiting the dhama are ordinary materialistic people.

4\.    To perform mundane activities while living in the holy dhama.

5\.    To earn money or make a business from deity worship or chanting the holy names of the Lord.

6\.    To think that the holy dhama belongs to a mundane country or province or, to think that the holy dhama is equal to other holy places connected to the demigods, or to try to estimate the area of the dhama by some material mechanism.

7\.    To commit sinful activities in the holy dhama.

8\.    To consider Vrindavana and Navadvipa to be different.

9\.    To blaspheme the Vedic scriptures that glorifies the holy dhama.

10\.   To be faithless and to think that the glories of the holy dhama are imaginary.

**Other Guidelines to Observe While Performing Parikrama**

A. One should always offer respect to the temple Deities, as well as to the cows, Vaishnavas, brahmanas, local residents, sacred trees, plants, kundas, and any other living entity, moving or none-moving, within the holy dhama.

B.    One should not become angry, curse, or offend any person, or any living entity while on parikrama; otherwise the benefits of the parikrama will be lost.

C.    While entering temples one should not wear shoes or leather items and one's clothing should be freshly washed. It is also recommended not to wear shoes when on parikrama.

D.    Before performing parikrama one should bathe and clean one's mouth and teeth and one should also observe celibacy.

E.    One should not perform parikrama at night.

F.    While walking on parikrama one must avoid crushing or injuring tiny living entities on the route.

G.    If one becomes sick while on parikrama one should rest and continue parikrama later.

H.    One should not leave parikrama incomplete.

## Chapter One: Introduction to Vraja Mandala

## Descriptions of the Transcendental Form of the Supreme Lord

The most celebrated description of Lord Shri Krishna is found in the Vedic classic known as the Brahma-samhita, a prayer composed by Prajapati Brahma, who was the first recipient of Vedic knowledge and from whose mouth the four Vedas originally became manifest:

“Krishna who is known as Govinda is the Supreme Personality of Godhead who possesses an eternal spiritual body. He is the origin of all and has no other origin, and is therefore the cause of all causes. I worship Govinda, the primeval Lord, the first progenitor who is tending the cows, yielding all desire in abodes built with spiritual gemstones, surrounded by millions of desire trees, always served with great reverence and affection by hundreds and thousands of Laksmis or goddesses of fortune. I worship Govinda, the primeval Lord, who is adept at playing on His flute, who has blossoming eyes like lotus petals, whose head is bedecked with a peacock’s feather, who possesses a figure of exquisite beauty, and whose complexion is tinged with the hue of blue clouds, and whose unique loveliness is charming millions of Cupids. I worship Govinda, the primeval Lord, around whose neck is a garland of forest flowers beautified with a moon-locket, whose two hands, adorned with jeweled ornaments, is holding His transcendental flute, and who always revels in pastimes of divine love, and whose graceful three-fold bending form of Shyamasundara is eternally manifest.”

## Descriptions of the Transcendental Abode of the Supreme Lord

The word dhama refers to the Supreme Lord’s eternal abode located in the spiritual world. This eternal abode (dhama) is known as Goloka Vrindavana, or sometimes as Swetadwipa, and being the abode of the Supreme Lord it is completely spiritual in nature. It is also non-different from the Lord Himself, just as the Lord’s name, form, and attributes are also non-different from Him. A description of the Lord’s eternal abode of Goloka Vrindavana is found in the Brahma-samhita, “I worship that transcendental abode known as Swetadwipa, where the goddesses of fortune known as gopis, in their unalloyed spiritual essence, engage in the amorous service of Lord Shri Krishna who is their only lover; where every tree is a transcendental desire tree, where the earth is made of wish-fulfilling gemstones, where all water is nectar, every word is a song, every gait is a dance, where the flute is the Lord’s favored companion, where the atmosphere is full of transcendental bliss; where numberless Surabhi cows provide transcendental oceans of milk; where there is eternal existence of transcendental time, which is ever present and without past or future, and thus not subject to the quality of passing away, not even for a moment. That transcendental realm of Goloka is known to only a very few self-realized souls in this world.”

## When the Lord Descends to Earth He Brings His Own Abode

The Supreme Personality of Godhead Lord Shri Krishna resides on the planet known as Goloka or Goloka-Vrindavana. The word Goloka means the planet (loka) of cows (go). On that spiritual planet there are an unlimited number of Surabhi cows known as Kamadhenus or wishfulfilling cows that can fulfill the desires of everyone and supply a great abundance of nectarine tasting milk to all the residents. This transcendental planet is situated in the far distant spiritual sky, but when the Lord desires to appear on earth along with His eternal associates, the gopis and gopas, He first manifests on the earthly plain, His own spiritual abode (dhama) where He will enact His transcendental pastimes for the benefit of the world. The Vraja-ritti-cintamani says that the spiritual abode of the Lord is non-different from Him, “The peerless and supremely sweet land of Vrindavana is the blissful abode where the Supreme Personality of Godhead enjoys pastimes. It is the incarnation of the Lord’s form and is non different from Him.”

That abode of the Lord, when manifested on earth is called Gokula or Gokula-Vrindavana. The word ‘Gokula’ means the ‘home’ (kula) of the ‘cows’ (go). The word ‘Vrindavana’ means ‘the forest (vana) of Vrinda’. The word ‘Vrinda’ refers to the forest goddess Vrinda Devi who manifests herself as the flora and fauna of Vrindavana forest and specifically as the sacred tulsi plant (Ocimum tenuiflorum), also called the ‘holy basil’, that grows in great abundance throughout that sacred forest. The forest goddess Vrinda Devi, an eternal associates of Lord Krishna and also appears as one of the prominent gopis who makes all the various arrangements for the Lord’s pastimes to take place.

The transcendental abode of Gokula-Vrindavana is also called Vrindavana Dhama; the word ‘dhama' means ‘spiritual abode’ and the Vrindavana Dhama covers an approximate area of 168 miles (chaurasi-kosa). Vrindavana Dhama is also known as Vraja Mandala; the word ‘vraja' means the ‘pasturing grounds’ where cows graze and the word ‘mandala’ means ‘area’. The 168 mile area of Vraja Mandala encompasses twelve sacred forests along with rivers, lakes, hills, groves, and gardens. The entire dhama is completely spiritual and is non-different from the original Goloka-Vrindavana in the spiritual world, even though it exists within the material world. In the Garga-samhita (2.1.53) it says, “Sri Varaha said: O beautiful one, you see transcendental Mathura-mandala (Vraja-mandala), which is part of the realm of Goloka, it is not destroyed at the time of cosmic devastation.”

The term Vraja Mandala specifically refers to the actual geographical area (mandala) of the Lord’s earthly abode of Vrindavana Dhama, which is demarcated by precise boundaries and can be easily located on a map of the world. Therefore, anyone from any place on earth can visit this transcendental abode of the Lord at any time. This is one of the reasons why Lord Krishna has manifested His abode on the earthly plane, so that those who wish to become His devotees and surrender their lives to Him can go there and experience His transcendental presence and visit the places of His transcendental pastimes, even long after He has left this world and returned to the spiritual world. Another reason for manifesting this abode on earth is to give information to the fallen souls that there is another world, where the Lord and His devotees enjoy an eternal life, completely free from all the pain and misery associated with life in this material world of repeated birth, disease, old age and death.

## The Timing of the Lord’s Descent on Earth

Five thousand years ago, at the time of Lord Krishna’s descent to the earthly plane, the world was being overrun by powerful demons in the form of impious and cruel kings, who were building up huge military forces for the purpose of world domination. The innocent people who were suffering under the yoke of these irreligious kings were fervently praying for the Lord to save them. In the Bhagavad-gita, Lord Krishna has personally said, “In order to deliver the pious and to annihilate the miscreants, as well as to reestablish the principles of religion, I descend to earth millennium after millennium.” Therefore, this is another reason for the Supreme Personality of Godhead Lord Shri Krishna, to appear on earth, when there is a general decline in piety and religion and the devotees of the Lord find themselves being persecuted. At that time, Lord Krishna descends to earth in His transcendental spiritual form and in order to save His beloved devotees and human society, He is forced to kill all the demons that are creating unnecessary disturbances. Nevertheless, by His unfathomable mercy, all the demons that He kills, automatically achieve liberation. After the Lord had exhibited His transcendental pastimes on earth for a period of one hundred and twenty-five years, and after annihilating all the demons, as well as having reestablished the principles of pure religion (Sanatana-dharma), He returned to His eternal abode of Goloka in the spiritual world.

## The Holy Dhama Was Known Even In Ancient Times

One of the earliest references to the holy dhama of Gokula Vrindavana is found in the Adi-Varaha Purana, which relates a conversation between the incarnation of Vishnu, Lord Varahadeva and His consort Bhumi Devi, goddess of the earth, which took place at Vishrama Ghata on the banks of the Yamuna at Mathura during the Satya-yuga, just after the earth had been rescued from the ocean of devastation by the Lord. In that conversation with Bhumi Devi, Lord Varaha enumerates the glories of all the various holy tirthas located within the area of Vraja Mandala.

Since very ancient times many saintly persons journeyed to the holy dhama of Vrindavana in order to perform tapasya and meditate on the lotus feet of the Supreme Lord, in order to achieve liberation and fulfill their innermost desires. Amongst them was the famous child-saint Dhruva Maharaja, who in the Raivata-manvantara underwent severe austerities in the celebrated Madhuvana forest just to please Lord Vishnu. Another was the saintly king Ambarisha Maharaja, who performed great penance in Madhuvana forest by observing an ekadashi-vrata for one year for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord. The famous grandson of Prahlada Maharaja, King Bali, worshiped the sun-god Surya Narayana and performed a great Vedic sacrifice (yajna) on the bank of the Yamuna in Madhuvana so that he could conquer the world. Maharaja Shantanu, the king of Hastinapura, also performed great penance at Satoya to please Surya Narayana, so that he could obtain a saintly and heroic son. Even the goddess of fortune, after hearing from Narada Muni about Krishna's Vraja-lila pastimes with the gopis, underwent severe penance in Bilvavan forest in order to become a gopi and take part in those transcendental pastimes.

The great sages, yogis, munis, and rishis, known to have performed tapasya and meditation in the holy dhama includes: Kapiladeva, Narada Muni, Kanva Muni, Vishvamitra Muni, Garga Rishi, Ashtavakra Muni, Durvasa Muni, Gautama Rishi, the Sapta Rishis, Dattatreya Rishi, Bhaguri Rishi, Bhagava Rishi, Chayavana Muni, Jamadagni, Parashurama, Parashara Muni and his illustrious son Shrila Vyasadeva. In fact it is said that Shrila Vyasadeva, the great compiler of Vedic literature, was actually born on an island in the Yamuna River near Mathura. Others like Maharishi Agastya Muni, performed many Vedic sacrifices at Akrura Ghata on the outskirts of Vrindavana and Saubhari Muni meditated deep inside the River Yamuna at Kaliya-hrada near Sanorakha. The devoted Sandilya Muni, who requested Vajranabha Maharaja to establish Krishna's pastime places in Vraja, also resided in the holy dhama.

## The Actual Meaning of Vraja

There are a number of meanings to the name Vraja, but the actual root meaning of the word 'vraja' is 'to go' or 'to move'. Therefore, the simplest definition of the word 'vraja' is the place where 'cows roam freely', which refers to Vrindavana, the transcendental land of the cows. Vraja can also mean the land where the cowherd boys with their large herds of cows roam unhindered from one forest to another. When Krishna appeared on earth, He also wandered about 'unhindered' with His herd of cows and cowherd boyfriends through the pasturing lands of Vraja. Therefore the word 'vraja' can also mean 'unhindered' as well as 'unlimited freedom'. Another meaning is derived from the Sanskrit stanza, “vrajati gacchati iti vrajah" which translates as, “That which moves around is Vraja,” which further implies that the Sanskrit word 'vraja' means 'to move around' or 'to go here and there unhindered', just as cows do when grazing in the pasturing grounds. According to the Sanskrit dictionary there are a number of related meanings to the word vraja including: a way, a road, wandering, roaming, as well as cattle-shed, pen, enclosure or place of herdsmen, a herd, flock, swarm, troop, host, or multitude.

A more deeply philosophical meaning is found in the Skanda Purana in the following verse, “Sandilya Rishi said, 'My dear Pariksit and Vajranabha, I will now tell you the secret of Vraja-bhumi, listen carefully. The meaning of the word 'vraja' is 'all-pervasive'. According to ancient opinion, this land is named Vraja because it is actually all-pervasive. It is an all-pervasive spiritual manifestation situated beyond the three modes of material nature. Therefore it is called Vraja.”

This verse from the Skanda Purana, gives us the information that the transcendental land of Vraja is different from any other place on earth, because it is beyond the effects of material nature and is a place where all our sufferings can be finally ended. Therefore, if we can surrender our hearts to Krishna and take shelter of His abode, allowing its all-pervasive spiritual nature to pervade our very own existence, the transcendental land of Vraja can, by its all-pervasive spiritual power, purify our very existence and bless us with divine love for Krishna and eternal life free from suffering.

## The Difference between Vraja Mandala and Mathura Mandala

In the Puranas, the area known as Vraja Mandala, was generally referred to as Mathura Mandala, and was associated with the pastime of Lord Vishnu, like Lord Varaha and Lord Prishnigarbha, but after Lord Krishna's advent on earth five thousand years ago at the end of the Dwapara Yuga, the name Vraja Mandala became exclusively associated with the places where Lord Krishna performed His pastimes. Although Mathura Mandala and Vraja Mandala cover the exact same area and exist simultaneously, the name Vraja Mandala refers to the place where Krishna performed His Vraja-lila pastimes with the gopas and gopis, and where He appears in His original form (svayam-rupa) as Govinda, the friend of the cows. On the other hand, Mathura Mandala generally refers to the place where Krishna appears in His plenary expansion as Vasudeva, and enjoys pastimes in various Vishnu forms including: Lord Hari, Mathureshwara, Dwarakadisha, Sankarshana, Prishnigarbha, Varahadeva, Parthasarathy and others.

This distinction made between Vraja Mandala and Mathura Mandala is meant to demonstrate the different varieties of pastimes and loving relationships Krishna enjoys with the various categories of His devotees. Before the advent of Krishna, the Vraja-lila pastimes were practically unknown and very few knew about them. The only concept people had of God, was as the Almighty Creator who was worshiped with great pomp, awe, and reverence. The special feature of Vraja is that Krishna is not even seen as God, but is thought to be an ordinary cowherd boy, the beloved friend of all the gopas and gopis and the darling son of Nanda and Yashoda. This is the unique and special feature of Vraja Mandala.

In Vraja, Krishna is able to live what appears to be an normal village life surrounded by all his friends and family members, and He is not recognized to be the Supreme Controller, but as someone who is completely under the control of His loving parents Nanda and Yashoda, as well as the gopis and gopas of Vraja. Therefore in Vraja Mandala, Krishna enjoys a very special and intimate kind of relationship with His devotees, which is not possible for Him to experience in either Mathura or Dwaraka where He is worshiped as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. This equality between God and His devotees is made possible by Krishna's powerful internal potency known as yogamaya, which causes the residents of Vrindavana to think of Krishna as an ordinary village boy. The most unique feature of the yogamaya potency is that Krishna Himself forgets His position as the Supreme Personality of Godhead and considers Himself one of the ordinary cowherd boys of Vraja.

Another important fact is that only in Vraja, does Krishna experience the transcendentally ecstatic states of divine love known as parakiya-bhava, vipralamba-bhava and maha-bhava, which are the highest form of all transcendental emotions and relished exclusively by Krishna and His most intimate associates the gopis of Vraja. Only the most spiritually advanced and exalted of all perfect yogis and pure devotees can achieve the position of gopis and take part in this aspect of Vraja-lila, the transcendental pastimes of divine love.

When Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu appeared on earth, He specifically glorified Krishna's Vraja-lila pastimes and said that the exalted devotional sentiments exhibited by the gopis of Vraja, is the highest stage of perfection that can be attained through any form of religious ritual or yoga practice. Before Lord Chaitanya appeared on earth and revealed the glories of Vraja, the importance of Vraja-lila was not generally understood. It was solely due to Lord Chaitanya and His senior-most disciples, the Six Goswamis, that Krishna's divine Vraja-lila pastimes and the holy dhama of Gokula Vrindavana has become known to the world. According to the Vedic scriptures, Lord Chaitanya was non-other than Krishna Himself, reincarnated on earth to reveal the secrets about Vrindavana and the loving pastimes between Krishna and the gopis for the benefit of all humanity.

## The Extraordinary Position Attained by the Gopis of Vraja

There are basically two categories of gopis, the first being those who descended from the spiritual world along with Krishna and known as nitya-siddha gopis. The second category are known as sadhana-siddha and kripa-siddha gopis, who in their previous lives had been great yogis and mystics engaged in severe penance and austerity to achieve pure love of God. The relationship of the gopis with Krishna is based entirely on the ecstatic emotions of pure spiritual love known as prema-rasa. Unfortunately, for those who have never experienced prema-rasa, it is almost impossible to understand the ecstatic pleasure derived from such pure unalloyed love of God. This ecstatic state of divine love can only be achieved by the most spiritually advanced persons who have completely removed all traces of mundane sexual desire from their consciousness. The pleasure of prema-rasa experienced by the gopis, is millions of times superior to the so-called pleasures of ‘kama-rasa', or mundane sexual pleasure, which arises from lust and ultimately ends in suffering.

Only when all desire for mundane sexual pleasure has been completely purified, can the ecstatic feelings of prema-rasa manifest within ones heart. Once prema has manifested within the core of a devotee's heart, then it is absolutely impossible to experience any form of mundane sexual desire. A devotee who has achieved freedom from mundane sexual desire is then qualified to be born as a gopi in Vraja and take part in Krishna's pastimes. Another very important fact to remember when hearing about the love affair between Krishna and the gopis of Vraja, is that these pastimes began when Krishna and the gopis were just seven years of age and continued only until their tenth year. Thus Krishna's amorous pastimes of gopi-lila were performed before the age of puberty, thus eliminating the opportunity by misguided persons to misinterpret the transcendental loving exchanges of prema-rasa between Krishna and the gopis as being expressions of mundane lust.

## Vajranabha Establishes Krishna’s Pastime Places in Vraja

The Mahabharata says that after Lord Krishna's disappearance from the world, the Pandavas also retired from their royal duties as the sovereign rulers over the kingdom of Hastinapura and departed for the Himalayas. At that time, Yudisthira Maharaja appointed Parikshit Maharaja as the king of Hastinapura and Lord Krishna's great grandson, Vajranabha Maharaja as the king of both Indraprashta and Mathura. Vajranabha Maharaja was the son of the great hero Aniruddha, who was the son of Pradyumna, the direct son of Lord Krishna and Queen Rukmini. At that time, Vajranabha was the only direct relative of Krishna left on the planet. As soon as Vajranabha Maharaja was enthroned at Mathura, many of Lord Krishna's great devotees led by Sandilya Rishi, who were all feeling the pangs of the Lord's separation, requested Vajranabha to establish temples and holy tirthas at all the places throughout Vraja Mandala where Lord Krishna had performed His transcendental pastimes. Vajranabha readily agreed and being guided by Vedic scriptures like the Adi-Varaha Purana, he identified and named every forest, grove, garden, lake, kunda, hill, rock, and village, connected to Krishna's pastimes within the entire area of Vraja Mandala.

## Vajranabha Installed Sixteen Important Deities in Vraja

It is said that Vajranabha installed at least sixteen very important Deities at various places around Vraja Mandala. The first Deities were established in the forest of Vrindavana and included: Madana-mohana, Govindaji, Gopinatha, and Sakshi-Gopala. Although Vajranabha was the son of Anirrudha who was himself the son of Pradyumna, Krishna own son from the womb of Rukmini, which made Vajranabha Lord Krishna's great-grandson, he was too young to have ever met Lord Krishna Himself, therefore In order to arrange for the Deities of Krishna to be carved in true likeness, he had to take help from his grandmother Uttara, the mother of Maharaja Pariksit, the only person still present on earth at that time who had actually seen Lord Krishna. Consequently, with the help of Uttara, Vajranabha immediately had three important Deities of Lord Krishna carved, namely: Madana-Mohana, Govindaji and Gopinathaji, who were to be installed in Vrindavana. After hearing the descriptions of Lord Krishna's form from Uttara, the three Deities were carved from pure black marble known as vraja-shila. When Uttara came to see the finished Deities, she exclaimed that Madana-Mohana perfectly resembled the Lord from His naval to His lotus feet; Govindaji perfectly resembled the Lord from His Navel to His neck. When Uttara saw the Deity of Gopinatha, it is said that she blushed in shyness while exclaiming that Gopinatha perfectly resembled the beautiful ever-smiling lotus face of the Lord.

The process of bhakti-yoga has three stages: sambandha, abhidheya, and prayojana, and the three most prominent Deities: Madana-Mohana, Govindaji and Gopinathaji, established by Vajranabha, represent the three eternal duties of all living entities trapped in the material world under the shackles of maya. Sambandha refers to establishing one's original relationship with the Supreme Personality of Godhead, abhidheya refers to acting according to that constitutional relationship, and prayojana is the ultimate goal of life, which is to develop love of Godhead. Madan-Mohan is the deity who establishes our relationship with Krishna; Govinda is the deity who accepts our devotional service, and Gopinatha is the Deity who fulfills our desires and attracts us to return back to Godhead. The diksha-guru or initiating spiritual master is the representation of Lord Madan-Mohan (sambandha). The shiksha-guru or instructing spiritual master is the representation of Lord Govinda Deva (abhidheya), and Lord Gopinath represents the ultimate goal of devotional service which is spontaneous attraction in pure love of Godhead (prayojana).

Sakshi-Gopala was also installed in Vrindavana but later the Deity moved to a village near Jagannatha Puri in Orissa. Other Deities installed at various places around Vraja included: Keshavadeva in Mathura, Harideva at Manasi-ganga in Govardhana, Shrinathaji (Gopala) at Aniyora Village on top of Govardhana Hill, and the Deity of Krishna's elder brother Lord Balarama (also known as Dauji or Baladeva) at Mahavana. Vajranabha also established four Shiva-lingas known as the dig-palas, or protectors of the holy dhama including: Bhuteshwara at Mathura, Gopishwara in Vrindavana, Cakreshwara at Govardhana Hill, and Kameshwara at Kamyavana. Vajranabha also established four Deities of Krishna's sister Yogamaya Devi, which are known as the four Devis of Vraja and include; Yogamaya Devi presently at the Yoga-pitha in Vrindavana, Vrinda Devi presently at Kamyavana, Manasi Devi at Govardhana, and Patala Devi in Mathura. Due to the turmoil that unfolded over the next five thousand years, with the ever-changing socio-political scenario and the numerous invasions of India, almost all of the holy places and Deities established by Vajranabha, either became abandoned, looted by invaders, hidden for safety, or just forgotten with the passage of time.

## The Sudden Decline of Bhagavata-dharma in India

From around 500 BCE, the invasion of India began, firstly with the Persians under Darius, then the Greeks under Alexander, then the Syrians under Seleucus Nicator, and eventually the whole of the North-west frontier of India was ultimately overrun by foreign invaders. The Greco-Bactrian's under Menander were the first to move southwards into the Indian heart-land and captured Mathura in 150 BCE. Then around 140 BCE, hordes of nomadic tribesmen known as the Sakas overthrew the Greco-Bactrian Empire in Northern India and also eventually captured Mathura. Another nomadic tribe known as the Kushans under Kanishka defeated the Sakas and by 50 BCE, they had conquered the whole of North India and Mathura became the southern capital of the Kushan Empire. The Kushan kings converted to Buddhism and Mathura became a major centre of Buddhist learning and culture, with many ancient holy places being turned into Buddhist shrines and monasteries. By the turn of the 5th century CE, the great Hindu king, Vikramaditya, drove out the Kushans and reestablished control over the whole of Northern India from the Ganges Delta to the Hindu Kush. He also retook the city of Mathura and rebuilt the Keshava Temple on a grand scale. Unfortunately, peace did not last long and within a few hundred years the invasions of India began once again, but with even greater ferocity, as the Huns, Arabs, Turks, Afghans, Routeans, and then the Mughals, conquered the sub-continent of India one after another.

## The 'Golden Avatara’ Lord Chaitanya Revives Bhagavata-dharma

According to references in the Vedic scriptures, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was a direct incarnation of Krishna, who appeared on earth at Navadwipa Dhama in Bengal in the year 1486 CE, principally for the purpose of spreading the yuga-dharma or the process of salvation in the modern age, which is the sankirtana-yajna. The sankirtana-yajna is the only Vedic sacrifice recommended in the age of Kali and is performed by the congregational chanting of God's holy names in the form of the maha-mantra, or the great chant of deliverance namely: Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.

Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is mentioned in the Vedic scriptures as being the 'Gaura-Avatara' or 'Golden Avatara', which means the 'golden hued incarnation' due to His effulgent golden-colored complexion. A far more secret and confidential reason for Lord Krishna to appear as Lord Chaitanya was to experience for Himself, Radharani's unique emotional mood (Radha-bhava) and the unparalleled love that She feels towards Him. The Chaitanya-charitamrita (Adi 1.5) says, “Shri krishna chaitanya, radha krishna nahe anya - Lord Chaitanya was an incarnation of both Radha and Krishna.” In other words, Lord Chaitanya was Krishna Himself who appeared with the same devotional mood and bodily complexion as that possessed by Shrimati Radharani.

The Vedas say that in the Kali-yuga the Almighty Lord does not appear as the Supreme Lord, but appears in the guise of a devotee of the Supreme Lord, who preaches the glories of the Supreme Lord's holy name. Therefore Lord Chaitanya is also called the 'Channa-Avatara' or hidden incarnation. Besides revealing the yuga-dhama of chanting the holy names, Lord Chaitanya's mission was to establish the Shrimad Bhagavatam as the foremost of all the Vedic scriptures and the means of salvation for all men.

The divine appearance of Lord Chaitanya marked the beginning of the great 'bhakti renaissance' of the middle-ages and the ultimate revival of Bhagavata-dharma in India. Lord Chaitanya revealed the purest forms of Vedic religion and established prema-bhakti as the highest spiritual achievement for all of mankind. Due to Lord Chaitanya's powerful preaching, the sankirtana movement that He started, not only spread throughout the entire Indian subcontinent, but eventually spread right across the face of the earth. The most important Vedic scriptures like Bhagavad-gita and Shrimad Bhagavatam became, for the first time in history, popular reading matter all over the world and the yoga process of prema-bhakti gained preeminence over all other yoga systems. By the mercy of Lord Chaitanya, the chanting of the holy names of Krishna became established as the most important of all the mantras of salvation and its popularity around the world is still spreading even today.

## Lord Chaitanya Inaugurates the Vraja Mandala Parikrama

After accepting the sannyasa order in 1510 CE, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu stayed at Jagannatha Puri in the company of His many followers, but He always yearned to visit the holy land of Vrindavana Dhama and see the places where Lord Krishna performed His transcendental pastimes five thousand years earlier. His most ardent desire was to rediscover all the important holy places that had been lost over time and to reestablish the important Deities of Vrindavana that were previously installed by Lord Krishna's great grandson Vajranabha Maharaja. Lord Chaitanya's intention was to establish Vrindavana as the most important religious centre in the world for spreading the sankirtana movement and the glories of chanting the holy name.

Just before the appearance of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in 1486 CE, a number of great devotees appeared on earth in order to prepare the way for Lord Chaitanya's divine advent and to support His mission to inundate the world with love of God. As the location of Mathura and the holy dhama of Vrindavana were known amongst the Vaishnava community, a number of prominent Vaishnavas from Bengal and Orissa visited the holy land of Vrindavana prior to Lord Chaitanya's own visit. Amongst these exalted Vaishnava devotees who came to Vrindavana on pilgrimage was the celebrated sannyasi Shrila Madhavendra Puri Goswami, a renounced ascetic who was the parama-guru of Lord Chaitanya. Shrila Madhavendra Puri became the guru of Shrila Isvara Puri who became the guru of Lord Chaitanya. Madhavendra Puri is credited as being the original preceptor of the Gaudiya Vaishnava sampradaya, because he was the parama-guru of Lord Chaitanya and the first Vaishnava devotee since the disappearance of Lord Krishna, to exhibit ecstatic symptoms of pure love of God. When Madhavendra Puri visited Vrindavana in 1749 CE, he would daily perform the parikrama of Govardhana Hill, where he also discovered the famous Deity of Lord Gopala, who was later moved to Nathadwara in Rajasthana and became known as Shrinathaji. Another great devotee to travel on pilgrimage to the Vrindavana in 1482 CE was Advaita Acarya, who became one of Lord Chaitanya's most intimate and confidential associates. Advaita Acharya performed bhajana on the bank of the Yamuna River in Vrindavana where he discovered the Deity of Lord Madana-Mohana near Dwadashaditya-tila. While staying in Vrindavana it is said that Advaita Acharya took initiation from Shrila Madhavendra Puri. During this same period, another important personality, Lord Nityananda Prabhu, also performed pilgrimage around Vrindavana Dhama while absorbed in complete transcendental ecstasy. Then much later in the year 1509 CE, two important followers of Lord Chaitanya, Lokanatha Goswami and Bhugarbha Goswami, arrived in Vrindavana after having received instructions from Lord Chaitanya in their dreams, that they should go to Vrindavana and locate the twelve sacred forests connected to Krishna's pastimes.

## The Vana-yatra Performed by Lord Chaitanya

According to the Chaitanya-charitamrta, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu arrived in Vrindavana Dhama in the year 1515 CE during the month of Ashwin, just prior to Sharad-purnima which marks the beginning of the holy month of Kartika. However, some Vaishnava scholars are of the opinion that Lord Chaitanya left Puri during the lunar month of Ashwin and arrived in Vrindavana on Kartika-purnima, which falls on the last day of lunar month of Kartika. The Chaitanya-charitamrita describes the arrival of Lord Chaitanya in Vraja. “In due course, He crossed the River Yamuna and came to Agravana, where Renuka-grama, the birthplace of the great warrior Parashurama, is situated. After taking darshana of the Yamuna, which always flows through Vrindavana, Mahaprabhu went to Raja-grama. At last Mahaprabhu entered Gokula and became overwhelmed with ecstatic love.” The Bhakti-ratnakara gives a similar account, "The inhabitants of Gokula would relieve their fatigue under this tree. Lord Gauranga also sat here. Who can describe in detail the arrival of Lord Chaitanya at this place. Mahaprabhu came to Agravana (Agra) from Prayaga and then went to see the ashrama of Jamadagni Muni at Renuka-grama which was named after Jamadagni's wife. Renuka-grama was also the birthplace of Parashurama. Mahaprabhu came to Gokula from Renuka via Raja-grama and sat under this tree.”

The Chaitanya-charitamrita says that on Lord Chaitanya's arrival in Mathura, He first bathed in the Yamuna River at Vishrama Ghata and then went to Krishna's birthplace and had darshana of Lord Keshavadeva. Lord Chaitanya stayed in Mathura for a number of days and with the help of a Sanadiya-brahmana disciple of Madhavendra Puri named Krishna Dasa, Lord Chaitanya visited all the important holy places in the city and He also bathed in all twenty-four sacred riverside ghatas along the bank of the Yamuna.

Accompanied by Madhavendra Puri's disciple Krishna Dasa, along with Balabhadra Bhattacharya and his brahmana assistant, Lord Chaitanya began His parikrama of Vraja Mandala with the intention to systematically visit all the twelve sacred forests of Vrindavana where Krishna had performed His transcendental pastimes. Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was the first to perform the 'vana-yatra' or the circumambulation on foot of all the twelve sacred forests of Vrindavana Dhama, which has now become famous and known the world-over as the Vraja Mandala Parikrama. After leaving Mathura, Lord Chaitanya first visited the forest of Madhuvana, and then gradually traveled to each of the twelve sacred forests, first on the western side of the Yamuna River, and then the eastern side, which took about a month to complete.

The Chaitanya-charitamrita provides the following description, “The Lord's ecstatic love increased a thousand times when He visited Mathura, but it increased a hundred thousand times when He wandered in the forests of Vrindavana. When Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was elsewhere, the very name of Vrindavana was sufficient to increase His ecstatic love. Now, when He was actually traveling in the Vrindavana forest, His mind was absorbed in great ecstatic love day and night. He ate and bathed simply out of habit.” (Madhya. 17.227-229)

During His parikrama around Vraja Mandala, Lord Chaitanya discovered a number of important holy places, but perhaps His most important discovery was the sacred lake known as Radha-kunda, which was Shrimati Radharani's most confidential bathing place and the lake where She enjoyed many transcendental loving pastimes with Krishna. While visiting Nandagrama, Lord Chaitanya discovered the Deities of Nanda and Yashoda along with a small Deity of Krishna, which were hidden inside a cave on Nandishwara Hill. After visiting Mahavana, Lord Chaitanya then visited the last of the sacred forests, Vrindavana, where He became immersed in bhajana and continued to stay there for an entire month.

After spending some two months in the holy dhama of Vrindavana, Lord Chaitanya left to attend the Kumbha-mela at Prayag before eventually returning to Jagannatha Puri. When Lord Chaitanya was on His return journey, He met with two of His senior-most disciples, Rupa Goswami and Sanatana Goswami at Prayag and Varanasi respectively. Lord Chaitanya ordered them to spend the rest of their lives in Vrindavana and gave them the specific instructions to excavate all the lost holy places around Vraja Mandala and establish temples dedicated to Lord Krishna. Lord Chaitanya also gave them instructions on how to develop Vrindavana into an important centre for spreading the sankirtana movement around the world.

Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was the embodiment of Radha-bhava, the highest form of love of God, which had never been exhibited by anyone else before in the history of the world. During Lord Chaitanya's parikrama around the holy places of Vraja, the intense fire of maha-bhava was ignited within His heart, and by the time He returned to Jagannatha Puri, He appeared to be a completely different person, being consumed day and night in the emotional feelings of Radha's mood of love in separation from Krishna. The intense mood of divine love in separation, also referred to as vipralamba-bhava, is considered to be the highest and most sublime stage of prema-bhakti, or divine love for God.

## The Goswamis Rupa and Sanatana Arrive in Vrindavana

The great revival of Bhagavata-dharma in India started with the rediscovery of Vrindavana by Lord Chaitanya, which directly lead to the rapid spread of the Krishna-bhakti movement throughout the Indian sub-continent and then eventually, during the next four centuries, to the rest of the world. This was possible due to the unprecedented contribution made by the celebrated disciples of Lord Chaitanya, Rupa and Sanatana Gosvamis. Their arrival in the holy dhama proved to be a watershed in the history of Vrindavana. The extraordinary work undertaken by them was a major contributing factor in the revival of Bhagavata-dharma and specifically the spreading of the sankirtana movement of Lord Chaitanya. During their lifetime, Rupa and Sanatana excavated innumerable holy places around Vraja Mandala and established two of the most important temples in Vrindavana, Govindaji and Madana-mohana. The present-day city of Vrindavana has become manifest simply due to the excavation work undertaken by Shrila Rupa and Sanatana Goswami. They also led the way in reviving the divine art of bhaktiyoga, the highest form of all yoga practice by writing a large volume of books on the scientific process known as sadhana-bhakti, which explains the esoteric principles and practices of unalloyed devotional service to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Shri Krishna.

## The Six Goswamis of Vrindavana

After receiving direct instructions from Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, to excavate Vrindavana's lost holy places, establish temples, and write books on the science of devotion, Rupa and Sanatana arrived in Vrindavana in 1516 CE. Within a short time they were joined by four other important disciples of Lord Chaitanya including: Gopala Bhatta Goswami, Raghunatha Bhatta Goswami, Raghunatha Dasa Goswami, and Jiva Gosvami, who assisted Rupa and Sanatana in their task. Along with Rupa and Sanatana, these sannyasi disciples of Lord Chaitanya became famous as the 'Six Goswamis of Vrindavana', and between them they established the precepts and the teachings introduced by Lord Chaitanya for all future generations of Gaudiya Vaishnavas. They exclusively propagated devotional service and the chanting of the holy names of God as the only means in the age of Kali-yuga to achieve liberation from repetition of birth and death.

The Six Goswamis of Vrindavana were also responsible for establishing the Gaudiya Vaishnava sampradaya founded exclusively upon Lord Chaitanya's unique achintya-bedabeda-tattva presentation on Vedic philosophy. The Goswamis were the first to introduce into the mainstream of religious life in India, the worship of Shrimati Radharani as the consort of Lord Shri Krishna. They established a number of important temples in Vrindavana that became pivotal in galvanizing the masses behind the sankirtana movement. Prior to the Six Goswamis, there were no temples of Radha-Krishna anywhere in India, but due to their efforts, there are now temples of Radha-Krishna not only in India but throughout the world. The Six Goswamis were supported in their mission by a number of other important followers of Lord Chaitanya, collectively referred to as the Gaudiya Goswamis including: Lokanatha Goswami, Bhugharbha Goswami, Krishnadasa Kaviraja Goswami, Shyamananda Pandita Goswami, Narottama Dasa Thakura, Shrinivasa Acharya, Madhu Pandita Goswami, Prabhodananda Saraswati Goswami and Raghava Pandita Goswami.

A total of seven important temples were established in Vrindavana by the Gaudiya Goswamis. These temples have now become famous throughout the world

## Narayana Bhatta's Contribution to the Vraja Mandala Parikrama

Another important personality, whose contribution towards establishing the Vraja Mandala Parikrama is very significant, was Shrila Narayana Bhatta, whose famous book Vraja-bhakti-vilasa describes every holy place within Vraja Mandala that is mentioned in the Adi-Varaha Purana and previously identified by Vajranabha Maharaja, Lord Krishna's great grandson. Shrila Narayana Bhatta is credited with having re-discovered the location of over one hundred important holy places around Vraja. Prominent amongst his many discoveries was Radharani's parental home of Varsana, where he also unearthed the small Deities of Radha-Krishna known as Larilylala (also called Ladlylala) which are the presiding Deities of Varsana. The words ‘larily' as well as ‘ladli' means a ‘young girl' and ‘lala' means a ‘young boy'.

It is said that after spending time under the tutelage of his siksha-gurus; Rupa and Sanatana Goswamis, and having received their mercy, Shrila Narayana Bhatta was able to find the many holy places of Vrindavana not already discovered by the Six Goswamis or their associates. Narayana Bhatta was the first to systematically demarcate the precise area and boundaries of Vraja Mandala and was also the first to organize the Vraja Mandala Parikrama on a large scale. He also introduced a number of different parikramas such as the Vraja Mandala Borderline-Parikrama and the Vana-yatra Parikrama that circumambulates the twelve sacred forests first performed by Lord Chaitanya, including the most suitable times to perform these various parikramas. The present day Vraja Mandala Parikrama that is followed by the Gaudiya Math and other Vaishnavas sampradayas was established by Shrila Narayana Bhatta

## Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Revives Vraja Mandala Parikrama

Shrila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Goswami, the great Vaishnava acharya and renowned Vedic scholar, was the founder of the Gaudiya Matha and established at least sixty-four Radha-Krishna temples throughout the Indian sub-continent for the purpose of propagating the teachings of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and the sankirtana movement. In the year 1932, Shrila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Goswami led a large group of over one-thousand Gaudiya Vaishnavas on a historic parikrama of Vraja Mandala, following the route taken by Lord Chaitanya around the twelve sacred forests. This was the first major parikrama of Vraja Mandala recorded in the modern era and it caused a revival of interest in Vrindavana and the holy places situated around Vraja. From that time onwards, the spiritual descendants of Shrila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati, the followers of the Gaudiya Math, have continued to perform the annual Vraja Mandala Parikrama. His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, the founder-acharya of ISKCON, who broadcast the glories of Vrindavana and the sankirtana movement all over the world, was the most brilliant disciple of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Goswami. The society he founded has turned the Vraja Mandala Parikrama into an annual international event with devotees attending the parikrama from almost every country of the world.

## Shrila Prabhupada Reveals Vrindavana to the World

His Divine Grace A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, the founder of ISKCON, the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, also known as the 'Hare Krishna Movement', became the first Vaishnava acharya in the history of the world to travel to the West and convert Americans and Europeans to Krishna Consciousness also known as Bhagavata-dharma. After traveling to America in 1965, He established hundreds of Radha-Krishna temples, not only in America but around the globe, and translated into the English language for the first time a large volume of books on the subject of Vedic culture and religion, including the Vedic classics Shrimad-Bhagavatam and Chaitanya-charitamrita. His unique translation of the celebrated Bhagavad-gita became the best selling edition of the Gita in history and his books are most highly appreciated by scholars, educators and academicians the world over.

Shrila Prabhupada was also the first Vaishnava acharya to introduce Westerners to the Vraja Mandala Parikrama when in 1972, he arrived in India from the West with a large party of Europeans and American devotees and personally took them to all the important holy places around Vraja Mandala including: Vrindavana, Govardhana Hill, Radha-kunda, Varsana, Nandagrama, and Gokula. He later established the famous Krishna Balarama Mandira in Vrindavana, where his foreign disciples could visit on pilgrimage and become purified of all contamination of the material world while spending their time appreciating the transcendentally surcharged atmosphere of the holy dhama, while engaging in yoga, meditation, chanting Krishna's holy names and performing parikrama.

In November 1977, during the last few days of his life, as Shrila Prabhupada lay ill in his rooms at the Krishna Balarama Mandira in Vrindavana, even though in a precarious state of health, he desired to be taken on parikrama to Govardhana Hill and requested that his disciples bring a bullock-cart in which he could travel to the various holy places. When a number of senior disciples objected saying that the ride would kill him, he challenged them saying that parikrama of Govardhana Hill would in fact give him life. Shrila Prabhupada also said that it was far better to die while on parikrama of Govardhana Hill, than to die while lying in bed, as it would be a far more glorious death. However, his senior disciples refused to allow him to go, in fear he would die at the first bump in the road.

On the third day after Govardhana-puja, which is the celebration of Krishna's pastime of lifting Govardhana Hill, Shrila Prabhupada breathed his last and entered into maha-samadhi and the eternal pastimes of Krishna's Vraja-lila. In order to fulfill Shrila Prabhupada's final wish, a parikrama was organized by his disciples and a Deity of Shrila Prabhupada was taken on parikrama around Govardhana Hill. It was decided to organize this parikrama as an annual celebration and it has been performed each year since then. A few years later, it was decided to perform the full Vraja Mandala Parikrama in honor of Shrila Prabhupada, and this particular parikrama is now organized every year in the holy month of Kartika, which has now become very popular with all ISKCON devotees from around the world who flock to Vrindavana to take part in this ecstatic parikrama.

## The Purpose of Performing the Vraja Mandala Parikrama

Besides being an important aspect of sadhana-bhakti, by performing Vraja Mandala Parikrama, one offers one's homage to the holy dhama by circumambulating the twelve sacred forests of Vrindavana, just as Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu had done on His pilgrimage to the dhama in the year 1515. The word ‘parikrama' is derived from the word ‘pradakshina' which means to circumambulate or walk in a ‘circular motion to the right' around a holy place of worship. The performance of pradakshina or parikrama is an important act of self-purification as well as an offering of devotion to the Lord. The goal of performing parikrama around Vraja is to increase ones smaranam, or remembrance of Lord Krishna, while seeing all the holy places where the Lord performed His transcendental pastimes five thousand years earlier. By performing parikrama around the sacred forests of Vrindavana, one's faith in the lotus feet of the Lord automatically increases with every step.

Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was the first to perform the circumambulation of the twelve sacred forests of Vrindavana and He chanted the holy names and danced in ecstasy in all the various holy places that He visited during His historic journey. Circumambulating the sacred forests had a very powerful effect on Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, especially after reaching the celebrated Imli-tala, the site where Radharani experienced the ecstasy of maha-bhava. After performing the Vraja Mandala Parikrama, Lord Chaitanya's mood drastically changed and after returning to Jagannatha Puri, He became more and more absorbed in the transcendental ecstasy of Radha-bhava, while experiencing Radharani's own intense feelings when She herself is separated from Her beloved Krishna.

While performing the Vraja Mandala Parikrama, besides circumambulating hundreds and thousands of holy tirthas, temples and sacred shrines, one also simultaneously performs many other important parikramas including the parikramas of Vrindavana, Mathura, Radha-kunda, Govardhana Hill, Kamyavana, Varsana, Nandagrama, and Gokula-Mahavana. Therefore it is said in the Vedic scriptures that those who perform the Vraja Mandala Parikrama are immediately freed from all their sins and will never take birth again in this material world.

## The Spiritual Benefits of Performing Vraja Mandala Parikrama

There are many benefits of performing the Vraja Mandala Parikrama and in the Vedic literatures one can find the following verses:

In the Skanda Purana it says, “Those who with firm faith and devotion for Lord Krishna, who perform the parikrama of Vraja Mandala - are freed from all sins and go back to godhead at the time of death.”

The Mathura Mahatmya says, “All sins accumulated through innumerable births can be destroyed in a second by staying in Vrindavana Dhama even for one day.”

The Mathura Mahatmya also says, “What is the need for any further consideration, anyone who simply hears about the glories of Vraja Mandala automatically delivers two hundred generations of both his paternal and maternal family members.”

The Adi-Varaha Purana says, “Those who visit the twelve sacred forests of Vrindavana will no longer suffer the pangs of hellish life.”

The Adi-Varaha Purana also says, “By bathing at any place in Vraja Mandala a person is redeemed of all his sins.”

In the Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu it says, “The result of travelling to all the pilgrimage places in the three worlds is achieved simply by touching the holy land of Vrindavana.”

The Garga Samhita says, “Visiting Vrindavana is equal to visualizing the Supreme Personality of Godhead Lord Shri Hari.”

The Garga Samhita also says, “Walking in the holy land of Vrindavana is equal to the merit of going to a different holy tirtha with every step”.

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “The unlimited happiness of Vraja Mandala can only be known, however, by one who is devoted to the holy dhama. Therefore, please chant the glories of the pastime places of Vraja-Dhama and all your desires will be easily fulfilled.”

## The Various Routes Followed by Vraja Mandala Parikrama

While performing Vraja Mandala Parikrama, there are a number of different routes followed by the various Vaishnava sampradayas which are based on four main literatures: Adi-Varaha Purana, Vraja-bhakti-vilasa, Chaitanya-charitamrita and Bhakti-ratnakara. The various parikrama routes may also change from time to, but the overall purpose of these parikramas is to circumambulate the twelve sacred forests of Vrindavana Dhama, whereas the places visited in between may differ according to preference. The Bhakti-ratnakara and Chaitanya-charitamrita trace out the parikrama route taken by Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu while the Vraja Mandala Parikrama followed by the Gaudiya Math is based upon Vraja-bhakti-vilasa. Besides the Gaudiya sampradaya, two other prominent sampradayas also conduct the annual Vraja Mandala Parikrama, the Nimbarka sampradaya and the Vallabhacharya sampradaya.

## The Vraja Mandala Parikrama of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu

The parikrama route followed by Lord Chaitanya is described in both the Chaitanya-charitamrita and Bhakti-ratnakara as follows:

Vishrama Ghata, Shri Krishna Janmasthana, Keshava Mandira, the twenty-four ghatas along the banks of the Yamuna (the Yamuna ghatas mentioned in Chaitanya-charitamrita are not in systematic order). The correct order is from north to south: Uttara-Koti Ghata, Vighnaraja Ghata, Dashashmavamedha Ghata, Chakra-tirtha Ghata, Saraswati-Patana Ghata, Soma Ghata, Brahma Ghata, Ghanta-Bharanaka Ghata, Naga Ghata, Dharapatana Ghata, Samyamana Ghata, Nava Ghata, Vishrama Ghata, Avimukta Ghata, Guhya Ghata, Prayag Ghata, Kankhala Ghata, Tinduka Ghata, Surya Ghata, Bata-Swami Ghata, Dhruva Ghata, Rishi Ghata, Moksha Ghata, Dakshina-Koti Ghata and Bodhi Ghata.

During His parikrama of Mathura Lord Chaitanya visited many holy places including: Kamsa's palace, the Mutra-sthana (where baby Krishna urinated on Vasudeva), Uddhava's house, the washer-man's house, Sudama the garland-makers house, Kubja's house (Kubja-kupa), Ranga-bhumi, Vasudeva's house, Ugrasena's palace, Kamsa-khali (Kamsa-tila), Kamsa Kupa (where Kamsa planned to throw Krishna's dead body), Agastya Kupa, Setabandhu-sarovara, Sapta-samudra-kunda, Mara-shila (where Kamsa killed Devaki's seven sons), Bhuteshwara Mahadeva, Jnana-vapi, Krishna Kupa and Saraswati Sangama. The Chaitanya-charitamrita says that Lord Chaitanya also had darshana of Dirgha-Vishnu, Swayambhu (Padmanabha), Gokarneshwara Mahadeva, and Mahavidya Devi.

After parikrama of Mathura, Lord Chaitanya then visited: Madhuvana, Talavana, Kumudavana and Bahulavana, Arit-grama (Radha-kunda and Shyama-kunda), Sumanas Lake (Kusuma Sarovara), Govardhana Hill, Harideva, Brahma-kunda, Manasa-ganga, Govardhana Hill, Govinda-kunda, Ganthhuli-grama, Kamyavana, Nandishwara (Nandagrama), Pavana Sarovara, Khadiravana, Seshashayi, Khela-tirtha (Kelanvana), Bhandiravana (Akshaya Vata), Bhadravana, Lohavana, Mahavana, Gokula, Yamalarjuna-bhanjana-tirtha (twin arjuna trees), Shri Krishna Janmasthana (second time), Akrura-tirtha (Akrura Ghata), Vrindavana, Kaliya Lake (Kaliya Ghata), Praskandana Ghata, Dwadasaditya-tila, Tentuli-tala (Imli-tala), Chira Ghata ( Chayana Ghata) and Keshi-tirtha (Keshi Ghata).
