As Rama was not interested in any woman other than Sita, having taken the vow of eka-patni - meaning only one wife, Supanakha felt rejected and she then approached Lakshmana, Rama's brother, who also refused her proposal. Utterly frustrated, she then flew into sudden rage and attacked Sita with her sharpened nails; Lakshmana immediately cut off her nose and disfigured her face. The word ‘supanakha' means 'one with sharpened nails'. Supeanakha then went to Lanka and complained to Ravana who subsequently abducted Sita as a reprisal. Later, Supanakha Surpanakha, still intensely in love with Lord Rama, went to Pushkara-tirtha to undergo penance in order to achieve Lord Rama as her husband. Lord Shiva finally gave her the boon that she would be able to enjoy the position of the Lord's wife when He incarnated as Krishna the Dwapara-yuga. According to the Gaura-ganoddesa-dipika, in Chaitanya-lila Kubja appeared as Kashi Mishra.

How To Get There: (See map No.1 & 1B).

## 11 Kamsa-tila / Ranga-bhumi

Kamsa-tila is situated on a small hillock that was formerly situated in the middle of a large showground known as Ranga-bhumi. A royal pavilion was erected on top of the hillock from where King Kamsa could view the festivities in the showground below. The word 'tila' means a 'hill' or a 'hillock''. Kamsa-tila is the actual place where Krishna killed the demon Kamsa inside the Ranga-bhumi arena. The Ranga-bhumi is also known as the Ranga-shala and it is the place where Kamsa had organized a large public celebration called the Dhanur-yajna or 'Sacrifice of the bow'. The word ‘ranga-bhumi' means a 'show-ground' and 'ranga-shala' means an 'arena' where festivals and public spectacles like wrestling matches, fairs, or Vedic sacrifices are held. The Ranga-bhumi was a vast open-spaced area of about a square mile, but now only a small enclosed area of the Ranga-bhumi can be seen here. On the day of the Dhanur-yajna sacrifice, a wrestling match had also been arranged and large crowds had gathered to see the great spectacle.

When Krishna and Balarama first tried to enter the Ranga-shala, the great elephant known as Kuvalayapida, who had been posted at the gateway of Ranga-bhumi by Kamsa, attempted to trample Krishna to death, however, Krishna very easily slew the great elephant. When Krishna entered the arena of the Ranga-shala sprinkled in blood and carrying on His shoulder the tusk of Kuvalayapida, Kamsa got the shock of his life. The Shrimad Bhagavatam (10.43.18) says, “When Kamsa saw that Kuvalayapida was dead and the two brothers were invincible, he was overwhelmed with anxiety.” Krishna then immediately broke the great sacrificial bow of Lord Shiva just as a child may break a dry twig, sending a great shattering sound reverberating in all directions.

Krishna and Balarama were then coerced into a wrestling match with Kamsa's enormous strongly built wrestlers, including the two champions Chanura and Mushtika, who had been ordered by Kamsa to kill both the brothers during the wrestling contest. However, after a titanic battle, Krishna and Balarama slew Chanura and Mushtika as well as all the other wrestlers employed by Kamsa, much to his great horror. After slaying Chanura and Mushtika, Krishna suddenly jumped on to the raised platform where Kamsa was sitting in his royal pavilion, and catching hold of him, threw him from the royal balcony on to the ground below. Krishna then dragged Kamsa around the arena by his hair in full view of the crowds. Krishna then killed Kamsa by striking him on the head with His powerful fist. Because Kamsa was killed near this hill, it became famous as Kamsa-khali, or the place where King Kamsa was delivered. Thus Krishna fulfilled the prophesy and put an end to the tyrannical reign of King Kamsa's by swiftly sending the demon to the kingdom of death.

After Kamsa had been killed by Krishna, his dead body was dragged down to the Yamuna to be cremated. Because Kamsa's huge body was so heavy it could not be carried but had to be dragged along the ground, and as it was dragged, it gouged out a deep channel in the earth starting from the Ranga-bhumi down to the Yamuna riverbank, which became known as Kamsa-khara. In his previous life, Kamsa had been born as Kalanemi, the son of the great demon Hiranyaksha, and in that previous life he had also been slain by Lord Vishnu.

How To Get There: (See map no.No.1 & 1B).

## 12 Rangeshwara Mahadeva Mandira

Situated near to the Ranga-bhumi is the temple of Rangeshwara Mahadeva, one of Mathura's most popular shrines. Lord Rangeshwara Mahadeva is one of the four ksetra-palas protecting Mathura. This famous temple is also known as the Siddhamukha-Rudra Mandira.

How To Get There: (See map No.1 & 1B)

## 12a Sapta-samudra Kupa

Located on the eastern side of the Rangeshwara Mahadev Mandira is the famous well known as Sapta-samudri-kupa which means the “well of seven oceans". According to legend, this well contains water from the sapta-sindhu, the seven great oceans that surround the island of Jambhudwipa.

How To Get There: (See map No.1 & 1B).

## 13 Keshava Gaudiya Matha

This is the famous temple where in 1959, Shrila Prabhupada accepted the order of tridandi-sannyasa from his beloved god-brother, His Holiness Bhakti Prajnana Keshava Maharaja. The Deity of Lord Chaitanya that can be seen standing on the simhasana next to Radha and Krishna was presented to the Keshava Gaudiya Math by Shrila Prabhupada when Shrila Prabhupada came from Allahabad on a visit to Mathura and Vrindavana. Shrila Prabhupada also spent some time at the Keshava Gaudiya Math in 1958, after leaving Jhansi were he had opened a preaching center under the name of 'League of Devotees'. While staying at the math Shrila Prabhupada was engaged in editing periodicals and training the younger brahmacharis in sadhana-bhakti.

How To Get There: (See map No.1 & 1B).

## 14 Shiva Tala

Built in sandstone and ornately designed with chatris around its perimeter, Shiva Tala is one of Mathura's most famous kundas and it is dedicated to Lord Shiva, who is said to have performed penance at this place in order to achieve the mercy of Lord Krishna. The word 'tala' means a 'lake', or 'large kunda'. The Vishnu Purana says, “Mahadeva executed his penances at Mathura.” The Skanda Purana says, “Is there any type of result which cannot be attained in Mathura, where Kshetrapala Mahadeva exists eternally.”

How To Get There: (See map No.1).

## 15 Kankali Mandira / Kankali-tila

This Deity of Kali Mata is said to have been personally worshiped by King Kamsa. The name 'Kankali' is derived from 'Kamsa-Kali' meaning 'the Kali worshiped by Kamsa'. The temple is located on a small hill known as Kankali-tila.

How To Get There: (See map No.1 & 1C).

## 16 Balabhadra-kunda

According to the Bhakti-ratnakara, Krishna and Balarama came here to sport in the waters of this kunda with Their cowherd boyfriends while they were roaming around the city of Mathura, sometime before attending the Dhanur-yajna or 'Sacrifice of the bow'. Nanda Maharaja and the cowherd men from Vrindavana were also in Mathura with their sons the cowherd boys to attend the Dhanur-yajna and were camped not far from this kunda, which was at that time located on the outskirts of Mathura City.

How To Get There: (See map No.1 & 1C).

## 17 Bhuteshwara Mahadeva Mandira

This is one of the most famous temples of Lord Shiva in the whole of Vraja. The Shiva-linga was established by Vajranabha five thousand years ago as one of the dig-palas, or protecting Deities of Vrindavana Dhama. Bhuteshwara is also one of the kshetra-palas protecting the western side of Mathura. It is said in the Vishnu Purana, “Mathura is the abode of Mahadeva, the Deity of all Deities and a great devotee of Lord Hari. Mahadeva executed his penances at Mathura.” Located in this same temple is the Deity of Pateleshvara Devi that was one of the four Deities of Devi established by Vajranabha Maharaja.

According to some traditions, the Vraja Mandala parikrama which starts on the dvadashi day after Janmasthami from Vrindavana's Madana-mohana Mandira, proceeds directly to the Bhuteshwara Mahadeva where prayers and sankalpa are offered. The next day which is trayodashi, the Vraja Mandala parikrama proceeds to Madhuvana.   Top

How To Get There: (See map No.1 & 1C

## 18 Jnana-vapi / Jnana-bavadi

The ancient tirtha of Jnana-vapi is located next to the Guru-Govinda Gaudiya Matha. This well is said to have been established by Dharmaraja (Yamaraja) in the Satya-yuga and according to the Adi-Varaha Purana, anyone who bathes here automatically removes the influence of malefic planets and achieves both jnana (knowledge) and Vishnu-bhakti (devotion). It is said that Lord Chaitanya came to this bavadi after having darshana of Lord Keshavadeva to perform achamana and bathe. Lord Chaitanya also stayed near here in the house of a sanadiya-brahmana who was a disciple of Madhavendra Puri Goswami, the parama-guru of Lord Chaitanya.

A very large well with steps going down inside it is known as a bavadi or bowri and from this word it appears the name vapi (as in Jnana-vapi) has been derived. At the present time this bavadi is dry and presently being used by Muslims who worship the shrine of a Sufi saint who once lived inside the well. It is also said that this Jnana-vapi is also connected to Krishna's dear friend Uddhava. It was while at this bavadi that Uddhava became overwhelmed with ecstatic love while thinking of Krishna's transcendental pastimes in Vrindavana. There used to be a small shrine dedicated to Uddhava nearby but it is no longer visible.

How To Get There: (See map No.1 & 1C).

## 18a Raja Bartrhari Samadhi

The samadhi of one of India's famous kings named Raja Bartrhari is located here at Jnana-vapi. At the height of his powers the king renounced his kingdom and all connection to worldly life and came to this sacred place to perform tapasya and meditation. After his death his samadhi was built on the banks of Jnana-vapi. At the present time the sacred well is in disrepair and the samadhi of Raja Bartrhari although visible is almost inaccessible.

How To Get There: (See map No.1 & 1C).

## 19 Potra-kunda

This large kund is believed to have been located within the walls of King Kamsa's prison and after giving birth to baby Krishna, mother Devaki came to Potra-kunda to bathe and also wash Krishna's baby-linen. It is said, “Being overcome with ecstatic love, Devaki happily washed Krishna’s cloth in the kunda”. Due to this pastime the kunda became known locally as ‘potra-kunda', which is said to be derived from the word 'putra' which means 'son'. Some researchers say that the kunda was formerly known as Pavitra-kunda, the word 'pavitra' means that which is ‘pure', but over the years it has become more commonly known simply as Potra-kunda, which they say is simply a corruption of the word pavitra. Top

How To Get There: (See map No.1 & 1C).

## 20 Prachin-janmasthana (Vasudeva-Devaki Mandira)

This is said to be the exact spot where the prison cell of King Kamsa was located and thus the actual place where Lord Krishna was born. The word 'prachin' means 'old' or 'original' and 'janmasthana' means 'birthplace'. The Prachin-janmasthana is also known as 'Kamsa Kara-garh', which means "Kamsa's prison cell'. The Prachin-janmasthana is situated in the area of Mathura known as Mallapura where the wrestlers employed by Kamsa, including Chanura and Mushtika, used to live. The wrestlers, who were part of the royal bodyguard, were given the responsibility to guard Vasudeva and Devaki during the period of their imprisonment. The word 'malla' means 'wrestler' and 'Mallapura' means the 'residence of the wrestlers', which further confirms that the Prachin-janmasthan at Mallapura is the actual site of Kamsa's prison. There is a small temple at the Prachin-janmasthana where the Deities of Vasudeva and Devaki along with baby Krishna can be seen. Local scholars and the people of Mathura have recognized this Prachin-Janmasthana as being the original birthplace of Lord Krishna since time immemorial.

The Chaitanya-charitamrita says that Lord Chaitanya also visited Krishna's birthplace before going for darshana of Lord Keshava Deva. The Bhakti-ratnakara also mentions that Raghava Pandita, Shrinivasa Acharya and Narottama Dasa also visited the room where Krishna was born during their parikrama of Mathura. Raghava Pandita Goswami informed his two companions, “This is the room of Devaki and Vasudeva where Krishna, the Supreme Lord, took His birth. According to the Skanda Purana, a person who fasts; chants japa and then takes darshana of this birthplace of Krishna is freed from all sins and is liberated. The Padma Purana says, “Anyone who once enters the janma-griha \[birthplace\] of Keshava during the month of Kartika achieves the eternal Absolute Truth, Lord Shri Krishna.”

It is interesting to note that the site presently advertised as the Shri Krishna Janmasthana, located at the rear of the new Keshava Mandira did not exist at the time of Lord Chaitanya or the period when Raghava Pandita, Shrinivasa Acharya and Narottama Dasa visited Mathura. It is quite evident that both Lord Chaitanya and Raghava Pandit and his companions visited the birth site of Lord Krishna which was in a separate location to that of the Keshava Mandira. Historical records show that from around the year 1951, when the land containing the ruins of the ancient Keshava Mandira was acquired by the Keshava Mandira Trust for building a new temple, a room in an old basement that was an extension of the Shahi Eidgarh mosque was advertised as being the actual site of the Janmasthana where Krishna was born. Previous to this, the Prachin-Janmasthana was the only place recognized by everyone as Krishna's birthplace. Gaudiya Vaishnava scholars have concluded that the new 'Janmasthana site' located next to the recently-built Keshava Mandira may be acknowledged as a smriti-sthala, which means a shrine of remembrance, while the Prachin-janmasthana should be recognized as the actual site of Lord Krishna's birth.

How To Get There: (See map No. 1 & 1C).

## 21 Kuvalayapida Badha-sthana

According to the local brahmana panditas this is the place where Lord Krishna slew the elephant Kuvalayapida before entering the Ranga-shala to take part in the danur-yajna. The Shrimad Bhagavatam (10.43.8-10) says, “Lord Krishna then grabbed the powerful Kuvalayapida by the tail and playfully dragged him twenty-five bow-lengths as easily as Garuda might drag a snake. Krishna then came face to face with the elephant and slapped him then ran away. Kuvalayapida pursued the Lord, managing to touch Him again and again with each step, but Krishna outmaneuvered the elephant and made him trip and fall.” It is said that during the fight with the elephant Kuvalayapida, Balarama also dragged the elephant around by its tail. The fight continued until it reached this spot when Krishna suddenly ripped out the elephant's tusk and delivered the final blow to its head that stopped the rampaging elephant dead in its tracks. How To Get There: (See map No. 1 & 1C)

## 22 Adi Keshava Mandira (Maratha Mandira)

In the year 1720, the armies of the Marathas defeated the Mughal forces and were successful in liberating the holy city of Mathura from the tyrannical rule of the Mohammedans. The Marathas went on to conquer the whole of Northern India ultimately driving the Mughals into oblivion. Because Aurangzeb had destroyed the original Keshava temple in 1669 and erected a mosque on the site, the Marathas built a new temple at this location next to the old temple which was completed in the year 1790 and known as the Adi-Keshavaji Mandira. The locals also refer to this temple as the Maratha Mandira as it was established by the Maratha chieftains. Although the original Deity of Keshavadeva, established by Vajranabha, had been moved to Rasadhan prior to Aurangzeb's attack, the original Vijay-murti from the old Keshavadeva Mandira was still in Mathura. Therefore the Vijay-murti was installed in the newly built temple. Vijay-murti is the replica Deity (pratibhu-murti) which is taken out on ratha-yatra processions during festival days. It is said that the body of this Vijay-murti is marked with the signs of the twenty-four primary avataras of Vishnu. Although the Adi-Keshava Mandira has since been renovated, the old gateway and part of the temple boundary wall originally built by the Marathas remains even today.

How To Get There: (See map No. 1 & 1C).

## 23 Krishna Kupa

This famous well known as Krishna Kupa has now been covered over and shops have been constructed on the spot. The Bhakti-ratnakara mentions that Krishna Kupa is one of the places where Krishna and Balarama sported with Their friends when they came to Mathura for the Dhanur-yajna. It was here that Lord Chaitanya sat for sometime surrounded by the people of Mathura. There used to be a large neem tree next to the well under which Lord Chaitanya sat and rested during His parikrama of Mathura. Krishna Kupa was situated at the northern gate of the Keshavadeva Mandira next to the place where the Maratha kings established a temple of Keshavaji. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “It was here that Shri Krishna Chaitanyacandra sat surrounded by people after His tour of Mathura. People were struck with wonder seeing the ecstatic condition of Mahaprabhu. The brahmana residents of Mathura spoke to one another, 'This so-called sannyasi must certainly be Lord Krishna Himself. This is extraordinary! Who can understand His transcendental activities? He has concealed His real identity by accepting this golden form.' Someone said, 'We are all very fortunate to see the Lord's visit to Mathura.” How To Get There: (See map No. 1 & 1C).

## 24 Keshava Mandira

This is the latest in a long line of temples built at this spot where the ancient Keshava Mandira was first built by Vajranabha Maharaja, the king of Mathura, more than five thousand years earlier. The temple is generally known as the Keshava Deva Mandira (Keshava Deo Mandira) or as Keshava Rai Mandira, and the original Deity of Lord Keshava Deva carved by Vajranabha was the residing Deity of this temple. It is said that the Deity of Lord Keshava Deva was carved out of pure black marble with large rubies for eyes.

The first temple of Lord Keshava Deva was built by Vajranabha soon after the disappearance of Lord Krishna. Three thousand years later a second temple was constructed on the same spot on a grand scale by the Gupta Dynasty ruler Chandragupta-Vikramaditya (Chandragupta II) who ruled from 380 to 415 CE. This second temple was destroyed in 1017 CE by the notorious Afghan-Turk invader Mahmud of Ghazni. According to an inscription found on a stone slab at the site, a third magnificent temple was built in 1150 CE by a wealthy landowner named Jajja under the patronage of the local ruler Raja Vijaypala Deva.

According to accounts by early European travelers in the 15th Century, at the peak of its glory, the Keshava Deva Mandira, which was constructed out of the finest red sandstone, was far greater in size than even the Jagannatha Temple at Puri in Odisha (Orissa). The base (plinth) of the Keshava Deva Mandira is said to have measured 217 x 34 yards, and its three shikaras or domes reached over 250 feet into the sky and clearly visible from a distance of at least twenty-five kilometers away. Tavernier, a French traveler who visited Mathura around 1650 CE says, "After Banaras, the most famous temple of India is situated at Mathura. It is octagonal in shape. Red sandstone has been used in it. All round the temple, the stone claddings have inscriptions of various kinds of animals. The Jagmohana is built upon one half of the temple's vast courtyard. At the center is the main Mandap. The temple has many windows and is so vast that it can be seen from a distance of 5 to 6 kosas." From the descriptions of the Italian traveler, Manuchi, it is clear that the gold canopied top of the temple could be seen even from Agra, which is at a distance of 18 Kosas (54 Kilometers). When lamps were lit on the occasion of Deepavali, at night the light could be seen by the Mughal Emperor from his fort in Agra.

It is said that the third Keshava Mandira built in 1150 CE was destroyed at the beginning of the 16th century by the soldiers of the Sultan of Delhi, an Afghan-Turk despot named Sikanda Lodhi, also called 'Butt Shikan', or the 'Destroyer of Hindu Deities'. Sikanda Lodhi ruled between 1486 and 1517 CE and it is said that the Keshava Mandira was destroyed towards the end of his reign. Historians mention that after the Keshava Mandira was destroyed by Sikander Lodi, a makeshift shrine (garbh-griha) was established within the ruins of the temple where the Deity of Lord Keshava Deva was being worshiped.

According to some researchers, when Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu arrived in Mathura on pilgrimage in 1515 CE, He visited the Keshava Mandira that was built during the rule of Raja Vijaypala Deva before it was destroyed by Sikander Lodhi, however others believe that this particular temple had already been destroyed and therefore Lord Chaitanya had darshana of the Lord Keshava Deva Deity when the Deity was being worshiped in the make-shift shrine. It has been mentioned in the Bhakti-ratnakara that upon seeing the beautiful Deity of Lord Keshava Deva, Lord Chaitanya chanted the holy names and danced in ecstasy before the Deity for many hours. Large crowds gathered to see the unusual spectacle of the Lord's exhibiting such ecstatic transcendental emotions as He danced in ecstasy and chanted before the Deity of Lord Keshava Deva. In the Bhakti-ratnakara Raghava Pandita Goswami says, “O Shrinivasa, look at Keshavadeva. In this place Shri Chaitanya once danced in ecstasy. Those who saw Him dance thought that He was Shri Krishna Raya Himself. Who can describe Keshavadeva’s glories? Whoever circumambulates Keshava in Mathura attains the virtue of circumambulating the earth with its seven islands. Singing Keshava Raya's glories will destroy sins committed in this age and in ages to come.”

During the reign of the Mughal Emperor Jahangir, a fourth temple was built by the Rajput prince Raja Vir Sinh Bundela, a vassal of the Mughals, who ruled over Orchaa in Bundelkhand from 1605 to 1627 CE. Raja Vir Sinh enjoyed a special favor with Emperor Jahangir on account of his support for his succession to the throne after the death of Akbar the Great. The temple built under the patronage of Raja Vir Sinh Bundela was one of the most magnificent temples ever built in India and enjoyed veneration throughout the Indian sub-continent. In the year 1670 CE, this magnificent temple was destroyed on the orders of Emperor Aurangzeb who visited Mathura to personally oversee its destruction. Aurangzeb then ordered that a grand mosque be built on the same raised plinth (foundation) where the Keshava Deva Mandira had once stood and the sandstone blocks from the demolished temple where used in the mosque's construction.

Just prior to the attack on the Keshava Mandira by Aurangzeb in January 1670, the Deity of Lord Keshava Deva was secretly taken to the village of Bhudauli near the town of Rasadhana in Kanpur District of Uttar Pradesh State. After destroying the Keshava Mandira, Emperor Aurangzeb built a mosque known as the Shahi-Eidgah where the Keshava Mandira had previously stood. During this period of Aurangzeb's attack on Mathura and Vrindavana, many important Deities were secretly removed for safe keeping. The famous Harideva Deity from Manasi-ganga at Govardhana was also taken to Bhudauli and both these Deities, Keshava Deva and Harideva, were being worshiped there from that time. Unfortunately, during the late sixties or early seventies, the Deity of Lord Keshava Deva was stolen by thieves and nobody knows its present whereabouts. However, the Deity of Lord Harideva is still being worshiped at Bhudauli.

Sometime later in the year 1803 CE, the Mughal armies were defeated by the British and Mathura came under the rule of the British East India Company. In 1815 CE, in order to appease the local Hindus, the East India Company sanctioned the sale of the vast Keshava temple compound known as the Katra-Keshavadeva, accept the area occupied by the Shahi Eidgarh Mosque and the adjacent Mohammedan graveyard. The Katra-Keshavadeva compound was immediately purchased by Raja Patnimal of Banaras. Some years later Raja Patnimal's heir Raja Krishna Das, who held the ownership rights over Katra-Keshavadeva was challenged in court on two separate occasions by the local Muslims of Mathura. However, in both the cases, the Allahabad High Court ruled that Raja Krishna Das was the legal owner of the Katra-Keshavadeva. Then in 1944, the nationalist leader Madan Mohan Malaviya acquired the Katra-Keshavadeva from Raja Krishna Das for the token sum of Rs. 13,000/-, which covered only the cost of fighting the two court cases and far less than the true value of the land.

Later in 1951, with the support and financial assistance from two prominent industrialists namely, Jugal Kishore Birla and Jaidayal Dalmia, a private trust was formed under the title of the Keshava Mandira Trust and in 1953 CE, construction began on the fifth and present temple of Lord Keshava Deva. The new temple was built on the land next to the place where the original Keshava Mandira once stood, now occupied by the Shahi Idgarh Mosque. The new temple built on a grand scale was opened in the year 1982 CE and in this temple one can have darshana the pratibh-murti of Lord Keshava Deva.

In an old basement room previously attached the Shahi Eidgarh Mosque that had been used as living quarters by the mosque's attendants; trustees of the Keshava Mandira Trust claimed that the room was the actual prison cell where Lord Krishna had been born. When this basement room was constructed by the mosque managers, by chance it protruded onto Katra-Keshavadeva land and fell under the control of the temple trust. There is absolutely no historical or shastric records to substantiate the claim that this basement room was the actual site of the Janmasthana. Previous to this claim, the Prachin-janmasthana located in the adjacent Mallapur area was recognized as Lord Krishna's actual birthplace. Gaudiya Vaishnava scholars have concluded that the Prachin-janmasthana should be recognized as the actual site of Lord Krishna's birth and the new janmasthana located behind the newly-built Keshava Mandira can be seen simply as a smriti-sthala, which means a shrine of remembrance with regard to Lord Krishna's birth.

How To Get There: (See map No. 1 & 1C).

## The Appearance of Lord Shri Krishna

The Srimad Bhagavatam says that Lord Shri Krishna was born on the stroke of midnight from the womb of Devaki in the prison cell of King Kamsa. The evil hearted Kamsa had imprisoned Devaki and her husband Vasudeva just after their wedding ceremony when Kamsa had heard an omen from the sky informing him that the eighth child of his sister Devaki would kill him. After imprisoning both Devaki and Vasudeva, Kamsa systematically slaughtered one by one all the babies born of Devaki, by dashing them on a large stone slab. Kamsa believed that the seventh baby must have been a miscarriage because after some period of pregnancy, no baby was born from Devaki's womb. Unknown to Kamsa, the baby, who was actually Lord Balarama, had been transferred by the power of the yogamaya potency, from Devaki's womb to the womb of Rohini, Vasudeva's second wife, who was at that time, for the sake of her safety, staying at Nanda Maharaja's house in Gokula.

According to the Vedas, Lord Krishna appears once in every day of Brahma in order to save His devotees and kill all the demons disturbing the world. When Devaki became pregnant for the eighth time, Kamsa remained vigilant and waited in great trepidation for this particular child to be born. On the stroke of midnight at the appointed time of His birth, Lord Krishna appeared before Vasudeva and Devaki, not as an ordinary baby, but in a four-armed form of Lord Narayana, dressed in shining yellow silk and holding the symbols of Vishnu in His four hands.

Understanding that the Supreme Personality of Godhead had been born as their son, Vasudeva and Devaki were struck with wonder and began offering their heartfelt prayers to the Lord. The demigods headed by Brahma and Shiva began showering flowers from the sky in great jubilation. At that moment, Lord Krishna spoke to Vasudeva and Devaki, informing them that in their previous lives, they had been born as Sutapa and Prishni and Lord Prishnigarbha had been born as their son, then in their next life they were born as Kashyapa and Diti and Lord Vamanadeva had been born as their son. After appearing before them as four-armed Narayana and having blessed them, Lord Krishna told Vasudeva that He should immediately take Him to the house of Nanda Maharaja in the village of Gokula for safety. After speaking these words, the Lord then manifested His two armed form as an ordinary baby boy.

Vasudeva suddenly became full of anxiety because he knew that when Kamsa comes to know about the birth of his eighth child, he would immediately dash this baby to death as he has done the others. At that moment, under the influence of yogamaya, the shackles attached to Vasudeva's feet suddenly slackened and fell off as the doors to the prison cell somehow miraculously opened. Outside the prison cell Vasudeva saw that all the guards had fallen fast asleep. Vasudeva quickly picked up the new-born child and placed Him in a wicker basket which he balanced on his head, and cautiously made his way out of the prison. Braving the stormy weather, Vasudeva headed for Gokula where his friend Nanda Maharaja lived. When he arrived at the bank of the Yamuna, Vasudeva saw the river was in full spate due to the storm. On entering the fast flowing river, Vasudeva suddenly lost his footing and baby Krishna fell out of the basket and was almost swept away by the strong currents, however, by the mercy of Yamunaji, Vasudeva could recover his son from the raging waters and then very carefully waded across the river and arrived at the village of Gokula. Mother Yashoda had just given birth to a baby girl and due to exhaustion was sleeping soundly on her bed. Under cover of darkness, on reaching Nanda's house, Vasudeva entered the delivery room and picking up the baby girl, replaced her with baby Krishna.

Returning to Kamsa's prison cell in Mathura, Vasudeva placed the baby girl next to Devaki and after closing the cell door, placed the shackles back on his feet and went to sleep. It was just before dawn when the guards heard the baby crying and ran to call Kamsa. Rushing to the spot, Kamsa entered the prison cell and ruthlessly snatched the baby away from Devaki's arms. Vasudeva pleaded that the eighth baby was a girl, and the omen had said a boy, not a girl would kill him, while pleading that this baby girl should not be killed. However, completely ignoring the words of Vasudeva, Kamsa angrily raised the baby girl in order to dash her on the ground, but suddenly the baby slipped from his grasp and rose into the sky while simultaneously assuming the eight armed form of the goddess Durga, an expansion of Yogamaya Devi. The goddess then informed Kamsa in a very grave voice that the eighth child, who was going to kill him, had already been born elsewhere. After saying this, the goddess suddenly disappeared into the sky leaving Kamsa totally bewildered and confused.

Meanwhile in Gokula, mother Yashoda woke up to the cries for milk from her newborn baby and holding Him in her arms, allowed the baby to suck her breast-milk. Due to the exhaustion of giving birth, Yashoda Mayi could not remember whether a boy or a girl had been born to her that night. Nanda Maharaja was overjoyed to see the birth of a son and immediately arranged for a great celebration and donated thousands of cows to the local brahmanas. In the prison cell of Kamsa; Vasudeva and Devaki, knowing that their eighth child was now safe and being overjoyed with happiness, began to meditate on giving away millions of cows in charity to the brahmanas.

End of Mathura Half-Parikrama

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 2

Including: \*Chakra-tirtha\*Ambarisha-tila\*Kamsa-kila\*Dirgha-Vishnu\*Mathura Devi\*Padmanabha Mandir.

## 5. Chakra-tirtha / Ambarisha-tila

Chakra-tirtha is the spot near the bank of the Yamuna River where Lord Vishnu's chased Durvasa Muni all over the universe. This Sudarshana-chakra came to rest after having place is also known as Chakra-tirtha Ghata and nearby is Ambarisha-tila, the hill (tila) where Ambarisha Maharaja performed a year-long Ekadashi-vrata. When Ambarisha was about to break his fast, Durvasa Muni suddenly arrived there. Ambarisha invited Durvasa to take prasada and join him in breaking the Ekadashi fast. Durvasa agreed but first wanted to complete his daily rituals by bathing in the Yamuna River. However, Durvasa did not return immediately and the proper time to break the fast was almost over. Therefore, after consulting his priests, Ambarisha took a little water in order to break his Ekadashi fast. As soon as Durvasa returned, he could understand that Ambarisha Maharaja had taken some water to break the fast. He became furious due to feeling insulted by the king. Durvasa then cursed Ambarisha to die and pulling a hair from his locks, he created a

demon that blazed like fire and was ready to kill the king. Suddenly the Sudarshana-chakra of Lord Vishnu appeared there and killed the demon. The Sudarshana-chakra then turned towards Durvasa who was forced to run for his life. Durvasa spent one year running from the Sudarshana-chakra but could not find shelter anywhere in the three worlds and no one could sav him; not even Lord Shiva or Lord Vishnu could save him. However, on the advice of Lord Vishnu, Durvasa Muni returned to Ambarisha-tila and begged forgiveness from Ambarisha Maharaja in order to be saved from the Sudarshana-chakra. Durvasa declared that the pure bhaktas of Lord Vishnu are even more powerful than the Lord Himself, as only Ambarisha had the power to save him. Ambarisha Maharaja immediately forgave Durvasa Mini and thus he was saved from being burned to death by the Sudarshana-chakra

How To Get There: (See map no.1D).

## 6. Kamsa-kila / Kamsa’s Fort

The ancient fortress of King Kamsa, also known as Kamsa-khila, is situated on the Mathura parikrama path. The Sanskrit word 'khila' means a 'fort' and it was built on a hilltop next to the bank of the Yamuna River. From the top of the hill one gets a wonderful panoramic view of the Yamuna River and in the far distance one can see the temples of Vrindavana. Raja Man Singh (1550-1614) the Rajput king of Amber (Jaipura) also established his palace on this hilltop amid the ruins of Kamsa's fort. Later a descendant of Raja Man Singh named Maharaja Jai Singh, a famous astronomer, around the year 1738, established a small-scale jantar-mantar or Vedic astronomical observatory within the palace compound which can still be seen by visitors to the fort.

How To Get There: (See map no.1D).

## 7. Dirgha Vishnu Mandira

This temple contains the Deity of the four-armed Dirgha Vishnu. The word ‘dirgha' means ‘huge' and refers to the very large form that Krishna showed to the cowherd boys because they doubted Krishna's strength and ability to fight with the powerful King Kamsa and his men. After Krishna manifested this form of Dirgha Vishnu, the cowherd boys were no longer in anxiety about Krishna's welfare and His ability to defeat Kamsa. Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu also visited this temple during His parikrama around Mathura.

How To Get There: (See map no.1D).

## 8. Mathura Devi Mandira

This small temple not far from the Dirgha Vishnu Temple contains the Deity of Mathura Devi, who is worshiped as the presiding Deity of Mathura Puri. Mathura Devi is one of the expansions of Yogamaya. In the Adi-Varaha Purana, the following statement is found, “Mathura Mandala extends throughout twenty-four kosas and is decorated with twelve forests, dvadasha-vanas, where Mathura Devi, the bestower of all accomplishments resides.” How To Get There: (See map no.1D).

## 9. Padmanabha Mandir

In this temple one can see the Deity of Lord Vishnu resting on the celestial serpent Ananta Sesha. The name Padmanabha refers to Lord Garbhodakashayi Vishnu, from whose navel (nabha), a lotus flower (padma) grew, which became the birthplace of Lord Brahma.

How To Get There: (See map no.1D).

End of excursion (Return Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 2 Madhuvana (Maholi)

In the Adi-Varaha Purana, Lord Varaha tells Bhumi Devi, “Oh Goddess, one who sees this forest of Madhuvana has all his desires fulfilled.” Madhuvana is one of the twelve sacred forests of Vraja and has an individual parikrama of around three miles (5km) that passes through all the important places of interest including Krishna-kunda and Dhruva-tila. In the Skanda Purana (Kashi-khanda) it is said, “The charming forest of Madhuvana is situated on the shore of the Yamuna. Madhuvana is the original place of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. It is very sacred to those whose hearts are fixed on Lord Hari. A sinful man who goes there becomes at once free from all sins.”

At the present time, Madhuvana forest has almost disappeared and a large village known as Maholi now stands where the sacred forest once stood. Madhuvana is one of the most famous amongst the twelve sacred forests of Vrindavana and gains mention in many ancient Puranas. Unfortunately, like many others in the holy dhama of Vrindavana, only a few trees remain of what was once a vast and verdant forest. It is said that Madhuvana is the only sacred forest of Vrindavana Dhama where the Supreme Personality of Godhead performed His transcendental pastimes in all the four yugas. In Satya-yuga of the Swayambhuva-manvantara,

He appeared there as Lord Madhusudana and slew a great demon named Madhu who had taken control of the sacred forest. He also appeared in the Satya-yuga of the Raivata-manvantara as Lord Prishnigarbha to give His blessings to Dhruva Maharaja, who was performing severe austerities in the Madhuvana forest. In the Treta-yuga of the Vaivaswata-manvantara, He appeared as Lord Shatrughna, the younger brother of Lord Ramacandra and slew the demon Lavanasura, the evil son of Madhu-daitya. Then in the last Dwapara-yuga, the Lord appeared in His original form as Lord Shri Krishna and performed many wonderful pastimes with the cowherd girls and boys of Vraja. In the present Kali-yuga, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, the incarnation of Krishna known as the 'Golden Avatara' visited the sacred forest of Madhuvana in the year 1515 during His Vraja Mandala parikrama and bathed in the sacred Krishna-kunda.   Top

How To Get There: From Vrindavana one has to proceed 6km to Chhatikara and then turn south-bound on the Delhi to Agra road. (National Highway No.2) and proceed 11km to the Maholi junction, where one can see on the right the large white marble temple of Jai-gurudev (resembling the Taj Mahal). At this junction turn right down this road for 2km until you reach Maholi village. Proceed straight through the village to the other side where one can see Krishna-kunda on the left. This kunda is considered to be the center of Madhuvana Forest (See map no. 2 & 2A).

## How Madhuvana Forest Got Its Name

The forest of Madhuvana, like all the sacred forests of Vrindavana Dhama, is eternally manifest in Lord Krishna's spiritual abode of Goloka Vrindavana which is located in the Vaikuntha planetary system. When Lord Krishna descends to earth to perform His transcendental pastimesfor the benefit of the conditioned souls, He first manifests on the earthly plane His spiritual abode along with its sacred forests and holy places including Govardhana Hill and the Yamuna River.

The Madhuvana forest is said to have been named after Lord Krishna due to the many transcendental pastimes that He performed in this forest. One of the meanings of the Sanskrit word 'madhu' is 'nectar' and because Lord Krishna engaged in many wonderful pastimes with the gopis of Vraja in this forest, it became known as Madhuvana, 'the forest of nectarine pastimes'. Another meaning of the word 'madhu' is 'honey' and Madhuvana was known as the 'forest of wild honey' The Madhuvana forest was an important place where Krishna and Balarama would regularly come with Their friends to enjoy madhupan-lila, the transcendental pastime of drinking wild honey liquor. After feeling intoxicated from drinking the honey, Krishna and Balarama would start singing and then They would dance in ecstasy along with Their cowherd boyfriends. The Vaishnava acharyas have given a number of other meanings to the name Madhusudana and they are: 'He who defeats the sweetness of honey (madhu)', 'He who destroys illusion', and 'He who can destroy all forms of grief'.

Lord Krishna is also known by the name Madhusudana because He slew the demon Madhu within the forest of Madhuvana. In this regard the Sanskrit word 'Madhu' means 'Krishna - the descendent of the Madhu dynasty' and 'sudana' means 'killer' or 'destroyer'; thus the name Madhusudana means 'killer of the Madhu demon'. The Skanda Purana says the forest of Madhuvana was so named because in this forest Lord Madhusudana slew the Madhu demon, “Who can find the limits to the glories of Madhuvana, the forest which contains Mathura Puri. Here the Lord killed the demon Madhu, hence it is known in Mathura as Madhuvana.”

## The Demons named Madhu and Kaitabha

It is mentioned in the Kalika Purana, the Devi-Bhagavata Purana, and also Mahabharata, that the original demons in the universe were the two brothers Madhu and Kaitabha. The Vayu Purana and Jayakhya Samhita both describe the appearance of these two demons who manifest from a wax-like secretion that came from the ear of Lord Vishnu as He lay in yoga-nidra. The first of these demons became eager to drink honey liquor (madhu) and thus became known as Madhu. He was a manifestation of kama, or lust. The second demon was a manifestation of krodha or anger and he became known as Kaitabha. Madhu and Kaitabha are sometimes called 'daityas' which in this regard means that they were 'giants' and not the progeny of Diti. These two demons conspired to rule over the earth and in so doing they not only stole the Vedas from Brahma, but also attempted to kill Him. Fearful of these two powerful demons, Lord Brahma cried out for Lord Vishnu to save him. However, Lord Vishnu was resting in yoga-nidra or deep slumber, and was unable to hear the cries of Brahma. Helpless to save himself from the terrible wrath of the demon brothers, Bramha called for Yogamaya to alert Lord Vishnu to the danger. On awakening from His slumber, Lord Vishnu decided to severely chastise the demons Madhu and Kaitabha and save the universe of the danger the two demons posed.

## The Madhu Demon Slain by Vishnu

The Skanda Purana (Mathura-khanda) says, “The demon Madhu-daitya was killed by Lord Vishnu in His Virata-rupa.” This verse implies that this particular Madhu demon was the same Madhu who was the brother of Kaitabha. These two demons Madhu and Kaitabha had stolen the Vedas from Lord Brahma and taken them to Patala-loka. When the brothers later tried to kill Brahma, he informed Lord Vishnu through the medium of Yogamaya Devi, and the Lord appeared in His Virata-rupa (Universal form) and slew the demons with celestial arrows. The only demons that are mentioned to have been killed by the Lord in His Virata-rupa form were the two brothers Madhu and Kaitabha.

In the Chaitanya-bhagavata (Adi-khanda.170) it says, “In the form of Hayagriva, You saved the Vedas by killing the original demons, Madhu and Kaitabha.” The brothers Madhu and Kaitabha were the first demons in the universe and appeared at the beginning of the universal creation just after the appearance of Lord Brahma.

In the Shrimad Bhagavatam (7.9.37) it says, “My dear Lord, when You appeared as Hayagriva, with the head of a horse, You killed two demons known as Madhu and Kaitabha, who were full of the modes of passion and ignorance. Then You delivered the Vedic knowledge to Lord Brahma. For this reason, all the great saints accept Your forms as transcendental, untinged by material qualities.” These two verses along with the previous verse from the Skanda Purana confirm that Lord Hayagriva who was a manifestation of the Virata-rupa killed the demon Madhu, the brother of Kaitabha.

## The Madhu Demon Invades Madhuvana Forest

The Vedas inform us that the holy dhama is eternal and is not destroyed at the time of the pralaya when the universe is annihilated. Thus the entire transcendental realm of Mathura Mandala (Vraja Mandala), which is part of the spiritual realm of Vaikuntha, remains above the waters of cosmic devastation and remains there until the next creation, when the dhama manifests once again on the earthly plane. The Jayakhya Samhita says that this transcendental land of Mathura Mandala is not created by Brahma but exists eternally and is part of the spiritual world. The Garga-samhita (2.1.53) also confirms this same truth when it says, “Sri Varaha said: O beautiful one (Bhumi), see the transcendental land of Mathura-mandala, which is part of the realm of Goloka, and is not destroyed at the time of the cosmic devastation.” The fact that Mathura Mandala is eternal and not destroyed at the time of the pralaya is again confirmed in the Garga Samhita (2.1.42) when Lord Vishnu told Prayag Tirtharaja, “Mathura-mandala is My home. It is My transcendental abode above the three worlds. At the time of cosmic devastation it is not destroyed.” This transcendental land of Mathura Mandala (Vraja Mandala) which is famous as the playground of Lord Vishnu (Krishna) was on one occasion seen by the demon Madhu who immediately desired to possess it as his own personal property. Madhuvana lies in the center of Mathura Mandala and it was here in this sacred forest that the Madhu demon established his citadel which he called Madhu Puri.

Seeing that the demon Madhu had taken possession of Madhuvana and built his citadel in the heart of the forest, in order to punish him for his many audacious and sinful acts, Lord Vishnu entered the Madhuvana forest in His transcendental form as Hayagriva - the horseheaded avatara, and slew the Madhu demon with celestial arrows. The Skanda Purana says, “Originally Mathura Puri was the forest of the demon Madhu who was slain by the almighty Shri Hari.” The Shrimad Bhagavatam (7.9.37) says, “My dear Lord, when You appeared as Hayagriva, with the head of a horse, You killed two demons known as Madhu and Kaitabha.” After the death of Madhu the Lord then killed his brother Kaitabha and it is said that the fat (medha) from their dead bodies nourished the earth. The Jayakhya Samhita says, “The earth became an abundant stream of wealth, because of their fat (medas) and from then on she (Bhumi) has been known as Medini (earth having the fat of fertility).” In other accounts it is said that the fat from the dead bodies of the demons Madhu and Kaitabha formed the seismic plates (also called tectonic plates), that are part of the earth's crust. The Hayagriva-mahatmyam says that the bodies of Madhu and Kaitabha disintegrated into twelve pieces (two heads, two torsos, four arms and four legs) and transformed into the twelve original seismic plates that cover the earth.

## The Other Demon named Madhu

During the Vaivasvata-manvantara there was another demon named Madhu who was a friend of Ravana. He also built a city named Madhu Puri in the forest of Madhuvana. This particular Madhu was the father of Lavanasura and without doubt a different personality from the Madhu demon, the brother of Kaitabha, who stole the Vedas from Brahma and was killed by Hayagriva. In the Uttarkhanda section of the Ramayana written by Valmiki Muni, it says that the demon named Madhu-daitya married Ravana's sister Kumbhanashi and the son born to them was Lavanasura. The demon Ravana appeared in the eleventh Treta-yuga during the seventh Manu in the Vaivaswata-manvantara, thus the time gap between the two Madhu's is almost two billion years by Vedic calculation. According to historical accounts, the only demon named Madhu who was slain in Madhuvana by Lord Vishnu was the brother of Kaitabha who stole the Vedas from Brahma.

The second Madhu demon, the father of Lavanasura, often referred to as Madhu-daitya, made his home in the Madhuvana forest and the Gopala-tapani Upanishad (2.39) confirms that a demon named Madhu once lived in Madhuvana. However, this particular Madhu was a daitya, which means that like Prahlada and Bali, he belonged to the race of daitya demons born from the womb of Diti, wife of Kasyapa Muni, who is the progenitor of the present Vaivaswata-manvantara. The Ramayana says that Madhu-daitya established his city in the forest of Madhuvana and named it Madhupuri. Although born in a family of asuras, he was a very pious personality and made friendship with demigods, consequently the demons and the demigods lived in peace for many years. Like most asuras, Madhu-daitya was a great devotee of Lord Shiva and being pleased with Madhu-daitya's pious disposition, Lord Shiva presented him with an expansion of his own infallible trishul, a three-pronged trident, for his personal protection. Madhu and his wife Kumbhanashi had a son named Lavanasura who possessed qualities that were completely opposite to those of his father. Lavanasura was so evil that even as a child he would often beat his play-mates and on some occasions even kill and eat them. Being thoroughly disgusted with his son's wicked ways, as soon as Lavanasura achieved adulthood, Madhu handed over the kingdom to him along with the infallible trishul. Madhu-daitya immediately left home and after taking shelter of Lord Varuna, he drowned himself in the ocean out of shame.

During the fourteenth Treta-yuga of the Vaivaswata-manvantara, which coincided with the time that Lavanasura inherited the kingdom of Madhupuri from his father Madhu-daitya, the Surya-vamsha king of Ayodhya named Mandhata Maharaja, was ruling over all the lands of the earth. Desiring to rule over the heavenly planets, Mandhata challenged Lord Indra that he should surrender the heavenly kingdom of Swarga-loka or fight with him in battle. Indra told Mandhata that if he could defeat Lavanasura, the most powerful demon on earth, then he would immediately give him the heavenly kingdom. Due to being instigated by Lord Indra, Mandhata went to Madhuvana and attacked the demon Lavanasura, but the demon very easily destroyed Mandhata's army and slew him in battle using the infallible trishul weapon inherited from his father Madhu-daitya.

## Lord Ramachandra Sends Shatrughna to Madhuvana

The demon Lavanasura let loose a terrible reign of terror throughout the region and was particularly inimical towards the rishis and brahmanas. Like all rakshasas he enjoyed feasting on human flesh and did not even spare the ascetics who frequented Madhuvana forest. Lord Ramachandra, after hearing the earnest petitions of the sages headed by Bhargava Rishi and Chayavana Muni, ordered His younger brother Shatrughna to accompany the sages to Madhuvana in order slay the demon Lavanasura. Before sending him on his journey, Lord Rama ordered Shatrughna to establish his own kingdom at Madhuvana and crowned him the King of Mathura Puri in an elaborate ceremony at Ayodhya performed by Vashista Muni.

Before leaving for Madhuvana, Lord Rama presented Shatrughna with an infallible quiver of arrows with which to kill Lavanasura. It is said that the celestial arrows had belonged to Lord Vishnu and were used to kill the two demon brothers Madhu and Kaitabha. Lord Rama also presented Shatrughna with an ancient Deity of Lord Varaha that was to be installed in the new city. This particular Deity was retrieved from the island of Lanka after the demon Ravana had been slain by Lord Rama. Ravana had taken the Varaha Deity from Lord Indra after defeating him in battle during his invasion of the heavenly planets. According to the Padma Purana, Lord Varaha, the boar incarnation of Lord Vishnu, is the original presiding Deity of the Mathura Mandala, and is eternally situated on the southern petal of the lotus of Vraja at a place known as Saukari-vateshwara (Batasar). According to the Puranas, whenever Lord Varaha advents Himself in order to save the world, He appears from His transcendental abode at Saukari-vateshwara.

## Lord Shatrughna Vanquishes the Demon Lavanasura

It was in the twenty-fourth Treta-yuga of the Vaivaswata-manvantara when Lord Vishnu incarnated on earth in the form of Lord Ramachandra along with His three brothers namely; Bharata, Lakshmana, and Shatrughna. Lord Rama's mission on earth was to destroy all the powerful demons like Ravana that were overburdening the world at that time in history. Lord Ramachandra and His three brothers represent the Chatur-vyuha, or four original forms of Lord Vishnu namely: Vasudeva, Sankarshana, Pradyumna, and Anirudha. According to the Uttarkhanda of the Ramayana, on the ardent plea of the sages who resided in and around Madhuvana forest, including Chayavana Muni and Bhargava Rishi, Lord Rama sent His brother Shatrughna to Madhuvanan in order to kill the demon Lavanasura and establish a kingdom there. Prior to his departure, after having been informed by Chayavana Muni and Bhargava Rishi, Lord Rama warned Shatrughna about Lavanasura's infallible trishul weapon with which he had slain the famous emperor of the Surya-vamsha dynasty Mandhata Maharaja, who was equal to Lord Indra in prowess. Chayavana Muni also advised Shatrughna that he should wait until such a time that Lavanasura was not carrying the infallible trishul before attacking him.

Travelling stealthily with his army, on his arrival in Madhuvana, Shatrughna waited patiently for the most opportune moment to attack the demon Lavanasura. Shatrughna had arrived at Madhuvana during the monsoon season and not suspecting an attack by kshatriyas in the rainy season, Lavanasura often went hunting without taking his infallible trishul. One day Shatrughna heard from his spies that Lavanasura had gone into the forest to hunt wild animals without taking his trishul. The Ramayana says that Shatrughna had his soldiers immediately block all the entrances to the Lavanasura's city so he could not enter and retrieve the trishul. It is said that Shatrugha himself waited at the eastern gate of city generally used by Lavanasura when hunting.

After some time, Shatrughna suddenly saw a ferocious looking giant immerging from the dense forest carrying under his arms a number of dead animals including: two tigers, a water buffalo, a huge snake, a crocodile and a baby elephant. Realizing that this was the great demon Lavanasura returning from his hunting expedition, Shatrughna came forward and challenged him to fight. Lavanasura wanted to run away as he was not carrying his infallible trishul, but Shatrughna challenged him saying that Lavanasura had sufficient weapons including a spear and should stand and fight. Infuriated by this challenge, a fierce battle broke out between Lavanasura and Shatrughna. Lavanasura used many weapons including large rocks and even uprooted trees, hurling them at Shatrughna with all his might, but Rama's young brother stood firm. When Shatrughna saw that the opportune time to gain victory was at hand, he slew the demon with a volley of celestial arrows. After killing Lavanasura, Shatrughna established the city of Mathura on the banks of the Yamuna. In the Vishnu Purana it is said, “Shatrughna founded Mathura after killing the powerful demon Lavanasura.” After his great victory, Shatrughna installed the Deity of Lord Adi-Varaha given to him by Lord Rama, and even today this Deity of Lord Varaha is still being worshiped in Mathura, at the temple of Adi-Varaha in the vicinity of the old city.

## Places Of Interest At Madhuvana

## 1 Krishna-kunda (Madhu-kunda)

In the Bhakti-ratnakara, it is said that in the sacred forest of Madhuvana one can see a very beautiful lake which is full of sweet transparent water and fragrant blue lotus flowers, and anyone who bathes there will achieve the fulfillment of all their desires. This sacred lake in Madhuvana forest is known as Krishna-kunda, as well as Madhu-kunda or Madhuvana-kunda. This celebrated kunda was the place where Krishna and Balarama performed many of Their transcendental pastimes and often brought Their cows to Madhuvana forest to graze on the sweet fresh grass that grew there. This pastime is known as ‘go-charana-lila' which means 'wondering with the cows' or sometimes as ‘ghoshta-vihara' meaning ‘pastimes in the pasturing grounds'. Such activities form an integral part of Krishna and Balarama's daily activities of taking the cows to pasturing grounds around Vraja. Once on a very hot summer day, when Krishna was grazing His cows in Madhuvana forest, He created this kunda by pushing His flute into the ground so that the cows and cowherd boys could quench their thirst. This lake then became famous as Krishna-kunda and Krishna and Balarama would enjoy many wonderful picnics along with Their friends on the banks of this beautiful kunda.

In the Vraja-bhakti-vilasa, all the presiding Deities of the sacred forests of Vrindavana Dhama are mentioned, along with all the various mantras and invocations to be chanted while performing achaman or bathing in the various kundas, but this is highly ritualistic and impractical for most pilgrims to follow, therefore it is recommended that one should simply chant the supremely powerful maha-mantra when bathing or performing achaman, either here at Krishna-kunda or at any other kunda in Vraja Mandala. When Lord Chaitanya was performing parikrama of Vraja Mandala, wherever He took bath or visited a temple, He simply chanted the Hare Krishna maha-mantra and danced in ecstasy.

How To Get There: After passing right through the Maholi village, Krishna-kunda can be seen on the left side of the road on the outskirts of the village (See map no.2 & 2A).

## 2 Balarama Temple (Dauji Mandira)

The Deity of Lord Balarama in this temple is considered to be the presiding Deity of the village. The word 'Dau' or 'Dauji' means elder brother, and a most affectionate name used by Vrajavasis to address Lord Balarama, the elder brother of Lord Krishna. It is believed that the Deity of Lord Balarama was established here at Krishna-kunda thousands of years ago. The original Deity was unfortunately lost in the course of time and the present Deity of Lord Balarama is the 'pratibhu-murti', or replica of the original Deity. The term 'pratibhu' means 'possessing the same spiritual potency'.

How To Get There: This temple is situated on the road-side just to the left of Krishna-kunda and at first glance resembles an ordinary house rather than a temple (See map no.2 & 2A).

## 3 Shatrughna Mandira

It is said that the Deity of Lord Shatrughna was originally installed here at Madhuvana during the Treta-yuga and is known locally as Madhuvana-Bihari, which means the 'Enjoyer of Madhuvana'. It is said that Lord Rama personally gave this name to his brother Shatrughna before sending him to Madhuvana. Unfortunately, the original Deity was lost many years ago and the present Deity is the pratibhu expansion. The old temple of Lord Shatrughna was built in the typical Vraja architectural style which became prominent during the period when the temples of the Six Goswamis were built in Vrindavana. The Goswami temples were constructed in the late 16th and early 17th Centuries, therefore, the old temple of Lord Shatrughna that can be seen here today dates back about 400 years.

How To Get There: This temple is to the right of Krishna-kunda and hidden from general view. It is situated in a side-lane that goes up a slight incline behind some houses. The temple is just 10mt up the lane on the right (See map no.2 & 2A).

## 4 Dhruva-tila

The word 'tila' means a 'small hill', and this is the exact spot in Madhuvana forest where the famous boy-saint Dhruva Maharaja performed austerities to please the Supreme Lord during the Satya-yuga. This is also the same place where Dhruva received the divine darshana of Lord Vishnu in His form as Lord Prishnigarbha. Dhruva Maharaja was a royal prince and son of the Aryan Emperor Uttanapada in the dynasty of Swayambhuva Manu, but due to being insulted at the instance of his step-mother named Suruchi, he decided to leave home. On the advice of his birth-mother Suniti Devi, Dhruva left for the forest in search of Lord Krishna, whom his mother said was the only person who could help him to remove his feelings of hurt and also fulfill his desires to obtain a kingdom far greater than that of his father.

By the will of providence, the great sage Shrila Narada Muni, came to know that the five year old Dhruva had left the comfort of his father's palace in order to live in the forest and perform penance. Therefore, Narada Muni went to meet Dhruva to enquire from him the reason why he left his father's opulent kingdom in exchange for a life of solitude and austerity in the forest. On hearing that Dhruva had been badly insulted and wanted to achieve a kingdom that would be superior to his father's own kingdom, Narada was very surprised that a mere boy of only five years of age could possess such a powerful kshatriya spirit. Narada was also moved by the child's sincerity and was extremely pleased that Dhruva was determined to directly meet the Supreme Lord in order to achieve his heart's desire. Narada Muni advised Dhruva to go to the Madhuvana forest and perform austerities there, as he would very quickly achieve the desired result. In the Shrimad Bhagavatam (4.8.42) Narada advises Dhruva by saying, “My dear boy, I therefore wish all good fortune for you. You should go to the bank of the Yamuna, where there is a virtuous forest named Madhuvana, and there be purified. Just by going there, one draws nearer the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who always lives there.” Narada also gave Dhruva a very powerful mantra by which he could propitiate the Lord directly. The mantra given by Narada to Dhruva was, “om namah bhagavate vasudevaya” which means, “I offer my respects to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Shri Krishna, the son of Vasudeva.” That a little boy of only five year of age was engaged in such severe forms of penance, like standing on only one leg and subsisting only on air, Lord Vishnu became very pleased with Dhruva's sincerity and appeared before him in His four-armed Narayana feature known Prishnigarbha. After hearing the heartfelt prayers of Dhruva, the Lord awarded the child the highest benediction of pure devotional service and liberation from repeated birth and death. The Lord also granted Dhruva a kingdom far greater than any earthly kingdom including that of his father and appointed him as ruler of the localized Vaikuntha planet known as Swetadwipa, which is also called the Pole Star.

On top of the hill known as Dhruva-tila, where Dhruva performed his austerities, is a temple known as the Dhruva-Narayana Mandir, where two important shrines can be seen. One shrine contains the Deity of Lord Vishnu in His merciful feature as Prishnigarbha, also called Dhruva-Narayana, seen giving His blessings to Dhruva, who is offering his obeisance's to the Lord's lotus feet. Also present in the same shrine is Shrila Narada Muni, as well as Garuda, the eagle carrier of Lord Narayana. In the second shrine are the Deities of Goddess Lakshmi and Lord Narayana, along with a Deity of Shri Nathaji and Lord Krishna's dear friend Uddhava.

How To Get There: From Vrindavana, follow the same directions for Madhuvana as far as Maholi junction, after turning right at Jai-gurudev Mandir, proceed for 1 km. Take a left turn at F.C.I. Warehouse & follow a narrow lane for 300mt to the Dhruva-Narayana Temple. From Krishna-kunda, return to the F.C.I. Warehouse & turn right. Alternatively, from Krishna-kunda, one can join the Madhuvana parikrama path at the back of the kunda and proceed across the fields for about 1km to Dhruva Tila and the temple of Dhruva-Narayana (See map no.2 & 2A).

## 5 Madhu Gufa (Cave)

This is said to have been the cave (gufa) where the demon Madhu once lived when he ruled the Madhuvana forest. It is also said that Madhu's son Lavanasura also lived in the same cave. Local people say that this cave goes underground for a few miles, but because the cave, over the period of many years, is continually shrinking, it is now far too narrow and dangerous to venture inside. Many demons preferred to make their homes in deep labyrinthine caves with a number of exits for easy escape in case of being attacked. There is now a shrine in the cave entrance dedicated to the monkey-god Hanuman.

According to the Ramayana and various Puranas, the demon Madhu lived in an opulent palace within a city which he had built in the Madhuvana forest known as Madhu Puri, which was later inherited by Madhu's son Lavanasura. Thus the cave may have been the demon's residence prior to him building the city of Madhu Puri.

How To Get There: This cave is at the foot of Dhruva-tila just 20mt. from the entrance gate leading up to the Dhruva-Narayana Mandir (See map no.2 & 2A).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 3

Including:\*Koila\*Karnawal.

## 9 KOLE GHATA (Koila)

This is the famous riverside ghata where Lord Krishna's father Vasudeva, crossed the Yamuna River on his journey to Gokula Mahavana. Vasudeva was carrying the newly-born Krishna in a wicker basket balanced on his head while on his journey from the prison cell of Kamsa to the safety of Nanda Maharaja's house at Gokula. Vasudeva crossed the Yamuna River at Kole Ghata, which is presently known as Koila Ghata, but due to a fierce storm raging that night, after entering the river, Vasudeva became overwhelmed by the strong waves and heavy currents and suddenly losing his balance, baby Krishna fell out of the basket into the river Yamuna. Fearing that He may drown, Vasudeva began franticly searching in the fast-flowing water for baby Krishna but could not find Him anywhere. It is said that this incidence was a pastime performed by Yamuna Devi, who was eager to receive Krishna's lotus feet on her head and also satisfy her desire to have baby Krishna sit in her lap. After embracing Him in her waves for a few ecstatic moments, Yamuna Devi returned baby Krishna to His father. At that moment Vasudeva suddenly saw baby Krishna floating in the water nearby and was overjoyed that his son had not perished in the raging current. Having got his baby Krishna back, Vasudeva once again attempted to cross the river but this time, by the grace of Yamuna Devi, who subdued her fastflowing current, he managed to get to the other side and reached Gokula and the house of Nanda Maharaja. According to the Sanskrit dictionary the word 'kole' refers to a person's 'lap' and in this particular case it means that Yamuna Devi had baby Krishna on her 'lap'. It is said that this holy tirtha was established by Maharaja Vajranabha. It is mentioned by historians that Maharaja Vajranabha became king of Mathura after the retirement of the Pandavas to the Himalayas. At the request of the local Vaishnava community, Vajranabha identified and named all the holy places connected to Krishna's pastimes within the area of Vraja Mandala.

How To Get There: This place is on the bank of Yamuna 10km south-east of Madhuvana following the road to Bad & 7km south of Mathura (See map no.2B).

## 10 Karnawali (Kanarwal)

This is said to be the place where Krishna and Balarama had Their ears pierced. The word 'karna' means 'ear' as well as 'earring' and 'wali' means 'the place', or in other words the place where the two brothers had Their ears pierced. There is an ancient well here known Karnabedha Kupa. The word 'karnabedha' means the place (bedha) of the 'ear-piercing' and 'kupa' means 'well'.

How To Get There: This place 2km south of Koila (See map no.2B).

End of excursion (Return to Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

End of chapter two

## Chapter Three: Talavana to Radha-kunda

## 3 TALAVAN (Tarsi)

Talavana is one of the twelve sacred forests of Vraja and it has a parikrama of three and a half miles (6km). It was in the Talavana forest that Lord Balarama killed the demon Dhenukasura, who was living in the forest in the form of a wild ass along with his family and friends. Unfortunately, at the present time the forest has completely disappeared and only a few tal trees remain of what was once a large forest. The present name of this place is Tarsi, or sometimes Tarasi and a fairly large village has now come up where the forest once stood. The important places to see here are the temple of Lord Balarama known as the Dauji Mandir and Sankarshana-kunda. The Adi-Varaha Purana says, “Oh goddess \[Bhumi\] by bathing here one becomes successful. The lake in this forest is full of clear water with many beautiful lotuses. By bathing and giving charity at this place one achieves great merit”.

As the name suggests, Talavana was a forest of tal trees, which is a type of palm that grows very tall and bears an extremely sweet and delicious fruit about the size of a grapefruit. The soft fleshy pulp of the tal fruit is saturated with a thick syrupy juice that tastes just like nectar. Because these wonderful fruits were of such high quality, King Kamsa ordered Denukasura to live at Talavana and protect the fruits from being plundered by others. King Kamsa firmly believed that all the delicious tal fruits in Talavan forest were meant only for his pleasure.

In his previous life, Dhenukasura had been known as Sahashika and was the son of Bali Maharaja, who was the son of Virochana, who in turn was the eldest son of Prahlada Maharaja. Once upon a time, Sahashika went to the Gandhmadana Mountain in the heavenly realm to sport with beautiful young girls. Unfortunately, Sahashika accidentally disturbed the great sage Durvasa Muni who was meditating in a cave on the mountain. In a sudden rage, Durvasa cursed Sahashika saying, "Oh ass-like fool, go to earth and become an ass.” After hearing the terrible curse pronounced by Durvasa, Sahashika begged Durvasa Muni for forgiveness. Being somewhat pacified by the humble submission of Sahashika, Durvasa told him that in the Dwapara Yuga, the Supreme Lord will appear on earth in the form of the divine brothers Krishna and Balarama, and by Their mercy he would eventually be redeemed.

## The Liberation of Dhenukasura

One day, Krishna and Balarama were enjoying pastimes in the forest of Vrindavana along with Their cowherd boyfriends. As the brothers lay beneath the shade of a tree, Their friends began to massage Their legs and started fanning Them with bunches of leaves. At that moment, a gentle breeze started blowing carrying the sweet aroma of newly ripened tal fruits that emanated from the nearby forest of Talavan. Upon smelling the delectable aroma of the newly ripened tal fruits, the cowherd boys began thinking how nice it would be to enjoy all those delicious fruits along with Krishna and Balarama. The cowherd boys knew that the nectar-filled fruits in Talavana forest were carefully guarded by a demon named Dhenukasura. Due to fear of the giant ass-demon Dhenukasura and his demonic friends, no one dared to enter the Talavana forest, not even birds or animals went anywhere near the place.

Desiring to enter the Talavana forest to eat the fresh tal fruits there, the cowherd boys headed by Shridama, Sudama and Stokakrishna began to address Krishna and Balarama, by first glorifying Them for Their heroic exploits in killing a large number of demons, simply by the power of Their immensely strong arms. In fact, the boys went as far as to say that only Krishna and Balarama were strong enough to kill the demon Dhenukasura, after which they could enjoy eating the ripened tal fruit. Upon hearing the request of the cowherd boys, Krishna and Balarama decided to enter the Talavana forest and confront the demon Dhenukasura. Leaving immediately, the two transcendental brothers soon arrived at Talavana, and accompanied by Their friends entered the forest. Ripened tal fruits not only hung down in great abundance from all the tree tops, but also lay scattered all over the forest floor. The sweet and aromatic scent of the delectable fruits filled the air in all directions.

Balarama, exhibiting the strength of an elephant, immediately started yanking on one tree after another, causing all the ripened fruits to fall to the ground making a tumultuous sound. The loud noise caused by all the falling tal fruits startled Dhenukasura who was resting nearby with his family members and friends. Neighing very loudly and in an angry mood, Dhenukasura immediately came to see what was causing all the noise. As the giant ass-demon hastily ran through the forest, the earth began to shake and the trees swayed 'to and fro' as if an earthquake was about to strike. Within moments the ass-demon Denukashura arrived and surveying the scene, concluded that Balarama was the main cause of all the commotion. Dhenukasura suddenly charged towards Balarama at great speed digging up the earth with his hooves as he galloped sending clumps of dirt flying in all directions. Coming in front of Balarama, the ass-demon, while roaring loudly, swiftly whirled around and began violently kicking Balarama's strong chest with all his might. At first Balarama seemed not to feel the kicking off the ass-demon, but then, without warning, Balarama suddenly caught hold of the ass-demon's hind legs and began to whirl him around over His head, as if the demon was nothing more than a ragdoll. Balarama then whirled the demon around with such power, that the demon's life air was immediately forced out from his body and he died instantaneously. Balarama then hurled the ass-demon's body up into the highest palm tree around, causing the tree to come crashing down under the weight of the demon's dead body, bringing down many other trees along with it like a pack of cards. It appeared as if a great tornado had just ripped straight through the Talavana forest. Thus the curse of Durvasa Muni had been fulfilled and just as Durvasa had said, the demon Dhenukasura achieved liberation at the hands of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

Seeing that their friend Dhenukasura had been killed, all the ass-demons came out of the dense forest and immediately started to attack Krishna and Balarama. One by one, the two brothers caught the ass-demons by their hind legs and began whirling them around over Their heads and then threw them up into the trees. Within a short time, all the ass-demons had been killed and their dead bodies lay suspended in the treetops appearing like clouds of various colors. Thanks to Krishna and Balarama, the cowherd boys were able to enjoy all the tasty tal fruits to their hearts content.

How To Get There: From Madhuvana, the Vraja Mandala Parikrama goes by a farm track to the sacred forest of Talavana situated just a few kilometers to the south. By road from Mathura proceed south-bound on the Delhi to Agra road (National Highway No.2) to the Bharatpur junction and then turn right on to the Bharatpur road. (This turn is on a flyover and one must come back on the other side of the road to reach it). Proceed along the Bharatpur road for 6km until to reach the Tarsi road junction on the right. Turn right over the railway lines and proceed another 2km to Tarsi village. Then go straight through Tarsi village for another 2km to reach Sankarshana-kunda and Talavana. (See map No.2B & 3).

## Places of Interest At Talavana

## 1 Sankarshana-kunda

This very large lake is generally known as Sankarshana-kunda, but is also known by the names Baladeva-kunda and Balabhadra-kunda. The various names of the kunda refer to Lord Balarama who killed the Dhenukasura demon here at Talavana. The local Vrajavasis usually refer to this lake as Talavana-kunda or Tarasi-kunda. It is said that while herding cows in the Talavana forest, Lord Krishna created this kunda by striking His cow-herding stick into the ground so that the cowherd boys and cows could quench their thirst.

How To Get There: (See map no. 3).

## 2 Baladeva Mandira (Dauji Mandira)

This ancient temple is dedicated to Lord Balarama who killed the Dhenukasura demon here at Talavana. Within the temple can be seen Lord Balarama along with His eternal consort Shrimati Revati Devi. This temple is known locally as Dauji Mandira. The word 'dauji' means 'elder brother' and refers to Lord Balarama who is Krishna's elder brother.

How To Get There: (See map No. 3).

## 4 Kamudavana (Kudarban)

In the Adi-Varaha Purana it is stated. “Hey Devi, this third forest, Kumudavana, is supreme. One who visits this place becomes worshipable in My abode.” Kamudavana is the smallest of the twelve sacred forests of Vraja with a parikrama of just one mile (1.5km). The sacred forest has now completely disappeared and a small village now stands here where the forest once stood. The village is known locally as Kudarban which is a corruption of the name Kamudavana. The word 'kamuda' or 'kamudini' refers to a special variety of lotus flower, similar to a water lily, which formerly grew in great abundance in Kamuda-kunda, and because of these kamuda flowers, this sacred forest achieved its name. The celebrated lake of Kamuda-kunda is still present here. It is said that Radha and Krishna used to enjoy many wonderful water sports (jala-krida) as well as many amorous pastimes (jala-vihara) in this sacred lake. The word jala’ means 'water' and 'krida' means 'sporting pastimes', the word 'vihara' means 'amorous pastimes'. Because many amorous pastimes (jala-vihara) took place in this lake, it is also known as Vihara-kunda.

Kamudavana is also one of the forests where ecstatic rasa-lila pastimes took place. In the Garga Samhita (2.29 & 38) it is said, "Then Sri Krishna went to Kumudvana forest, which was filled with the sounds of humming bees, and enjoyed the rasa-dance with the gopis. With many different dances, with amorous gestures, and with sidelong glances the gopis gave great pleasure to Krishna." The great sage and incarnation of Lord Vishnu, Kapila Muni, also spent considerable time at Kamudavana performing austerities on the banks of Kamuda-kunda and there is a small temple known as the Kapila Mandira here on the bank of the kunda containing the Deity of Lord Kapila. Because Kapila Muni spent time here engaged in meditation and austerities, this kunda is also known as Gangasagara-kunda, after the famous ashrama of Lord Kapila situated at the mouth of the Ganges in Bengal, known as Shri Gangasagara. In the Adi-Varaha Purana it is said, “One who bathes in this kunda will achieve ten times the benefit of a pilgrimage to Shri Gangasagara.” As all the tirthas of the world have their origins in Vraja it appears from this verse that Kamuda-kunda is the original Gangasagara-tirtha. This famous kunda is also known as

Padma-kunda and it is said that anyone who bathes here will acquire all the knowledge of the Vedas. The word 'padma' generally means a 'lotus flower', but can also refer to enlightenment through transcendental knowledge.

Krishna and Balarama used to regularly bring Their cows to Kamudavana and while the cows were grazing in the forest, the two brothers would enjoy water sports (jala-krida) in this kunda along with Their cowherd boyfriends.
