## 34 Paraso (Palson)

When Akrura was taking Krishna and Balarama to Mathura on his chariot, he passed through this village. The gopis were following behind the chariot in a distraught condition, sobbing piteously and sometimes falling on the ground in a state of acute separation. Seeing the forlorn condition of the gopis, Krishna tried to pacify them by promising to return 'the day after next'. The word 'paraso' means 'the day after tomorrow' and because Krishna made this promise here, thus the village achieved its name. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, "See here is Paraso-grama. As Krishna rode in the chariot to Mathura, He became disturbed seeing the condition of the gopis. In order to pacify them He said, 'Tomorrow or the day after \[parasu means the day after tomorrow\] I will return and meet you.' For this reason the town is called Paraso.” How To Get There: This village is 10km north of Govardhana (See map no.13).

## 35 Si-Grama (Sigram)

During Krishna's journey from Nandagrama to Mathura, the gopis continued to follow the chariot from one village to the next and they eventually arrived at the village of Si-grama. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, "Nearby Paraso is a town called Si-grama. Let me describe briefly how it was named. Krishna became impatient here seeing the condition of the gopis and told them again and again that He would return quickly from Mathura. The name of Si-grama comes from the word ‘sighra' which means 'quickly'. Krishna then left on the road to Mathura while the gopis, bereft of Krishna's association, were left for dead. The torrent of tears shed by all the gopis mixed with the anjana (mascara) from their eyes and flowed down their breasts to the ground. The combined tears formed a river which everyone said looked just like the Yamuna. This is the place where the gopis cried in ecstatic love. Only the most fortunate persons see this place.” Although Akrura tried to avoid the main highway to Mathura so that the Vrajavasis could not know which road he was traversing, fearing they would try to stop him from taking Krishna and Balarama to Mathura, nevertheless, he could not avoid the gopis who appeared to be following the chariot wherever it went.

How To Get There: This village is 2km south of Daholi (See map no.13).

## Holy Places to The South of Govardhana Hill

## 36 Rinmochan Kunda / Papamochan-Kunda

Rinmochan-kunda has recently been renovated by the 'Braja Foundation'. It is said that anyone who bathes in these two kundas would be freed from the sins of killing a brahmana and even the sin of killing a cow. The word 'mochan' means to release, liberate or deliver' one's soul from all kinds of sins (rin). Lord Krishna manifested all the holy places of Bharata-varsha within Vraja Mandala and Rinmochan-kund is said to be the embodiment of the sacred Vishnupada at Gaya, where people traditionally perform the pinda-dhana, or shradha ceremonies for the benefit of their departed ancestors. The Bhakti-ratnakara says that one who bathes in Rinmochan-kunda also becomes free of all debts to the ancestors, demigods and sages. Papamochana-kunda is located a few hundred meters from Rimmochana-kunda on the road to Parasauli (Mohammadpur).

How To Get There: (See map no.13 & 13B).

## 37 Indra Dvaja Vedi

This is the spot where Krishna's father Nanda Maharaja and the Vrajavasis used to worship Lord Indra, the king of heaven. When the Vrajavasis cancelled the annual 'Indra-pu/a' on the advice of Krishna, and instead performed Govardhana-pu/a, this caused Lord Indra to become very angry and in retribution he inundated the land of Vrindavana with torrents of rain. How To Get There: This place is situated on Mathura road just after the bus stand (See map no.13 & 13B).

## 38 Pali Brahmanan

According to the parikrama detailed in Bhakti-ratnakara, after Narada-kunda and Ratna-simhasana, the next tirtha mentioned just before Indra-dwaja-vedi is Pali, which has been identified as being the village of Pali Brahmanan. It is mentioned in the Bhakti-ratnakara that Pali is the village of the gopi Palita, who was a 'yutheshwara", a group leader of younger gopis who she would train in the service of Radha and Krishna. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Pali is the beautiful garden where Palita-yutheshwara used to stay.” A village with the appellative 'Brahmanan' attached to its name generally implies that the village is predominantly inhabited by brahmanas. Pali Brahmanan is one of the villages along with Janmanta and Parasauli, where a channel of the Yamuna River once flowed. One can see the light-grey colored silt that is unique to the Yamuna river-bed six to ten feet below the topsoil.

How To Get There: This village is located 1mile to the north of Janmanta on the opposite side of the Govardhana to Mathura road (See map no.13).

## 39 Yamuna Mata (Janmanta)

This is the famous village where it is said a channel of the Yamuna River once flowed. The local Vrajavasis like to show interested visitors the light-grey colored silt that is unique to the Yamuna river-bed lying some six feet or so below the topsoil. To commemorate the fact that the Yamuna River once flowed here, there is a famous temple in the village that is dedicated to Yamuna Devi, the river goddess. There can be a number of explanations how the Yamuna River came to be flowing at this place. During the monsoon season great rivers like the Yamuna inevitably swell with excess rain-water and often burst their banks thus creating vast flood plains as well as new channels. These new channels would at some point lead back to the main course of the river. In the nearby village of Pali Brahmanan, a short distance north from Yamuna Mata village, as well as at Parasauli to the south, there is evidence that the same channel of the Yamuna River was also running through these two villages. According to mineralogical studies, the same light-gray silt which is found in the present-day Yamuna river-bed, which is composed of grey colored granite sediments that have been carried by the rivers powerful currents from the high Himalayas, is clearly present in these villages.

It is important to note that every few hundred years the course of a river may go through considerable change, especially during the monsoon season, with new channels opening and old ones closing. In Vrindavana, the Yamuna no longer flows at the famous Pani Ghata or the revered Akrura Ghata, and has now moved a few kilometers away to the east. It is said that about two hundred years ago, the Mana-sarovara at Belvana was situated on a large island with the Yamuna River flowing on both sides until the eastern branch of these two channels completely disappeared. The Shrimad-Bhagavatam also reveals that there was a great flood that completely inundated Vrindavana when Lord Indra in great anger wanted to punished the Vrajavasis and he sent the samvartaka clouds of devastation that unleashed great torrents of rain that flooded the entire land. Due to the great deluge of water, the Yamuna would also have overflowed her banks and created new channels.

Based on a survey conducted by the Photo-geology & Remote Sensing Division of the Geological Survey of India, an ancient channel of the Yamuna River once existed about five thousand years ago and was located to the west of the Yamuna's present-day course. This ancient channel formerly flowed from somewhere north of Seshasayi and then flowed past the forest of Kamyavana, then towards Nandagrama and Varsana, before flowing east of Govardhana Hill past the villages of Pali Brahmanan, Yamuna Mata and Parasauli. Then the river passed through the forest of Kamudavana and Talavana before rejoining the main course of the Yamuna just north of Mathura. Shrila Sanatana Goswami in his commentary on Brihad-bhagavatamrita (1.6.108) says, “The glorious Yamuna flows in the midst of Vrajabhumi, but during Kirshna’s manifested presence some of her branches flowed in parts untouched by her today. Thus many of the forests of Krishna’s land were graced by Sri Yamuna’s water and her grassy, tree-lined banks.”

It appears from the Brihad-bhagavatamrita commentary of Shrila Sanatana Goswami that the river Yamuna had many sub-branches that flowed through different parts of Vraja. This is also confirmed by the survey conducted by the Geological Survey of India which reveals many ancient sub-channels that meander through the entire Vraja region. In the Garga Samhita (2. 3.14-17) it says, “Wishing to attain Lord Krishna, the Original Supreme Personality of Godhead, as her husband, Kalindi assumed a splendid spiritual form and performed great austerities. Even today she stays in a water-house her father made for her. Then the Kalindi swiftly entered Vraja-mandala. Then she flowed through Vrindavana, beautiful Mathura, and beautiful secluded Mahavana. As the very beautiful leader of many gopis, Sri Yamuna made her home in Vrindavana to perform the rasa-dance with Sri Krishnacandra.” Also in the Garga Samhita is the famous stotra known as the Yamuna Sahasra-nama that reveals the numerous places where the Yamuna River flows as she courses through the holy land of Vrajabhumi, “Talavana-sthita - she flows through Talavana, Kumudavana-nadi - she flows through Kumudavana, Govinda-kunda-nilaya - she is the home of Govinda-kunda, Govardhini - she flows by Govardhana hill, Govardhananka - she carries the mark of Govardhana, Govardhana-tati bhava - she is situated near Govardhana, Lalita-kunda-ga - she stays at Lalita-kunda, Visakha-kunda-mandita - she is decorated with Visakha-kunda, Nanda-grama-mahi-dvara -she flows by Nanda-gram, Kamavanancita, Kamatavi - she flows by Kamavana, Nandisvara-samanvita - she flows by Nandisvara hill, Nandi-grama-sthala-sthita -she is situated at Nanda-grama.”

How To Get There: This place is situated on the southern side of Mathura road (opposite the road to Pali Brahmanan) and 2.5km from Govardhana Town (See map no.13).

End of excursion (Rejoin Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 18 Parasauli (Mohammadpur)

In the Bhakti-ratnakara it says, “O Shrinivasa, behold this village of Parasauli! Here Shri Krishnachandra danced the rasa in spring. Look at the peerless Chandra-sarovara! Here Krishna rested after dancing the rasa. This village is where Radha and Krishna performed Their wonderful rasa-lila pastimes in springtime and also where the greatly celebrated lake known as Chandra-sarovara is situated. The ancient name of this place was Parasauli, but during the Mughal rule it was changed to Mohammadpur.”

The Vraja-bhakti-vilasa says that Parasauli is one of the famous sub-forests of Vrindavana Dhama. It is also said that a former branch of the river Yamuna, which passed through the villages of Pali Brahmanan and Yamuna Mata, also flowed in this direction and ran through the village of Parasauli and according to the Puranas, Krishna performed rasa-lila on the banks of that same Yamuna River at Parasauli. The forest of Parasauli is famous as the site of the Vasanta-lila, or spring-time pastimes, where Krishna and the gopis performed rasa-lila every night during spring; corresponding to the lunar month of Phalguna (February - March). The rasa-lila site at Parasuali is sometimes referred to as Govardhana Rasa-sthali due to its proximity to Govardhana Hill. In the Stavavali it says, “This is Rasa-sthali, where during the month of Vasanta, Shrimati Radharani, who is known as Madhava-priya, danced with Krishna. She was surrounded by beautiful sakhis, each worshiped by hundreds of Lakshmis, and Her neck was decorated by the sweetly fragrant hands of Krishna. Which fortunate person will not take shelter of this exalted Govardhana Rasa-sthali.”

With reference to the Vasanta-lila spring pastimes, in Shri Govinda-Vrindavana (4649) it says, “The Lord showed them the forest called Vrndavana, a forest filled with many trees and Kamadhenu cows, a forest opulent with many beautiful forest groves, a forest served by the pleasures of spring. In that place was a hill named Govardhana, a beautiful hill filled with clear streams, beautiful caves, graceful birds, and many jewels and minerals. In that place was the Yamuna, the best of rivers. Both its banks were studded with jewels. It was filled with many swans and lotus flowers. In that place were many gopis intoxicated by tasting the nectar of many kinds of rasa-dances.”

In the Sri Krishna Bhavanamrita-mahakavya it says, "Sakhi, this Rasathali named Parasauli is where You enjoy the rasa dance every night. Let us rest here for a while on the jeweled platforms." When They did so, Vrindadevi, the keeper of the forest, brought Hari His honey wine. When Shri Radhika looked into the silver cup to see how sweet the honey was, She saw Priyatama's face reflected in it and began to drink the nectar of His face, considering it to be sweeter than the honey.” The name 'Priyatama' means 'most dearly beloved' and is sometimes used by Radharani when talking to Her divine paramour Shri Krishna. It was at Parasuali where rasa-lila was performed on the occasion the Vasanta-purnima, the night of the full-moon in spring, which was transformed by Krishna into a night of Brahma, a very long duration of time covering many millions of years. By Krishna's mystic potency, although it appeared by human calculation that only one night had passed, the gopis felt that it was equal to a night of Brahma, an incredible duration of 4.32 billion solar years.

According to the Sri Krishna Bhavanamrita-mahakavya, the forest where the springtime pastimes took place is located on the eastern side of Govardhana Hill and known by the name 'Vasanta-sukhada' meaning 'giving joy in the spring-time'. The forest at Parasauli where Vasanta-lila took place is also located on the eastern side of Govardhana Hill. A verse from Sri Krishna Bhavanamrita-mahakavya says, “While Krishna heard Radhika's ambrosial words, which are not heard even by the Vedas, He came to the forest named Vasanta-sukhada, where the mango trees are dripping from top to root with drops of honey that makes the earth very happy. Krishna said, “O, Radha! Here, Cupid is the King. The sweet spring is his minister and the Malaya breeze is his invincible general. The bees are his spies and the flocks of cuckoos are his chastisers. The uncooperative Vraja-gopis are punishable and the mountain caves are the prisons.”

It is said that the rasa-lila performed on the occasion of Vasanta-purnima at Parasauli, was enacted by Krishna for the special satisfaction of Shrimati Radharani and all the eternally liberated nitya-siddha gopis, who descended along with Krishna in order to take part in the Lord's transcendental pastimes on earth. Included amongst the eternally liberated gopis are the ashta-sakhis, the eight principle girlfriends of Radharani, along with the various groups of their friends and assistants. Also included amongst the nitya-siddha gopis is Chandravali and her close friends and assistants. It is said that during the maha-rasa-lila at Govinda Ghata in Vrindavana, the nitya-siddha gopis were unable to fully exhibit their innermost feelings of love for Krishna, due to the presence of so many new gopis. These new gopis numbering thirty-two individual groups, were either sadhana-siddha or kripa-siddha gopis that were entering Krishna's pastimes for the very first time.

Included amongst these new gopis were the sages of Dandakaranya forest, who had received blessings from Lord Ramachandra that they would be born in their next life as gopis in Vrindavana. Due to a benediction given by Lord Seshashayi Vishnu, the personified Vedas also took birth as gopis. Another group of new gopis were the Apsaras or heavenly dancing girls, who attempted to seduce Nara-Narayana Rishi and after having failed, received the benediction from the Lord that they would be born as gopis in Vrindavana in their next lives and take part in Krishna's conjugal pastimes. Other new gopis included the women of Barhishmati City, who saw Lord Prithu and became overwhelmed with love for Him and were thus blessed by Atri Muni to become gopis in Vrindavana. Then there were the aboriginal girls known as Pulindas, who by seeing Krishna walking in the Vrindavana forest, were overcome with passionate love for Him and lustily smeared the red vermilion fallen from His lotus feet up on their breasts; thus during the rasa-dance they attained the association of Krishna. Others had been the women of Sutalaloka who became gopis by the blessings of Lord Vamanadeva. The Garga Samhita mentions that another group of gopis were the medicinal plants of the earth that became useless and ineffective after the disappearance of Lord Dhanvantari. To regain their powers they transformed themselves into women and performed severe austerities. After four yugas had passed, Lord Hari blessed them that at the end of Dwapara-yuga they would become flowering vines in the forest of Vrindavana and would transform into gopis at the time of the rasa-dance.

Having understood the inner feelings of the nitya-siddha gopis headed by Radharani and Chandravali, Krishna enacted the rasa-lila at Parasauli so that the nitya-siddha gopis could, without feeling any constraint or inhibition, fully manifest their most wanton feelings of amorous love in the full-bloom of parakiya-bhava. The rasa-lila at Parasauli is said to have lasted for a 'night of Brahma', and while witnessing the ecstatic dancing of Krishna and the gopis, the moon became stunned and remained completely stationary in the night sky.

Although the most famous spring-time rasa-lila was performed at Parasauli, the pastimes of Vasanta-rasa were performed in a number of other places around Vraja including Viharavana and Basonti. Rasa-lila pastimes also took place during the different seasons of the year and the famous rasa-lila performed at Seva-kunja in Vrindavana took place during the Sarat season in the lunar month of Ashvin (September to October).

How To Get There: This village is 2km south of Govardhana Town on the road to Sonk (See map no.13 & 14).

## 19 Chandra-Sarovara

According to the Bhakti-ratnakara, the enchanting lake known as Chandra Sarovara is located within the forest of Parasauli which is also known as 'Vasanta-sukhada', meaning 'the forest giving joy in spring-time'. During the vasanta-rasa-lila, after having spent the whole night ecstatically dancing with the gopis, Krishna, while still wearing His special rasa-lila dress, came here to Chandra Sarovara in order to rest on the banks of sacred lake. The gopis also came here and began massaging Krishna's limbs and also fanned Him in order to relieve His fatigue.

It is said that this lake is also very dear to the moon-god Chandra, because at this place he witnessed the Vasanta-rasa-lila pastime between Radha and Krishna. Due to experiencing transcendental ecstasy after witnessing the rasa-dance, the moon-god Chandra became momentarily stunned and while ceasing all external movement remained completely stationary in the night sky. (The astronomical explanation for the moon to remain stationary in the night sky is known as Lunar standstill. Every 18.6 years, the angle between the moon's orbit and earth's equator reaches a maximum of 28°36', the sum of earth's equatorial tilt (23°27') and the moon's orbital inclination (5°09') to the ecliptic. This is called major lunar standstill. Around this time, the Moon's declination will vary from -28°36' to +28°36'). Thus it appears that on that occasion, the Lunar standstill perfectly coincided with the rasa-dance at Parasauli, allowing the moon-god a unique vision of Krishna's transcendental pastimes.

Chandravali, who is sometimes called Chandramukhi, the gopi with the moon-like face, is considered second only to Radharani in attracting Krishna's love and attention, and just like the moon-god, Chandravali also has a very special relationship with this lake. It is said that just as Radha-kunda is very dear to Radharani, so Chandra-sarovara is very dear to Chandravali. This celebrated lake is famous all over Vraja because of the spring-time rasa-lila that took place here. Even Lord Balarama became stunned when He witnessed the extraordinary rasa-lila at Chandra-sarovara as He stood on the top of Govardhana Hill. The place from where Lord Balarama saw the Vasanta-rasa-lila is known as Doka Dauji. The word 'doka' is a corrupted form of the word 'dekna' which means to 'look', or to 'see'.

Chandra-sarovara is the site of many other wonderful pastimes where Krishna and the gopis would regularly meet and engage in singing, dancing, playing sports, as well as drinking the beverage known as varuni, or honey-liquor. The honey drinking pastimes known as madhupan-lila were very popular, not only with Krishna and Balarama, but with the gopis and the cowherd boys as well. The word 'madhu' means 'honey' and 'pan' means to 'drink'.

On the banks of this lake, Krishna often engaged in decorating Radharani by applying mascara and other cosmetics on Radha's moonlike face and decorating Her transcendental limbs with gem-encrusted ornaments and golden jewelry. Krishna would also comb Radha's long black hair into braids and then decorate Her braids with sweet smelling forest flowers. There is a shrine here on the banks at Chandra-sarovara known as the Shringara Mandira that commemorates this particular pastime. The word 'shringara' means 'dressing', or 'decorating with ornaments'. Surrounding this lake are a number of other shrines including the bhajana kutir and samadhi of the blind Vaishnava saint named Sura Dasa, who composed two well-known poetry books: Sura-sagar and Sura-padavali. There is also the baithaka, or sitting place of Vallabha Bhatta and his son Vitthalanath. Raghunatha Dasa Goswami appointed Vitthalanatha as the head priest of Madhavendra Puri's famous Deity named Gopala Raya (Gopala Natha) that was later moved to Nathadwara in Rajasthan and became known as Shri Nathaji. Shriman Vallabha Bhatta met Lord Chaitanya a number of times at Puri and also at Prayag where he had his residence; he later moved to Mathura with his sons and eventually founded the Vallabhacharya sampradaya. Top How To Get There: This place is next to Parasauli Village (See map no.13 & 14).

## 20 Paitha (Petha)

This village achieved its name after the celebrated pastime of Krishna's hiding from the gopis near this village. The places of interest here include: the Chaturbhuja-Narayana Mandir, Narayana-sarovara, Lakshmi Kupa, Aintha-kadamba, Ksira Sagara, and Balabhadra-kunda. The word 'paitha' means 'went into', or 'entered', and refers to Krishna's two extra arms that were manifested at the time He exhibited His Chaturbhuja-Narayana form before the gopis, which later 'entered' into His body when He saw Radharani's intense mood of separation. Once during the rasa-lila at Parasauli, which is not very far from Paitha, Krishna wanted to witness for Himself the pure and unadulterated love of Radha and the intensity of Her mood in separation from Him, referred to as vipralambha-bhava. Therefore, He suddenly disappeared from the arena of the rasa-lila and assuming the four-armed form of Lord Vishnu, hid Himself in a secluded forest grove. In great anxiety Radharani and the gopis started to search for Krishna everywhere. When arriving at the forest grove where Krishna was hiding, the gopis saw the four-armed form of Lord Vishnu, and after paying their obeisances, they moved on in search of Krishna. However, when Radharani came there in search of Him, Krishna could not bear to see Radharani's distraught and pitiable condition while in the mood of acute separation from Him. Krishna was so moved by Radharani's intense feelings that He was unable to maintain His four-armed feature any longer, thus two of His four arms suddenly disappeared and Krishna immediately came forward to surrender Himself before His beloved Radha in order to mitigate Her intense feelings of sorrow. According to the Gaudiya Vaishnava philosophy, this important pastime establishes the supremacy of Radharani over all other gopis including Chandravali, Her main rival in attracting Krishna's love. This is because Radharani alone is the very embodiment of 'maha-bhava-svarupa', and no other gopi possesses this supreme transcendental attribute of divine love. Because Radharani is the epitome of maha-bhava or 'maha-bhava-svarupa', Her own ecstasy of maha-bhava exceeds that of all the other gopis and this unique feature is known as Radha-bhava. Due to this special quality, Radha is able to bring even Krishna under Her control, which is due to Her unparalleled love and complete devotion towards Him.

Another reason for the village to be named Paitha has been mentioned in various scriptures including Gopala-champu. During Krishna's pastime of lifting Govardhana Hill, He came to Paitha where there was a very deep cavern that ran straight below Govardhana Hill. Krishna 'entered' (paitha) the cavern so that He could get underneath Govardhana Hill and easily lift it up in order to give shelter to the residents of Vrindavana from the torrential rain. There were formerly many large caves all over Govardhana Hill, but in course of time, most of these caves have shrunk in size or disappeared altogether, or otherwise closed by the authorities because of the danger of collapse. There are many stories of local people entering these deep caves, which in some cases ran for miles underground, never to be seen again. It is also said that once Krishna had lifted Govardhana Hill, the Vrajavasis also entered under the Hill from this place. The word 'paitha' also means 'entered'. It has been described by Shrila Jiva Goswami that the Vrajavasis took shelter within a large cavernous arena below the mountain once it had been lifted by Krishna.

Before lifting Govardhana Hill, the cowherd boys, who had all assembled at Paitha, were trying to convince Krishna not to attempt such a 'Herculean' feat because His body was so soft and delicate. Therefore, in order to test Krishna's strength and also convince themselves, the cowherd boys asked Him to twist the trunk of a nearby kadamba tree, which He easily accomplished with great ease. Feeling satisfied the cowherd boys agreed to let Krishna lift Govardhana Hill and dressed Him up in a wrestler's costume along with a beautiful silken sash around His waist. The kadamba tree at Paitha that Krishna twisted as a test of His strength became known as the Aintha-kadamba (twisted kadamba). Unfortunately, this particular kadamba tree disappeared some years ago.

How To Get There: This village is 3km east of Parasauli on the road that goes to Sonk (See map no.14).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 9

Including: \*Sabala\*Ratu\*Vatsagrama\*Sonk.

## 40 Sabala (Sabla)

At this place Krishna and the cowherd boys used to bring their cows for grazing on the fresh grass that grew here. There were also many aromatic wild flowers here, which gave great pleasure to Krishna and His friends.

How To Get There: This village is 2km south of Petha (See map no.14B).

## 41 Ratu (Nagla Ratanu)

This place is famous due to the erotic pastimes known as rati-krida that took place here between Krishna and the gopis of Vraja. The village is called Ratu or sometimes Ratanu and is derived from the word 'rati', which means 'transcendental lust'.

How To Get There: This place is 2km south of Sabla (See map no.14B).

## 42 Vatsavana (Bachgaon)

This is one of the places where Krishna and Balarama and Their cowherd boyfriends would bring their calves for grazing. One day the cowherd boys headed by Shridama and Madhumangala informed Krishna that they were feeling extremely hungry and requested Krishna to arrange something nice to eat. Krishna, the Supreme Mystic, who is also known as Yogeshvara the master of all yogis, sat beneath a kadamba tree and began to play on His flute. Suddenly pots containing all kinds of tasty preparations started to appear in front of Him. There were pots containing: sweet rice, fresh cream, yogurt, butter, lassi, paya, rabari, burfi, laddus, and many other delectable items, the cowherd boys therefore enjoyed a wonderful picnic in this forest. There are a number of kundas at this place celebrating Krishna's pastimes including: Rabari-kunda, Vimala-kunda, Adavara-kunda, Rama-kunda, Sankara-kunda, Jnana-kunda, Sahasra-kunda and Kanaka-kunda (Kanaka Sagara). It is said that anyone who bathes in any of these kundas will be freed from all the sins of his previous lives. There are also two temples known as Vatsa-bihari Mandira and Makhana-chora Mandira.

It has been said that Nanda Maharaja used to keep his grown-up calves here. These calves no longer suckled milk and were kept separated from their mothers. The words 'vatsa' as well as 'bachhra' means a 'calf' and 'vana' means forest. Therefore the name 'Vatsavana' can mean 'the forest of the calves', or 'the forest where calves enjoy grazing'. Although this particular Vatsavana is different from the one near the village of Sei where Brahma stole the calves and cowherd boys, they are both connected to the same pastime. During the year that the calves and cowherd boys had gone missing, (having been stolen by Brahma), Krishna, unknown to anyone, had expanded Himself to become all the calves as well as the cowherd boys. One day, when Krishna and Balarama were grazing Their calves near Vatsavana, the elderly cowherd men were grazing their cows on top of Govardhana Hill. As soon as the cows on top of Gavardhana Hill noticed their calves in the valley below, mooing loudly they started running down the hill towards them, much to the chagrin of the herdsmen. On reaching their calves they started to lovingly lick their bodies while exhibiting uncommon affection towards them. When the herdsmen arrived there and suddenly saw all their young cowherd sons, they forgot their chagrin and also became overcome by affection and began to lovingly embrace their sons.

Observing the whole scene along with Krishna, Balarama was completely struck with wonder at the ecstatic reunion going on between the cows and their calves, and between the cowherd men and their sons. Balarama began to reflect on what He had seen and concluded that such an exalted level of ecstatic love and affection, shown by both the cowherd men and the cows, could only be shown towards Krishna and no one else, and therefore He concluded that all the calves and the cowherd boys must be direct expansions of Krishna. Once Balarama had solved the puzzle, Krishna explained to Him all the facts regarding Brahma stealing the calves and cowherd boys, because on that day Balarama did not go to the pasturing grounds as it was His birthday. Because the pastime concerning the calves and their mothers occurred here, this is another reason why this forest is celebrated as Vatsavana.

How To Get There: This place is 2km south of Nagla Ratanu and 2km west of Sonkh (See map no.14B & 14C).

## 43 Saunkh (Sonkh)

The name Saunkh is derived from the word 'chaunke', sometimes pronounced as 'chownk' or 'chaunce', which refers to the frying of spices in ghee for the purpose of flavoring vegetables and other preparations. One day, Radharani and the gopis were searching for Krishna in the forest near here. Noticing all the many varieties of wild vegetables that were growing within the forest in such great abundance, the gopis suggested to Radharani that they should cook all these wonderful forest vegetables and Krishna would surely come there to enjoy the feast. Radharani responded by saying that they had no pots, no utensils, no ghee, no spices, and no water, so how could they possibly cook anything!

Suddenly, the gopis noticed all the things they needed lying here and there in the forest. The gopis then started to cook varieties of forest vegetables and wild roots, and many kinds of wild spinach. Radharani then prepared a most wonderful chaunkh and the aroma of the fried spices spread throughout the forest. Meanwhile, Krishna informed His friend Madhumangala that the gopis must have started cooking for them somewhere in the forest. Taking Madhumangala with Him, Krishna followed the aroma of the chaunkh until He finally found the place where the gopis were cooking. Krishna and Madhumangala then sat down to enjoy the most wonderful feast prepared by the gopis.

How To Get There: Sonkh is 6km south of Petha (See map no.14B).

## 44 Suryapatanvana (Khera)

The name Khera is derived from the Sanskrit word khora which means 'cows hoofprint' and indicates that it was the place where the cows and calves were herded together in the late afternoon by Krishna and the cowherd boys before they returned to the goshala. The village is also known as Khera Bramanan because it is a village where primarily brahmanas are residing. It is said that Suryadeva the sun-god descended to earth and worshiped Lord Krishna at this place and thus the ancient name of the village was Suryapatnavana, which means 'the forest where Surya descended'. The temple of Surya is located about two miles (3km) to the west of the village where one can also see a small kunda known as Surya-tala. One can also see within Khera village: Gopala-kunda and Gwala-kunda, the Gopala Mandira and Bihariji Mandira.

How To Get There: Khera is 2km south of Sanwain (See map no.14B).

## 45 Samai (Sanwain)

This is the place where Krishna dressed up as one of the gopis named Shyama-sakhi and this is how the village got the name Samai, which is derived from the word sanvari meaning one with a blackish complexion, or in other words Shyama-sakhi, the sakhi with the dark (shyama) complexion. One day due to some lovers tiff, Shrimati Radharani, being extremely angry with Krishna, came here in a sullen mood and sat beneath a forest bower to lament. Feeling unhappy at seeing His beloved Radha in such an anguished condition, Krishna devised a means to relieve Radharani of Her 'mana'. Expertly disguising Himself as one of Radha's confidential advisers in matters of love, named Shyama-sakhi, Krishna came before Radharani and began to pacify Her by speaking sweet words of encouragement while heaping praises on Krishna by saying He was a great hero and a devoted lover and was unable to live for a moment without His beloved Radharani. Within a short time, the imitation Shyama-sakhi was able to completely dispel Radharani's 'mana' and had also cleverly made arrangements for Radharani to meet Her pining lover Krishna in a nearby forest grove.

How To Get There: This village is 2km south of Shyamadhak (See map no.14B).

End of excursion (Rejoin Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 21 Shyama Dhaka (Shyamadhak)

This secluded forest of ancient palasa trees is famous as one of the sites where Krishna and the gopis performed the pastime of 'rasa-lila'. The name Shyama Dhaka means the holy place (dhaka) where the trees are imbued with a bluish-black hue (shyama). Nearby is a kadamba-kandi when Krishna and the cowherd boys play various games, they would also use the leaves of kadamba trees as cups for drinking buttermilk during their forest picnics. The places of interest here include: Gopatala-kunda where the cowherd boys would sit to take their lunch, Gopa Sagara where the cowherd boys used to swim, Rasa-sthali where the rasa-lila took place and Vitthalanatha-baithaka, the sitting place of Vitthalanatha, who was appointed by Raghunatha Dasa Goswami as the head pujari of Madhavendra Puri's Gopala Deity. The main temple here is known as the Shyamakunda Mandira which stands in front of the lake known as Shyama-kunda.

How To Get There: This place is 1.5km from Punchari village (See map no.14, 14B, 14C & 15).

## 22 Gulala-Kunda

The word 'gulala' refers to the powdery 'bright-red pigment' used in religious ceremonies all over India. Once, on the occasion of the annual Holi-mela also known as the 'festival of colors', after having thrown red colored gulala powder on each other, Radha and Krishna came to this kunda near Ganthuli village to bathe. After They had bathed and sported in the kunda for some time, the water of the kunda turned 'gulali' or a reddish color, due to the red gulala powder that had been thrown on the 'divine lovers' during the holi festivities. Top How To Get There: This kunda is 1km from Jetipur on the road that goes to Gantoli village (See map no.14A &15).

## 23 Ganthuli (Gantholi)

The name of this village has been derived from the word 'gantha' which means 'knot' and refers to this being the place where the 'knot' was tied. One day, Radha and Krishna accompanied by the gopis, came here to play holi, by throwing red colored powder (gulala) on each other. During the course of the festivities, Radha and Krishna sat down together on a nicely decorated throne prepared by the gopis. While Radha and Krishna were engaged in talking together, Lalita-sakhi, Radha's close friend, sneaked up behind the throne and secretly tied the corner of Radha's saree to Krishna's dhoti. This tying together of a girl's saree and a boy's dhoti is always done at the time of a marriage ceremony, signifying the union of oneness between husband and wife. When the holi festivities came to an end and it was time for Radha and Krishna to take Their bath at Gulala-kunda, when They stood up, to their surprise they found that Their clothes were tied together. At that moment, all the gopis suddenly started laughing and clapping their hands in great happiness at seeing the 'divine couple' tied together, as if They had just been married. Top

How To Get There: The village of Gantholi is situated 300mt from Gulala-kunda and 1.5km north of Jetipur, and 3km west Govardhana Town (See map no.14 & 15).

## Lord Chaitanya Visits Ganthuli Grama

While on His parikrama around Vraja Mandala, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu arrived at Govardhana Hill, but refused to climb the sacred hill to visit the Gopala Temple situated on hilltop. This was because according to Lord Chaitanya's spiritual vision, Govardhana Hill was non-different from Lord Krishna Himself, and therefore He refused to place His feet on the hill. Even though the Vedic scriptures confirm that Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was an incarnation of Lord Krishna, He appeared in the form of an ordinary human being and behaved just like any other humble Vaishnava devotee of Lord Krishna. During His life-time, Lord Chaitanya strictly observed all the rules and regulations of sadhana-bhakti and set the highest standards of devotional behavior for all future generations of devotees to follow. Even to this day, the followers of Lord Chaitanya who are known as Gaudiya Vaishnavas, do not step on Govardhana Hill, remembering Lord Chaitanya's own example.

While performing parikrama of Govardhana Hill, Lord Chaitanya had darshana of Lord Harideva where He danced in ecstasy for hours. After leaving the temple of Harideva, He began to think about Lord Gopala, the Deity discovered by Shrila Madhavendra Puri, the celebrated guru of His own guru, Shrila Ishvara Puri. Lord Chaitanya began lamenting that because the temple of Lord Gopala was on top of Govardhana Hill, He would never be able to have darshana of the Deity, as He had decided not to set His foot on the sacred hill. The next day, continuing with His parikrama, Lord Chaitanya arrived at Govinda-kunda where He took His bath. At that moment, news arrived that the Deity of Lord Gopala had been moved to the village of Ganthuli Grama for safety; because a rumor had spread that there was going to be an imminent attack by a rampaging horde of Mohammedan soldiers out on a looting spree. Upon hearing this incredible news, Lord Chaitanya felt great ecstasy and immediately left for Ganthuli Grama to have darshana of Lord Gopala. After arriving at Ganthuli and seeing the extraordinary beauty of Lord Gopala, Lord Chaitanya entered into a state of transcendental bliss and while incessantly chanting the holy names of the Lord, He began dancing in great ecstasy. The Deity of Lord Gopala remained at Ganthuli Grama for three days and Lord Chaitanya also remained there, totally immersed in the mood of ecstatic love.

According to the Chaitanya-charitamrita, the threat of an attack by the Mohammedan soldiers was a transcendental trick performed by Lord Gopala, as a pretext for giving darshana to Lord Chaitanya at Ganthuli. It has also been said by others, that Lord Gopala actually desired to have darshana of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, the incarnation of divine love and the embodiment of ‘Radha-bhava'. This celebrated Deity of Shrila Madhavendra Puri was very famous for His many extraordinary pastimes and there are innumerable stories where the Deity interacted directly with His devotees. A few years after giving darshana to Lord Chaitanya, Lord Gopala made a similar arrangement when He gave darshana to Lord Chaitanya's most senior disciples, Rupa and Sanatana Goswamis at Mathura, where the Deity had been taken for safety on the pretext of another imminent attack by Mohammedan soldiers. Some years later all the Deities of the Gaudiya Goswamis were moved to Rajasthan for safety during the despotic rule of the Mughal tyrant Aurangzeb the Deity of Lord Gopala was moved to Nathadwara under the patronage of the king of Udaipura. The Deity is still residing there even today and is presently known as Lord Shri Nathaji.

The tradition amongst Gaudiya Vaishnavas of not setting foot on Govardhana Hill has been adhered to by all Gaudiya acharyas including the Six Goswamis. It was only on the direct order of Lord Gopala that Shrila Madhavandra Puri stepped on the sacred hill, because Lord Gopala wanted to be installed on the top of Govardhana Hill and asked Madhavendra to install Him there and also build a temple. This means that the pujaris serving the Deity had to climb Govardhana Hill every day to perform the seva-puja. Therefore, a large govardhana-shila was installed at the base of the sacred hill at Jetipura which is known as the dandavata-shila. The pujaris of Lord Gopala would circumambulate this shila seven times while paying dandavata-pranams and it is said that this was equal to performing dandavata-parikrama around the entire Govardhana Hill, by performing this particular ritual the pujaris would free themselves from any aparadha incurred while climbing Govardhana Hill.

End of Chapter Four

## Chapter Five: Raheja to Unchagrama

## 24 Raheja (Bahaj)

The name Raheja is derived from the word 'behaya' which means 'remorse' as well as 'shame'. According to Bhakti-ratnakara, Lord Indra, after realizing how offensive his behavior had been towards the lotus feet of Lord Krishna, and feeling full of remorse and shame, he came to this place accompanied by Surabhi Devi. Lord Indra thoroughly condemned himself for daring to challenge the authority of Lord Shri Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Indra had impudently attempted to devastate the land of Vrindavana by sending torrents of rain which caused flooding and great hardship to all the Vrajavasis. It was Lord Brahma who advised Indra to take help from the Surabhi Devi, the mother-goddess of all cows, by asking her to speak to Krishna on Indra's behalf. This was because Brahma knew that Krishna, as the well-wisher of the cows, would naturally fulfill any request made by mother Surabhi. It is said that Lord Indra dismounted from his elephant carrier at Raheja and as a sign of remorse, walked barefoot all the way to Govardhana Hill. At that time Krishna was walking on Govardhana Hill when Surabhi Devi approached with Indra's humble request for forgiveness. Lord Krishna agreed to Surabhi's plea and Indra immediately came forward and while shedding an ocean of tears, fell down just like a stick before the lotus feet of the Lord. The place where Indra bowed down while asking for forgiveness is known as Indra-pranama-sthali or sometimes as Indra Puja; the torrent of tears shed by Indra formed a small pool which became known as Indra-kunda.

How To Get There: Bahaj is 6km west of Gantholi on the road from Govardhana to Dig (See map no.15).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 10

Including:\*Nagla Moti\*Nagla Khapan\*Devsaras\*Mundsaras.

## 46 MOTI (Nagla Moti)

At this place it is said that Shri Krishna threaded a string of fine quality pearls into a necklace and hung it around the neck of His beloved Radharani. The word 'moti' means 'pearl' and 'nagala' means a 'hamlet' (small village).

How To Get There: This hamlet is 3km north-west of Bahaji (See map no.15 &15A).

## 47 Khabara (Nagla Khapan)

It is said that the name of this village is derived from the word 'khabara' which means 'news' or 'information' and refers to Krishna receiving 'news' from one of His messengers. Krishna had just presented the wonderful gift of a pearl necklace to His beloved Radharani when a message arrived and Krishna suddenly left that place. Wondering why Krishna had left so suddenly, Radharani enquired from Her girlfriends as to where Krishna had gone after receiving the message (khabara).

How To Get There: This place is just 600mt north of Nagla Moti (See map no.15A).

## 48 Devasirsha Sthana (Devsaras/Devseras)

The word 'sirsha' means 'foremost' and refers to all the prominent demigods in the universe. According to the Bhakti-ratnakara, there is a very beautiful lake here known as Devasirsha-sthana-kunda, where the foremost amongst the demigods assembled to offer their prayers in glorification of Lord Shri Krishna, “Another very potent pastime place named Devasirsha-sthana-kunda is beautifully situated here. The devatas joyfully offered their prayers to Lord Krishna here as He herded the cows with His friends.”

How To Get There: This place is 4km north of Gantholi (See map no.15A).

## 49 Malapura (Malipur)

The word 'mala' pronounced as 'mal' refers to any kind of 'goods' including 'provisions' as well as 'food'. The village has derived its name from a pastime where Krishna had to produce some 'mala' for His friends to dissipate their hunger. Krishna used to come here with His cowherd boyfriends to graze the cows in the surrounding forests. One day, knowing that His friends must be hungry, Krishna suddenly exclaimed that He could accomplish any wonderful thing He wanted at any time He pleased. Hearing Krishna's words, the cowherd boys decided to test Krishna's ability. Because the cowherd boy's favorite pastime was enjoying picnics in the forest, they informed Krishna that in order to prove His statement, He would have to produce all kinds delicious mala so that they could enjoy a wonderful feast in the forest. The cowherd boys also stipulated that after they had eaten, all the mala should remain as if nothing had been eaten; then only it could be considered a truly wonderful thing.

Krishna is the master of all mystic powers and known as Yogeshvara, the Lord of all yogis and mystics. From His mind only, the whole universe with its innumerable stars and planets and myriad number of living beings has been created, therefore, to create a wonderful feast in the middle of the forest was not a very difficult thing to do. Therefore, by Krishna's mystic potency, large quantities of food preparations (mala) in earthen pots suddenly appeared in front of the cowherd boys. There was a wonderful variety of preparations including: laddus, milk cakes, milk sweets, sweet-rice, condensed milk (kshira), rabari, gulabjamuns, halva, malpuras, yogurt, cream and butter. There were so many varieties of mala that no cowherd boy could count them all. The cowherd boys wasted no time in relishing all the mala while glorifying Krishna for such an incredible display of mystical power. After everyone had eaten to their full capacity, the cowherd boys were astonished to see that the pots still remained full.

How To Get There: This village is 2.5km west of Devsaras (See map no.15A).

## 50 Munisirsha Sthana (Mundsaras/Mundseras/Mudseras)

The word 'muni' refers to a 'self-realized soul' and 'sirsha' means the 'foremost' or 'topmost'. In other words, the foremost amongst the self-realized munis' assembled here on the banks of the Munisirsha-sthana-kunda. These munis had achieved perfection by performing austerities while remembering the pastimes of Lord Shri Krishna. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, "See here the most pleasant Munisirsha-sthana-kunda where the munis achieved Krishna by performing austerities. At these sites Krishna and Balarama performed various pastimes with Their friends as They tended their cows.”

How To Get There: This place is 8km north of Malipur via Iklahra (See map no.15A).

End of excursion (Rejoin Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 25 Dirghapura (Dig/Deeg)

Dirghapura gains mention in the Skanda Purana with regard to Nanda Maharaja's journey from Gokula to Nandagrama. After leaving Gokula, Nanda Maharaja first stayed at Shakatikara (Chhatikara). From Shakatikara, Nanda Maharaja moved to Dirghapura where he stayed for some time before moving to Kamyavana and then finally to Nandagrama, where he built his permanent residence. Besides Dig, the name of this town is sometimes spelled as Diga or as Deeg. However, the word ‘dig' means 'direction' as in ‘digpal' (dikpal) meaning 'guardian of the directions' in reference to Lord Shiva as the protector of the holy dhama. Some scholars say that the name of this town is derived from the word ‘diga' or 'dirgha' which means ‘to slacken' or 'loosen' like the reigns of a horse-drawn chariot when riding. The word 'dirgha' can also refer Krishna, who could slacken the strict moral principles kept by Radharani and the gopis, simply by His charm, His incredible beauty, or by the sound of His transcendental flute.

Local historians have said that in the Treta-yuga, when Lord Rama's brother Shatrughna established His kingdom at Mathura, His brother Lakshmana established his kingdom here at Dirghapura. There is a very ancient temple in the town dedicated to Lakshmana, who it is said was the family Deity of the local Jat kings. Historians also say that Rama's other brother Bharata established His kingdom at nearby Bharatapura. In more recent history, Dig was the capital of the great Jat kingdom founded in 1722 CE and was at one time ruled over by one of the most famous Jat kings, Suraj Mal. This kingdom encompassed the same area as the ancient kingdom of Matsya, which now forms part of the modern-day Bharatpur District. During the British rule, the great fort at Dig became a bastion and stronghold of the Jat forces and was the scene of many a fierce battle. Dig Fort could not be captured by the British due to its strength and impregnability, which withstood the fire-power of a large battery of British cannons.

There is a story that a former king of Dig was most unhappy because the Vraja Mandala Parikrama did not visit his city as it was not one of the tirtha-sthanas, but instead took another route to Adi-Badrinatha via Devashirsha, Munishirsha, and Paramadana. Therefore the king pleaded that as Dig fell within Vraja Mandala, the parikrama should also visit his town. The king jokingly said that if the devotees performing parikrama did not come to Dig voluntarily, he would send the local police-force with canes (lathis) and forcibly bring the parikrama devotees to Dig. Due to seeing the great desire of the king to host the devotees and have the Vraja Mandala Parikrama visit Dig, the parikrama route was changed and the devotees started coming to Dig and spending the night at the hospitality of the king. From that time on, the Vraja Mandala Parikrama began to visit Dig. It is said that to please the king, one devotee jokingly gave Dig the name of Lathavana, or the 'forest of canes', with regard to the king threatening to send his police with lathis to coerce the Vraja-yatris

The town of Dig is sometimes pronounced as Deeg and it has become a popular destination with foreign tourists who visit the famous Dig Fort and the exquisite Monsoon Palace (also known as Gopala Bhavan), with its unique water-gardens containing over five hundred fountains. There is also a large lake at Dig which is known as Rupasagar where the famous lakeside Jal Mahal palace is located.

How To Get There: Dig is 14km west of Govardhana Town and 3km west of Bahaj (See map no.15A).

## 26 Didavali

This is said to be the village where Krishna's paternal grandmother lived. Her name was Variyasi Devi, and she was the wife of Parjanya Maharaja, the father of Nanda Maharaja.

The word ‘didima', means 'grandmother', and the name of the village is derived from the word ‘didavali', or the ‘grandmother's place'. In the village one can see Didavali-kunda and a temple dedicated to Lord Narasinghadeva.

How To Get There: This village is 5km north of Dig on the Kaman road (See map no.15A & 16).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 11

Including: \*Paramdara\*Ghaata\*Setu-kandara\* Saugandha-shila\*Pahalwara\*Guhana\*Badri\*.

## 51 Pramodana Grama (Paramdara/Parmadra/Paramadan)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “This is Pramodana-grama where Krishna sportingly gave pleasure \[pramoda\] to the ladies of Vraja. For this reason the village was known as Pramodana, although people now call it Paramadana.” This place is known as Pramodana because it was here that Krishna gave great pleasure to the gopis. The name Pramodana is derived from the Sanskrit word 'pramoda' which means 'pleasure' or 'delight'. One day the gopis were searching the forest for Krishna but they were not able to find Him anywhere. Eventually they came to this place and suddenly feeling such intense separation from Krishna, they began to weep uncontrollably. Out of utter despair at not seeing Krishna, some of the gopis began embracing the dark-blue colored tamala trees because those trees reminded them of Krishna's own bodily complexion. Some of the gopis simply fainted on the ground and remained lying there motionless as if dead. All of a sudden Krishna arrived at that place and the gopis were immediately revived by His transcendental presence. The gopis became filled with delight and experienced the greatest pleasure at seeing their beloved Krishna once again. On another occasion, the gopis came to this place to get water from the kunda. On seeing the darkish color of the water, they immediately thought of their beloved Shyamasundara and thus swooned and fell to the ground. Krishna very quickly came there and revived the gopis by lovingly embracing each gopi and thus fulfilled their innermost desires. In the village one can see two ancient kundas known as Krishna-kunda and Charana-kunda. The word 'charana' means Krishna's lotus feet.

How To Get There: This place is 4km north of Didavali on the road to Kaman (See map no.16).

## 52 Ghata (Ghaat)

One day Krishna was herding His cows at this place along with the cowherd boys when He suddenly began remembering all the wonderful pastimes He had enjoyed with His beloved Radharani. Because of this, Krishna gradually became so overwhelmed with loving emotions as He thought of Radharani, that He was forced to sit down and simply remained there almost motionless. The word ‘ghata' has a number of meanings one of which is to 'think deeply', or to be 'overwhelmed by thoughts'. Thus the village received the name of Ghata because at this place Krishna was completely overwhelmed by thoughts of His beloved Radharani.

How To Get There: This place is 5km north of Parmadra (See map no.16).

## 53 Setu-Kandara (Jadkora Dhama)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, "This is Setukandara, a most enchanting place.” Krishna used to come here to graze His cows in this area. Setu-kandara is situated between two mountains and famous for its scenic beauty. This most isolated and picturesque place is also known as Sue or Seu-kandara and the name implies 'a place located near a mountain' or 'a ridge that divides the flatlands'. The word 'kandara' can also mean 'a mountain of loose rocks' or 'a rock-strewn mountain ridge'. This holy place is also known locally as Jadkhora Dhama and it is a place where yogis and ascetics are engaged in sadhana. All the mountains in this area are part of the Adi-Badri Hills, which stretch from here southwards to Alipura Village and the holy shrine of Adi-Badrinatha. The mountains in the western part of Vraja including Govardhana Hill belong to what is known as the Bharatpura range of the Aravali Mountains which start just south of New Delhi and continue southward through the states of Haryana and Rajasthana as far as Mount Abu on the border of Gujarat.

How To Get There: This place is 3.5km south-west of Ghaat (See map no.16).

## 53a Saugandha-Shila

Located at Setu-kandara is the famous saugandha-shila where Lord Krishna once took a vow in front of the gopis that He would never ever leave Vrindavana. The Vrajabasha/Hindi word ‘saugandha' means 'vow'. (The word saugandha should not be confused with the word 'sugandha' which means 'fragrance'). The fact that Krishna never left Vrindavana has been confirmed by Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and in the Chaitanya-charitamrita it is mentioned that Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu told Rupa Goswami, “The Krishna known as Yadukumara is Vasudeva Krishna. He is different from the Krishna who is the son of Nanda Maharaja. Yadukumara Krishna manifests his pastimes in the cities of Mathura and Dwaraka, but Krishna, the son of Nanda Maharaja never leaves Vrindavana.” In the Brihad-gautamiya-tantra, Lord Krishna tells Narada Muni, "The five yojanas of Vrindavana forest are like My body and the spinal cord of the body is the Kalindi River, which flows with nectarine water. Deities and other spirits live here in invisible bodies. And I, living within every being, never leave this place.” This fact has been confirmed by Uddhava and others. This aspect of Krishna remaining present in Vrindavana but unseen is called His aprakata-lila, or un-manifested pastimes, whereas the prakata-lila is the manifested or visible pastimes.

How To Get There: This place is located at Setu-kandara (Jadkhor Dhama) (See map no.16).

## 54 Pahelabada (Pahalwara/Pahalavada)

This is where Krishna and the cowherd boys held a wrestling match. The challenge was that Krishna would have to single-handedly fight with all the boys together at the same time, and then He could genuinely claim the grand title of the 'pelawan', which means the 'strongman'. Therefore, the cowherd boys began circling around Krishna looking for the opportunity to jump on top of Him. As they were hesitatingly circling around Krishna, one boy said to another boy. "Oh Brother, you go first”. Then that boy replied. “Nehi bhaiya, tum pehle jao, hum bada me ayenge”, which means, "No brother, you go first - I will go later". Thus this village became known as 'Pahelabada' after the words 'tum pehle jao, hum bada me ayenge'. How To Get There: This place is 2km south of Setu-kandara (Jadkhor Dhama) (See map no.16).

## 55 Guhana (Guhana/Gohana)

This is the village where Krishna's dear friend Sudama was born. When Krishna came here while herding His cows, He met with Sudama and they became very close friends. It appears that the name of this village is derived from 'godrstavana', which means 'the forest where cows gather' and this is one of the places where Krishna would call all His cows together and count them before returning to Nandagrama in the evening.  Top

How To Get There: This place is 2km east of Pahalwara & 1.5km west of Parmadra (See map no.16).

## 56 Budhe-Badri (Badri)

The word ‘budhe' means 'old' as well as 'original' and therefore the name 'Budhebadri' means 'Old Badri', or 'original Badri'. This place is accepted by a number of Gaudiya scholars to be the original Badrinatha where Krishna brought His father Nanda Baba for darshana. This is further confirmed in the Bhakti-ratnakara when, after visiting Pramodana, Raghava Pandita led Shrinivasa Acharya and Narottama Dasa northwards to this place while informing them that this was Adi-Badri, the ancient shrine of Lord Badri-Narayana and the place where Krishna brought His father Nanda Maharaja to have darshana of Badrinatha Dhama. There is an old temple here of Lord Budhe-Badrinatha containing the Deity of Badri-Narayana and nearby is Alakananda-kunda. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “See here the most merciful Adi Badri-Narayana. He is served in a most unique way by fragrant stones on this enchanting mountain within the forest. Krishna removed the lamentation of Nanda Maharaja and the other cowherd men by bringing them here for darshana of Narayana.”

It is interesting to note that Raghava Pandita and his companions did not go to Adi-Badrinatha near Alipura, neither did they visit Kedarnatha, but went directly from Pramoda to Budhe-Badri and then after visiting Kadamba-khandi, they went to Kamyavana via Ghat and Indroli. Some researchers have concluded that the route taken by Raghava Pandita Goswami in this part of Vraja must be the same route taken by Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, as they were more or less attempting to retrace Mahaprabhu's footsteps. The shrine of Adi-Badrinatha near Alipur was discovered by Narayana Bhatta who also discovered the Adi-Kedaranatha shrine. Top How To Get There: This place is 1km north of Guhana (See map no.16).

## Lord Krishna Visits Badrinatha with Nanda Maharaja

One day Nanda Maharaja, Krishna's father, had a great desire to go on pilgrimage and take darshana of Badrinatha Dhama in the Himalayas. According to the Vedic custom, the four Vaikuntha Dhamas in India (Bharata-varsha) should be visited by all religious people at least once before they die. These four dhamas are: Badrinatha, Dwaraka, Jagannatha Puri, and Rameshwaram, and they represent the planets of Lord Vishnu in the spiritual world. The dhama of Vrindavana represents the Lord's supreme abode on the planet called Goloka-Vrindavana which is far beyond the realm of Vaikuntha.

However, Krishna did not like the idea that His father should leave Vrindavana Dhama and therefore asked him why he should take so much trouble to go all the way to the Himalayan Mountains, when the very same Badrinatha Dhama was present in Vraja. Krishna then brought Nanda Baba and all the Vrajavasis to this place and declared its glories before them, saying that this was the original Badrinatha and thousands of times more spiritually potent than the Badrinatha in the Himalayas. When Nanda Maharaja wanted to leave Vrindavana to bathe in the River Ganges, Krishna objected and instead took his father to Manasi Ganga at Govardhana. Krishna was conveying the message that one should never leave Vrindavana, because Vrindavana itself is the greatest of all the holy places within the material universe, and every other holy place in the universe has its original form in Vrindavana. Some of the original holy places found in this part of Vraja include: Kedarnatha, Gaya, Pushkara, Dwaraka, Varanasi (Kashi), Prayag (Allahabad) and Rameshwaram, which are all located near Kamyavana.

## 57 Maharaniya (Nagla Maharniyan)

The name of this village is derived from the word 'maharani', which means 'queen'. One day the gopis assembled here and decided to dress Radharani up as a queen, or maharani. They sat Her down on a very nicely decorated throne and began adorning Her with many kinds of beautiful and aromatic forest flowers. They then declared Radha to be their beloved maharani and started playing various musical instruments while dancing in a circle around Her. Some gopis also sang songs in praise of Radharani, glorifying Her as the Queen of Vrindavana forest. Because of this pastime the village became known as Maharaniya.

How To Get There: This place is 1.5km south of Guhana (See map no.16).

End of excursion (Rejoin Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 27 Khonha (Khoh)

At this place it is said that Radha and Her girlfriends used to play one of their favorite games called 'kho'. When Radharani saw the sakhis and manjaris playing the game of kho, which is a game especially for girls, it gave Her great pleasure. The village of Khoh derives its name from the gopi's pastime of playing the game of kho at this place.

How To Get There: This place is 2.5km west of Nagla Mahaniyan (See map no.16).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 12

Including; \*Kalyanpura.

## 58 Kalyanpura (Kalyanpur)

One day Krishna and Balarama were herding Their cows at this place. In order to have some fun, the cowherd boys began to play various games. In one of the games the cowherd boys began paying their prostrated obeisances before Krishna and Balarama as if they were great saintly sages. Krishna and Balarama in turn began giving their blessings to each of the cowherd boys by saying, “Kalyana ho! Kalyana ho!" meaning 'may you be blessed with auspiciousness', just as the great saintly sages do. Therefore this village became known as Kalyanpura.

How To Get There: This place is 1.5 km north of Khoh (See map no.16).

End of excursion (Rejoin Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

NOTE: The Vraja Mandala Parikrama path from Khoh to Shanara Shikara and beyond is usually impassible for motor vehicles and this journey must be made on foot. For those travelling in vehicles, after visiting Shanara Shikhara on foot, return to Khoh and take the main road to Alipur and Adi-Badrinatha via Bhadari, Kayareeka & turn left at the Pausopa road junction.

## 28 Shanara Shikhara (Kadamba-khandi)

The village takes its name from the mountain named Shanara Shikhara. The word 'shikhara' in this regard means 'pinnacle' or 'crest'. This mountain is also known as Dhavala Parvata because of its light creamy-colored rocks. The word 'dhavala' refers to a 'white' or an 'off-white' color. Another name for this mountain is Navanita Parvata, because it appears to be the color of butter (navanita). At Shanara Shikara there is a famous kadamba forest that is called Kadamba-khandi or Kadamba-kanana. This is the place where Radha and Krishna enjoyed many of Their pastimes during the month of Sravana, like the swing pastimes known as jhulana-lila.

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “See ahead the sacred Kadamba-kanana where Radha-Krishna happily enjoyed Their many different pastimes with the sakhis. During the month of Shravana They enjoyed Their swing pastimes here.”

Other mountains located here including the Nila Parvata and there is a pass (ghati) through this mountain known as Anandadri. From Sinara Shikhara, the parikrama path goes to Karmooka village and then to Adi-Badrinatha via Alipur through isolated mountain passes.

How To Get There: This place is 750mt south-west of Khonha (See map no.16 & 16A).

## 29a Adibadri Grama (Alipura)

This village was formerly known as Adibadri Grama, but during the Mughal rule it was changed to Alipura. This is the place where the Himalayas of Vraja referred to as the Adi-Badri mountain range, begin to rise and these mountains also mark the gateway to Adi-Badrinatha, which lies just one kilometer to the south.

How To Get There: This village is 4km west of Shanara Sikhara & 6km from Khoh by road via Bharadi & Kayreeka (See map no.16 & 17).

## 29 Adi-Badrinatha (Badrikashrama)

This is one of the more isolated and wildly beautiful parts of Vraja, being surrounded with tree lined hills and dense forests. It is also the haunt of hundreds of peacocks and a variety of exotic birds, as well as many species of wild animals. Nestled in the heart of this exotic landscape is the famous shrine of Adi-Badrinatha, dedicated to Lord Nara and Narayana Rishi, the twin incarnations of Lord Vishnu. It is said that this holy tirtha was discovered by Shrila Narayana Bhatta. The incarnation of Lord Nara Narayana Rishi is the predominating Deity of Bharata-varsa (India) and worshiped specifically by Narada Muni at Badrikashrama in the Himalayas. It is stated by Lord Garbodakshayi-Vishnu in the tenth-canto of Shrimad-Bhagavatam, that Krishna and Arjuna are both incarnations of Nara-Narayana Rishi. This refers to the two-armed Narayana feature when the Lord is present at places outside Vrindavana like: Mathura, Dwaraka, Hastinapura and the battlefield of Kurukshetra, or whenever He is engaged in pastimes with Arjuna. Whenever Krishna kills the demons that enter Vrindavana, He does so in His Narayana feature (Vishnu) and not in His original form as Krishna the cowherd boy. This two-armed Narayana form is also known as Vasudeva-Krishna, Yadukumara and Dwarakadisha.

The word 'adi' means 'first' or 'original' and Adi-Badrinatha in Vraja is considered to be the original Badrinatha, with Badrinatha (Badrikashrama) located in the Himalayas as its expansion. This is because Vrindavana Dhama and all its holy places are part of the eternal spiritual sky and therefore not created at any time, unlike the temporary material world, which is created at a particular time. All the incarnations of Godhead have descended from the spiritual world and when They descend, They bring with Them their own original abodes or dhamas. Therefore, all incarnations and holy dhamas have their origins in the spiritual world. And just as Lord Shri Krishna has His eternal abode in Goloka Vrindavana, Lord Nara-Narayana is eternally residing at Badrinatha Dhama that is situated in one of the Vaikuntha planets.

On the simhasana in the Adi-Badri shrine one can be see the Deity of Lord Nara in His 'chatur-bhuja' form with four arms holding the four symbols of Vishnu that includes a lotus, chakra, conch, and club. Next is the Deity of Lord Narayana, who is sitting in the yoga-asana, or the meditation pose. Next is Shriman Uddhava, Krishna's dear friend who after Krishna's departure from the world, went to the Himalayas to take refuge of Nara-Narayana Rishi at Badrikashrama. Other Deities that can be seen here include Shrila Narada Muni, the 'rishi amongst the demigods', who, during the winter season when it snows in the Himalayas and humans cannot stay there, assumes the position of the temple pujari to perform the seva-puja of Lord Nara-Narayana. Next is Kuvera the treasurer of the demigods, whose ancient kingdom on earth was situated in the Himalayas north of Badrinatha, and who also performs the duties of a pujari during winter. In the same temple are Deities of Shri Shri Radha Krishna and also Lord Shri Nathji holding Govardhana Hill. There is also a Deity of Annapurna Devi, the mountain-goddess who has a range of mountains in the Himalayas named after Her.

Situated in the compound of the shrine can be found the Tapta-kunda, the water of which is stone-cold the whole year round and bathing there is always a great tapasya. The word 'tapta' or 'tapa' is derived from the word 'tapasya' which means 'austerity'. Paradoxically, the kundas at Badrinatha in the Himalayas are boiling-hot due to underground sulphur springs, and bathing there is another type of tapasya. The water of these sulphur kundas is so hot that sadhus often cook food like rice, chapatti doe and vegetables, within the kunda by wrapping the items in cloth and then lowering it into the steaming hot water.

It is mentioned in the Shrimad-Bhagavatam, that after His appearance on earth, Lord Nara-Narayana Rishi went to meditate and perform tapasya on the Gandhamadana Mountain, which is sometimes called the Nara-Narayana Parvata. The word 'parvata' also means mountain. That same Gandhamadana Mountain is also present here at Adi-Badrinatha, along with all the other important holy places found in the Himalayan ranges in Northern India, including: Trikut Parvata, Nishada Parvata and Keshava Parvata, the holy rivers Alakananda (Ganga), Yamuna, and Saraswati, the holy places Haridwara and Har-ki-pauri, Rishikesh, Lakshmana-jhula and Tapovana, are all to be found here. There is also the famous Triveni Sangama and Dashashmavedha Ghata. Adi-Badri is also mentioned to be one of the upavanas or sub-forests of Vraja.

How To Get There:: Adi-Badrinatha is 1.5km south of Alipur, 15km from Dig, and 50km from Vrndavana (See map no.16-16A ,16B & 17)

## The Apsaras Tempt Nara-Narayana Rishi

Isolated high in the Himalayas is the abode of Nara-Narayana Rishi known as Badrinatha Dhama, where Lord Nara-Narayana Rishi, who is a strict niashtika-brahmachari, is engaged in severe penance for the benefit of the entire human race. Once, the demigod Indra who is the king of heaven became extremely envious of the extraordinary tapasya being undertaken by Nara-Narayana Rishi. King Indra was thinking that Nara-Narayana Rishi was some ordinary yogi undergoing austerity to achieve the heavenly planets. Indra always feared that some very pious man or powerful yogi, after performing severe tapasya and austerities, might try to usurp his position as the King of heaven and take away his great wealth. Every wealthy man fears losing his money and property and due to anxiety cannot sleep peacefully at night. Similarly, a man with an exalted post in society dreads to lose his high status and engages in all kinds of political intrigue simply to save his position. Indra was no different and therefore plotted the downfall of Nara-Narayana Rishi.

Due to the fear of losing his position, Indra the King of heaven, sent many beautiful dancing girls known as Apsaras to seduce Nara-Narayana Rishi in the hope of making Him falldown to lusty desires and abandon His severe penance. The dancing girls from heaven arrived scantily clad before Nara-Narayana Rishi and started to perform their highly erotic dance performance. With their ankle bells ringing melodiously and bangles jingling, the Apsaras did their utmost to seduce the great Rishi from his meditation; nevertheless, Nara-Narayana Rishi remained completely absorbed in samadhi. While dancing before the great Rishi, the Apsaras suddenly saw many extremely beautiful girls appearing from the body of Nara-Narayana Rishi, and their exquisite beauty easily defeated the beauty of the heavenly Apsaras. Seeing this powerful display of mysticism, and having failed in their attempts to seduce Nara-Narayana Rishi, the Apsaras immediately left and returned to Indra's abode in the heavenly planets.

This incident proves that the Supreme Lord can never become victimized by mundane lust or be brought under the control of a beautiful woman, because He Himself is the original creator and source of all the beautiful women in the universe and this particular creation forms only a minute aspect of His total creative energy. This episode also helps clarify Krishna's position in regard to the gopis of Vrindavana, who are all expansions of Krishna's own spiritual body for the purpose of His transcendental enjoyment of prema-rasa, or divine love. This exhibition of the Lord's prema-rasa is always misunderstood by materialists, who foolishly equate Krishna's gopi-lila pastimes, with their own pursuit of gross sexual pleasure. This misunderstanding is due to the failure to realize the scientific difference between spiritual prema-rasa and the materialistic kama-rasa. When the pure spirit soul falls from the spiritual world, his original love of God (prema) becomes perverted by contact with the material energy and is transformed into lust (kama). The goal of bhakti-yoga and chanting the holy name of the Lord is to purify the soul of mundane lust (kama) in order to regain the soul's original platform of prema, pure love for God.

Excursion to other holy places (Not on the parikrama route) Including: \*Kayareeka\*Bhadradi.

## 59 Kayarika (Kayreeka) / Bhayari (Bharadi)

It is said that at Kayarika the gopis were playing a game of 'kho' till very late in the day. After the game had finished the gopis started walking home towards Varsana, but by the time they had gone just a short distance, it started to get very dark and the gopis became very afraid (bhaya). The village where they became afraid is known as Bhayari (Bharadi) and it is just over a mile south from Kayarika. Full of fear because of the dark, the gopis began calling out for Krishna to save them saying “Oh Krishna, it is very dark and we are afraid so please come and take us back to our homes in Varsana”. All of a sudden Krishna arrived there and it is said that He was able to illuminate the path ahead because as He smiled at the beautiful gopis the light emanating from His moon-like teeth shone as brightly as the full-moon. The gopis were therefore able to safely reach their houses.

How To Get There:: Kayareeka is 2km north of Alipur. Bharadi is 1 km south-east of Kayareeka (See map no.16 &17).

End of excursion (Rejoin Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 30 Pasopa (Parsaupa/Pausopa)

The beautiful and tranquil landscape of this area with its rolling hills and rustic forests is truly breathtaking. Situated on a nearby hill overlooking the village is the temple of Shri Shri Jugala-kishore, the dual form of Radha and Krishna entwined together in a loving embrace. The name of the village has been derived from the words 'pa' meaning 'hoof-print' and 'pashu', meaning an 'animal' such as a cow. Or in other words 'pasopa' means the 'hoof-print of cows'.

One day, when Krishna and Balarama were herding Their cows in a nearby forest, Krishna wanted to show Balarama just how much Their cowherd boyfriends really loved Them. Therefore, while the cowherd boys were absorbed in playing games, unseen by them, Krishna very stealthily took Balarama to another forest. However the cows noticed that Krishna and Balarama were going to another forest and while still grazing on the grass, slowly followed behind Them.

While absorbed in playing games, the cowherd boys all of a sudden realized that both Krishna and Balarama had disappeared along with all the cows. They immediately stopped playing and started searching from one grove to the next. Becoming almost mad at the loss of their two dear friends, they began shedding tears in separation and crying out the names of Krishna and Balarama. While franticly searching throughout the forest, the cowherd boys suddenly noticed the 'pashu-pa', or hoof-prints of the cows. They then started to follow these tracks which led them to this village where they suddenly saw Krishna and Balarama waiting with open arms to greet them. The great misery that had momentarily engulfed the cowherd boys immediately dissipated as they embraced Krishna and Balarama to their heart's content. Thus Krishna was able to show Balarama just how much the cowherd boys actually loved Them. Top How To Get There: Pasopa is 3km north of Alipur and 6km west of Khonha (See map no.16 &17).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 13

Including:\*Birar.

## 60 Virara (Birar)

It is said that Krishna performed the 'rasa-lila' at this place with sixteen thousand gopis. After dancing for the whole night, the gopis felt that Krishna must be feeling fatigued and brought Him to this place to rest. The gopis made a soft bed of fragrant forest flowers where Krishna could lie down and relax. The word 'virara' is derived from the word 'vishrama' or sometimes 'virama', which means 'to rest'.

How To Get There: This village is 2km west of Sabrana (See map no.17).

End of excursion (Rejoin Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 31 Adi-Kedarnatha (Kedarnath/Kedarnath Dhama)

Situated on the top of a mountain is the famous shrine dedicated to Lord Shiva known as Adi-Kedarnatha. One has to climb up three hundred steps to reach this sacred shrine. From the mountain top one gets a panoramic view of the surrounding country-side. This place is considered to be the original Kedarnatha, which like Adi-Badrinatha, has its secondary expansion in the Himalayas. This shrine is situated inside a cave where one can have darshana of Kedarnatha Mahadeva in his deity form of a Shiva-linga as well as Lord Shiva's eternal consort Gauri Devi (Parvati). At the foot on the mountain there is a small pond known as Gauri-kunda. This holy tirtha and the Deity of Lord Shiva are said to have been discovered by Shrila Narayana Bhatta during his excavations of Vraja.

How To Get There: This shrine is 10km north of Pasopa and 1km west of Bilonda (See map no.17, 17A & 17B).
