## Excursion to Other Holy Places 14

Including: \*Badli\*Karmooka.

## 61 Badali (Badli)

Once during the hot summer months, Krishna and the cowherd boys were grazing their cows at this place. Due to the intense heat that day, all the cowherd boys began praying to Krishna to provide them some relief. Suddenly, huge dark clouds began to appear in the sky and cool breezes started blowing which gave great pleasure to everyone. Suddenly it began to rain and in great happiness the cowherd boys began to glorify Krishna due to His wonderful activities. The word 'badala' refers to very dark clouds in the sky that are pregnant with heavy rainfall.

How to Get There: Badali is 500mt north of Kedarnatha (See map no.17B).

## 62 Karamuka (Karmooka)

There was formerly a verdant forest located here where one day Krishna came to meet with His beloved Radharani to enjoy transcendental pastimes in the forest.

How To Get There: This place is is 2.5km north-east of Bilond (See map no.17B).

End of excursion (Rejoin Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 32 Charana Pahadi

Situated on top of a large hill which is considered to be a divine manifestation of Lord Shiva, one can see the lotus foot-prints of Lord Shri Krishna impressed upon a rock. In the same area, besides Krishna's lotus foot-prints, one can also see the foot-prints of the gopis, the gopas (cowherd boys), and the cows. The word 'charana' means 'lotus feet' and 'pahadi' means a 'mountain', or a 'hill'. Sometimes this place is also called Charana-chinnha; the word 'chinnha' means that the impression of the Lord's lotus feet is 'indented' on the rocks. This is the most famous amongst the three important 'Charana Pahadis' found in Vraja, the other two being located at Nandagrama and Chota Bathain.

Lord Krishna used to come to this area for grazing His cows along with the cowherd boys. One day Krishna climbed to the top of the hill and started playing on His flute. The enchanting sound of Krishna's flute suddenly captivated the minds of the gopis who were bathing at a nearby kunda and they immediately started to climb the hill in search of Krishna. The cowherd boys also became attracted by the sound of Krishna's flute and they also began to climb the hill to search for Krishna. Similarly, the cows also became enchanted by Krishna's flute playing and they also made their way to the top of the hill. At that same time the hill also became completely enchanted by the sound of Krishna's flute and the rocks began to melt in ecstasy. The place where Krishna stood became so soft that His lotus feet became indented on the rock. Similarly, because all the gopis, the cowherd boys and their cows had also reached the top of the hill, their foot-prints also became indented on the rocks.

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Here is Shri Carana-chinnha on top of the mountain. Here at Krida-kunda Krishna played games \[krida\] in the water. Here are the five beautiful Gopa-kundas beginning with Shridama's. See also this very beautiful Ghosarani-kunda.

Ghosarani was the daughter of Yashodara, a king of the cowherds. He arranged the marriage of his daughter here. Look at Vihvala-kunda, where Radha was overwhelmed (vihvala) after hearing the sound of Krishna's flute.”

Surrounding Charana Pahadi are a number of sacred kundas although most are only visible in the monsoon season when they are filled with rainwater. From the top of the hill one can see Dhyana-kunda where Shri Krishna meditated on His beloved Radha. Nearby is Vihvala-kunda where Radha became overwhelmed after having heard the enchanting sound of Krishna’s flute, and Krida-kunda where Krishna played water-sports with His friends. Near Angrawali village are the five kundas named after Krishna’s cowherd boyfriends called the Pancha-sakha-kundas, also called the Gopa-kundas. These five friends are said to include: Rangila, Chabila, Jakila, Matila, and Datila. However, the Bhakti-ratnakara mentions Shridama as one of the five gopas. In the far distance looking eastwards is Luk-luki-kunda where Krishna and the gopis would play hide and seek. In the southern direction is Ghosarani-kunda, where mother Yashoda’s brother named Yashodhara gave away his daughter in marriage. It is said that the whole area on this side of Kamyavana was being ruled by mother Yashoda’s father whose name was Samukha Maharaja. It is also said that Ghosarani-kunda is also connected to the family of Yashoda’s mother whose name was Patala Devi. Top

How To Get There: Charana Pahadi is 3.5km north of Kedarnatha. It is 1.5km west of Vilond on the Jhanjpuri to Kaman road. From Kaman Town it is 3.5km on the road going to Gopalagarh just after passing through the village of Lahasar (See map no.17B & 17C).

## 33 Luklukana-Micali (Luk-luki-kunda)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “This place is called Luklukana-micali where Radha and Krishna performed many pastimes. Michali means closed eyes. As They would play hide and seek at this place Their happiness increased. Here the beautiful Luklukana-michali-kunda is situated within this very dense dark forest.” There used to be a beautiful forest here named Luklukana-micali, where Radha and Krishna enjoyed many wonderful pastimes along with the gopis. There was also a very beautiful lake known as Luklukana-micali-kunda. The word 'michali' means that was enjoyed here by Krishna and the gopis. When the gopis would close their eyes Krishna would hide in the forest, or sometimes in a cave on the mountain known as Luk-luki Kandara, or sometimes under the water of the kunda. Although the forest has almost disappeared the shallow kunda is still visible and is located in the middle of a rice-paddy. The mountain Luk-luki Kandara is still visible next to Charana Pahadi but the cave has disappeared. One day the gopis challenged Krishna to a game in Luklukana-micali-kunda, the winner would be the one who could hold their breath and stay under water the longest. When Krishna and the gopis dipped their heads under the water, the gopis cheated and again popped their heads above the water waiting for Krishna to surface.

When the gopis saw Krishna’s head coming up from the water, they would take a deep breath and immediately dip under the water and Krishna would think that He was the first to surface.

The gopis would then pop their heads above the water and claim victory. This went on game after game and each time the gopis were victorious. In the next game the gopis placed a wager on their winning the next round. Again everyone dipped below the water and once again the gopis cheated and popped their heads up waiting to see Krishna's head begin to surface. Then, as the gopis waited for Krishna's head to surface, nothing happened. The gopis aguishly waited and waited, but Krishna's head did not come to the surface.

Suddenly realizing that Krishna may have drowned while trying to defeat the gopis in the game, the gopis became distraught and franticly began searching in the water. Not finding Krishna in the kunda, they began searching on the land and in the nearby forest. Not finding Krishna either in the water or in the forest, or anywhere else, they began to lament and while shedding torrents of tears, began blaming themselves for Krishna's death. They condemned themselves over and over again for having cheated in order to win the game of 'hide and seek', and thus had now lost their beloved Krishna forever. Understanding that the gopis were deeply regretting their cheating activities in the game and were feeling devastated due to His loss, Krishna suddenly appeared before them and the gopis immediately forgot their lamentation and became ecstatic due to having got back their beloved Krishna, the very life-breath of their existence.

How To Get There: This kunda is 500mt from Charana Pahadi on the parikrama path going to Gaya-kunda and Kaman Town (See map no.17B).

## 34 Kamyavana (Kaman)

Kamyavana is one of the sacred forests of Vraja and today the town of Kaman stands on the spot where the ancient forest of Kamyavana once stood, although some of the ancient kundas still survive, very little of the great forest now remains. Kamyavana, was the largest forest of Vrindavana with a parikrama of fourteen miles (20km). The word 'kamya' in Kamyavana means 'charming' as well as 'attractive' and the word 'vana' means 'forest', therefore the name 'Kamyavana' means a very 'charming and attractive forest'.

In the Vraja-riti-cintamani it says, “Because of the many charming (kamya) forests, groves, and lakes, where Lord Krishna relishes the sweetness of His pastimes, this place is known as Kamyavana.” The Vishnu Purana specifically mentions that there are eighty-four sacred kundas and eighty-four sacred simhasanas in Kamyavana forest. However most of these simhasanas and kundas have now disappeared. Some Puranas mention that there were over three hundred sacred kundas as well as over one hundred different simhasanas within in the sacred forest. The word 'simhasana' in this case refers to a throne, but the altar in a temple where the Deity stands is also called a simhasana.

Kamyavana is also called Kamavana, and the word 'kama' usually means mundane 'desire' or 'lust', but in the case of Kamavana, this is not ordinary mundane lust or desire, but a highly elevated transcendental form of lusty desire called 'rati' which can only be experienced by pure devotees of Krishna, like the gopis of Vraja. According to the Puranas, Lord Gopinatha, who is also known as Kamadeva or the transcendental Cupid, is the presiding Deity of Kamavana (Kamyavana) and therefore the word 'kama' in the name 'Kamavana' also refers to Lord Gopinatha, the transcendental Cupid. Thus the 'kama' in the name Kamavana also refers to the transcendental kama (rati) of the gopis to fully satisfy the desires of Lord Gopinatha. With regard to the pastimes between Krishna and the gopis of Vraja, it must be clearly understood that the spiritual kama or rati of the gopis is completely different from the mundane kama or lust of this material world. Kamyavana (Kamavana) is also a forest where all one's desires can be fulfilled. In the Adi-Varaha Purana, it says that the forest of Kamyavana (Kamavana) can fulfill all the desires of the devotees as well as the demigods, and any pilgrim who visits this forest becomes glorified even in Vishnuloka. In the Skanda Purana (Mathura-khanda) it is said, “O king next is Kamyavana, where Lord Hari stayed in His childhood. Simply by bathing here, any person will attain all his desires.”

Nanda Maharaja stayed at Kamyavana for sometime while on his journey from Shakatikara (Chhatikara) to Nandagrama and it is said that Krishna enjoyed a number of His boyhood pastimes in this forest during the last period of His pauganda-lila. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Krishna performed many wonderful pastimes here. Just see all the many kundas. O Shrinivasa, see Vishnu-simhasana and Shri Charana-kunda where Krishna washed His feet. How can I describe the glories of these places when even Lord Brahma cannot understand their unlimited glories?”

It is also said that the Pandavas spent some time living at Kamyavan during the period of their exile and some of the pastimes mentioned in the Mahabharata occurred in this forest. It is said by some scholars that the Pandavas also spent a part of their childhood living in the area of Kamyavana. The Puranas mention that the Pandavas spent over five years of their exile in this region moving between two great forests known as Kamyaka and Dwaita that encompassed an area covering modern-day Haryana and Northern Rajasthan, through which the fabled river Saraswati once flowed. The forest of Kamyavana would have been on the southern periphery of these great forests. Another name of Kamyavana is in fact Kamyakavana. During the final year of their exile, the Pandavas lived incognito in the nearby kingdom of Matsya, identified as the present day Bharatapur District of Western Rajasthan of which Kamyavana is a part. The Matsya kingdom was being ruled by King Virat, who was a member of the Yadava confederacy.

Kamyavana also became celebrated as the place where the three important Deities of the Gaudiya Goswamis namely: Govindaji, Gopinatha, and Madana-mohana, as well as the Deity of Vrinda Devi, were kept after they had been secretly smuggled out of Vrindavana in bullock carts, just prior to an attack on the holy city by soldiers of the tyrant Emperor Aurangzeb in 1670. After some time when it became safe to travel, the Deities were then taken from Kamyavana to Amber in Rajasthan that was still under the rule of Hindu Rajput kings. The Deity of Vrinda Devi remained at Kamyavana because by some miracle she had become too heavy and could not be moved. In 1727, after the city of Jaipur was founded by Maharaj Jai Singh II, the Gaudiya Goswami Deities, Govindaji, Gopinatha, and Madana-mohana, were moved to permanent locations within the newly built city.

Due to the great transcendental pleasure that the local people of Kamyavana had experienced by having the Deities of the Gaudiya Goswamis in their town, it was decided to establish temples containing the 'pratibhu-murtis' of these three Deities. The term ‘pratibhu' means the ‘empowered replicas' of the original Deities. Therefore, the temples of Govindaji, Gopinatha, and Madana-mohana were duly established here at Kamyavana and the original Deity of Vrinda Devi, who stayed behind at Kamyavana was subsequently installed in the temple built for Govindaji.    Top

How To Get There: Kamyavana is 55km northwest of Vrindavana, 9km from Varsana, 11km from Nandgoan and 23km from Dig. The quickest way to get there from Vrindavana is to go to Chhatikara and then by the Agra to Delhi road (N.H.2.) to Chatta, and then turn left on the road to Nandagrama and then continue to Kaman (See map no.18)

## Kamyavana Interior Parikrama

NOTE: Some say that the traditional Kamyavana parikrama starts with a sacred bath in Vimala-kunda but Kamyavana parikrama can start from any place of one's choice. Many devotees prefer to start Kamyavana inner parikrama by visiting the Gaudiya Goswami temples located in the city area starting with the darshana of Shrimati Vrinda Devi, the presiding Deity of Vrindavana Dhama, who resides at the Radha Govinda Mandira, then devotees usually visit the nearby Madana-Mohana Mandira. After visiting the Vrinda Devi and Madana-mohana, devotees usually proceed to Chaurasi-khambha (the Gopinatha Mandira can also be reached on foot from Chaurasi-khamba but generally it is visited after Gaya-kunda). Then next is Vishnu Simhasana and Chandra-sarovara (Chandrabhaga-kunda). The next is Kameshwara Mahadeva Mandira, followed by Pancha Pandava Mandira, Dharma Kupa, and Dharma-kunda, then to Vimal-kunda and Manokrama-kunda. Next are Yashoda-kunda, Rameshwara Setubandha and Gaya-kunda, after which darshana at the Radha Gopinatha Mandira and finally Surabhi-kunda (Some devotees prefer to visit Surabhi-kunda on their way to Bhojana Thali).

## 1 Govindaji Mandira / Vrinda Devi

The Deity of Govindaji was originally established in Vrindavana by Lord Krishna's great grandson Maharaja Vajranabha, who was the king of Mathura just after Krishna's disappearance around five thousand years ago. During the course of time the Deity was lost and eventually rediscovered by Shrila Rupa Goswami hidden in a hole on the hill-top known as Goma-tila, also called the Govindaji Yoga Pitha, the place where the Govindaji Mandira now stands.

Here in this temple one can see the original Deity of Vrinda Devi alongside the 'pratibhu-murti' of Lord Govindaji and also a Deity of Lord Jagannatha Swami. When the Deities of the Gaudiya Goswamis were brought from Vrindavana, they were kept at different locations in Kamyavana for safety. At this particular location, the Deities of Govindaji and Vrinda Devi were kept for three or four days before Govindaji was moved to Amber, then finally to Jaipura in Rajasthan. When the pujaris tried to move the Deity of Vrinda Devi, she became too heavy to move; the pujaris therefore concluded that Vrinda Devi, the presiding Deity of Vrindavana forest, was not willing to leave the holy dhama. Consequently, Vrinda Devi remained at Kamyavana and was later installed in this temple along with the pratibhu-murti of Govindaji.

This very beautiful Deity of Vrinda Devi has ten arms holding her various symbols and is said to have been originally installed in Vrindavana by King Vajranabha, five thousand years earlier. During the course of history, the Deity was lost but was subsequently rediscovered in Brahma-kunda by Shrila Rupa Goswami after she appeared in a dream informing him where she lay hidden. Rupa Goswami then installed Vrinda Devi in the Govindaji Mandira in Vrindavana. Vrinda Devi is the gopi after whom the forest of Vrindavana has been named (the vana of Vrinda). Along with Purnamasi, Vrinda Devi is responsible for making all the various arrangements for the loving pastimes between Radha and Krishna within the groves of Vrindavana. Shrimati Tulasi Devi is considered to be the partial expansion of Vrinda Devi, who is herself an expansion of Yogamaya Devi.

How To Get There: This temple is in the center of Kaman Town on a secluded back road not far from Chaurasi Khamba (See map no.18).

## 2 Madana-mohana Mandira

In this temple one can see the 'pratibhu-murti' of Lord Madana-mohana. The original Deity of Madana-mohana was worshiped at Dwadashaditya-tila, a hill-top on the bank of the River Yamuna in Vrindavana by Shrila Sanatana Goswami. The Deity was established by King Vajranabha around five thousand years earlier, but in the course of time was lost and rediscovered by Shrila Adwaita Acharya, at the place known as Adwaita Vat just below Dwadashaditya-tila. When Adwaita Acharya returned to Nadia he arranged for a local brahmana named Choube to continue the worship of the Deity, thus, according to the Bhakti-ratnakara, Madana-Mohana was being worshiped at a temple in Mahavana by the Choube family. When Sanatana Goswami was living in Vrindavana, he received instructions in a dream from Madana-Mohana that he should personally take charge of the seva-puja and brings the Deity back to Vrindavana, which he did. After some years a temple was built for Lord Madana-Mohana at the place where Sanatana Goswami performed his bhajana on the hill known as Dwadashaditya-tila. Some years later due to an imminent attack on Vrindavana by the Muslim tyrant Aurangzeb in 1670, the Deity of Madana-Mohana was moved along with Govindaji, Gopinathaji and Vrinda Devi to Radha-kunda, then to Kamyavana, where they remained for three or four days before being taken to Jaipura exceptn for Vrinda Devi who refused to leave the holy dhama. Later the Deity of Madana-mohana was again moved to Kiraoli near Bharatapura.

How To Get There: This temple is near the Govindaji Mandira on the road going to Vimala-kunda (See map no.18).

## 3 Gopinatha Mandira

In this temple can be seen the 'pratibhu-murti' of Lord Gopinatha. The original Deity of Lord Gopinatha was established by King Vajranabha almost five thousand years earlier in Vrindavana, but like the other important Deities that he established, Lord Gopinatha was in due course of time lost. The Deity was again rediscovered at Vamsi Vata by Paramananda Goswami and the seva-puja was reestablished by Paramananda's close friend Madhu Pandita Goswami, an important associate of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. When the Deities of the Gaudiya Goswami's were moved from Vrindavana due to the fear of an attack by the soldiers of Aurangzeb in 1669, the Deity of Lord Gopinatha was brought to Kamyavana via Radha-kunda along with Govindaji, Madana-mohana and Vrinda Devi. Lord Gopinatha is presently being worshiped in Jaipur. The exquisitely beautiful and all-attractive Lord Gopinatha, who is also referred to as being the transcendental Cupid or Kamadeva, is considered to be the presiding Deity of Kamyavana forest. How To Get There: This temple is situated behind Chaurasi Khamba a short distance from Gaya-kunda (See map no.18).

## 4 Chaurasi Khamba (Nanda Bhavana)

The word 'chaurasi' means eighty-four and 'khamba' means pillars, in other words a palace with eighty-four stone pillars. This ancient ruin is one of the famous landmarks of Kamyavana and lies on a hilltop between the Govindaji and Gopinatha temples. The Chaurasi Khamba at Kamyavana is said to have been discovered by Shrila Narayana Bhatta, the author of Vraja-bhakti-vilasa and a great authority on Vraja Mandala parikrama. It is said that this palace was built by the celestial architect Vishvakarma and was one of the three palaces of Nanda Maharaja, the others being Gokula and Nandagrama. It appears very similar to King Nanda's palace at Gokula, but on a much larger scale. Some historians have said it was used by the Pandavas during their exile while others have said it was originally built by Mother Yashoda’s forefathers who ruled the area around Kamyavana.

Some of the local historians claim that Chaurasi-khamba was reconstructed from the ruins on Nanda Maharaja's palace by a Hindu king named Kamasena Maharaja who ruled over the area. It is said that Kamasena Maharaja excavated and reestablished many important holy places around Kamyavana including Vimala-kunda, but as historical records are practically non-existent such claims are difficult to substantiate. During the Islamic rule over this region it is said that it was used as a mosque and there are a number of Urdu and Persian inscriptions found there.

How To Get There: This place is in the center of Kaman Town and situated at the far end of the main bazaar (See map no.18).

## 5 Vishnu Simhasana

This is the most famous of the eighty-four ancient simhasanas of Kamyavana. The word 'simhasana' means the 'lion seat' and generally refers to throne or the altar on which the temple Deities are situated. The word 'simhasana' can also mean the 'throne of a king'. The Vishnu Simhasana is the place where the marriage ceremony of Lord Narayana and the goddess Lakshmi Devi is celebrated by the people of Kaman every year. Situated nearby was the famous Charana-kunda where Krishna once washed His lotus feet, but this kunda has now disappeared. How To Get There: This shrine is near the main bus stand on the road from Nandagrama (See map no.18).

## 6 Chandra Sarovara

This very beautiful and isolated lake is also called Chandrabhaga-kunda and there is a famous temple of Shiva here known as Chandeshwara Mahadeva. It is one of the largest kundas that remains of the eighty-four sacred kundas of Kamyavana mentioned in the Vishnu Purana. How To Get There: This kunda is some distance from the bus stand along the bypass road to Dig (See map no.18).

## 7 Kameshwara Mahadeva Mandira

Karmeshwara Mahadeva is one of the four famous 'dig-pala' Deities that were established by King Vajranabha to give protection to the holy dhama. The word 'dig' means 'direction' and 'pala' means 'protector'. The other 'dig-pala' Deities are Bhuteshwara in Mathura, Chakreshwara in Govardhana, and Gopishwara in Vrindavana.

How To Get There: This temple situated on a back street and is not far from Vimala-kunda (See map no.18).

## 8 Pancha Pandava Mandira

This temple near to the Kameshwara Mahadeva Mandira is dedicated to the five Pandavas and is also known as the Dharmaraja Mandira. The name Dharmaraja is another name of Yudhisthira Maharaja, as he was religion (Dharma) personified as well as the son of Dharmaraja (Yamaraja). Some local panditas say that this was the spot where the Pandavas actually lived during their stay at Kamyavana when they were undergoing their period of exile. How To Get There: This temple is near the Kameshwara Mandira (See map no.18).

## 9 Dharma Kupa

This is a large well known as Dharma-kupa which is located very near to Dharma-kunda. The word 'kupa' means a 'well' for drawing drinking water.

How To Get There: This well is located near Dharma-kunda (See map no.18).

## 10 Vishoka Simhasana

Near to Dharma-kunda is another of Kamyavana's famous simhasanas, the ancient thrones or sitting places of which there used to be a total of at least eighty-four. The local Vrajavasis say that this particular simhasana belongs to Dharmaraja, which is another name of Lord Yamaraja, who is the Lord of Dharma and the demigod responsible for judging the dead.

How To Get There: This simhasana is located near Dharma-kunda (See map no.18).

## 11 Dharma-kunda (Pancha Pandava-kunda)

Dharma-kunda is a small kunda situated in an isolated area surrounded by open fields. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “This is Dharma-kunda where Narayana in the form of Dharma performs indescribable pastimes.” The sacred Dharma-kunda is also known as Pancha Pandava-kunda. The word 'dharma' means 'religion' as well as 'religious duties' and the name ‘Pancha Pandava' refers to Yudhisthira, Arjuna, Bhima, Nakula, and Sahadeva, the five (pancha) sons of Maharaja Pandu, who were collectively known as the Pandava brothers. When the Vedas speak of Dharma or Dharmaraja it usually refers to Lord Yamaraja, who passes judgment on the departed souls and who is one of the great Mahajanas, or those who perfectly understand the import of the Vedas.

How To Get There: Dharma-kunda is about 250mt from the Karmeswara Mandira and is situated in a field some distance from the road (See map no.18).

## A Yaksha Tests Yudhisthira Maharaja

Is has been said that when the Pandavas first arrived at Kamyavana after having traveled a great distance, they all felt very thirsty and Maharaja Yudhisthira asked Bhima to bring some water for Draupadi and his brothers in a pot. Bhima went in search of water and arrived on the bank of this kunda. He was about to draw water when a Yaksha appeared there and forbade him to take the water without first answering a riddle, otherwise he would immediately die. Not caring for the words of the Yaksha, the thirsty Bhima began to drink water and immediately fell down dead. After Bhima did not return, Yudhisthira sent Arjuna to fetch the water. Arjuna arrived at the kunda and was about to drink water when the same Yaksha appeared and forbade him to drink the water, without first answering a riddle, otherwise he would immediately die. Being very thirsty, Arjuna ignored the Yaksha and as he began to drink the water, he fell down dead. As Arjuna did not return with any water, Yudhisthira sent Nakula who also met the same fate. Yudhisthira then sent Sahadeva and when he did not return, he decided to go himself to bring water.

Arriving on the banks of the kunda, he suddenly noticed his brothers lying either dead or unconscious at different spots around the kunda. The same Yaksha suddenly appeared before Yudisthira and also forbade him to drink water without first answering a riddle, otherwise like his brothers he would also die. Yudhisthira agreed to answer the Yaksha's riddle, and one by one answered each of the riddles correctly. The riddles asked by the Yaksha and the answers Yudisthira gave are as follows:

Who raises the sun? - Brahma raises the sun.

What is heavier than the earth? - One's mother.

What is higher than the sky? - One's father.

What travels faster than the wind? - One's mind.

What is more numerous than grasses on the earth? - The desires of the mind.

What is the best kind of dharma? - Mercy.

What is the best kind of forbearance? - To tolerate the dualities of life.

What is the worst enemy? - One's mind.

What is the worst disease? - One's greed.

Who is a holy man? - One who does good to all.

Who is not a holy man? - One who cannot control his senses.

Who is happy? - Those without debt, not living in a foreign land, and who can digest their food. What is the greatest wonder? - Although a man sees all around him people are dying, even in youth and sometimes unexpectedly, yet he thinks that he will not die.

What is life's true path? - The path of the maha-bhagavata is the true path for all.

What is newsworthy? - That time devours all men.

The Yaksha was very satisfied with Yudhisthira and informed him that as he had answered all the riddles correctly, he could revive one of his brothers. Yudhisthira then chose Nakula. The Yaksha was surprised by the choice, saying that surely it was better to choose either Arjuna or Bhima, as they were not only senior in age but also great warriors on the battlefield. Yudhisthira replied that as his father Maharaja Pandu had two wives, Kunti and Madri, and that because he himself was the son of Kunti, it was only right according to dharma, that one of Madri's sons should also live. Being very happy at Yudhisthira's perfect understanding of dharma and his choice of bringing Nakula back to life, the Yaksha declared that all of Yudhisthira's brothers could be brought back to life. At that moment the Yaksha revealed his true identity as Lord Yamaraja, who had appeared there in the form of a Yaksha just to test Maharaja Yudhisthira. Lord Yamaraja is also known as Dharmaraja, because he is a Mahajana and the knower of all religious principles and the judge of all departed souls. Being the seminal father of Yudisthira Maharaja, he was extremely happy to see that his son was so firmly situated in the principles of dharma.

## 12 Vimala-kunda

When Nanda Maharaja stayed at Kamyavana, Krishna and Balarama used to graze Their herds nearby and along with Their cowherd boyfriends, They enjoyed various games as well as sporting pastimes in Vimala-kunda. This is the largest and most well maintained of the kundas at Kamyavana and also the most famous. In the Adi-Varaha Purana it is said, “By bathing in Vimala-kunda, all one's sins are destroyed and on leaving the body will attain My eternal abode.” There are many important temples situated around this sacred kunda including those dedicated to: Dauji, Surya-narayana, Nilakanteshwara, Kamyavana-bihari, Govardhana-natha, Madana-gopala, Murli-manohara, Vimala-bihari, Vimala Devi, Ganga Devi, Yamuna Devi and Gopalaji. In the month of Kartika on the occasion of the second dvadashi day, a festival is held here and thousands flock to Vimala-kunda where ghee lamps are offered to the sacred kunda along with flowers and numerous other offerings.

How To Get There: This kunda is 500mt east of the Kaman Town on the road to Dig (See map no.18).

## The Appearance of Vimala-kunda

Once during 'chaturmasya', all the sacred 'tirthas' or holy places in the world visited Kamyavana to pay their homage to Krishna, but the sacred lake Pushkara Tirtharaja failed to come. Therefore, in order to compensate for Pushkara Tirtha's failure to appear, Krishna caused a very powerful jet of water to come shooting out of the ground which eventually created a large kunda. Within that flow of water, a very beautiful young girl appeared and began to serve Krishna in different ways. In no time a lake formed and after sporting and enjoying various pastimes in the lake with the beautiful young girl, Krishna blessed her saying that from this day onwards, she would be known as Vimala Devi and this sacred kunda would be named after her. Krishna also said that by bathing only once in this kunda, it would be equal to bathing seven times in the sacred lake of Pushkara. The Puranas say that the goddess Vimala Devi eternally resides here in this holy kunda.

There is another famous story related in the Bhavisya Purana as well as the Garga Samhita concerning Vimala-kunda. It is said during the advent of Lord Krishna, there was a noble and pious king from the city of Champak Nagari in Sindhu-desa named Raja Vimala, who although having many wives, had no children. On petitioning the great ascetic Yajnavalkya Rishi, the king was blessed with sixteen thousand beautiful daughters. It is said that all these girls had in their previous life been living in Ayodhya and had desired Lord Ramacandra as their husband. When the time came to select husbands for his daughters, the king was advised by Yajnavalkya to approach Lord Krishna, who was the only person who was actually qualified to accept such highly cultured and beautiful princesses. Lord Krishna immediately accepted the king's proposal and brought all the princesses from Campak Nagari to the beautiful forest of Kamyavana. It is said that Krishna expanded Himself to be with each and every princess and enjoyed endless pastimes in Kamyavana forest, including the celebrated 'rasa-lila'. The long-cherished desire of the beautiful princesses, to serve Lord Rama in a conjugal relationship was thus fulfilled by Lord Krishna in Kamyavana forest. The tears of happiness that flooded from the eyes of those beautiful princesses is said to have created a large kunda that became celebrated as Vimala-kunda. It is said that anyone who is fortunate enough to bathe in the tear-filled Vimala-kunda, will certainly have all their desires fulfilled.

In order to clarify the various stories about the appearance of Vimala-kunda, as well as other histories of Krishna's pastimes here in Kamyavana, the local panditas have said that these histories of Kamyavana may relate to different time periods and cover at least five different kalpas, or days of Brahma. This is because Krishna appears on earth to perform His pastimes once in a day of Brahma, and that sacred places like Vimala-kunda may appear in each and every kalpa. As the Puranas are not recorded in any chronological order, it sometimes creates confusion for those reading the Puranic histories. The learned panditas have also ascertained that in each of the different kalpas, Krishna's pastimes have been centered in different parts of Vrindavana Dhama and say that in a previous kalpa, Kamyavana was the focal point of Krishna's pastimes, in another kalpa it was Chandra-sarovara, and in this present kalpa it was Seva Kunja and Vrindavana, where the maha rasa-lila took place.

It is interesting to note that before Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's parikrama of Vraja Mandala in 1515, Vrindavana and its more than two hundred holy places were completely unknown, in fact, many believed that Kamyavana was the real Vrindavana and the actual place where Krishna performed His earthly pastimes five thousand years earlier. However, the importance of Vrindavana was revealed to the world when Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu spent more than one month engaged in bhajana in Vrindavana and each day took darshana of such places as: Kaliya Ghata, Seva Kunja, Imli-tala, Chayana Ghata and Keshi Ghata, thus revealed the glories of Vrindavana before the whole world. After Lord Chaitanya returned to Puri, He sent His senior-most disciples Rupa and Sanatana Goswamis to complete the excavation of Vrindavana and establish the important Deities there like Madana-mohana, Govindaji and Gopinatha.

## Durvasa Muni Visits the Pandavas at Kamyavana

During their time in exile, after having been banished from their kingdom by Duryodhana, the Pandava brothers: Yudhisthira, Arjuna, Bhima, Nakula, and Sahadeva, along with their wife Princess Draupadi, stayed for some time in the sacred forest of Kamyavana. One day while visiting the city of Hastinapura, the great ascetic Durvasa Muni was very pleased with the reception given by Duryodhana, and offered him a boon. Duryodhana then requested that Durvasa and his ten thousand disciples should visit his cousin brothers the Pandavas, who were at that time staying in the forest at Kamyavana. Duryodhana asked Durvasa to reach the Pandavas residence by the third 'prahara' of the day so that he and his disciples could be fed a very sumptuous meal that would be prepared by Princess Draupadi. The evil minded Duryodhana knew full well that Draupadi would have finished serving lunch by then and would be unaware that Durvasa would be arriving. Duryodhana's despicable plan was based on the premonition that because Durvasa Muni was very easily angered, he would arrive too late to get his midday meal and would therefore become angry and thus curse the five Pandavas.

In due course of time, Durvasa arrived with his disciples at the time given by Duryodhana. After greeting the Pandavas, Durvasa informed Yudhisthira that before taking his lunch, he and his disciples would first take their bath in Vimala-kunda. After Durvasa left to take his bath, Draupadi informed Yudhisthira that there was no more food available to feed Durvasa, what to speak of his ten thousand disciples. Even though Draupadi possessed a celestial cooking pot, given to her by Surya, the sun-god, which could produce inexhaustible amounts of food, but only as long as Draupadi herself had not eaten and that there was still some food remaining inside the pot. Once it was washed clean, the pot could no longer produce any more food. In great anxiety, Draupadi began to cry, fearing that on his return from bathing, Durvasa would undoubtedly curse the Pandavas for not having received him in the proper manner, and for not providing food for him and his hungry disciples.

Being a great devotee of the Lord, Draupadi began to pray to Krishna for help to save her dear husbands'. Just at that moment, Lord Shri Krishna arrived from Dwaraka to meet the Pandavas and upon hearing about their dilemma, He requested Draupadi to bring Him the sungod's inexhaustible cooking pot. Draupadi informed Krishna that she had already taken her meal and the magical cooling pot had been rinsed and there was no food remaining inside it. Nevertheless, Krishna insisted that the pot be brought to Him. On inspecting it, Krishna discovered a minute particle of leafy vegetable stuck on the side of the pot and immediately ate it. He then smilingly told Bhima to call Durvasa and all his disciples. Meanwhile, on the banks of Vimala-kunda, Durvasa and all his disciples having finished bathing, were suddenly feeling completely bloated, as if they had just eaten a very large meal. Not feeling even slightly hungry, and not wanting to insult Yudhisthira Maharaja by refusing to eat the meal that he thought the Pandavas must have prepared for him, Durvasa and his ten thousand disciples immediately slipped away from Kamyavana unseen by anyone.

## 13 Manokramana-kunda

This small kunda is located next to the Kashi-Vishvanatha Mandira and is dry most of the year except during the monsoon season. This somewhat neglected kunda is also known as Manokramana-ganga-kunda.      Top

How To Get There:: Manokramana-kunda lies a few hundred yards to the west of Vimala-kunda (See map no.18).

## 13a Kama-Sarovara

This famous kunda is no longer visible having been filled-in and ploughed over by local agriculturists a number of years ago. This is the plight of many ancient kundas of Vraja that are not being protected.

## 14 Yashoda-kunda

When Nanda Maharaja was moving from Gokula to Nandagrama, he stayed at a few places including Shakatikara, Dig and also Kamyavana, where his residence was said to have been located near Yashoda-kunda. In the Bhakta-ratnakara it says, “Here is the supremely pure Yashoda-kunda where Krishna in jubilation, herded His cows.” It is said by some authorities that Samuka Maharaja, mother Yashoda’s father, was at one time staying at this place and therefore Yashoda spent some of her childhood pastimes at this place. There is also a spot next to the kunda where it is said mother Yashoda used to churn butter and also wash her pots. There is an ancient temple here dedicated to Chamunda Devi, a form of goddess Durga. Chamunda is famous for killing the two powerful demons named Chanda and Munda.

There is a nice story about the potency of this sacred kunda mentioned in the Adi-Varaha Purana. Once there was a vaishya (trader) who very expertly worshiped the brahmanas and consequently in his next life, he was born as a king. His name was Subhajit and his kingdom was known as Mahismati, but even though he had conquered all his enemies and accumulated great wealth, he was not happy. The reason for his unhappiness was due to not having a son and heir. On behalf of the king, the royal priest went to the forest to consult the great ascetic Loma Rishi, who informed the priest that although the king was a very pious vaishya in his previous life, he had once committed an offence against a cow. Loma Rishi further explained that in his previous life, the vaishya, while on a business trip during the hot season, had become very thirsty and began searching for a well. After finding a well, the vaishya lowered a vessel into the well to draw water. At that moment, a cow also came there searching for water. Not caring for the cow, the vaishya quenched his thirst and continued on his journey thus neglecting the cow. Loma Rishi further explained that because in his previous life the vaishya had diligently worshiped the brahmanas, he was reborn as a king, but because he had neglected to serve the thirsty cow, he was thus condemned to be childless.

Loma Rishi further advised the royal priest that he should take the king to the sacred forest of Kamyavana and take bath in the celebrated Yashoda-kunda, and thus the desires of the king would be fulfilled. The royal priest then arranged for the king to travel to Kamyavana and take bath in Yashoda-kunda. Within a short time, the wife of the king gave birth to a very beautiful baby boy, whose effulgence filled the four directions and brought unbounded happiness to King Subhajit, including the people of his kingdom. It has also been said in the Puranas that Yashoda-kunda is so supremely pure, that even if one does not take bath in the kunda, but simply hears about its glories, one will achieve the same result as if one had actually taken a bath there.

How To Get There:: Yashoda-kunda is situated on the parikrama path from Vimala-kunda going towards Rameshwara and Gaya-kunda (See map no.18).

## 15 Rameshwara Setubandha

Rameshwara Setubandha is the place in Kamyavana where Krishna enacted the pastimes of Lord Ramachandra. The word 'setu' means ‘bridge’ and 'bandha' means to ‘link-up’ or to 'join' one place to another. At this isolated spot on the Kamyavana parikrama path one can see a temple of Lord Shiva known as Rameshwara Mahadeva, which is a manifestation of Rameshwaram Dhama in Southern India. Setubandha is the place from where Lord Ramachandra built a stone bridge and crossed the Indian Ocean to the island of Lanka. Here in Kamyavana, the Rameshwara Mahadeva temple lies at one end of a stone bridge that runs across a small lake called Setubandha-sarovara, which is a manifestation of the Indian Ocean; the stone bridge leads to a small hill called Lanka Puri, representing the demon Ravana's fabled city of Lanka. This shallow lake is dry for most of the year, except during the rainy season. Unfortunately, most of the stones used to make the bridge have now disappeared. There was also a small forest nearby known as Ashokavana, which was a manifestation of the Ashoka grove in Lanka where Sita Devi was kept as a prisoner by Ravana.

One day Shri Krishna was enjoying pastimes with the gopis at this spot. At that moment a troupe of monkeys appeared from the nearby forest, and due to it being a very hot summer's day, the monkeys in order to cool off started to jump from the trees into the lake. Seeing the monkeys reminded Lalita-sakhi about the adventures of Lord Rama. She told Vishakha-sakhi, that once when the demon Ravana kidnapped Sita Devi and took her away to Lanka, the monkeys built a bridge out of large stones across the ocean and on the order of Lord Rama, all the stones miraculously floated on the water. Lord Rama and his army were then able to cross the ocean and reach Lanka by walking on those stones. Hearing the talks between Lalita and Vishakha, Krishna suddenly declared that He was that very same Lord Rama and that in His previous life He had appeared in Ayodhya as the son of Maharaja Dasaratha. The gopis started laughing at Krishna's boasting words and Lalita informed Krishna that if He was actually Lord Rama, He should take the help of the monkeys and immediately build a bridge by floating large stones over the lake, then only would the gopis believe that He was actually Lord Rama.

Taking up the challenge of the gopis and with the help of all the monkeys, Krishna assembled many large stones and after touching them with His lotus feet they began to float on the water, much to the amazement of the gopis, and within a short time a stone bridge had been erected across the lake. Seeing this wonderful and miraculous pastime, the gopis unanimously declared Krishna to be the very same Lord Ramachandra and gave the lake the name of Shri Rameshwara Setubandha. This same lake is also known as Lanka-kunda as well as Setubandha-sarovara. It is said that Shri Krishna personally established at one end of the stone bridge, the Shiva-linga known as Rameshwara Mahadeva, which is considered to be the original Rameshwaram in Vraja. Rameshwaram in Southern India is the place where Lord Ramachandra worshiped the Deity of Lord Shiva in order to kill the demon Ravana, because Ravana was a staunch and devoted follower of Lord Shiva. From this location at Rameshwara Setubandha one gets a very good view of the Kaman fort and the palace of former king of Kaman known as the Sheel Mahal, or the 'Eagle Palace', which is perched on top of same hill on which the Chaurasi Khambha is also located.

How To Get There: Rameshwara is situated in an isolated place on the parikrama path from Yashoda-kunda. to Gaya-kunda. It can also be reached from Gaya-kunda (See map no.18).

## 16 Gaya-Kunda

This sacred kunda is situated on the outskirts of Kaman Town and it is one of the famous kundas of Kamyavana and considered to be the original Gaya, or Adi-Gaya, with its expansion situated in Bihar state, where Hindus traditionally offer 'pinda' once a year to their departed forefathers. Nanda Maharaja used to come here to Gaya-kunda and offer 'pinda' to his forefathers, as do many Vrajavasis even today. Some authorities have said that there are many different kundas, now not visible, that were situated around Gaya-kunda including: Prayaga-kunda, Kashi-kunda, Pushkara-kunda, Gomati-kunda, Mana-kunda, Balabhadra-kunda, Narada-kunda, and Dwaraka-kunda, which represent the various holy tirthas found in India. Others say these kundas were actually situated within Gaya-kunda depending at which side of Gaya-kunda one bathed, and it was possible to bathe in all these various holy places one after another by moving clockwise around Gaya-kunda.

How To Get There: Gaya-kunda is 1km southwest of Kaman Town on the road to Jhanjpuri (See map no.18).

## Kamyavana Exterior Parikrama

## 35 Surabhi-Kunda (Prabhodananda Saraswati Bhajana Kutira)

The very beautiful and tranquil Surabhi-kunda is the place where Prabhodananda Saraswati Goswami performed his bhajana for some period of time before he moved to Kaliya Ghata in Vrindavana. Prabhodananda Saraswati was a devoted follower of Vaishnava Dharma and a prominent spiritual teacher belonging to the Shri sampradaya of Ramanujacharya; he hailed from Srirangam (Rangapatnam) in Southern India and was the uncle as well as initiating spiritual master of Gopala Bhatta Goswami.

Shrila Prabhodananda Saraswati Goswami first met Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu at Srirangam in Andhra Pradesh during the Lord's tour of South India, when He spent the rainy season staying at the house of Gopala Bhatta's father, Venkata Bhatta, who was Prabhodananda's brother. At that time, Prabhodananda had the opportunity to associate with Lord Chaitanya and became so convinced about the Lord's mission and philosophy, that he left the Shri sampradaya and joined Mahaprabhu's Gaudiya sampradaya. After leaving Shrirangam and moving to Vrindavana, Prabhodananda stayed in the holy dhama for the rest of his life. He was an intimate associate of the Six Goswamis and wrote a number of important books on the science of bhakti-yoga. His samadhi is at Kaliya Ghata in Vrindavana where he also performed bhajana during the latter part of his life. The Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika says that Prabhodananda Saraswati was one of the ashta-sakhis named Tungavidya Devi in Krishna's Vrindavana pastimes. How To Get There: (see map no. 18).

## 36 Pichalni-Shila /Cowherd Boys Slide (Kalavati)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “On Chandrasena-parvata is pichalni-shila. At this place Krishna plays along with His friends. Sitting in a bending form they slid down the rock again and again.” Situated on the side of a hill is this natural rock slide that is used even today by the local children. Krishna and His friends used to come here for herding the cows and would enjoy many long hours playing on this slide. The word 'pichalni' means 'sliding stone' and ‘shila' means a 'stone', or 'rock'. The Bhakti-ratnakara says that the side of the hill on which the pichalni-shila is located is called Chandrasena Parvata, or Indrasena Parvata, or sometimes as Indranila Parvata. However, this hill is known locally as Pichal Pihari. The word 'pichal' refers to the 'slide' and 'pihari' means a 'mountain'. Locals also refer to this rock slide as khisasini-shila, or pishalini-shila, which are both corruptions of the word pishalni-shila. The cowherd boys slide is located in the village of Kalavati. The word 'kalavati' means the 'place of the dance' and it was here where the gopis assembled and engaged in singing songs glorifying Krishna and dancing in circles with one-another. When Krishna heard the rhythmic jingling of the gopi's ankle bells and the sweet sound of their singing, He came here to witness the wonderful dancing of the cowherd girls. Top How To Get There: This place is 2km outside Kaman on the road to Pahari Town and situated behind the village of Kalavata (see map no. 18 & 18A).

## 37 Vyomasura Gufa

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Chaursyakhela is the mountain where Vyomasura hid the cowherd boys and was then killed by Krishna.” Situated on the side of a mountain is the cave or gufa of the demon Vyomasura. Located nearby are Krishna's lotus handprints and the imprints of His flower garland and Kaustuba necklace. On the opposite side of the road are the lotus footprints of Lord Balarama. The Bhakti-ratnakara mentions that this is the site where Shri Krishna killed the demon Vyomasura. This particular part of the mountain is known as Chaursya-khela Parvata because Krishna and the cowherd boys were playing a game (khela) of cops and robbers and the word ‘chaursya', or ‘chaur' means ' thief'. Thus the game named ‘chaursya-khela' means ‘cops and robbers'.

The term 'vyoma' refers to a type of demon or asura that by dint of mystic powers can fly in the sky at will. The word ‘vyoma' means ‘sky'. The demon Vyomasura, in his previous life, had been a king named Bhimaratha who ruled the kingdom of Kashi. He was a devotee of Lord Vishnu and was always performing sacrifices. Eventually he left the kingdom to his son and retired to perform penance on the Malaya Mountain in Southern India. One day the great sage and son of Lord Brahma, Pulastya Muni, arrived at Bhimaratha's ashrama, but due to his false pride in being a great personality and performer of severe penances, Bhimaratha failed to receive the great sage in the proper manner and neglected to either rise from his seat or offer any respects to such an exalted visitor. Infuriated at the insulting behavior of Bhimaratha, the great sage Pulastya cursed him by saying. “O great rascal, immediately become a demon.”

Within a short time, Bhimaratha left his body and in his next life took birth as Vyomasura, the son of the asura Maya Danava. During the despotic rule of King Kamsa, many great demons were engaged in helping him in consolidating his hold on power and expanding his dominance over other kings. The demon Vyomasura was also one of Kamsa's supporters and one day he was asked by Kamsa to go to Vrindavana and kill the cowherd boy named Krishna. The Bhagavatam says that on that particular day, Krishna was at Govardhana Hill with His cowherd boyfriends playing a game of 'cops and robbers'. However, the Gopala-campu of Shrila Jiva Goswami says that Krishna was playing near Kamyavana and not Govardhana. Some boys played the part of police constables, some played the part of thieves, and others played the part of lambs. The game involved the police trying to catch the thieves who were stealing the lambs. Arriving on the scene, Vyomasura, by dint his mystic power, assumed the form of a cowherd boy and played the part of a thief. One by one he began stealing the cowherd boys that were playing the part of lambs, and after carrying them away, hid them in a cave and rolled a big rock in front of the cave entrance to close it. Gradually the demon stole almost all of the cowherd boys playing with Krishna.

Krishna was wondering where all the cowherd boys have gone, as only four or five boys remained playing the game. Contemplating the situation, Krishna then noticed that a very cunning demon was masquerading as one of the cowherd boys. Without any warning Krishna suddenly caught hold of the demon in the same way that a lion catches a lamb. Feeling the strong grip of Krishna and fearing for his life, the demon Vyomasura began to expand his body into a gigantic size and attempted to escape by flying high into the sky. Nevertheless, he could not free himself from Krishna's powerful grip. A fierce battle then ensued between the demon Vyomasura and Krishna, sometimes they fought on the land and sometimes in the sky. The whole earth began to shake as if an earthquake was about to strike and Balarama had to press His foot down firmly on the ground to keep the earth steady. As the demon flew in the sky, all of a sudden Krishna lost His grip and fell to the earth on all fours, leaving behind the imprints of His hands on the rocks along with His flower garland that fell off. Krishna's Kaustuba necklace also fell off and landed nearby. In an angry mood, Krishna suddenly reached up into the sky and catching the demon Vyomasura by the arm Krishna pulled him down and slammed him into the ground with such force, that the demon died on the spot. Krishna then released all the cowherd boys from within the cave where they had been hidden.

Regarding the Shrimad-Bhagavatam saying that the cowherd boys were playing at Govardhana Hill, Shrila Jiva Goswami has clarified this point by saying they were playing at Chaursyakhela Parvata. The Vaishnava acharyas are empowered representatives of Vyasadeva and his son Sukadeva Goswami and therefore have the authority and vision to clarify any apparent contradictions. Factually all the mountains in the west of Vraja belong to the mountain range known as the Aravallis, and Govardhana Parvata is recognized as one its major peaks. It could be that at some time in history the entire mountain range was known as Govardhana. The Aravallis are considered amongst the world's oldest mountains dating from the pre-Cambrian period more than five hundred million years ago. It is also a geological fact that the entire Aravalli mountain range, including Govardhana Hill, is slowly disappearing. Therefore, it can be said that modern science confirms the statements found in the ancient Vedic literatures that Govardhana Hill is slowly sinking into the earth due to the curse of Pulastya Muni.

How To Get There: Follow the same directions for Pichalina-shila, but continue along the main road to Pahari for another 100mt and the cave is situated on a hill to the right (see map no. 18 & 18A).

## 38 Balarama Charana-Chinnha

This is where one can see the lotus footprint of Lord Balarama impressed upon a rock. When Krishna was fighting the demon Vyomasura, the earth started shaking so violently that Lord Balarama had to press His foot down very hard on the ground to steady it. The word 'charana' means 'lotus feet' and 'chinnha' means 'indented'.

How To Get There: Follow the same directions for Vyomasura's Cave and Balarama Charana-chinha is on the opposite side of the road from the cave (See map no. 18 & 18A).

## 39 Bhojana Thali (Bhojana Sthali)

This is the site of the famous Bhojana Thali where Shri Krishna enjoyed a great feast with His cowherd boyfriends. The word 'bhojana' means 'food', or sometimes 'taking food' and the word 'thali' means a 'plate'. At this spot one can clearly see on the floor the impression of the plates (thali) and cups (katori) used by Krishna and His friends when they all sat down together and took their lunch. Nearby is the spot where Balarama spilled His condensed milk or 'kshira', which ran down across the floor and created a kunda that became known as Kshira Sagar, or the 'ocean of condensed milk'. A white line can be seen that marks the place where Balrama's condensed milk was spilled. One can also see Krishna's special sitting place known as a simhasana and the bhajana-shila, which is a rock with a hollow center that makes a sound like a bell when struck. Some of the cowherd boys were expert in playing tunes on these musical rocks. The word 'bhajana' means 'singing' or 'playing' musical instruments and 'shila' means a 'rock'.

Situated nearby on a small hill behind Bhojana Thali is the Parashurama-tapabhumi where it is said Lord Parashurama, the incarnation of Lord Vishnu, once performed austerities. It is said that Lord Parashurama was born in the holy dhama of Vrindavana at the village of Renuka Grama on the bank of the Yamuna near Agravana (Agra), where the ashrama of his father Jamadagni Rishi was situated. There were also a number of sacred kundas surrounding Bhojana Sthali but they have now disappeared including: Narasimha-kunda, Prahlada-kunda, Matsya-kunda, Govinda-kunda, Gopala-kunda, Shantanu-kunda, Avantika-kunda, Haridwara-kunda and Gupta-ganga.

How To Get There: This place is 2km from Kaman on the right side of road to Pahari Town just 100mt past the village of Kalavati, just opposite to Vyomashuras Cave (see map no. 18 & 18A).

End of Kamyavana external parikrama

## 63 Paigram (Pai)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “It was in Paigrama where Shri Radhika and Her sakhis caught hold of Krishna after searching for Him.” One day Radha and Krishna were playing hide and seek along with the gopis. When it was Krishna's turn to hide the gopis couldn't find Him anywhere. After searching here and there for a long time, the gopis naturally started to feel separation from their beloved Krishna. They then began crying out saying. “We can't find Him? We can't find Him?” Then all of a sudden they arrived at the place where Krishna was hiding and quickly catching hold of Him they excitedly began shouting. “We found Him, We found Him.” The word ‘pai' means to obtain and thus the village became known as Paigrama, the village where the gopis obtained Krishna.

How To Get There: This place is 19km northwest of Kaman (See map no.19).

## 64 Nagla Vanachariya

A vanachari is someone who lives in the forest. Once, some of the gopis were talking amongst themselves saying that Krishna was a vanachari, because He was always found roaming in the forests of Vraja. He always wears a garland of forest flowers and often sits under the trees in the forest playing on His bamboo flute; we also see Him playing with His friends on the banks of the Yamuna. Because the gopis were talking about Krishna being a vanachari at this place, the village became known as Vanachariya and the word ‘nagla' means a hamlet.

How To Get There: This place 4km south-east of Pai (See map no.19).

## 65 Parehi

Krishna often boasted about His prowess in front of the gopis who usually laughed to hear Krishna's boasting words. While at this place Krishna requested the gopis that they should no longer laugh at Him, or try to make fun of Him, or tease Him, as they had done in the past, as it was really vexing for a great hero like Himself. The word ‘pare' as in ‘ke pare' means ‘in the past' and ‘paresan' means ‘vexing', or ‘troubling' and thus the village received the name Parehi. How To Get There: This place is 6Km south of Pai & 2.5km south-west of Nagla Vanchariya (See map no.19).

## 66 Patharali

According to legend, this is the place where the gopis waited for a long time for Krishna to return to engage in loving pastimes with them. The gopis sat near the pathway on which Krishna had left after He had assured them that He would soon return. The gopis waited for a very long time and kept looking down the pathway to see if Krishna was returning. The gopis kept telling each other that Krishna will soon come back and repeatedly looked towards the path in expectation of Krishna's return. Therefore the village became known as ‘Patharali', which means the ‘forest pathway' where the gopis waited for Krishna to return.

How To Get There: Not located

## 67 Naganya

The local legend says that one day the gopis were fetching water for their families when their minds became captivated by the enchanting sound of Krishna's flute. Although they wanted to abandon their duties and run to Krishna, they could not and therefore felt frustrated at not being able to enjoy pastimes with Him. The following day the gopis complained to Krishna saying “why were you playing your flute at a time when we were all engaged in our household duties.” Krishna feigned ignorance of the matter and then the gopis said, “Who was that person sitting under the tamala tree playing such attractive tunes on the flute?” Krishna then replied by saying, “Ham nehi gaya, ham nehi bolaya - I didn’t go there and I didn’t call you.” Therefore the name of the village became ‘Naganya' and is derived from the words ‘nehi gaya'.

How To Get There: Not located

## 68 Shatona / Satvasa (Satwas)

This village was known as Shantanu, but later it became Satoya, then Satona and later Satvasa, and presently Satwas. The village was formerly named Shantanu because it is said that a sage named Shantanu Muni once worshiped Lord Krishna at this place. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “In Shatona-grama Shri Shantanu Muni worshiped Krishna.” According to the local legend, Satrajita Maharaja, who was the father of Queen Satyabhama, one of Lord Krishna's wives in Dwaraka, is said to have performed austerities here to please the sun-god Surya, thus the village became known as Satvasa after Satrajita Maharaja. According the Shrimad-Bhagavatam, after being pleased with the great tapasya of Satrajita Maharaja, Surya fulfilled his desire and awarded him a fabulous gem-stone called the Shyamantaka-mani; this powerful gem was by its own power was producing a large quantity of gold-dust every day. This gemstone made Satrajita a very wealthy man but ultimately led to his downfall when he was mercilessly killed by those who wanted to possess the gemstone. In the village one can see Surya-kunda and a temple dedicated to the sun-god Surya-Narayana. According to the Vraja-riti-chintamani (2.52) while describing the holy places around Kamyavana, it says that Shrimati Radharani also worshiped the sun-god Surya at this same place, "By a lake there, at the place the people call Shantanu-vasa, is a sun-god Deity Shri Radha worships. On the pretext of seeing him She gives that Deity a chance to see Her."

How To Get There:: This place is 3km south of Parehi (See map no.19).

## 69 Papadi

The word papadi' means a leaf or flower-petal that has fallen from the tree, which usually occurs during the autumn season. At this place the gopis made a throne from these flower petals and leaves, thus the village became known as Papadi. After sitting Radha and Krishna on the flower petal throne they presented Them both with very beautiful crowns made from fresh flowers and they also offered Radha and Krishna nice garlands and other items all made from sweet smelling flowers.

How To Get There: This place is 1.5km east of Satvasa (See map no.19).

## 70 Nandera

It is said that many dear friends and associates of Nanda Maharaja used to live in this village but now most of the inhabitants are Mohammedans.

How To Get There: This place is 2.5km south-west of Satwasa (See map no.19).

## 71 Nagla Sitarama

Once Radha and Krishna met with the gopis at this place to have some fun, they dressed Krishna as Lord Ramacandra and dressed Radharani as Sita Devi and imitated the Lord's pastimes described in the Ramayana. Thus the village became known as Sitarama. The word 'nagala' means a 'hamlet', or a small village.

How To Get There: This place is 2km east of Nandera & 2.5km south of Papadi (See map no.19).

## 72 Kanabada (Kanwari)

It is said that one day the gopis dressed-up Radharani as the Queen of Vrindavana, one gopi became the gatekeeper and others became footservants. To have some fun, Krishna and His friends Subala and Sudama, dressed up as gopis and came to this place and asked the gatekeeper if they could see the greatly noble Queen Radha. The gatekeeper then went and informed the queen that some unusual looking gopis had come to see to Her. Speaking in a very stern and grave voice, the queen said, “What do they want here?” Hearing these very sharp words of the queen, Krishna and His friends decided that it might be safer if they very quietly left that place otherwise they might be arrested as imposters by the footservants of the queen and given a good slapping.

How To Get There: This place is 3.5km east of Nagla Sitarama (See map no.19).

## 73 Udha Grama (Udaka)

According to the Bhakti-ratnakara, Krishna's friend Uddhava stayed here when he was on his way from Mathura to Nandagrama to deliver Krishna's message to the gopis.

How To Get There: This place is 3km south of Kanwari & 2.5km north-east of Kaman (See map no.19).

## 74 Dhulauda Grama (Dilawati)

In the Bhakti-ratnakara it says, "O Shrinivasa, see here Dhulauda Grama where the sky became filled with the dust raised by the cows.” The word 'dhula' means 'dust' which was raised by the cow's hooves' and 'uda' means that the dust was 'flying around'. When cows are being herded there are always clouds of dust being raised by their hooves as they walk along the dusty trails. This dust raised by cows is considered to be very auspicious and is one of the symbols of Vedic religion. Shri Krishna Himself was always covered in this same sacred dust when He would return from the pasturing grounds in the evening. This dust which covered the Lord's body, hair, and lotus face, simply increased the beauty of His transcendental form. The gopis would congregate in the evenings waiting for Krishna to return home to Nandagrama with the cows, just to get a glimpse of His exquisite beauty while covered in 'dhula'.

How To Get There: This place is 2km north-east of Udaka (See map no.19).

End of excursion (Return To Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 40 Kanovaro / Kanva (Kanwar)

It is mentioned in the Bhakti-ratnakara that this is the place where the great sage Kanva Muni had an ashrama and where he performed penance, "O Srinivasa, see Kanoyaro-grama where Kanva Muni performed austerities.” In the Shrimad-Bhagavatan, an incident has been recounted where Vishvamitra fell down from his vows and engaged in coitus with the beautiful heavenly Apsara named Menaka, who had been sent by Indra to break the Muni's severe penance. The result was a baby girl who neither Menaka nor Vishvamitra wanted, and who was then abandoned in the forest. Finding the baby girl in the forest, out of compassion Kanva Muni rescued her and raised her in his ashrama. The girl's name was Shakuntala and she grew up to become one of the most beautiful women in the history of the world.

One day, while on a hunting trip, the great king Maharaja Dushmanta of Hastinapura visited the ashrama of Kanva Muni and upon seeing the incredible beauty of Shakuntala, immediately fell in love with her and made a proposal of marriage. According to the rites of the 'gandharva-vivaha', Shakuntala accepted Maharaja Dushmanta as her husband and after spending some time together, the king eventually returned to his kingdom. Within due course of time, Shakuntala gave birth to a son who later became very famous and was known as Bharata Maharaja, who was a partial expansion of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. All the rituals of birth were performed by Kanva Muni who gave the child the name Sarvadhaman. As the child grew up he became so strong that he would play with lions the same as other children play with kittens. He would catch a lion and after opening its mouth count how many teeth it had. When the child reached youth-hood, Shakuntala took him to meet his father Maharaja Dushmanta, the Chandra-vamsha Emperor, in his capital city. Because none of the citizens knew about the king's gandharva-vivaha marriage to Shakuntala, when Maharaja Dushmanta was informed that his son had arrived at the palace, not knowing about the birth, he did not at first acknowledge the existence of any son. At that moment there was an ominous voice from the sky, which proclaimed that this boy was in fact the king's legitimate son, whose name would now be Bharata. Hearing the omen, Dushmanta immediately accepted both Bharata and Shakuntala and they remained with the king at Hastinapur.

After the death of King Dushmanta, his son Bharata Maharaja ascended the throne in 25 million BCE, and expanded the kingdom from the Bay of Bengal to Iran, Turkey, and Greece, and it included all the heavenly varshas, such as Ketumala and Ramnaka, which lay to the west of Meru. These same varshas were later conquered by Parikshit as well as Pradyumna. He became as equally famous as his namesake, Bharata, the son of Lord Rishabha Deva. He also delivered the demigods from the torment of the demons and in recognition the demigods named the tract of land he ruled as Bharatavarsha. (The Bhagavatam says that Bharatavarsha was named after Rishabha's son, Bharata Maharaja). After becoming the Emperor of the world, Bharata Maharaja the son of Dushmanta, performed ninety-nine ashvamedha-yajnas at all the holy places along the banks of the Ganga. He also performed a great sacrifice to Lord Indra in Vraja on the bank of the Yamuna near present-day Agra. (Some say the incident of Bharata's birth from the womb of Shakuntala occurred in the Shivalik Hills where Kanva Muni also had an ashrama; however the Bhakti-ratnakara says that Kanva Muni's ashrama was located at Kanavaro).

How To Get There: This place is 5km south of Kamyavana on the minor road to Varsana (See map no.19 & 20).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 16

Including: \*Indrauli\*Murara.

## 75 Indroli (Indrauli)

It is said that after Indra had been defeated by Krishna he came here and engaged in meditation to properly understand Lord Krishna's position as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. In the Bhakti-ratnakara it says, “This town is called Indroli. At this place Indra engaged in meditation on Lord Krishna.” According to some, Indroli is the village of the gopi Indulekha who is one of the ashta-sakhis or intimate girlfriends of Radharani. There is a kunja located here bearing her name and known as Indulekha Kunja. Indulekha is an expert in chanting mantras and also charming snakes. She knows many arts including palmistry, gemology, weaving, and stringing necklaces. She also carries messages on behalf of the 'divine couple'. However, local legends say Indulekha was born in the village of Anjanauka near Varsana.

How To Get There: This place is 3km south-west of Kanvar (See map no.20).

## 76 Murali (Murar/Murara)

At this place Krishna experienced great pleasure to see the cowherd boys singing and dancing to the rhythmic sounds of His flute playing. The word murali means 'flute' as well as being one of Krishna's names meaning the 'flute player' and thus the village was named Murali. At the present time the village is known as Murar.

How To Get There: This village is 2.5km south of Indroli (See map no.20).

End of excursion (Return to Vraja Mandala Parikrama route

## 41 Kadamba-Khandi

The word 'khandi' means a 'forest grove' containing the same variety of trees and therefore the term kadamba-khandi refers to a large grove of sweet smelling kadamba trees. At this place surrounded by kadamba trees, one can see the Kadamba-khandi Mandira. Although the majority of trees are kadamba there are also some very large banyana trees growing here. There is also a large kunda about one hundred meters to the south of the Mandira known as Krishna-kunda (Ratna-kunda) and a smaller kunda known as Panihari-kunda where the gopis would collect water. One can also see a kadamba tree entwined with a tamala tree, which Vrajavasis believe represents the 'divine lovers' Radha and Krishna. Kadamba-khandi is the place where Radha and Krishna performed 'rasa-lila' pastimes with the gopis on the crest of the nearby hill where there is a Rasa-mandala shrine that commemorates the event. There is also a rasa-mandala platform 500 meters to the south, on the road to Kanvara, where rasa-lila pastimes were also performed and where a large garden maintained by the Nimbarka-sampradaya is located.

Every year during the month of Bhadra (August/September) a festival is held at Kadamba-khandi where dramatic performances of krishna-lila are enacted in front of large crowds. Shrila Narayana Bhatta was the first to introduce the tradition of krishna-lila dramas that are now part of Vrajavasi folk-culture. It was Narayana Bhatta who discovered Kadamba-khandi and spent some time living here engaged in bhajana. He established the tradition of rasa-lila performances as a means to keep alive the memory of Krishna's pastimes.

Kadamba-Khandi was also the place where the famous tyagi-baba named Nagaji Maharaja performed his bhajana. The word 'naga' or 'nagaji' indicates a naked ascetic and the word 'kathiya' means a large wooden shackle or belt worn around the waist as an act of penance. It is believed that Nagaji was born at Paya Gaon and is one of the few Vrajavasis to renounce the world and follow an ascetic lifestyle. It is said he became the 39th acharya in the Kathiya-baba lineage belonging to the Nimbarka sampradaya and became known as Chatur-chintamani Devacharya. There is a shrine in the temple here that is dedicated to Nagaji, however at the present time most of the ascetics performing bhajana here and managing the Kadamba-Khandi Mandira and ashrama belong to the Gaudiya sampradaya.

How To Get There: This place lies 3.5km east of Kanwar near the village of Harnarayana (See map no.20A & 20B).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 17

Including: \*Nagla Harnarayana\*Nagla Harasukh\*Nandola\*Dana\*Bhajera.

## 77 Hara Narayana (Nagla Harnarayana)

At this place Shri Krishna assumed the form of Lord Narayana. Such pastimes where Krishna appears as Lord Narayana are specifically meant to please the cowherd boys and sometimes to test the love of the gopis.

How To Get There: This place is 500mt north Kadamba Kandhi (See map no.20B).

## 78 Harasukha (Nagla Harasukh)

The word 'Hara' refers to 'Krishna' and the word 'sukha' means 'pleasure' or 'satisfaction'. At this place, Krishna who is also known as Harideva, the lifter of Govardhana Hill, gave immense pleasure to the gopis by fulfilling each gopi's inner desire to satisfy Him through intimate embraces and other exchanges of transcendental love.

How To Get There: Harasukha is 500mt south of Harnarayana on the road to Mullaka (See map no. 20B).

## 79 Nandola

At this place the gopis made a nice bed of flower petals where Radha and Krishna could rest after performing rasa-lila at nearby Kadamba-khandi.

How To Get There: This place is north of Kadamba Kandhi (See map no.20B).

## 80 Dana

One day the cowherd boys were passing by this place when they suddenly noticed a peacock's feather lying on the ground. Seeing that the peacock's feather was showing signs of wear and tear, they concluded that this was proof that their beloved friend Krishna must have danced at this place along with the peacocks. In the local language, the word 'dana' means a 'peacock-feather' but it can also mean a 'gift' or a ‘donation', which implies that the peacocks leave behind their beautiful feathers as a 'dana' or gift, and this is how the village got its name. How To Get There: This village 1km north of Nandola &1km east of Bhajera (See map no.20B).

## 81 Bhajera

This village is the birthplace of the twin sisters Sudevi and Rangadevi who are amongst the eight most intimate gopi friends of Radharani known as the ashta-sakhis. Sudevi always combs and arranges Radha's hair, anoints Her eyes with mascara and massages Her body with scented oils. Rangadevi likes to joke around with Radha especially when She is with Krishna. She also likes to fan the ‘divine couple' when They are sitting together. Rangadevi is also an expert in both logic and diplomacy and due to past austerities she has attained a mantra whereby she can attract Krishna. She also has the power to control various forest animals. Both sisters are yutheshvaras, or leaders of their own group of younger gopis.

How To Get There: This place is 1km west of Bana (See map no.20B).

End of excursion (Return to Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 42 Svarnahara (Sunhera)

In the Bhakti-ratnakara it is said, “Krishna had many pastimes at Svarnahara, which is also known both as Sonar and Sonhera. The happiness enjoyed by Krishna as He used to herd His cows around the mountain is impossible to describe.” It is said that the village was so named due to its proximity to the mountain known as Suvarnachala, which means the ‘Golden Mountain'. The words 'svarna', 'sonar' and 'sonhera' all refer to gold. Another reason for the name of this village being Swarnahara, is because of a fabulous golden necklace that Radharani was once wearing while performing worship of Lord Shiva at this place. The gopis often worshiped the demigods like Shiva and Durga simply to get Krishna as their husband. Therefore, because the goal of worshiping the demigods was only to achieve Krishna's pure devotional service, it is not considered to be on the mundane material platform. Needless to say, such activities should not be imitated by devotees not on the same level as the gopis of Vraja. Some say that the ashta-sakhi gopi named Champakalata was born in this village and in Chaitanya-lila she appeared as Lord Chaitanya's close associate Shivananda Sena. The twin sisters Sudevi and Rangadevi were born in nearby village of Bhajera.

How To Get There: This village is about 2km east of Bhajera & 3km west of Unchagram (See map no.20B &21).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 18

Including: \*Akata\*Radha Nagari.

## 82 Ata Grama (Akata)

This secluded and peaceful place is where Krishna was playing with His friends. They became so absorbed in their pastimes, that they completely forgot what time of day it was. It is mentioned in the Bhakti-ratnakara, that Krishna and His friends played non-stop for twenty four hours, which is equivalent to eight praharas or ‘atho praharas'. Thus the name of this village became Ata Grama derived from the word atho, or ashta, meaning eight. Now the village is known as Akata which is a corrupted form of the ancient name Ata Grama.

How To Get There: This place 1km north-east of Akata & 3km north of Sunhara (See map no.19).

## 83 Radha nagari

Local legend says that one of Radha's dear girlfriends used to live in this village. One day this particular girlfriend began to feel intense pangs of separation from Radha and while crying piteously, began calling Radha's name over and over again. In Varshana, Radha heard the piteous cries of Her girlfriend and leaving everything She immediately ran to this village to pacify Her friend. Thus the village where Radha's friend lived became known as Radha Nagari, which means the village that was blessed by Radha.

How To Get There: This place is 2km north-west of Unchagram (See map no.21).

End of excursion (Return to Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 43 Lalita Grama (Unchagrama)
