After many long hours of rasa-dancing, Balarama was feeling a little fatigued and desired to relax in the cooling waters of the Yamuna. Feeling too intoxicated to walk to the river, Balarama called Yamuna Devi to bring her soothing waters to where He was resting, so that He might refresh Himself within the river. Thinking that Balarama was simply too intoxicated with varuni liquor to know what He was saying, Yamuna Devi mistakenly ignored His request. Realizing that Yamuna had ignored His order and refused to come there, Balarama became suddenly very angry and His eyes turned a fierce red color. Picking up His personal weapon the celebrated plough (haladhar), He immediately began to drag the Yamuna towards the arena of the rasa-dance. Realizing her great mistake, Yamuna Devi immediately came before Balarama and throwing herself at His lotus feet, begged for forgiveness. Balarama’s anger was thus pacified by Yamuna's prayers and He entered the river to relax in the cooling water with His many girlfriends. In the Gopala-champu it says that during that full-moon evening, Balarama married all the gopis that came to dance with Him in a special marriage ceremony known as gandharva-vivaha, solemnized simply by the exchange of flower garlands.

Lord Nityananda also visited Rama Ghata during His pilgrimage to Vrindavana and stayed here for a few days absorbed in the mood of a cowherd boy. In the Bhakti-ratnakara it says, “During His pilgrimage, Shri Rasa-vilasi Rama, Nityananda Raya, passed some days here. He played with the cowherd boys and ate curd, milk, roots, and fruits whenever He felt hungry. He was perplexed, trying unsuccessfully to conceal His identity as Baladeva. The local people said, 'this must be Rohini-nandana traveling in Vraja as an avadhuta.' Seeing Nityananda's divine performance, all the people, young and old alike, were bewildered.” Raghava Pandita also showed Shrinivasa and Narottama the sakata-vriksha (Sakata tree), a twig from which Nityananda used to clean His teeth. The Bhakti-ratnakara continues, “At Rama Ghata there was a brahmana who could not live for a moment without the thought of Baladeva. To satisfy his devotee, Nityananda gave him darshana as Baladeva. Here also Kalindi, (Yamuna Devi), offered her prayers to Nityananda. Even the demigods could not restrain their tears of ecstasy as they watched Nityananda sporting at this place. When Nityananda slept on a bed of dust beneath the trees He would call out again and again in His dream, 'When will the emancipation of these wretched souls take place? When will the Lord of Navadwipa advent Himself? I will go and see Him with My own eyes.' No one could understand the meaning of His words.”

How To Get There: This place is 3km east of Shergarh (See map no. 33).

## 60 Viharavana (Biharvan Gaushala)

Viharavana is one of the upavanas or sub-forests of Vrindavana mentioned in the Vraja-bhakti-vilasa. This isolated forest is a place where Krishna and the cowherd boys would bring the cows for grazing. It is also one of the places where Krishna performed rasa-lila pastimes with the gopis. There is a temple here known as Radha-bihari Mandira which is maintained by devotees of the Nimbarka sampradaya. Within this forest is a place known as Kacchavana because there is a kunda located there called Kacchavana-kunda, where Krishna and Balarama and the cowherd boys would play in the water and enjoy themselves by pretending to be turtles. The word 'kaccapa' or 'kacchua' means a turtle. The kunda, which is also called Krishna-kunda as well as Vihara-kunda, is teeming with small turtles. The pastime place of Viharavana is said to have been rediscovered by Shrila Narayana Bhatta.

How To Get There: This place is 1.5km south of Rama Ghata (See map no. 33).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 29

Including: \*Bhushanavana\*Gunjanavana.

## 140 Bhushanavana (Vehata)

This forest is called Bhushanavana because it was here that the cowherd boys decorated Krishna with ornaments made from forest flowers. The word 'bhushana' means 'ornaments'.

How To Get There: This place is 2km east of Viharavana (See map no. 33).

## 141 Gunjanavan

This is where Radharani and the gopis decorated Krishna with ornaments and garlands made from gunja flowers (gunja-mala). After this, Krishna began to decorate Radharani with similar adornments and garlands made from gunja flowers.

How To Get There: This place is just south of Bhushanavana (See map no. 33).

End of excursion (Return to Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 61 Akshaya Vata / Bandira Vata (Kajarotha/Kajraut)

This is the sacred place known as Akshaya Vata where a very large forest of banyana trees stood during Krishna's pastimes. At the present time only one large banyan tree remains which is very famous and known as Akshaya Vata. The word 'akshaya' means 'everlasting' or 'that which never diminishes' and the word 'vata' means a 'banyana tree' (Ficus benghalensi). The famous Bandira Vata (Akshaya Vata) is also mentioned as being one of Vraja Mandala's sixteen famous banyana trees. The Gopala-champu says that this banyana tree located just south of Rama Ghata, was so vast that its roots and sub-branches spread out right across the Yamuna River and the cowherd boys could cross the Yamuna to the other side simply by walking on its branches. The Bhakti-ratnakara says that the forest which lays to the south of Rama Ghata and just north of Tapovana, is called Bhandiravana. This forest is also called simply as Bhandira and the famous banyana tree known as Akshay Vata, is also known as Bhandira Vata. This is the place where Krishna and Balarama used to graze Their calves and enjoy playing games with Their cowherd boyfriends. This same Bhandiravana (Akshaya Vata) is the place where Krishna enjoyed many pastimes with gopis including the famous wrestling match between Radha and Krishna. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “One day as Krishna sat beneath a tree in Bhandira, He played His flute in such an enchanting tone that it could drive the whole world mad. When Radha heard the sound of the flute She became agitated and ran to meet Krishna along with Her friends. In great ecstasy They enjoyed various sporting pastimes here along with the sakhis.”

There is overwhelming evidence that this particular Bhandiravana at Aksaya Vata, lying on the western bank of the Yamuna south of Rama Ghata, is the place where Balarama killed the demon Pralambhasura. There is a small village close to Akshaya Vata called Gadhibhima which is celebrated as the actual spot where the demon Pralambhasura was slain. Therefore this Bhandiravana at Akshaya Vata should not be confused with the sacred forest of Bhandiravana mentioned in the Adi Varaha Purana which is situated on the eastern bank of the Yamuna south of Bhadravana at the village of Chhanhari where the cowherd boys used to take their lunch and where Lord Brahma performed the marriage ceremony of Radha and Krishna.

How To Get There: Akshaya Vata (Bhandira Vata) is 2km south of Viharavana (See map no. 33, 33A & 34).

## The Mystery of the Two Bhandiravana’s

There are some who believe that Pralambhasura was killed in the Bhandiravana (Chhanhari) on the eastern bank of the Yamuna, based on a reference in the Shrimad-Bhagavatam's tenth-canto, but the Bhandiravana mentioned in tenth-canto is without doubt the Bhandiravana at Akshaya Vata, because all the pastimes performed during Krishna's pauganda-lila, when He stayed at Shakatikara and took care of the calves, actually took place on the western bank of the Yamuna River in the area known as Vatsa-krida, or sometimes as Nanda's Vraja. There is no evidence that Krishna performed pastimes on the eastern bank during His pauganda-lila. Only later when Krishna entered His kaishore-lila did He and the cowherd boys cross the Yamuna to the eastern bank for herding the cows.

With regard to Akshaya Vata being the Bandiravana mentioned in the Bhagavatam's tenth-canto, in the same tenth-canto we find a reference saying that Krishna was playing at Govardhana when He killed the Vyomasura demon, however, Shrila Jiva Goswami has clarified that Vyomasura was killed at Kamyavana and not at Govardhana. Elsewhere in the tenth-canto it often says that after having spent the day herding the calves and cows, Krishna returned to Vrindavana in the evening along with the cowherd boys. However, Krishna was in fact returning to either Shakatikara, where He lived during the period of His pauganda-lila or Nandagrama, where He lived during the period of His kaishore-lila. Therefore it is important to hear the opinion of the Gaudiya Vaishnava acharyas in order to properly understand the meaning of the Bhagavatam's verses. In this regard Shrila Raghava Pandita Goswami, one of the foremost authorities on Vraja Mandala, has stated that Pralambhasura was killed near Akshaya Vata. Another important authority is Shrila Narayana Bhatta, who extensively researched Vraja Mandala and wrote the famous book Vraja-bhakti-vilasa, and he also concurs that Pralambhasura was killed at Akshaya Vata.

The Bhakti-ratnakara mentions, “While traveling on the path from Rama Ghata, the great beauty of the Bhandira forest created restlessness within the minds of Raghava Pandita, Shrinivasa, and Narottama”. This verse confirms that there was a forest named Bhandira lying to the south of Rama Ghata. The Bhakti-ratnakara further states, "Look at this beautiful place called Bhandira Vata, presently people call this place as Akshaya Vata. At this place Balarama and Krishna enjoyed their sports. As they played games with Their sakhas, the demon Pralambasura in disguise also joined them. Balarama in fun killed Pralambha and in this way Krishna and Balarama enjoyed various pastimes with the sakhas here.” This verse from Bhakti-ratnakara confirms that Pralambhasura was killed at Akshaya Vata, which is also called Bhandiravana.

In the Bhakti-ratnakara it is said, "Just see Ara Grama and Munjatavi near Bhandira where Krishna swallowed the forest fire to rescue the cows and cowherd boys.” Ara Grama is a few kilometers west of Akshaya Vata. The Vraja-riti-chintamani by Shrila Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura mentions that Gopi Ghata and Munjatavi, which lie on the western bank of the Yamuna, are both within the Bhandiravana forest, thus further confirming that Bhandiravana, Bhandira Vata and Akshaya Vata, are one and the same place. This same Bhandira Vata where Balarama killed Pralambhasura is also the place where the wrestling pastimes between Radha and Krishna took place and where Krishna called the gopis with His flute. The Bhandiravana south of Rama Ghata presently called Akshaya Vata is without doubt the more prominent of the two forests called Bhandiravana. This is confirmed by numerous Gaudiya Vaishnava authorities through their writings on Vraja including, Raghunatha Dasa Goswami, Jiva Goswami, Narahari Chakravarti Thakura, Kavi Karnapura, Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura and Narayana Bhatta.

The Gopala-champu also confirms that Bhandira Vata (Akshaya Vata) located in the forest of Bhandiravana is on the western bank of the Yamuna when it says, "On the western bank of the Yamuna to the north of Bhandiravata is Rama Ghata.” This verse places Bhandiravata, now called Akshaya Vata, just south of Rama Ghata and on the western bank of the Yamuna. Thus there is ample evidence that whenever the Gaudiya Goswamis mention Bhandira Vata or Bhandiravana in their writings they are referring to the place presently known as Akshaya Vata.

The Chaitanya-charitamrita also establishes Akshaya Vata as being called Bhandiravana in the following verses, “Afterwards, Shri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu saw Khela-tirtha (Kelanavana) and then went to Bhandiravana. Crossing the Yamuna River He went to Bhadravana. He then visited Shrivana and Lohavana and then went to Mahavana and saw Gokula.” These verses from Chaitanya-charitamrita confirm that this is the Bhandiravan that Shri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu visited located on the western bank of the Yamuna just south of Rama Ghata. Thus according to the vision of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, Akshaya Vata is the actual location of the Bhandiravana, where Krishna enjoyed His transcendental pastimes especially those pastimes that took place during the period of His pauganda-lila. Furthermore, there is no record that Lord Chaitanya ever going to the Bhandiravana on the eastern side of the Yamuna, which the Bhakti-ratnakara calls Bhandari Grama, although Lord Chaitanya must have passed nearby to that place on His way to Bilvavana.

It is quite evident that at the time of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and the Six Goswamis, the sacred banyana tree at Akshaya Vata was recognized as being the famous Bhandira Vata of Vraja Mandala and the surrounding forest was known as Bhandiravana, where Krishna's pauganda-lila pastimes took place and again during His Kaishore-lila, this is where Radha and Krishna enjoyed many transcendental pastimes like the wrestling match. There will always be a number of divergent opinions amongst the research scholars regarding Bhandiravana, besides other holy places in the region of Vraja. There is very little historical evidence available other than that written by the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, therefore one should accept the opinion of the great liberated souls (nitya-siddhas) and the empowered acharyas in the line descending from the 'Golden Avatara' Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, including the Six Goswamis and their followers, who were the first to excavate and write about the holy places of Vraja Mandala. It is only through their empowered writings that we can ascertain the actual truth regarding the location of Krishna's pastime places.

Another reason for the confusion between the two Bhandiravanas arises because the Adi-Varaha Purana mentions Bhandiravana as being the eleventh sacred forest of Vrindavana (the eighth forest visited by Vraja Mandala Parikrama), which lies on the eastern bank of the Yamuna just south of Bhadravana. Nevertheless, there is sufficient evidence to show that there are two Bhandiravanas, with the one at Akshaya Vata being the more prominent and the place where a majority of Krishna's transcendental pastimes took place. It should also be noted that in different kalpas the twelve sacred forests (dwadasa-vanas) are sometimes located in different places. In some Puranas, the names of the twelve sacred forests vary and Kokilavana is listed as one of the dwadasa-vanas in place of Khadiravana. Another confusing factor is the false propaganda by local panditas promoting their own version of events for material gain. Many Sanskrit scholars have complained that one or two of the Puranas have also been interpolated in order to present a version favorable to a particular group or sampradaya as happened in the case of a scurrilous version of the Brahma-vaivarta Purana, which unreservedly promotes the interests of a particular sampradaya.

## Radha and Krishna’s Pastimes at Bhandira Vata

There were many famous pastimes at Akshaya Vata between Radha and Krishna and in the Bhakti-ratnakara it is said, “One day Radha asked Krishna in Her soft voice, 'How do you play with your friends at this place?’ Krishna answered, 'I dress as a wrestler and I wrestle with my friends. No one knows wrestling like Me and I win very easily.’ Lalita smiled and requested Krishna again and again to show them His wrestling while dressed-up in His wrestlers dress. They then changed into wrestlers costumes, but Krishna was very proud of His dress. Radha smiled sweetly when She saw Krishna’s wrestling costume and They both entered the wrestling arena. There was no question of winning or losing in that wrestling match and Kandarpa, the god of love, was satisfied to watch the game. In this way, various wonderful pastimes were performed in Bhandiravana. Who can describe them all?” The Bhandiravana mentioned here in this verse from the Bhakti-ratnakara is the one located at Akshaya Vata as this verse is found in the section of the book describing Akshaya Vata.

In the Vraja-vilasa-stava of Raghunatha Dasa Goswami it says, “In the forest of Bhandira, my beautiful queen, proud Shri Radha, started a wrestling competition amongst Her closest friends. When She eagerly wrestled with Lord Krishna, the enemy of Bakasura, She brought great happiness to Cupid, the god of love. Let me worship that forest of Bhandiravana.” Because the Gaudiya Goswamis always refer to Bhandiravana as being the forest located to the south of Rama Ghata, these references from the writings of Shrila Raghunatha Goswami obviously refer to the Bhandiravana at Akshaya Vata.

The Bhakti-ratnakara gives another description of the transcendental pastime that occurred at Akshaya Vata, “One day, Krishna sat beneath a vata tree in Bhandira, He played his flute in such an enchanting tone that it could drive the whole world mad. When Radha heard the sound of the flute, She became agitated and ran to meet Krishna along with her girlfriends. In great ecstasy, Radha and Krishna then enjoyed various sporting pastimes here along with Their sakhis.” This verse from Bhakti-ratnakara is found in the section describing Akshaya Vata. However, Krishna enjoyed pastimes with the gopis at both the Bhandira Vata’s located on the western as well as eastern banks of the Yamuna.

How To Get There: Akshaya Vata (Bhandira Vata) is 2km south of Viharavana (See map no. 33, 33A & 34).

## The Slaying of Pralambhasura at Bhandira Vata

One day while herding Their calves in the vicinity of Akshaya Vata, Krishna and Balarama along with Their cowherd boyfriends, began a game where those who lost had to carry the winners on their shoulders. Having been ordered by King Kamsa to kill Krishna and Balarama, the demon Pralambhasura, who by dint of his mystic power, had assumed the form of a cowherd ‘boy’, and cleverly mingled with the other boys, but his intention was to kidnap Krishna and Balarama and then kill Them. The demon disguised as a cowherd boy, joined Krishna’s team and in the next round of the competition, Krishna’s team lost, therefore Krishna had to carry Shridama on His shoulders and the demon Pralambha had to carry Balarama. While carrying Balarama on his shoulders, Pralambhasura began running at great speed and carried Balarama faraway with the intention of killing Him. However, Balarama appeared to be getting heavier and heavier by the minute, and therefore Pralambhasura was forced to assume his original demonic form. Balarama suddenly noticed that the cowherd boy carrying Him had abruptly changed his appearance and had transformed into giant black colored demon with long sharpened teeth. At that moment, Balarama decided it was time to slay this sinful and ugly looking rascal and immediately struck the demon on the head with His powerful fist. Pralambhasura immediately cried out in great pain and while spewing blood from his gaping mouth, fell to the ground dead. Krishna then arrived there with all the cowherd boys and congratulated Balarama for His heroic feat in killing the demon Pralambha.

## 62 Tapovana (Gopi Ghata)

Tapovana is mentioned in the Vraja-bhakti-vilasa to be one of the upavanas or subforests of Vrindavana. This sacred tirtha near the banks of the Yamuna is where the gopis performed tapasya during the month-long katyayani-vrata to achieve Krishna as their husband. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, ”In Tapovana the daughters of the cowherd men performed tapasya.” The name Tapovana is derived from the words 'tapa' or 'tapasya' which means to perform 'austerities', and 'vana' means 'forest'. There is a temple here known as the Radha Gunja-bihari Mandira. It is said that the gopis who performed tapasya at Tapovana were the kripa-siddha and sadhana-siddha gopis who took birth in Vrindavana to take part in Krishna's pastimes. Amongst these new gopis were those who had been the sages of Naimisharanya and had received the benediction from Lord Ramachandra to take their next birth as gopis in Vrindavana and achieve the divine association of Krishna. Another group were the Apsaras who were blessed by Nara-Narayana Rishi to achieve the position of gopis in Krishna's Vrindavana pastimes.

Gopi Ghata is the name of the bathing place on the Yamuna River at Tapovana where the gopis would take their ritualistic bath during the brahma-muhurta, as part of their month long austerities during the katyayani-vrata. The gopis performed this vrata during the cold season simply to achieve Krishna as their husband. On the last day of the katyayani-vrata, the gopis went to Chira Ghata to worship the Deity of Katyayani Devi.

How To Get There: This place is 1km east of Akshaya Vata (See map no. 33A & 34).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 30

Including: \*Gadhi Bhima\*Agaryala\*Randhera \*Naugawan\* Sedapura.

## 142 Gadhi Bhima

This place is famous amongst the Vrajavasis as the actual spot where Lord Balarama slew the demon Pralambhasura. On the order of King Kamsa, Pralambhasura had entered Vrindavana and after disguising himself as a cowherd boy, he had planned to kidnap both Krishna and Balarama and then kill Them. However his evil plan did not work out and he was instead killed by Lord Balarama.

How To Get There: This place is 2km northwest of Akshaya Vat (See map no. 33 & 34).

## 143 Munjatavi/Ara Grama (Agaryala Grama)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Just see Ara Grama and Munjatavi near Bhandira, where Krishna swallowed the forest fire to rescue the cows and cowherd boys.” Munjatavi forest is located near Ara Grama, which is known today as Agaryala, and is the place where Krishna swallowed the forest fire. In the Shrimad-Bhagavatam it says that the forest where Krishna swallowed the forest fire was named Isikatavi, but they both appear to be the same place known by two different names, Munjatavi and Isikatavi. One day, Krishna and Balarama were absorbed in playing games with Their cowherd boyfriends at Bhandira Vata. Without anyone noticing, the cows slowly drifted away and entered the very dense Munjatavi forest, being attracted by the lush green grass that was growing there. Within a short time, the cows suddenly found themselves being surrounded by a raging forest fire and being trapped began crying out.

Meanwhile, the cowherd boys noticed that their cows had disappeared from Bhandira Vata and began worrying that they may be lost. They then began to search for the cows by following their hoof prints as well as the path of eaten grass and after arriving at Munjatavi, they could hear the crying of the cows. Krishna began calling the cows and when the cows responded, the cowherd boys were able to locate them, but by then, the cowherd boys were also surrounded by the blazing forest fire. Being severely afflicted by the suffocating smoke, the cowherd boys began to collapse on the ground. Having no other shelter, the cowherd boys looked to the transcendental brothers Krishna and Balarama to save them. Assuring the cowherd boys by speaking telepathically through His eyes, Krishna immediately inhaled His breath and simultaneously sucked all the fearful flames into His mouth. When the cowherd boys regained consciousness, they saw that all of them along with the cows had been saved by their friends Krishna and Balarama. The boys then began thinking that Krishna was not an ordinary boy, but must be a demigod that had taken birth amongst them.

How To Get There: This place is 4.5km south of Gadhi Bhima (See map no.34).

## 144 Randhera (Ranhera)

Local legend says that the gopis came here to fetch water and just at that moment Krishna also arrived there while herding His cows and said, “Oh Radhera! I am feeling very thirsty, please give Me some water to drink”. Radharani then gave Krishna some water to drink. 'Radhera', or Radhe, are the 'pet' names used to address Radharani.

How To Get There: This place is 6km west of Agaryala (See map no.34).

## 145 Naugawan (Naugaon)

The word 'naugawan' or 'naujawan' means a 'fresh youth' (naya-jivani). Local legends say that one day Krishna, who had just entered His kaishora-lila as a newly blossoming youth, was out herding the cows when the gopis began to feel intense separation from Him and desired to see His beautiful form. Thus they split into two groups and began searching for their beloved Krishna here and there and eventually came to this place. One group of gopis asked the other if they had found their beloved Krishna and the group of gopis replied “no, we could not find Krishna even after searching everywhere”. The gopis then became distraught and began to cry thinking that Krishna must be lost somewhere in the vast forest.

How To Get There: This place is 8km south-east of Ranhera (See map no.34).

## 146 Sedapura (Saidpur)

One day, Krishna and Balarama were playing here so intently along with Their cowherd boyfriends, that trickles of sweat began rolling down Their lotus faces. The word 'seda' means a 'trickle' of perspiration, and thus the village became known as Sedapura.

How To Get There: This place is 5km west of Naugaon (See map no.34).

End of excursion (Return to Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 63 Chira Ghata (Siyaro)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, "The gopis joyfully worshiped Katyayanidevi at Chira Ghata. They put their clothes here on the bank of the Yamuna as they entered the water for taking bath. Krishna secretly stole their clothes and climbed into a kadamba tree to see the fun. When the gopis realized they had no clothes, they were greatly ashamed and bade Krishna to return their clothes while remaining in the water. After revealing His mind, Krishna jubilantly returned their clothes. The gopis then dressed themselves, but only after they had dedicated themselves to Krishna.”

This is the celebrated ghata where Krishna stole the clothing of the gopis. The word 'chira' means 'clothing'. After following the katyayani-vrata for one month by undergoing austerities at Tapovana, the gopis came here on the final day of the vrata to make a clay image of Katyayani Devi and perform puja by offering incense, flowers, and ghee lamps to the goddess, who is worshiped in her form as eight-armed Durga riding her carrier, a tiger. Before starting the katyayani-puja, the gopis went to take their ceremonial bath in the Yamuna and kept their clothing on the river bank. Meanwhile, understanding the minds of the gopis to obtain Him as their husband, Krishna arrived there and after gathering all the gopi's clothes, climbed into a nearby kadamba tree. Krishna then called the gopis to come and collect their clothing - one at a time, saying He wanted to enjoy the beauty of each slender wasted gopi as she collected her clothing. The gopis were the most beautiful women in the whole universe, far exceeding the beauty of heavenly Apsaras, or even the Lakshmis of Vaikuntha.

At first the gopis strongly protested Krishna's actions, but inwardly they felt very satisfied that Krishna wanted to see them naked and admire their exquisite beauty. In Vedic culture, a young woman should only exhibit her naked beauty before her husband and no one else, therefore, Krishna was assuming the position of each gopi's husband, by seeing them stand before Him in their naked splendor. The gopis realized they had no option but to come out of the Yamuna one at a time. Slowly, each naked gopi emerged from the river to collect her clothing from Krishna's hand, allowing Him to see the incredible beauty of their delicately formed limbs, thus fulfilling the gopi's desire to have Krishna as their husband. After enjoying their beauty, Krishna gave a promise to the gopis that in the near future, during the autumn season, they would be able to enjoy Him as their husband, by engaging with Him in conjugal pastimes in the forest of Vrindavana.

There is a temple here dedicated to goddess Katyayani Devi that commemorates the transcendental pastime that took place here. It is said that this tirtha was re-discovered by Shrila Narayana Bhatta and Shrila Jiva Goswami has confirmed that this is the original Chira Ghata and the actual spot where the gopis worshiped goddess Katyayani and had their clothing stolen by Krishna. Near to Keshi Ghata in Vrindavana, there is another Chira Ghata, although its proper name is Chayana Ghata, where Krishna simply hid the outer garments of the gopis while they bathed in their underwear after performing rasa-lila at Seva Kunja.

How To Get There: Chira Ghata is 1km from Tapovana, and 2km south of Akshaya Vata (See map no.34).

## 64 Gangrauli

It is said that this is the village where Gargamuni, the family priest of Nanda Maharaja had his ashrama and where he had his meeting place (baithaka). Gargamuni, who is also known as Gargacharya, performed the name giving ceremony of Krishna and Balarama and also made various astronomical calculations about both past and future events in Their lives. It is also said that both Krishna and Balarama came here to this ashrama to receive instructions from Gargamuni. There is a Radha Krishna temple in the village containing the Deity of Gargamuni. Next to this temple is Dhoni-kunda, where it is said Krishna was once milking a cow and knocked over the milk pale (dhoni), and the milk that spilled out of the pale caused this kunda to form.

How To Get There: This village is 2km south of Chira Ghata (See map no.34).

## 65 Nanda Ghata (Baigram)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Here at Nanda Ghata, Nanda and the other cowherd men took their bath in the Yamuna River. After fasting on the Ekadashi, Nanda was entering the Kalinda (Yamuna) to take his bath on the Dvadashi. While bathing, a servant of Varuna abducted Nanda, but Krishna easily rescued him. As Nanda had become afraid in this place, Krishna’s great grandson, Vajra, the son of Aniruddha, named this place Bhaya.”

This is the famous ghata on the Yamuna River where Nanda Maharaja was arrested by the servants of Varuna Deva, the demigod of the waters. It so happened that on the occasion of Ekadashi, Nanda Maharaja, Krishna’s father, had fasted the whole day and the following morning, the day of Dwadashi, he decided to take an early morning ritualistic bath in the River Yamuna before breaking fast. Unfortunately, he arrived at the river bank before the appointed hour and as soon as he entered the water to bathe, he was immediately arrested by the servants of Varuna Deva, who accused him of bathing at an improper time and took him away to the court of Varuna to be punished. The moment that Nanda Maharaja was arrested, Nanda’s companions immediately informed Krishna and Balarama about the sudden turn of events. The two transcendental brothers could immediately understand the situation and straight away left for the abode of Varuna to rescue their father Nanda Maharaja.

As soon as Krishna and Balarama arrived at the abode of Varuna, They were welcomed with great respect. Varuna Deva humbly addressed Krishna and Balarama by saying that it was his great fortune to be able to see the Supreme Personality of Godhead present before his eyes, and because of seeing Them, he would not have to take birth again. Varuna also said that because he was personally seeing Krishna and Balarama before his eyes, his life was now perfect. Varuna Deva also apologized on behalf of his servants, who he said had inadvertently arrested Nanda Maharaja and informed Krishna and Balarama that They could now take Their father back home. Varuna further said that it was only by the will of providence that this whole incident had been allowed to take place.

Nanda Ghata is situated near the village of Baigram sometimes called Bhogoan, which are corruptions of the ancient name Bhaya Grama, the name given by Vajranabha Maharaja. The word 'bhaya' means ‘fear’ and the village was so named because both Nanda Maharaja and the cowherd men experienced great fear at this place after Nanda had been arrested by the servants of Varuna. There is a temple here containing the Deities of Nanda Maharaja and mother Yashoda along with Krishna and Balarama.

How To Get There: This place is 3km south of Chira Ghata (See map no.34).

## Jiva Goswami’s stay at Nanda Ghata

Shrila Jiva Goswami spent some time staying at Nanda Ghata where he lived inside an old disused crocodile hole on the bank of the Yamuna. Due to his youthful enthusiasm, he was banished from Vrindavana by Shrila Rupa Goswami because he dared to challenge Vallabha Bhatta, thus displeasing Rupa Goswami, his uncle and spiritual master. One day Vallabha Bhatta, who was later known as Vallabhacharya, paid a visit to Rupa Goswami’s bhajana-kutira at Seva Kunja. When he arrived, Rupa was working on the invocation to his book Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu (Nectar of Devotion). On glancing at the mangalacharana or invocation, Vallabha, who was a greatly learned Sanskrit scholar, pointed out what he thought were some slight discrepancies in the text and offered to edit it. Although Rupa accepted this criticism by Vallabha with great humility, Jiva was disturbed that Vallabha had the audacity to find fault with Rupa Goswami's writing.

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Once Shri Rupa was writing a book in a very quiet place in Vrindavana. It was a hot day, and to dry the sweat from Rupa's body, Shri Jiva would stand nearby fanning him. The beauty of both Shri Rupa and Shri Jiva was effulgent. At that time Shri Vallabha came to visit Rupa. When he saw the mangalacarana of Rupa's Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu, he told Rupa, “I shall edit it.” When he went to bathe in the Yamuna, Shri Jiva followed on the pretext of taking water from the Yamuna.” When Vallabha went to the Yamuna to bathe, Jiva followed him and raised the issue of Vallabha's critique regarding the invocation written by Rupa Goswami. Jiva then systematically refuted with shastric evidence each of the points raised by Vallabha, thus proving to Vallabha that he was wrong in his opinions and that what Rupa had written was actually perfect and needed no editing. Confronted by Jiva's superior knowledge of Sanskrit grammar, Vallabha was defeated and forced to admit, his critique was misguided.

On returning to Rupa's kutira, Vallabha mentioned his encounter with the young sannyasi and the discussion that had ensued, informing Rupa that the original invocation was perfect and needed no correction. Sometime later, when Jiva returned, Rupa Goswami was very upset that Jiva had dared to challenge such a senior devotee and greatly learned scholar like Vallabha Bhatta. Admonishing Jiva for being too proud and lacking in proper Vaishnava humility, Rupa ordered him to return to his home in Bengal until he had learned more about Vaishnava etiquette and humility. He further said that Vallabha Bhatta was only trying to help and that due to Jiva's passionate nature, he had unnecessarily challenged him.

After being rejected by Rupa Goswami, Jiva was on the path out of Vrindavana when he decided it was better to remain in the holy Dhama and undergo severe penance in order to redeem himself in the eyes of Rupa Goswami. He then went to Nanda Ghata and remained there living in an old crocodile hole. Later the Vrajavasis built him a kutira of thatched leaves. He subsisted by performing madhukari, begging a little flour from the local Vrajavasis and after mixing it with water from the Yamuna ate it raw. No one in Vrindavana knew the whereabouts of Jiva until one day, Sanatana Goswami was traveling to some of the holy places nearby, when someone mentioned to him about a young and much renounced sannyasi living at Nanda Ghata. Sanatana was informed that the young sannyasi was very frail and thin due to subsisting only on raw flour and water. Sanatana could immediately understand that the young sannyasi must be his nephew Jiva. After going there and meeting Jiva at Nanda Ghata and hearing everything from him, Sanatana returned to Vrindavana to meet Rupa, whose writing work was suffering due to not having Jiva there to help him. It was Jiva who used to make by hand the paper for writing and he also edited all of Rupa's books.

On arriving in Vrindavana, Rupa Goswami was talking with other Vaishnavas on the subject of giving mercy to all the jivas (living entities). After the talks, Sanatana spoke to Rupa and enquired about the work on his most important book, the Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu. Rupa explained that his book was finished, but since their nephew Jiva's absence, the editing work was incomplete and not going so well. Sanatana then told Rupa that although he was lecturing others about giving mercy to all the jivas, he himself was not. Rupa Goswami could immediately understand the meaning of Sanatana's comment.

After hearing about Jiva's whereabouts from Sanatana, without further delay, Rupa Goswami made arrangements to bring Jiva Goswami back to Vrindavana and after nursing him back to full health, entrusted him with the task of editing the Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu, the most important book on the science of devotional service ever written. Under the direct guidance of his two uncles Rupa and Sanatana, Jiva Goswami went on to become the greatest ever Sanskrit scholar and philosopher that has ever lived. So great was his scholarship, that when the Benares Hindu University was established, a Sanskrit department was named in his honor. After the disappearance of both Rupa and Sanatana, Jiva Goswami was the undisputed leader amongst Lord Chaitanya's followers and became the next acharya of the Gaudiya Vaishnava sampradaya. He went on to write over twenty-five important books of which Sat Sandharba and Gopala-champu are the most well-known.

NOTE: According to historical records, during Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's parikrama of Vraja Mandala, He crossed the Yamuna River at Nanda Ghata and proceeded towards the forest of Bhadravana on the eastern bank of the river. The Vraja Mandala Parikrama followed by ISKCON, also crosses the Yamuna River at Nanda Ghata and proceeds to Bhadravana. According to the Bhakti-ratnakara, during the parikrama of Raghava Pandita, Shrinivasa Acharya and Narottama Dasa Thakura, before crossing the Yamuna at Nanda Ghata, they traveled southward down the western bank of the Yamuna and visited a number of pastime places in this area of Vraja that are related to Krishna's pauganda-lila when He stayed at Shakatikara. The parikrama detailed in the Vraja-bhakti-vilasa also visits these same places. This part of Vraja is spacifically referred to as being 'Nanda's Vraja', where Krishna and Balarama performed Their childhood pastimes of herding the calves and thus it is also known as 'Vatsa-krida' meaning 'playground of the cowherd boys and calves''. After going as far as the village of Atasa, Raghava Pandita and his companions retraced their steps and returned to Nanda Ghata where they crossed the Yamuna River in order to continue their parikrama of Vraja Mandala on the eastern bank of the Yamuna River.

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 31

Including: Basai Buzurg\*Sei\*Vatsavana\*Barahra\*Rasoli\*Bhajana\*Parkhama\*Janai\*Balahara\*Sakroya \*Sapauli\*Taroli/Varoli\*Chaumuhan\*Sihana\*Ajhai\*Jait\*Devi Atas\*Sonarakh.

## 147 Basai (Basai Buzurg)

It is said after stealing all the calves and cowherd boys, Lord Brahma left for his abode in Brahmaloka, however, feeling somewhat anxious about his having stolen the cows and calves, Lord Brahma immediately returned to see what was happening. Although only a few minutes had elapsed of Brahma's time, on earth one whole year had already passed by. From his position hidden in the clouds above this village, he was completely surprised that Krishna was present in the pasturing ground with all the same calves and cowherd boys that he thought he had just stolen. Thus Lord Brahma became completely bewildered by what he saw. The word ‘buzurg' in the name ‘Basai Buzurg' means ‘patriarch' or ‘ancestor' and is a reference to the universal patriarch Prajapati Brahma.

How To Get There: This place is 3km south-west of Nanda Ghata (See map no.35).

## 148 Sei

This village is near the place where Brahma stole the calves and cowherd boys. After Brahma returned to see what had happened, he became bewildered by seeing all the calves and cowherd boys still present with Krishna. Lord Brahma was saying to himself, “Kya ye sei hai." Meaning “Is it true.” Or in other words, Brahma was saying. “Is it true that these are the same calves and cowherd boys that were stolen by me?” The word ‘sei' means the ‘truth', or whatever has been spoken is ‘truthful'. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “At this place Sei which is known by all, Brahma was bewildered by Krishna’s maya. After stealing the cowherd boys and calves, Brahma kept them hidden. But when he returned to Vatsavana, he saw what he thought must be the same boys and calves. Being overwhelmed he repeatedly said, 'Those are these or these are those? Thus the village became known as Sei.”

How To Get There: This village is 2.5km south-west of Basai Buzurg & 6km south-west of Nanda Ghata (See map no.35).

## 149 Vatsavana / Bachavana (Bachwan)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “See here Vatsavana where Brahma stole the calves.” The Vraja-vilasa-stava gives the following description, “I sing the glories of Vatsa-harana-sthali where Brahma, being inquisitive about the glories of Lord Krishna, stole the calves and cowherd boys. To satisfy the long cherished desire of the mothers of the calves and cowherd boys, Krishna then manifested Himself as calves and cowherd boys to eat the food given by their mothers.” Local brahmanas confirm this is the actual spot where the cowherd boys and the calves were stolen by Brahma. Vatsavana is presently known locally as Bachwan, or Bachpan, and both names mean 'children’s forest’ or, 'cowherd boy’s forest’. It is also said that Vatsavana is the place where Krishna slew the demon Vatsasura. The word 'vatsa' can mean a 'calf’ as well as a 'boy’, and 'vana' means 'forest’. Vatsavana is one of the forests where Krishna used to bring His calves and it is also known as 'Vatsa-krida’, which in regard to Krishna’s cow herding pastimes means, the 'playground of the cowherd boys and calves’. This place is less than a kilometer from the village of Sei and in ancient times the forest of Vatsavana covered the area between the villages of Sei and Mai, two miles to the south, with the Yamuna River forming the forest’s eastern border. Unfortunately today, only a few trees remain of what was once a vast and verdant forest.

At Vatsavana one can see the temple of Vatsavana-Bihari, also known locally as Bachapan-Bihari, where one can have darshana the ancient four-armed Deity of Chaturbhuja-Narayana, the same form that Brahma saw manifested by Krishna when he returned from Brahmaloka to review the situation after stealing the calves and cowherd boys. Nearby is the Gwala Mandali where Krishna sat in a circle (mandali) with all the cowherd boys to take their lunch. The word 'gwala' pronounced as 'gowala' means a 'cowherd boy’. Nearby is the sitting place of Vallabhacharya who spoke on Bhagavatam at this place. There is also a drinking water well known as Ganga-bhowari; the word 'bhowari' means a 'large well with steps going down inside it’. Not far away is the Gwala-kunda, which is also known as Brahma-kunda.

How To Get There: This place is 500mt east from the village of Sei (See map no.35 & 35A).

## Brahma Steals the Calves and the Cowherd Boys

This particular pastime of Brahma stealing the calves and cowherd boys occurred when Krishna was residing at Shakatikara and taking care of the calves. Although it is stated in the Bhagavatam that Krishna returned to Vrindavana in the evening with his calves, factually He was returning to Shakatikara. This same description of Krishna returning to Vrindavana in the evening is used even when Krishna was living at Nandagrama. This is because both these places, Shakatikara and Nandagrama, are within the greater Vrindavana forest. This same greater Vrindavana area is also called 'Nanda’s Vraja’ which forms the inner core of Vraja Mandala. Although Vrindavana Dhama (Vraja Mandala) is spread over an area of eighty-four kosas (chaurasi-kosa), which is equal to twenty yojanas or one hundred and sixty-eight miles, there is an inner core measuring just five yojanas which is referred to as being the greater Vrindavana forest. This inner core of Vrindavana covers an area stretching from Seva Kunja to Nandagrama and encompasses the entire region on the western bank of the Yamuna as far north as Kelanvana and then westward to Nandagrama, Varsana and Govardhana. In the Brihad-gautamiya-tantra it says, “The forest of Vrindavana consists of five yojanas.” Thus five yojanas is equal to forty miles which is the distance from Seva Kunja to Nandagrama and this area is repeatedly being mentioned in the Bhagavatam as being Vrindavana. Therefore, whether Krishna is returning to Shakatikara or Nandagram, in the evening with the cows, the Bhagavatam always says that Krishna was returning to Vrindavana.

One morning, after Krishna had gone to the pasturing grounds with His cowherd boyfriends, the powerful demon named Aghasura had attempted to kill Krishna along with all the cowherd boys, but instead, the demon Aghasura was very easily killed by Krishna. Lord Brahma, who was hiding within the clouds along with the host of demigods, had witnessed this extraordinary event. Brahma became somewhat doubtful about Krishna's true identity and began to wonder how this little cowherd boy could exhibit so much power and kill so many big demons that even the demigods were unable to challenge. Brahma pondered on whether or not this cowherd boy could actually be the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as some of the demigods believed. Wishing to see more of Krishna's wonderful activities, and also have some fun, Brahma devised a plan in order to test the prowess of this young cowherd boy.

The Bhagavatam says that on that day, after killing the demon Aghasura, Krishna and the cowherd boys arrived by the banks of the Yamuna at Vatsavana and while the calves grazed nearby, the cowherd boys all sat around in a circle to enjoy their lunch along with Krishna. Balarama did not come on that day because it was His birthday and He stayed at home. While Krishna and His friends were absorbed in taking lunch and talking amongst themselves, the calves wondered off into the distance. Just then, the cowherd boys noticed that the calves had wondered off and they informed Krishna, who told them that they should all finish their lunch, while He would go Himself and fetch the calves.

Krishna began to search for the cows but it appeared that they had just simply vanished and therefore He returned to the place where the cowherd boys were taking lunch. To His surprise, He found that the cowherd boys had also vanished. Krishna, due to His omnipotency, immediately realized that this was a trick being played by Brahma. Not being able to return home without the calves or the cowherd boys, because it would create great distress amongst the boy's mothers, as well as the calves' mothers. Krishna decided that He would expand Himself through His internal potency and take the place of all the missing cowherd boys and calves. He then returned to Vrindavana as if nothing had happened along with all His expansions in the form of the various cowherd boys and their calves. In the Vraja-vilasa-stava of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami it is said, “I sing the glories of Vatsa-harana-sthali where Brahma, being inquisitive about the glories of the Lord, stole the calves and the cowherd boys. To satisfy the long cherished desire of the mothers of the calves and the cowherd boys, Krishna then manifested Himself as calves and cowherd boys to eat the food given by their mothers.”

After Lord Brahma had stolen all the calves and cowherd boys and put them to sleep by his mystic power, he left for his own abode, but then decided to return to see the fun. He was also a little apprehensive and doubtful about his activities, thinking that if Krishna was in fact the Supreme Personality of Godhead, then stealing Krishna's calves and cowherd boyfriends might be deemed as an offense. When Brahma decided to return to Vatsavana, although only a short space of time had elapsed for Brahma, on the earth, a whole year had already passed. Arriving at Vatsavana, Lord Brahma was amazed to see that all the cowherd boys and the calves were still present there along with Krishna. Brahma could not believe what he was seeing and in a state of total bewilderment, he immediately went to the place where he had hidden the calves and cowherd boys and saw they were still sleeping soundly. Brahma again returned and to his great surprise he saw that all the cowherd boys and calves had become transformed into four-armed Vishnu forms. Brahma was absolutely dumbfounded by seeing such an incredible display of Krishna's mystic potency, realizing that it was a grave mistake to display his own feeble power before Krishna as he foolishly attempted to test the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The Shrimad-Bhagavatam (SB.10.13.19) says, “By His Vasudeva feature, Krishna simultaneously expanded Himself into the exact number of missing cowherd boys and calves, with their exact bodily features, their particular types of hands, legs and other limbs, their sticks, bugles and flutes, their lunch bags, their particular types of dress and ornaments placed in various ways, their names, ages and forms, and their special activities and characteristics. By expanding Himself in this way, beautiful Krishna proved the statement samagra-jagad vijnumayam: "Lord Vishnu is all-pervading."

Immediately Brahma came before Krishna and threw himself on the ground just like a stick, begging for forgiveness and offering heartfelt prayers to the lotus feet of the Lord. After Krishna had accepted his apology, Brahma brought all the calves and cowherd boys back to Vatsavana, and when they awoke, they had absolutely no clue of what had happened, or that one whole year had passed by. As it was time to return home, the cowherd boys gathered all the calves and accompanied by Krishna they made their way back to Vrindavana. When they arrived in home, they began telling everyone about how Krishna had killed the demon Aghasura in the morning and how He saved all of them from impending death. The cowherd boys were unaware that due to Brahma's mystic power they had been asleep for a very long period of time and that the Aghasura demon had actually been killed exactly one year earlier.

## The Slaying of Vatsasura

In the forest of Vatsavana, Krishna killed the demon named Vatsasura who assumed the form of a calf in order to kill Krishna and Balarama. After Krishna had moved to Shakatikara and started to look after the calves, Vatsasura was the first of the demons to be killed. In his previous life, Vatsasura was known as Pramila, the son of the demon Maru. He was so powerful that he could fight with the demigods and also defeat them. One day this demon was passing the hermitage of the great sage Vashishta Muni when he saw Vashishta's wish-fulfilling surabhi cow named Nandini. Pramila disguised himself as a brahmana in order to enter the hermitage and steal the cow. Nevertheless, Vashishta Muni, by dint of his mystic power attained through great austerities, could understand that Pramila was not a brahmana but a cow thief. He became exceedingly angry and cursed Pramila saying, “O fool! Because you dared disguise yourself as a brahmana in order to steal this surabhi cow and its calf, then you can now take birth in the bovine species and become a calf yourself.” Pramila was very sorry when he heard the curse and fell at the feet of Vashishta Muni while begging for forgiveness. Being somewhat pacified, Vashishta informed him that in the near future, the Supreme Lord Shri Krishna would appear on earth and while performing His pastimes, would liberate him from the form of a calf. The demon Pramila eventually took birth as Vatsasura and became a close associate of King Kamsa.

When Nanda Maharaja had moved his residence from Gokula to Shakatikara in the forest of Vrindavana, Krishna and Balarama were given charge of grazing the calves. One day Krishna and Balarama, while in the company of Their cowherd boyfriends, were grazing Their calves on the banks of the Yamuna at Vatsavana. After receiving the order from King Kamsa to kill the cowherd boy Krishna, the demon Vatsasura, who possessed the form of a calf, secretly mingled with the other calves in order to get close enough to attack Krishna. But Krishna knew each and every one of His calves by name and quickly noticed that a strange new calf had entered the herd. Turning to Balarama, He asked whether He had also seen this strange new calf mingling with the herd.

The transcendental brothers both realized that this was no ordinary calf but a demon sent by Kamsa to kill Them. The brothers then devised a plan to kill the demon before he had a chance to attack Them. While moving through the forest with the calves, the brothers cleverly doubled back and sneaked up behind Vatsasura, without him being aware of it. Suddenly catching the calf demon by the hind legs and tail, and with the force of a powerful tornado, Krishna whirled the calf-demon around and then catapulted him up into the nearest tree top. The demon was already dead from the powerful whirling even before he reached the tree top. The demons body then fell from the top of the tree to the ground with a thud. Having seen Krishna whirling the demon around and then killing him, the cowherd boys began praising Krishna's prowess in slaying the demon. It is said that Krishna deliberately threw the calf-demon into a very tall bilva tree so that all the sweet bilva fruits would fall to the ground so the cowherd boys could enjoy eating the ripened fruits The demigods, who had gathered in the sky to witness the slaying of this demon, began to shower flowers on the earth as they played drums, cymbals and other musical instruments while praising Krishna's wonderful deeds.

Sometime later when the cowherd boys were herding their calves near Govardhana Hill, some of them were feeling somewhat perplexed that although Vatsasura was a demon, he had appeared in the form of a calf and consequently to kill a calf is considered to be very sinful. Therefore, the cowherd boys requested Krishna to purify himself of the sin by bathing in the River Ganges. Krishna happily agreed to the cowherd boy's proposal, but not wishing to leave Vrindavana, Krishna manifested the River Ganges from His mind and took his bath in her sacred waters. The Ganges where Krishna took His bath became known as Manasi-ganga, the Ganges manifested from the mind (manasa) of Krishna.

## 150 Varahara (Barahra)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “In Varahara village, Krishna played with His friends by assuming the form of Varaha.” This rather remote village lies on the old bank of the Yamuna River where Krishna played with the cowherd boys and exhibited His transcendental form as Lord Varaha, the boar incarnation of Vishnu. The Yamuna River has moved away from this place over the period of the last fifty years and is now located more than a mile to the east.

How To Get There: This place is 1.5km southeast of Sei (See map no.35).

## 151 Harasali (Rasoli)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “See Harasali-grama where Krishna performed His rasa.” Krishna and the gopis once performed the rasa-lila dance at this place which was formerly located on the banks of the Yamuna River. The Yamuna has since moved away from here due to a change in her course and presently lies over one mile to the east. Nearby is a temple dedicated to Garga Muni known as the Gargacharya Mandira.

How To Get There: This hamlet is 300mt south of Barahra (See map no.35).

## 152 Bhajana (Bajana)

After Krishna had slain the Aghasura demon, the demigods, who were assembled in the sky near this place, began glorifying Him by singing and dancing accompanied by musical instruments. The name of the village is derived from the word 'bhajana' which means 'to sing and play' musical instruments.

How To Get There: This place is 500mt north-west of Jonai (See map no.35).

## 153 Parikhama (Parkham)

During Krishna's killing of the Aghasura demon at nearby Sapauli, Lord Brahma stayed behind and concealed himself in a cloud above this village. Brahma wanted to observe Krishna's activities more closely to further ascertain whether or not He was the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as the demigods were claiming. Thus Brahma hatched a plan to steal all the cowherd boys along with their calves as a test (pariksha) to see what the little cowherd by named Krishna would do. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “In Parikhama, Brahma wanted to test the power of Krishna.” The word 'pariksha' means to 'question', to 'ascertain' or to 'test', thus the village achieved the name 'Parikham' which is derived from the word 'pariksha'.

How To Get There: This place is 2km south of Jonai & 4kn south of Sei (See map no.35 & 36).

## 154 Unai (Janai/Jonai)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “In Unai, Krishna and His boyfriends ate all sorts of food”. Some commentators have said that from this place Lord Brahma observed the cowherd boys taking their lunch. However, the place where the cowherd boys ate their lunch has been identified as Vatsavana near the village of Sei which is five miles north-east from Unai. Therefore the verse quoted above from the Bhakti-ratnakara about Krishna and the cowherd boys 'eating all sorts of food' at Unai village appears to describe a different pastime altogether.

How To Get There: This place is 3.5km west of Barahra & 2km south-west vai Sei on the Parkham road (See map no.35).

## 155 Balahara

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “In Balahara, Brahma felt delighted as he stole all the cowherd boys.” The name of this village is Balahara which comes from the word ‘bala' meaning 'boys' and 'hara' meaning ‘stolen’. Lord Brahma was feeling great delight while believing that he had played a clever trick on Krishna by taking away all His cowherd boyfriends along with their calves.

How To Get There: This place is presently untraceable.

## 156 Sakrasthana (Sakaroya/Sakraya)

This place was known in ancient times as Sakrasthana or sometimes as Sakaroya which is derived from Sakra, one of the names of Lord Indra, the King of heaven. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Sakrasthana was later named Sakaroya. This place is famous because it was here that Sakra (Indra) became afraid after causing the terrible rain in Vraja.” After having caused a devastating flood in Vrindavana, Lord Indra was surveying the scene of destruction in this region of Vraja while remaining concealed within the clouds. Indra became fearful due to his mistake of trying to punish the Vrajavasis, simply because they had stopped the performance of the Indra-yajna. After Krishna lifted Govardhana Hill and saved all the Vrajavasis from the torrential rain, Indra felt totally defeated and realized that Krishna was in fact the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus he became fearful and full of remorse thinking that his actions were highly offensive to the lotus feet of the Lord.

How To Get There: This place is 3km east of Janai and 6km east of Parkham (See map no.35).

## 157 Sapauli \\ Aghavana (Pasoli/Pasauli)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “In Aghavana Krishna killed Aghasura, but people now call the place Sapauli.” The present name of this village is Pasauli which is derived from the ancient name of Sapauli, sometimes called Sarpa-sthali. The name 'Sapauli' means ‘the place of the snake'. The word 'sarp' means a 'snake' and because the giant snake-demon Aghasura was killed here, the village achieved its name. This place is also known as Aghavana, because in this forest (vana) the great enemy of the demigods named 'Agha' was killed by Krishna. In the Vraja-vilasa-stava it is stated, “May Sarpa-sthali be my protector, for it was here that the powerful Murari watched as His friends entered into the burning, poisonous stomach of the sinful Aghasura. He followed His friends, who are dearer to Him than His own life, and being angry at the demon, killed the giant snake in order to rescue them.”

The word 'sarp' can also mean 'curse' and this village is also known as the place of the curse, or Sarpa-sthali. In the Mahabharata it says that the two sons of Shantanu Maharaja by his second wife Satyavati, whose names were Chitravirya and Vichitravirya, both died of a curse that is believed to have been placed upon them at this place, hence the name Sarpa-sthali. Although they both ascended the throne of Hastinapura, due to the curse, both brothers died while still very young and without leaving heirs. Chitravirya, also known as Chitragada, was killed by a Gandharva of the same name, and Vichitravirya died of consumption. Just before entering the village from Parkham, one can see Manasa-kunda, where it is said Satyavati and her two sons formerly stayed. Locals say this kunda was created from Krishna's mind (manasa) in order to provide drinking water for the cows. This kunda is surrounded by a thick pilu forest.

How To Get There: This place is 5km north-west of Parkham (See map no.35 & 36).

## The Killing of the Serpent Aghasura

One day the demon Aghasura, the son of Sankhasura, was enjoying the company of many young girls in the vicinity of the Malaya Hills in Southern India. While there he noticed the great sage Ashtravakra Muni, who possessed a body that was bent in eight different places due to being deformed from birth. Being proud of his own beauty, Agha foolishly derided the sage by calling him both crooked and ugly. Ashtravakra became angry due to the impudence of the demon and cursed him by saying. “Oh fool! On this earth the snake species are also very crooked and ugly, therefore you will now become a snake.” After hearing the curse pronounced by the sage, Agha became repentant and begged the sage to forgive him. Ashtavakra then informed Agha, that although his words could not be changed, when the Supreme Lord Shri Krishna descends to earth in the Dwapara-yuga, at that time he would be redeemed.

The demon Aghasura eventually took birth in Vrindavana and became a close associate of King Kamsa. He was the brother of Vatsasura and Putana, who were both slain by Krishna. Due to mystic power, demons like Aghasura, Putana and Vatsasura, could also create various forms including human-like forms by which they could move about in human society. Having been ordered by Kamsa to kill Krishna, the demon in the form of a huge python waited in the forest for Krishna and His friends to arrive there. It is the nature of a python to simply lie on the ground and wait for its prey to arrive. In the same way, Aghasura lay in wait on the pathway through the forest for Krishna and the cowherd boys to arrive there for grazing their calves.

After some time the cowherd boys arrived along the path with Krishna following close behind them. Upon seeing the great serpent lying on the forest pathway, the cowherd boys stopped and began discussing amongst themselves about the unusual object and what might it be. At first they concluded that it was the statue of a great serpent, but then decided it must actually be a real serpent that seemed to be waiting there simply to devour them. It seemed that the serpent was at least eight miles long. Its mouth was open wide and its upper lip appeared to touch the sky. Its tongue looked like a highway and its breathing caused hot winds to blow which sounded like a hurricane, while at the same time a strong fishy smell emanated from its intestines. Nevertheless, with a sense of great bravado and invincibility, the cowherd boys decided they would enter the serpent's mouth all together and because there were so many of them, it would be impossible for the serpent to devour them. They also reasoned that if there was any danger, their dear friend Krishna would undoubtedly save them and slay the serpent.

Following some distance behind, Krishna saw all His cowherd boyfriends joyfully enter into the giant serpent's mouth and He could also understand that this statuesque figure was actually a demon. As Krishna thought what action He should take, the last of the cowherd boys disappeared into the mouth of the giant serpent. Aghasura's mouth remained open as he waited for Krishna to also enter, thinking that he would now avenge the death of his sister Putana. Meanwhile Krishna concluded that the only way to save his friends was to also enter the gaping mouth of the giant serpent. As Krishna entered Aghasura's mouth, the demigods who had assembled in the sky to witness the event, suddenly became perplexed, thinking that now Krishna would certainly be finished. When the demigods saw Aghasura's mouth close, Krishna could hear their anguished cries as they exclaimed. “Alas! Alas!”

After entered the serpent's mouth, Krishna began to expand His body while standing in the demons throat, all of a sudden the demon could no longer breathe properly and slowly started to suffocate. Aghasura was immediately forced to open his mouth and desperately tried to gulp for air while his eyes moved violently and bulged from their sockets. As the serpent could no longer breathe he suffocated to death and his life air, which had nowhere to go, suddenly burst through the top of his skull. When the demon was dead, Krishna began searching for His friends and found them lying dead in the demon's belly. Krishna then cast His merciful gaze over the cowherd boys and brought them all back to life. Seeing Krishna emerge triumphantly from the mouth of the serpent along with the cowherd boys, the demigods heaved a great sigh of relief and began a tumultuous kirtan with drums, cymbals and other musical instruments amid the chanting of, “Jaya! Jaya! Jaya!,' which means “Victory! Victory! Victory to Krishna!”

Hearing the great tumult, Lord Brahma descended from Satyaloka to see what all the commotion was about. Lord Brahma listened as the demigods praised Krishna as 'Maryard Purushottama', or the Primeval Lord incarnate on earth in human form. Even though he had witnessed Aghasura's life air enter Krishna's lotus feet, Lord Brahma had some doubt about whether this talkative cowherd boy could actually be the same Lord Narayana, and he decided to closely observe this unusual cowherd boy for some time before reaching any conclusion. As the cowherd boys slowly made their way along with the calves towards the bank of the Yamuna at Vatsavana, Lord Brahma began to follow them unseen from within the clouds.

## 158 Taroli / Varoli (Tarauli-Janubi/Barauli)

These two villages were the site of Krishna's cow herding pastimes (gocharana-lila) and according to the Bhakti-ratnakar, the two villages were given their names by the cowherd men, "See the two villages Taroli and Varoli which were named by the gopas.” There are no holy places to be seen in these two villages, but there is a kunda at Taroli known as the Swami Baba-kunda, also called Taroli- kunda, which is said to possess medicinal properties because once a 'siddha baba' performed penance there. It is said that a variety of skin diseases like white leprosy can be cured by covering one's body with mud and then bathing in the kunda. The village of Varoli is 2km to the west of Tarauli.

How To Get There: This place is 5km northwest of Parsoli (See map no.35).

## 159 Chomuha (Chaumuhan)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, "In Chomuha-grama Brahma approached Krishna and, repenting his audacity, offered prayers to the Lord.” The name Chomuha is derived from the word 'chaturmukha' which is one of Brahma's names, meaning one who possesses four (chatur) faces (mukha). Therefore the term 'chaturmukha' is applicable only to Brahma who possesses four heads in order to control the four directions of the universe. After having stolen Krishna's calves and cowherd boyfriends, Lord Brahma suddenly realized his grave mistake in trying to test Krishna's power. The Bhakti-ratnakara says that Lord Brahma, with tears in his eyes, approached Krishna at this place and in a repentant mood, repeatedly offered his dandavata-pranams while offered prayers of glorification at Krishna's lotus feet. The Shrimad-Bhagavatam says that Lord Brahma, whose complexion is golden, appeared to be like a golden rod, as he again and again threw himself down on the ground in front of Krishna. This falling on the ground like a rod is called dandavata-pranama and is considered to be the best way of paying ones obeisances, especially in front of the Supreme Lord, or the Deity in the temple, as well as before the spiritual master. The word 'danda' means a 'rod' or a 'stick' and 'pranama' means to offer one's most humble respects.

In the Vraja-vilasa-stava it says, "I sing the glories of the place called Bhirucaturmukha. It was here that Brahma repented for his offense of stealing the cows and cowherd boys and fell on the ground at the feet of Mukunda the gently smiling son of Maharaja Nanda. With his eyes filled with tears, Brahma sang the glories of the Lord.” There is a famous temple of Lord Brahma here, dedicated to the pastime of the 'Brahma Vimohana-lila', or the 'bewilderment of Brahma' and is known as the Chaturmukhi Brahmaji Mandira. There is also a lake nearby called Chandra-sarovara.

How To Get There: This place is situated 3.5km west of Parsoli (See map no.36).

## 160 Sayano (Suhana/Sihana)

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Krishna killed Aghasura in a clever \[sayana\] way, therefore this village was given the name Soyano or sometimes Sehona.” The word 'siyano' means 'very clever' and after hearing about the killing of Aghashura, all the Vrajavasis began to praise Krishna saying, He had very cleverly killed the great serpent by entering its throat and after expanding His body, the demon was unable to breath and thus choked to death. There is an ancient temple here on a hill in the centre of the village dedicated to the four Kumaras: Sanaka, Sananda, Sanat and Sanatana. Unfortunately, the Deities of the Chatur-Kumara, along with Deities of Radha-Krishna, were stolen long ago because they were made of a precious metal called ashta-dhatu, which contains gold and silver. At the present time the small Deities of Banke-Bihari are being worshiped in this temple. To the east of the village there is a large lake known as Kshira Sagar where the temple of Seshashayi-Vishnu, known locally as Podanatha Mandira, once stood. This Deity was also stolen and over time the temple fell into ruins and disappeared. To the west of the village one can see Krishna-kunda which also called by the locals as Vishnu-Kunda, or sometimes as Dubala-kunda.

How To Get There: This place is 4km west of Chaumuhan (See map no.36).

## 161 Krishna-Kunda-Tila

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Raghava took Narottama and Shrinivasa up a small hill called Krishna-kunda-tila and as they looked in all directions they felt intense pleasure.” This hill is located in the center of Sihana village on which the temple of Chatur-Kumara is located. From the roof of the temple one gets a panoramic view of Vraja and one can see both Varsana and Nandagrama in the far distance some twenty-five kilometers to the west.

How To Get There: This hill is in the center of Sihana village (See map no.36).

## 162 Ajhai (Ajhai Kurd)

There are two very nice gardens here known as Ramabhaga and Syamabhaga and also a large lake. It is said that the name 'Ajhai' is derived from the word 'aja' which means 'today'. After Krishna had killed the serpent Aghasura, nobody knew because the cowherd boys had been stolen by Brahma and put to sleep for one year under the influence of Brahma's mystic power. When the cowherd boys woke up they were not aware that one whole year had passed by, therefore they thought that Krishna had killed the Aghasura demon in the morning of that same day. Therefore on the way home, the cowherd boys started to tell all the Vrajavasis that Krishna killed the demon Aghasura 'today' (aja), although unbeknown to them, it happened one year earlier.

How To Get There: This place is 2.5km south of Chaumuhan (See map no.36).

## 163 Jayeta (Jait)

After Krishna had slain the serpent Aghasura, the demigods who saw the event from the sky, began a tumultuous kirtana accompanied by drums, cymbals, and various other musical instruments while showering flowers on the earth. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “In Jayeta-grama the demigods glorified Krishna, 'Jaya! Jaya! All glories to the Supreme Personality of Godhead!' and then showered Him with flowers.” The demigods were chanting in unison, “Jayate! Jayate! Jayate!" This loud chanting by the demigods means, "Victory! Victory! Victory to Krishna!” and it was so loud it could be heard by the people in this village and therefore the village achieved the name of Jayeta, which has now become Jait. There is a large lake in the village where there is a statue of the serpent Aghasura.

How To Get There: This place is 3km south of Ajhai Khurd & 6km south of Chaumunhan (See map no.36).

## 164 Atasu (Devi Atas)

The name of Atas is a corrupted form of Atasu, which is derived from the name of Ashtavakra Muni, who according to the Bhakti-ratnakara, performed austerities near here on the old bank of the Yamuna River, “In Atasu-grama, the saint Ashtavakra performed austerities.” Astavakra Muni gains mention in many of the Puranas and spent a lot of his time in Vrindavana Dhama. As his name suggests, he was crippled and his bones were bent in eight different places. The word 'ashta' means 'eight' and 'vakra' means 'bent'. Whoever ridiculed him or passed derogatory comments about his ugliness was inevitably cursed. According to the Brahma-vaivarta Purana, Ashtavakra Muni eventually sat in meditation on the banks of the Kusuma-sarovara, patiently waiting for the pastimes of Radha and Krishna to begin. One day, he suddenly glimpsed both Radha and Krishna enjoying Their loving pastimes with the gopis on the opposite bank of the lake and in transcendental ecstasy he gave up his body. His samadhi can be seen on the eastern bank of Kusuma-sarovara near a small Shiva Shrine.

There are three villages situated within two kilometers of each other, all with name including: Devi Atas, Bara Atas, and Chota Atas. The most important of these is Devi Atas, where the famous temple of Devi Ma (the mother goddess) is situated. In this temple are two separate Deities of Devi, one is of Ekanamsa Devi, Krishna's sister, who is non-different from Yogamaya Devi and the other Deity is Yogamaya's expansion of Manasa Devi. The goddess Yogamaya Devi along with all her various expansions, is generally worshiped as Goddess Durga, for the purpose of achieving material benefits. The Gaudiya Vaishnavas worship Yogamaya Devi as Krishna's internal potency in order to achieve pure devotional service to Krishna, just as the gopis did.

When Krishna was born in Kamsa's prison cell as the son of Devaki, Ekanamsa (Yogamaya) was born as His sister in Gokula from the womb of Yashoda Mayi. When Vasudeva exchanged Krishna for Ekanamsa and brought her back to the prison cell, Kamsa tried to kill her by dashing her on the ground. But instead she escaped his grip and flew into the sky while manifesting her eight armed form of Durga. After admonishing the sinful Kamsa, she informed him that Devaki's eighth child was alive, Ekanamsa, sometimes called Ekananga, then disappeared from that place and is said to have come to Atasu to live in the forest of Vrindavana, where she remains even today. It is also said that the Deity of Manasa Devi was also worshiped for some time by Ashtavakra Muni. In some Puranas it is said that Ekanamsa, after chastising Kamsa, departed for the Vindhya Mountains where she is known by the name Vindyavali.

How To Get There: This place is 4km north-east of Jait (See map no.36).

NOTE: Sunrakh was not visited during this part of the parikrama undertaken by Raghava Pandita, Shrinivasa Acharya and Narottama Dasa Thakura, but was visited at the beginning of their Vrindavana parikrama. As Sunrakh is not part of the present-day Vrindavana Parikrama it has been included here due to its proximity to Devi Atas.

## 165 Sanorakha (Sunrakha)

This place was formerly on the bank of the River Yamuna where Saubhari Muni performed his penance. He is one of the sages who find mention in the Rig Veda and after establishing his ashrama at Sanorakha, he would spend long periods of time meditating deep inside the River Yamuna. There is a temple located here on a small hill which contains the Deity of Saubhari Muni. Formerly this place was situated on the banks of Yamuna, but since a long time the river has changed course and is now located over one kilometer to the east. From this place there is a good view of the Madana-mohana Mandira in Vrindavana and Kaliya-hrada, the lake where the poisonous serpent Kaliya Naga used to live and which previously stretched from Sunrakh up to Kaliya Ghata.

Whenever Garuda, the eagle carrier of Lord Vishnu, used to visit Vrindavana, if he felt hungry, he would catch fish in the Yamuna River for his lunch. One day, Garuda caught a large fish that was a prominent leader among the other fish and his death created a disturbance amongst the fish community. Consequently, all the other fish complained to Saubhari Muni who was engaged in meditation within the Yamuna. Because of having spent long years engaged in severe austerities and impersonal speculation, when he heard the complaint of the fish, Saubhari Muni became consumed with anger and immediately pronounced a curse on Guruda, saying that if he ever came to this part of the Yamuna again to eat fish, he would be immediately burnt to ashes on the spot. When the black snake Kaliya Naga, who lived in mortal fear of being eaten by Garuda, heard about the curse of Subhari Muni, that Garuda could no longer visit the Yamuna River in Vrindavana, Kaliya decided to move to the Yamuna as he would be much safer living among the fish that were being protected by Saubhari Muni.

Some people are surprised to hear that Garuda, the servant of Lord Vishnu ate fish, which, like all types of flesh is forbidden for Vaishnavas. But it must be remembered that Garuda is an eagle and like many other species of eagle, survives on fish, as well as snakes, and similar other prey. If an animal kills and eats flesh there is no sin. Another point to consider is that by killing and eating poisonous serpents, Garuda is fulfilling the Vedic edict that a serpent must be immediately killed. Similarly a kshatriya warrior must kill the enemy as a religious duty. A warrior must the practice the art of killing by slaying animals in the forest as a part of kshatriya training in the martial skills which is done as an act of religious duty, and thus there is no sin. When a soldier, out of duty kills an enemy on the battlefield, he is sinless. Garuda, besides being an eagle, is also considered as a kshatriya, because he also fights on the battlefield as part of his duty to serve Lord Vishnu, so in both cases Garuda is completely sinless.

Due to this curse of Saubhari Muni, Garuda was unable to enter the inner-most region of Vrindavana known as Seva Kunja where the rasa-lila and other intimate pastimes took place. Instead, he used to stand at Shakatikara (Chhatikara) and offer his obeisance's from the spot where the Garuda Govinda Mandira now stands. Meanwhile, Saubhari Muni who had committed a grave offence by cursing a great Vaishnava like Garuda, fell down from his position. It so happened that Saubhari Muni, who was meditating deep within the water of the Yamuna, happened to witness two fish engaged in sex-life. Almost immediately his mind became polluted and the desire to enjoy sexual intercourse arose within his heart.
