## Vrindavana Parikrama

The Vrindavana Parikrama is undoubtedly the most popular parikrama in the region with many local residents performing parikrama every single day of their lives. The Vrindavana Parikrama path is approximately six miles (10km) long and can take around two hours to complete. The parikrama of Vrindavana is known as the Pancha-kosi Parikrama because the original parikrama path covered a distance of ten miles or ‘pancha-kosi' (a kosi is approximately two miles). However, today the parikrama covers just six miles because urban development has altered the course of the parikrama path and has inevitably shortened it by a few miles. Whoever performs Vrindavana Parikrama simultaneously circumambulates over five thousand temples of Radha and Krishna located within the holy city, including the seven Goswami temples.

On major festival days of the Vedic calendar, a steady stream of pilgrims can be seen performing parikrama around Vrindavana from the early morning till late at night. Important parikrama days are: Ramanavami, Janmashtami, Radhashtami, Dipawali, Govardhana Puja, Bhai-dooj (Yama-dwitiya), Hariyali-teej, Akshaya-navami and a rare evening parikrama known as the Vana-vihara Parikrama on dvitiya in the lunar month of Jyeshta (Krishna-paksha), the third day after Narasimha-caturdasi.

During the sacred leap-month known as Purushottama-mas, thousands do parikrama every day of the month and many perform the arduous dandavata-parikrama, by offering their obeisances while lying full length on the ground, then standing up and moving forward a few paces to again offer dandavata obeisances at the spot where their fingertips have touched the ground. The dandavata-parikrama can take around twelve to fifteen hours or more and many pilgrims spend the entire day and night performing dandavata-parikrama. On each Ekadashi day which occurs twice a month, many thousands can be seen performing Vrindavana Parikrama as part of their Ekadashi-vrata. The big Ekadashi parikamas occur at the time of Holi (Rang-vihara-ekadashi) and on Devosayana-ekadashi as well as Devottana-ekadashi. There is also a parikrama on each full-moon day (purnima) as well as on the dark-moon day (amavasya).

## The Jugal-Jodi Parikrama

The Jugal-Jodi Parikrama means the complete circumambulation of the two holy cities of Mathura and Vrindavana in a combined parikrama, which covers a distance of about twenty-six miles. In this regard the word ‘jugala' means 'combined', or in other words Vrindavana-Mathura combined parikrama. The word 'jodi' means 'partner' referring to married couples, brothers and sisters, close friends, or any members of the same family. It is the tradition that this parikrama is performed by partners (jodi), however anyone can perform the Jugal-Jodi Parikrama. The first Jugal-Jodi Parikrama of the year is performed on Akshaya-tritiya, the third lunar day of the bright fortnight (shukla-paksha) in the month of Vaisakha (April/May). The next Jugal-Jodi Parikrama occurs on Devasayana-ekadashi during the bright fortnight (sukla-paksha) in the month of Ashadha (June/July). This particular Ekadashi in Ashadha marks the day when Lord Vishnu and the host of demigods take rest during the chaturmasya, the four-month period of the rainy season. There is another Mathura-Vrindavana Jugala-Jodi Parikrama on Akshaya-navami during the bright fortnight (shukla-paksha) in the month of Kartika (October/November) just two days before Devotthana-ekadashi. Then after two days there is the Teen-van Parikrama on the occasion of Devotthana-ekadashi, the day when Lord Vishnu and the host of demigods awaken from their slumber at the end of the rainy season. The word 'teen' means 'three' and 'vana' means 'forests' and this parikrama circumambulates the three sacred forests of Madhuvana (Mathura), Bahulavana (Garuda-Govinda), and Vrindavana, covering a distance of around fifty-five kilometers.

## The Vrindavana Parikrama followed by Raghava Pandita.

In the Bhakti-ratnakara it says that after leaving Bhojana-sthala on the last leg of their Vraja Mandala Parikrama, Raghava Pandita, along with his companions Shrinivasa Acharya, and Narottama Dasa, jubilantly started towards the most sacred forest of Vrindavana. Going to the northern most point where the Yamuna River first meets Vrindavana, they stopped at Sonorakha (Sonrakh), which was situated at the far end of the Kaliya-hrada. This is the lake within the Yamuna in which the serpent Kaliya Naga had previously lived, where Subhari Muni had his ashrama and where he performed meditation while submerged within the waters of the sacred river. Next they visited Kaliya Ghata, Dwadashaditya Ghata, Prashkandana Ghata, Surya Ghata, Advaita Vata, Shringara Vata, Govinda Ghata, Rasa-sthali, Chira Ghata (Chehan Ghata), Keshi Ghata, Nidhuvana, Dhira Samira, Vamsi Vata, Gopishwara Mahadeva, Brahma-kunda, Venu Kupa, and then to Davanala-kunda. After that, they went to meet Shrila Jiva Goswami at the Radha Damodara Mandira to inform him about all the places they had visited on their ecstatic parikrama around Vraja Mandala.

The parikrama of Vrindavana mentioned in the Bhakti-ratnakara began at Sunrakh village, which is not considered to be a part of the present day Vrindavana Parikrama, thus the nearest point on the present-day parikrama to Sonorakha (Sonrakh) is Ramana Reti. The Vrindavana Parikrama mentioned in this book starts from the Krishna Balarama Tree in Ramana Reti. However, one can start Vrindavana Parikrama from any point on the parikrama path, but it must end at the same place for it to be considered to be a full parikrama of Vrindavana.

## The Inner and Outer Parikrama Paths

There are two basic parikramas of Vrindavana: the outer-parikrama, which goes around the perimeter of Vrindavana known as the 'Pancha-kosi Parikrama', and the inner-parikrama known as the 'Sad-Goswami Parikrama' which follows the Pancha-kosi Parikrama path part of the way, but then veers inside to the interior of Vrindavana while visiting the 'Seven Goswami temples' and many other important holy shrines. The word 'sad', or 'sat', as in 'Sad-Goswami' means 'seven'. At the time of the Vraja Mandala Parikrama by Raghava Pandita, Shrinivas Acharya and Narottama Dasa Thakura, the temples of the Gaudiya Goswamis had not been constructed, however, today the Goswami temples can be included in the Vrindavana section of the Vraja Mandala Parikrama. The Sad-Goswami Parikrama (inner-parikrama) was first established during the Vraja Mandala Parikrama conducted by Shrila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Goswami, the founder-acharya of the Gaudiya Math, in the year 1932. Since that time the Sad-Goswami Parikrama has now become part of the Vraja Mandala Parikrama path. While passing the various temples on the Sad-Goswami Parikrama, devotees may simply offer obeisances from outside the temple if darshana is not available. Just by seeing the kalash (water-pot), or even the flag, at the top of the temple spire (shikhara), is considered equal to having darshana of the Deity, and therefore offering obeisances outside a temple is acceptable according to the Gaudiya acharyas.

While proceeding along the Pancha-kosi Parikrama path, the Sad-Goswami Parikrama (inner-parikrama) begins at Govinda Ghata, where one leaves the 'Pancha-kosi Parikrama' path and proceeds to Radha Damodara Mandira. In accordance with the traditions of the Sad-Goswami Parikrama, in order to complete a full parikrama of Vrindavana, after visiting Govindaji Mandira and the Sixty-four Samadhi Pitha, one should rejoin the Pancha-kosi Parikrama patha (outer parikrama) at Pani Ghata, and then proceed to Adi-Badri Ghata, Raja Ghata and then to Mahaprabhu's Baithaka. Then after veering off the pancha-kosi parikrama path once again to visit Davanala-kunda, one rejoins the pancha-kosi parikrama path before it passes the ancient well known as Radha-kupa. One can then complete the parikrama at Ramana Reti by taking darshana at the Krishna Balarama Mandira.

How To Get There: (See map no.46).

## Start of Vrindavana Parikrama

## 1 Ramana Reti / Krishna Balarama Tree

The name 'Ramana Reti' literally means the 'pleasure sands' and during the time that Krishna and Balarama lived at Shakatikara (Chhatikara), the two transcendental brothers used to come here with Their cowherd boyfriends and enjoy playing on the soft silky sands located at this place. Unfortunately, the wonderful rolling sand dunes that could once be seen here have now disappeared due to urban development in the area. Radha and Krishna also used to enjoy pastimes in the adjoining forest grove of Viharavana that formerly covered this entire area. It is also said that They would sometimes meet at this place and then proceed together with the gopis to Seva Kunja. There were two trees entwined together here that were being worshiped by the local Vrajavasis as representing Krishna and Balarama and known as the Krishna-Balarama tree. Unfortunately one of the trees, the white colored tree representing Lord Balarama, has now disappeared. The Vrajavasis worship many such trees that are entwined together as representing Krishna-Balarama, Radha-Krishna, or Lakshmi-Narayana. For the Vrajavasis this is a form of smriti or remembering their beloved Thakurjis when seeing unusually formed trees around Vrindavana.

How To Get There: (See map No.47).

## 2 Varaha Ghata

It is said that this is where Krishna showed His form as Lord Varaha, the boar incarnation of Vishnu to the gopis. At Varaha ghata one can see a very rare Deity of Lord Varaha holding the earth on his tusk in a temple located here and known as the Varaha Mandira. There is also another place about two kilometers north of here on the old bank of the Yamuna known as Varaha Grama, (Barahara), where Krishna showed His form of Varaha to the cowherd boys. Lord Varaha is one of the presiding Deities of Vraja Mandala and His eternal residence is at Saukari-vateshwara (Batasar) just south of Agravana on the southern petal of the lotus of Vraja. After killing Hiranyaksha and lifting the earth from the Garbha Ocean, Lord Varaha rested at Mathura's Vishrama Ghata where He spoke the Adi-varaha Purana to Bhumi Devi.

How To Get There: (See map No.47).

## 3 Gautama Rishi Ashrama

It is said that this is the place where the great sage Gautama Rishi performed penance and presently there is an ashram located here bearing his name. The ISKCON founder-acharya His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada belongs to the gotra, or genealogical line from Gautama Rishi. There are forty-nine established gotras that have descended from the eight great sages, the mind-born sons of Lord Brahma including: Gautama, Bharadwaja, Vishvamitra, Jamadagni, Vasishtha, Kashyapa and Atri. Agastya is also generally included in this group. These eight sages are called gotrakarins from whom all the forty-nine gotras (especially of the brahmanas) have evolved. The members of a gotra do not necessarily have to be blood relatives, but could be the descendants of a guru's pupils, as in the case of Shrila Prabhupada, whose father belonged to the disciplic descendants or gotra of Gautama Rishi. Sanatana and Rupa Goswamis belonged to the Bharadwaja gotra, which indicates that they belonged either to the family or the disciplic succession of Bharadwaja Muni.

How To Get There: (See map No.47).

## 4 Cowherd Boys Trail (Old Yamuna River-bed)

This trail used by the cowherd boys formerly ran along the old bank of the Yamuna as far as Keshi Ghata where the cowherd boys used to play ball games. This trail now forms part of the Vrindavana Parikrama path.

How To Get There: (See map No.47).

## 5 Madana Ter Ghata

In a beautiful garden located here, Krishna was once enjoying pastimes with the gopis when it is said that Kamadeva (Cupid), who is also known as Madana, arrived there with the intention of firing his arrow of attraction at Krishna. But upon seeing Krishna, he became so attracted by the Lord's transcendental beauty that he became completely bewildered and fell unconscious on the ground. Also located at Madana Ter Ghata one of Vrindavana's ancient wells known as Krishna Kupa.

How To Get There: (See map No.47).

## 6 Go Ghata / Ram Gol Ghata

It is said that after Krishna had successfully subdued the poisonous snake Kaliya Naga, feeling immense gratitude that Krishna was saved from the coils of the great serpent, Nanda Maharaja came to this place and gave away a large number of cows in charity to the brahmanas. (According to some commentators this occurred at Gopala Ghata). There is now a goshala under the care of Iskcon next to this same ghata.

How To Get There: (See map No.47).

## 7 Kaliya Ghata

This is where Krishna subdued the multi-hooded and venomous serpent known as Kaliya Naga, by ecstatically dancing on the snake's many hoods until he was completely exhausted and on the verge of death. One can still see the original kadamba-vriksha tree known as Kali-kadamba that Krishna climbed when He jumped into the Yamuna River in order to chastise the serpent Kaliya Naga. Some claim that this is an offshoot of the original kalpa-vriksha tree which is considered non-different from the original. The old sandstone ghatas that were erected in the 16th century by Holkar Roa are still visible.

After Kaliya Naga heard that Garuda, the eagle carrier of Lord Vishnu, could no longer enter Vrindavana due to a curse pronounced on him by Saubhari Muni, Kaliya decided to move his residence to this location where a large lake had formed within the River Yamuna, because he felt he would be safe from any attack by Garuda, who is the mortal enemy of all snakes. Due to Kaliya's presence, this part of the lake became highly poisonous and all the fish died, any animal that drank the water would die immediately, even birds that by chance flew over the lake would fall down dead after inhaling the toxic fumes. Understanding the great danger to everyone concerned, especially the cows who used to drink water from the river, Krishna decided that He must rid the Yamuna of this poisonous serpent forever.

Climbing a nearby kadamba tree, Krishna jumped into the water and began splashing about to attract the attention of Kaliya Naga. Sure enough, the envious serpent soon arrived on the spot to see who was causing all the commotion. The great snake immediately grabbed hold of Krishna in its powerful coils and attempted to crush His delicate body. Kaliya Naga exerted all his strength but to no avail. Hearing that Krishna had been captured by a venomous snake, all the Vrajavasis ran to the spot including Nanda Maharaja and mother Yashoda. When Krishna saw all the Vrajavasis on the riverbank crying and falling unconscious on the ground due to anxiety that He might be killed, He decided it was time to exhibit His own strength. Immediately freeing Himself from the serpent's coils, Krishna jumped on the Kaliya's hoods, and while playing His flute, He began to dance ecstatically from one hood to the next. As Krishna rhythmically stamped His feet down on the serpent's hoods as He danced, it felt to Kaliya that he was being struck on the head by thunderbolts. Very soon, Kaliya was completely exhausted due to the heavy pounding he received, leaving him battered and bruised with blood oozing from his mouths. The wives of Kaliya Naga known as the naga-patnis, immediately came before Krishna begging Him to spare their poor husband, who appeared to be on the verge of death. After hearing the heartfelt prayers of the naga-patnis, Krishna decided to release the Kaliya serpent, but ordered him to leave the vicinity of the Yamuna River and depart with his wives and children to the ocean, where he could cause no harm to anyone. Kaliya Naga readily agreed to the proposal and after bowing his hoods in submission, quickly left the Yamuna along with his family forever.

In a conversation between Lord Varaha and His consort Bhumi Devi, the Adi-varaha Purana says, “O Vishalakshi, the panditas have visualized many transcendental things in this place. That kadamba tree which is situated on the eastern side of the Kaliya Lake has many scented branches. O Vishalakshi, this charming and auspicious tree blooms throughout the twelve months of the year and brightens the whole world. In the Saura Purana it says, “This sin destroying holy place named Kaliya-tirtha is where Krishna danced on Kaliya's heads. Whoever takes a bath and worships Vasudeva in this holy place achieves the service of Lord Krishna, which is completely unobtainable by vile persons.”

How To Get There: (See map No.48).

## 8 Prabhodananda Saraswati Bhajana-kutira and Samadhi

This is the place where the great Vaishnava saint Prabhodananda Saraswati Goswami performed his bhajana and where his samadhi is located. Prabhodananda was the uncle and initiating guru of Gopala Bhatta Goswami. After meeting Lord Chaitanya at Shrirangam in South India, he surrendered to the Lord. He then came to Vrindavana and spent the rest of his life performing bhajana, and writing books about Krishna's pastimes and the glories of the holy Dhama. He also spent some time at Surabhi-kunda at Kamyavana, but towards the end of his life he came to this place to perform bhajana. He was an intimate associate of the Six Goswamis and amongst his works Shri Vrindavana Mahimamrita, Shri Vrindavana Sataka, and Radha-rasa-sudha-nidhi, are the most celebrated and well known.

How To Get There: (See map No.48).

## Excursion to other holy places 37

Including; \* Kaliya Mardana Mandira.

## 177 Kaliya Mardana Mandira

In this temple one can see a very ancient Deity of Lord Kaliya-mardana, which is said to be five thousand years old. This small Deity of Lord Krishna can be seen subduing the poisonous serpent Kaliya Naga, and the naga-patnis, the wives of Kaliya, can be seen offering prayers to the Lord while begging Him to forgive their sinful husband. The Sanskrit word ‘mardana' means 'defeated', or 'subdued' as well as 'crushed, bruised, pained, or tormented', which perfectly describes the physical condition of the Kaliya Naga after Lord Krishna had stamped on his hoods while forcing him to leave the sacred waters of the Yamuna River.

How To Get There: (See map No.48).

End of excursion (Return to Vrindavana Parikrama Route)

## 9 Prashkandana Ghata / Prashkandana-tirtha

On the hill above Prashkandana Ghata is the place where the twelve forms of the sun-god appeared to provide warmth to Krishna, who was feeling very cold, having spent a long time in the waters of the Yamuna River while subduing the Kaliya serpent. The combined heat of the twelve Adityas very quickly warmed Krishna's body to such a degree that He started to perspire. The combined water from Krishna's body then ran down the hill-side and entered the Yamuna at this place, which became known as Prashkandana Ghata. The word 'prashkandana' means 'perspiration' and thus this celebrated ghata achieved its unusual name. Until about one hundred years ago, the Yamuna used to flow past this ghata but unfortunately the river eventually changed its course and moved away.

How To Get There: (See map No.48).

## 10 Suraj Ghata / Surya-tirtha

In the Adi-varaha Purana it is said, “Hey Vasundhare! Whoever takes a bath at Surya-tirtha gets the darshana of Aditya and goes to Suryaloka having had all his desires fulfilled.” Situated along the old bank of the Yamuna River is Suraj Ghata; Suraj is a name of the sun-god Surya-Narayana. This famous ghata named after the sun-god is also known as Surya Ghata or Surya-tirtha, and it is said that in ancient times the sun-god Surya Deva came to this place by the Yamuna and underwent severe austerity in order to have darshana of Lord Krishna.

During the pastime of subduing the serpent Kaliya, after Krishna had emerged from the waters of the Yamuna River, He was shivering with cold. Shrimati Radharani came here to Surya Ghata along with the gopis and prayed to Surya-Narayana to provide warmth to Krishna so that He could quickly recover from the cold. At that moment all twelve expansions of the sungod known as the Adityas, appeared simultaneously in the sky to warm Krishna's body. Although the old ghata is no longer visible, the nearby ruins of the ancient temple of the sun-god can still be seen. It is also said that Radharani often visited this ghata by the banks of the Yamuna in order to perform Surya-puja and offer flowers to the sun-god. The Vraja-ritti-cintamani (77) says, “To the south-west, located in a jasmine garden is Suryaspada, where Sri Radhika worships the sun-god with a newly blossomed red rose.”

How To Get There: (See map No.48).

## 11 Dwadashaditya-tirtha / Dwadashaditya-tila

After spending a long time in the water while subduing the serpent Kaliya Naga, Krishna was feeling very cold and came here to this hill (Dwadashaditya-tila), to lie down for some time in the sunshine. Understanding that the Lord was feeling rather chilly and was also shivering due to being cold, all the twelve (dwadasha) forms of the sun god known as the Adityas, appeared there and provided their combined heat in order to warm Krishna's body. Thus this hill became known as Dwadashaditya-tila and the place on top of the hill where Krishna rested became known as the Dwadashaditya Yoga-pitha. Another name that is used to describe this same place is 'Dwadasha-surya-tirtha', which means the 'holy place of the twelve suns' and located just below the hill is Surya Ghata, where Shrimati Radharani used to come and offer flowers to Surya, the sun-god.

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Raghava then pointed out Dvadasaditya-tirtha, which according to the Puranas fulfills the desires of all men. There is no doubt, whoever takes a bath in this holy place on a Sunday, which is the last day of the month, gets the satisfaction of having his desires fulfilled. Pointing out one hill, Shri Raghava told Shrinivasa that after chastising Kaliya in the Kaliya Lake, Krishna came to that place. When the twelve sun-gods understood that Krishna was very cold they increased their heat to warm the Lord. The Vraja-vilasa-stava says, “I eternally take shelter of this holy place, Dvadasasurya, where magnanimous Murari was stricken with cold. He who is always engaged in wonderful pastimes, surrounded by affectionate men, women, and lowing cows, was then served by twelve suns, who with great devotional love and ecstasy gave intense heat to warm the Lord.”

How To Get There: (See map No.48).

## 12 Madana-Mohana Mandira

The famous temple of Lord Madana-Mohana was established by Shrila Sanatana Goswami and it is the first of the 'Seven Goswami Temples' that is visited during the parikrama of Vrindavana. The temple was built on the spot where the celebrated Deity of Madana-Mohana was being worshiped by Shrila Sanatana Goswami on top of the small hill known as Dwadashaditya-tila. The name 'Madana-Mohana' means 'He who attracts even Cupid', the god of love - whose name is also Madana. The temple of Madana-Mohana was the first temple built in Vrindavana since the time of Vajranabha Maharaja five thousand years earlier. King Vajranabha, who was Lord Krishna's great grandson, established a number of important temples in Vrindavana, such as: Madana-Mohana, Govindaji, and Gopinathaji, but during the course of time these temples disappeared and the Deities were lost.

In the year 1670, just prior to the attack on Vrindavana by the soldiers of the Mughal tyrant Emperor Aurangzeb, the Deity of Lord Madana-Mohana, along with the other important Gaudiya Goswami Deities including Govindaji and Gopinathaji, were secretly taken out of Vrindavana and hidden at Radha-kunda. During the attack by Aurangzeb's soldiers, Vrindavana's most important temples including Madana-Mohana, Govindaji, and Gopinathaji, were desecrated and Aurangzeb's soldiers dismantled the shikara (turret) of these temples. When it became safe, the three Deities were then taken from Radha-kunda to Kamyavana, and then finally to Jaipura in Rajasthan, where the Deity of Madana-Mohana was worshiped for many years. Sometime later, when a princess of the Jaipura royal family married a prince from the kingdom of Karauli near Bharatpura, it is said the princess, unable to bear the separation of Lord Madana-Mohana, took the Deity with her and established His worship in Karauli, where the Deity remains even to this day.

Madana-Mohana was the first Deity installed in Vrindavana and all Gaudiya Vaishnavas are advised to worship this Deity in order to reestablish their long-lost relationship with the Supreme Lord. In the beginning stages of sadhana-bhakti, it is Lord Madana-Mohana who has the power to attract us and help to nullify our false attachment to the sensual pleasures of this material world. Just as He has attracted Cupid, He can also attract the fallen souls and raise them to the platform of experiencing the transcendental mellows of devotional service. The initiating spiritual master, who engages his disciples in following the regulative duties (abhidheya) of devotional service, is the direct representative of Lord Madana-Mohana. Unless one can achieve the mercy of Lord Madana-Mohana and his representative, the spiritual master, the path of pure unalloyed devotion is difficult to ascertain. For this reason the disciples of Lord Chaitanya, headed by the Goswamis Rupa and Sanatana, established the three principle Deities in Vrindavana for the benefit of all aspiring Vaishnavas. Whereas Madana-Mohana represents the principle of sambhandha, or the soul's relationship with the Lord, Govindaji represents abhidheya, or the regulated activities for reviving that relationship, and Gopinatha represents prayojana, or the ultimate goal of life.

Before writing the Chaitanya-charitamrita, which was completed in the year 1681, Shrila Krishnadasa Kaviraja Goswami came to Vrindavana from Radha-kunda where he was staying. His purpose was to obtain the permission of Lord Madana-Mohana before attempting to write about the pastimes of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. As Krishnadasa Kaviraja bowed down before the Deity, a garland fell down from Deity's neck and all the devotees present understood that Lord Madana-Mohana's permission had been granted. The pujari then offered the garland to Krishnadas Kaviraja as loud cries of the Lord's holy name filled the air. In the Chaitanya-charitamrita it says, “Lord Madana-Gopala, the chief Deity of Vrindavana, is the enjoyer of the rasa dance and is directly the son of the King of Vraja.” (Cc.Adi.5.212

How To Get There: (See map No.48 & 48A).

## The Story of Lord Madana-Mohana

When Sanatana Goswami first came to Vrindavana, he performed his bhajana on the hill known as Dwadashaditya-tila. Sometime later when he obtained the Deity of Madana-Mohana, he began worshiping the Deity at this same place and is said to have kept the Deity in the crevice of a tree until a temple was eventually built. The first seva-puja of Madana-Mohana was believed to have been performed in the year 1534 on the basis of ancient hand written records known as Seva-prakatya and Ishtalabha.

There are a number of local legends of how Sanatana Goswami actually obtained the Deity of Madana-Mohana, but they are not based on any true facts. It is well known that some years earlier Advaita Acharya had discovered the Deity of Madana-Mohana at Advaita Vata during the time he performed his bhajana there. According to most scholars, this Deity was the original Deity installed by Vajranabha named Madana-Gopala. When Advaita Acharya was leaving Vrindavana and returning to Bengal, it is said that Madana-Gopala did not want to leave Vrindavana, therefore Advaita Acharya asked a brahmana named Choube from Mathura to look after the Deity in his absence. Based on actual historical records known as the Istalabha and Seva-prakatya, it says that in 1534, Sanatana Goswami obtained the Deity of Madana-Mohana from a Mathura brahmana living at Mahavana named Parashurama Choube, and Sanatana Goswami established the first seva puja of the Madana-Gopala in the same year, which was on the second day of the bright-moon or dwitiya-shukla in the month of Magh (Jan-Feb 1534). It appears that at the instillation ceremony, Sanatana Goswami gave the Deity the name of Madana-Mohana due to the many bewildering (mohana) pastimes that the Deity enacted. After the instillation, Sanatana appointed his disciple Krishna Dasa Brahmachari as the pujari. The details found in the Seva-prakasya appear accurate and it must be concluded that Advaita Acharya originally gave the Deity of Madana-Gopala to Choube, who later gave the Deity to Sanatana Goswami. The surname Choube is short for Chaturvedi, and they are a well-known brahmana community from Mathura, who are also priests at the famous Keshava Mandira.

The generally accepted story of how Sanatana received the Deity from Choube is as follows. According to the Bhakti-ratnakara, Sanatana Goswami was staying at Mahavana when he first saw the Deity of Madana-Gopala, he had noticed a very unusual cowherd boy with the most beautiful features playing with the other cowherd boys in the vicinity of Ramana reti near the banks of the Yamuna. Sanatana was convinced that this boy was non-other than Krishna playing as an ordinary village boy with the other cowherd boys. When he returned home after playing, Sanatana followed him to see where he went. The boy entered a temple and Sanatana followed, but once inside, he found the place deserted accept for the Deity of Madana-Gopala. Sanatana immediately bowed down before the Deity and without uttering a word to anyone, and in a deep mood of contemplation, returned to his cave near Nanda Bhavan in Mahavana Village. After this incident, when Sanatana went out to collect alms he would also have darshana of Madana-Gopala. Lord Chaitanya also had darshana of this same Deity when He visited Mahavana, and so did Lord Nityananda when He came to Mahavana on pilgrimage some years earlier.

The Bhakti-ratnakara says that Sanatana Goswami went every day to the temple of Madana-Gopala for darshana. The Madana-Gopala temple was managed by the brahmana Choube and his wife, who both lived on the temple premises. On one occasion while visiting the temple, Sanatana felt somewhat shocked at the irreverence being shown to the Deity, when he saw the Choube's children playing with the Deity, and also the way in which Choube's wife was serving the Deity, without following any rules of Deity worship. Sanatana mildly reprimanded the brahmana's wife, who was supposedly looking after the worship of the Deity and wanted to know why they were not following the specific rules governing temple worship. Choube's wife admitted her fault and agreed to be more conscientious in the future. However, that night Sanatana had a dream in which Madana-Gopala told Sanatana that He had been very happy playing with Choube's children, but since Sanatana had asked the family to be more reverential in their Deity worship, they had now introduced so many rules and regulations, that He was no longer happy staying at Choube's house, and told Sanatana to take Him back to Vrindavana.

The next day, feeling great remorse that the Deity was no longer feeling happy, Sanatana returned to the Choube's house to apologize for his somewhat over-exuberance in encouraging them to be more reverential in their Deity worship. However, Choube requested Sanatana to take the Deity of Madana-Gopala, as he had also received a dream in which the Deity had informed him. “As you already have so many children and Sanatana had none, therefore please hand Me over to Sanatana.” After hearing the words spoken by Choube, Sanatana replied that as he was in the renounced order of life and subsisted by begging alms, he was in no position to worship the Deity in the proper way, and for this reason could not accept Choube's offer. That night, Sanatana received another dream in which Madana-Gopala again appeared before him and once again asked Sanatana to take care of Him, saying this would make Him very happy. The Deity further said that whatever simple things Sanatana could offer, He would gladly accept it. After this dream, Sanatana agreed to take the Deity from Choube, and after bringing the Deity to Vrindavana, began to worship Him on top of Dwadashaditya-tila.

Because of being in renounced order and subsisting simply on alms given to him while performing madhukari, Sanatana's only offering to the Deity, besides water and wild flowers, were dry chapattis - small flat rounded pieces of unleavened wheat bread cooked over an open fire. One day, after having made an offering of dry chapattis, Sanatana heard the Deity asking for some salt to put on His dry chapattis. Sanatana replied by saying. “Just see, now You want salt, and tomorrow You will want sweets; I am an old man and have so many books to write, so please be satisfied with these dry chapattis.”

It so happened that on the same day, a merchant hailing from Multan in Punjab, named Ramadas Kapoor (some say his name was Ramadasa Sadagara from Amritsar), was ferrying salt and other goods by boat down the Yamuna River to the city of Agra, and while passing Dwadashaditya-tila, his boat got stuck on a sandbank in the middle of the river. In great anxiety and fearing his goods may be lost, the merchant came ashore in order to get help. Ramadasa could not see anyone around accept a young cowherd boy sitting near the riverbank. Some say the cowherd boy was actually Madana-Mohana taking part in one of His pastimes for which He was very famous. Ramadasa asked the cowherd boy if there was anyone who could help to free his boat and the cowherd boy informed him that there was a sadhu performing bhajana on the nearby hill who might be able to help. Climbing the hill, Ramadasa humbly approached Sanatana and asked him to help free the boat. Sanatana said that as he was old and also quite weak, he was not in any position to give much help, but advised Ramadasa to seek help from his beloved Deity Madana-Mohana, who was sitting in the nearby tree. With full faith, Ramadasa bowed down and offered heart-felt prayers to Lord Madana-Mohana and very humbly requested His help in saving his boat.

Suddenly dark clouds filled the sky and there was the deafening sound of thunder and within moments torrential rainfall began to inundate the whole area. Within a short time, due to the heavy downpour, the large deluge of rainwater began to swell the Yamuna River and the merchant's boat became freed from the sandbank. Being overcome with joy, Ramadasa repeatedly offered his obeisance's to Madana-Mohana and profusely thanked Sanatana, asking him what service he could perform in gratitude. Sanatana suggested that Ramdasa could help in building a temple for Madana-Mohana and also requested a little salt for the pleasure of the Deity. It is said that Ramadasa eventually returned to Vrindavana, and provided the funds needed to build a temple for Lord Madana-Mohana.

Lord Madana-Mohana was one of the two famous gopala-murtis carved by Vajranabha, with the other being Sakshi-gopala. Previously Sakshi-gopala was known only as Gopala, but His name was later changed to Sakshi-gopala after the pastime of His becoming a witness (sakshi). The Deity Sakshi-gopala is different to the Gopala Deity discovered by Madhavendra Puri at Govardhana, which was one of the two natha-murtis carved by Vajranabha and also known by other names like Gopala-Raya, Gopala-Natha, and also Shri-Natha. The other natha-vigraha carved by Vajranabha was Gopinatha who was installed in Vrindavana.

## The Mystery of the Two Temple Towers

During the parikrama of Vrindavana conducted by Raghava Pandita, although they had darshana of Govindaji, there is no mention of them taking darshana of the celebrated Madana-Mohana Deity, nor is there any mention of a temple being located at Dwadasaditya-tila. Even more surprising is the fact that the Bhakti-ratnakara does not even mention that the Deity of Madana-Mohana was being worshiped on this hill-top. It is quite clear from the Bhakti-ratnakara that both Sanatana Goswami (1558) and Rupa Goswami (1564) had disappeared by the time that Raghava Pandita, Shrinivasa and Narottama's performed parikrama of Vraja, thus their parikrama would have taken place somewhere between the years 1564-1579, because by the year 1580, the temple of Madana-Mohana was opened and this would definitely have been described in the Bhakti-ratnakara. It can be conjectured that the Deity of Madana-Mohana was perhaps being worshiped at some other location after Sanatana Goswami’s disappearance and returned to Dwadasaditya-tila once the temple was constructed in 1580.

It is believed that the temple of Madana-Mohana was erected with the financial help of the Multan merchant Ramadasa Kapoor. However, Hindus were not allowed to be built temples during the repressive Mohammedan rule in India that began from the 14th century onwards. It was only after permission was granted by the Mughal Emperor Akbar in 1570, that any Hindu temple was allowed to be built in Vrindavana, which at that time in history had been renamed by the Mughals as Mohammedpur. Consequently, the first temple of Madana-Mohana was the one built under the supervision of Raja Man Singh of Jaipur which opened in 1580.

In 1760, when Aurangzeb's came to this temple they smashed the motifs, frescos and sculptures in and around the temple and according to historical accounts, they dismantled the top of the temple turret, as per the orders of Aurangzeb, who wanted that all the temple turrets be reduced in height. It is important to note that the temple turret situated right next to the temple shows clear signs of desecration and the chakra at the top of the temple turret (shikara) has been dismantled. On the other hand, the second turret on the left (viewed from the west), has absolutely no structural damage whatsoever and in fact appears like a more recent addition. Another point is that the actual architectural design with two temple turrets is quite different, which conveys the idea that the second temple turret was added some years after the desecration of the first temple by Aurangzeb's soldiers

Yet another important observation is that the second turret has no precedent in traditional temple architecture. The fact that the second turret has the Deities doors facing the outer courtyard is another clue to the fact that it was a much later addition once the original temple had been abandoned due to its desecration. It appears certain that the temple tower on the left was built during a different era as the sandstone is of a different quality and the exterior design and motifs are very different from the temple tower on the right. This alludes to the fact it was built by different artisans during another time period altogether, sometime after the year 1760, because there are no signs of desecration at all and it appears intact in every detail.

## Places of Interest at The Madana-Mohana Mandira

## 12 Bhajana-kutira of Sanatana Goswami

This is the spot on the top of Dwadashaditya-tila where Sanatana Goswami performed his bhajana. The word ‘bhajana' means 'to chant or meditate' and ‘kitira' or ‘kuti' means a ‘thatched hut'. When Sanatana Goswami first came to Vrindavana in the year 1516, he lived beneath the trees without caring for any shelter. Even when he began worshiping the Deity of Madana-Mohana, he kept the Deity in the crevice of a tree. It was only at a much later date that he, or any of the other Goswamis, accepted bhajana-kutiras which were made of simple of bamboo canes and thatched leaves.

When Lord Chaitanya first sent Sanatana Goswami to Vrindavana, He gave him a number of specific tasks to fulfill. In the Chaitanya-charitamrita it is said that Lord Chaitanya told Sanatana, “Your body is My principle instrument for executing many necessary functions. By your body I shall carry out so many tasks. You shall have to ascertain the basic principles of being a devotee, love of Godhead, Vaishnava duties, and Vaishnava characteristics. You will have to explain Krishna’s devotional service, establish centers for cultivating love of Krishna, excavate the lost places of pilgrimage, and teach people how to adopt the renounced order. Vrindavana is My very own abode and I want to do many things there to preach Krishna consciousness and I have to do this work through your body”. The essence of Lord Chaitanya's instructions formed the basis for one of Sanatana Goswami's most celebrated books known as the Hari-bhakti-vilasa.

How To Get There: (See map No.48 & 48A).

## Sanatana Goswami’s Early Life

Sanatana Goswami was believed to have been born in the year 1488 at Jessore (now in Bangladesh) on the banks of the Ganges River and was named Amar by his parents. He took birth in a saraswata-brahmana family that originally hailed from Karnataka in South India, where his forefathers were known to have been powerful kings in the region. According to Shrila Jiva Goswami, Sanatana Goswami’s nephew, their family ancestors belonged to the Saraswata Bharadvaja-gotra. Other biographers have said that the family surname was Bhatta and they belonged to the Saraswata-brahmana community from Telangana, who had emigrated to Karnataka. At some point in time, some of their family members eventually moved to Bengal and this is where Amar (Sanatana) and his two younger brothers, Santosh (Rupa) and Anupama (Shri Vallabha), were later born. Amar and his brothers were highly educated having studied under the great Sanskrit scholars Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya and his brother Vidyavachaspati, and were thus highly proficient in Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, Urdu, Hindi, and Bengali, and acknowledged to be amongst the most learned scholars of the day.

Based on the Gaudiya Vaishnava Abhidhana and other sources, Sanatana’s grandfather Mukundadeva, was engaged in government service as private secretary during the reign of Barbak Shah (1460-1470). After the death of Barbak Shah, his son Yusuf became king, followed by his son Fateh Shah. While in the service of Fateh Shah Mukunda departed from the world. During the reign of Fateh Shah, the Abyssinian generals in the ranks of the army led a coup in which Fateh Shah was assassinated. The Abyssinian generals ruled for five or six years and during this period, the future ruler Hussain Shah, a Pathani army general, became the wazir or prime minister under the last of the Abyssinian rulers, Sultan Shams-ud-Din Muzaffar Shah, who Hussain Shah later conspired to assassinate. After assuming the seat of power, Hussain Shah established the first Sultanate of Bengal in 1493 and his reign over Bengal lasted until 1519.

Mukundadeva’s son Shri Kumaradeva had a number of sons but three gained prominence: Amar (Sanatana Goswami), Santosh (Rupa Goswami) and Anupama (Shri Vallabha). Because of their profound scholarship and reputation as greatly learned men proficient in a number of languages, Hussain Shah, after hearing of their reputations, induced the three brothers to join his government and take up important administrative posts. While in government service it appears that Amar was soon elevated from the position of private secretary to the post of prime minister, while Santosh held another ministerial post and later became the finance minister. The youngest of the three brothers Anupam, was appointed as superintendent of the royal mint. Hussain Shah gave each of the brothers a royal title; Amar received the title of Sakara Mallik, while his brother Santosh was given the title of Dabir Khas and the youngest Anupama was given the title of Anupama Mallik. Hussain Shah also presented the three brothers with a large amount of wealth and land in Ramakeli where the brothers constructed palatial residences befitting their high posts in the government.

As no one from the brahmana community was willing to be associated with the Mohammedans for fear of being ostracized, at first the brothers refused, but when Hussain Shah threatened to persecute and kill innocent Hindus if the brothers did not join his government, they were forced to agree, not wanting to see innocent lives lost on their account. The brothers then moved from their ancestral home in Naihati to Ramakeli, the capital of the Sultanate of Bengal. At that time in history, Bengal had come under the subjugation of the Mohammedans from the year 1203, when Muhammad-bin-Bakhtiyar Khilji, an Afghani-Turkic military commander, owing allegiance to the Delhi Sultanate, overran Bengal defeating in battle the Hindu king Lakshman Sen and captured his capitol city of Gaur. Consequent invasions eventually consolidated the Mohammedan rule over the whole of Bengal.

Hussain Shah's long reign of more than a quarter of a century was a period of peace and prosperity, which was in striking contrast to the period that preceded it. The liberal attitude of Hussain Shah towards his Hindu subjects is also an important feature of his reign. Hussain Shah was known for his religious tolerance and when he came to know about Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's huge following amongst his subjects, he ordered his kazis (local magistrates) not to injure him in any way and allow him to go wherever he liked. After the three brothers Amar, Santosh and Anupama, joined the government of Hussain Shah, the rigid and ultra-orthodox smrta-brahmana community immediately ostracized them. However, as they had long been acknowledged to be great Vaishnavas and highly learned Vedic scholars, they continued to have many sincere followers amongst the brahmana community and would also spend long hours engaged in reading the Shrimad-Bhagavatam and other Vedic scriptures with their close associates.

## Sanatana Goswami Surrenders to Lord Chaitanya

After hearing from their brahmana friends about the wonderful activities of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and His sankirtana movement, both Amar and Santosh resolved in their hearts to surrender themselves to Lord Chaitanya and wrote letters to Him begging for His mercy and imploring Him to somehow or other try to save them. Lord Chaitanya, after accepting the sannyasa order in 1510, had moved to Jagannatha Puri in Orissa, but after staying at Puri for some months, He decided to go on a preaching tour of Bengal. After visiting Navadwipa, Lord Chaitanya proceeded to Ramakeli where thousands came to greet Him. Amar and Santosh accompanied by their younger brother Anupama eagerly went to meet the Lord and after placing straw between their teeth, very humbly approached Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and immediately fell on the ground like rods before the Lord’s lotus feet. They then begged the Lord, saying that because of serving the Mohammedan Government, they were the most abominable and fallen persons and therefore they should be saved first. Lord Chaitanya immediately accepted them as His disciples and gave them their spiritual names; Amar became Sanatana, Santosh became Rupa, and Anupama became Shri Vallabha. The three brothers immediately decided to retire from government service in order to join Lord Chaitanya’s sankirtana movement. The Lord told the three brothers to go and live in Vrindavana.

Although Rupa and Shri Vallabha managed to leave the service of the government and proceeded to Vrindavana, Sanatana was not so lucky. When Nawab Hussain Shah came to know that Sanatana was planning to leave his post, he immediately locked him in jail. When Nawab Hussain Shah left on a military campaign to conquer Orissa, Sanatana took the opportunity to bribe the jailer with a large sum of money who then released him. Sanatana immediately went to meet Lord Chaitanya at Benares (Varanasi), where he received the Lord’s personal instructions. Lord Chaitanya ordered Sanatana to immediately proceed to Vrindavana to join Rupa and Shri Vallabha, who had gone to Vrindavana sometime earlier. After his arrival in Vrindavana, Sanatana Goswami set about fulfilling the mandate given to him by Lord Chaitanya. He left Vrindavana only once to meet Lord Chaitanya for the last time at Jagannatha Puri and then immediately returned to Vrindavana. Sanatana Goswami spent the remaining forty two years of his life living in the holy Dhama performing the important tasks personally given to him by Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

## 12a Krishna Kupa

It is said that Lord Madana-Mohana created this well by pushing His flute into the ground so that Sanatana could easily obtain drinking water. The word 'kupa' means 'well'.

How To Get There: (See map No.48 & 48A).

## 12b Dwadasaditya-tila

This is the hill which Krishna climbed in order to lay down in the sunshine. He was feeling very cold after having spent time in the chilly waters of Yamuna River while subduing the serpent Kaliya Naga. Shrila Sanatana Goswami chose this sacred spot on top of Dwadasaditya-tila to perform his bhajana and where he worshiped his Deity Lord Madana-mohana. After some time with the help of a wealthy merchant named Ramdas Kapoor, a temple for Madana-mohana was built on top of the same hill.

How To Get There: (See map No.48 & 48A).

## 12c Dwadasaditya Yoga Pitha

There is a shrine here that marks the exact spot where Krishna rested while being warmed by the twelve Adityas, who were the twelve different manifestations of the sun-god. Their names are: Vishnu, Aryama, Indra, Tvashtha, Varuna, Dhata, Bhaga, Parjanya, Vivasvan, Anshuman, Mitra, and Pushya. The twelve Adityas appeared in the sky simultaneously to provide their combined heat in order to stop Krishna from shivering from the cold. Each month there is a different Aditya who takes over as the sun-god and on this occasion all twelve Adityas appeared at one time in order to serve Krishna. The twelve Adityas only appear together at the time of universal devastation but on this occasion, after hearing the prayers of Radharani and the gopis, they combined together to serve Lord Krishna. The heat from the twelve Adityas was so great that Krishna became so warm that He began to perspire, and a small stream formed from the accumulated perspiration ran down the hill-side and created a pool within the Yamuna.

How To Get There: (See map No.48 & 48A)

## 13 Sanatana Goswami Samadhi

This is the Samadhi Mandira where in the year 1558, Shrila Sanatana Goswami was laid to rest. Sanatana Goswami departed on the occasion of Guru-purnima at Manasi-ganga near Govardhana Hill where he was performing bhajana. His sacred body was then brought in a procession to Dwadashaditya-tila in Vrindavana and entombed next to where his beloved Deity Madana-Mohana was being worshiped. He wrote a large number of books on the science of devotion, the most famous being Brihad-bhagavatamrta and Hari-bhakti-vilasa. According to the Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika, he was known by the name Rati-manjari or sometimes as Lavanga-manjari in Krishna's Vrindavana pastimes and in the form of Lavanga manjari, he serves Srimati Visakha-sakhi just as Rupa Manjari (Rupa Goswami) serves Lalita-sakhi. The Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika says that Sanatana Goswami is accepted to be an extension of the body of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, as well as being an incarnation of Sanatana Kumara, one of the four Kumara sons of Lord Brahma.

How To Get There: (See map No.48 & 48A)

## 13a Tapan Mishra and Chandrasekhara Acharya Pushpa Samadhis

When Lord Chaitanya was on His historic journey from Jagannatha Puri to Vrindavana, He spent around ten days at Benares (Varanasi) and stayed at the house of His old friend Tapan Misra, who was an acquaintance of Lord Chaitanya from Bengal. Tapan Misra was the father of Raghunatha Bhatta Goswami, who while still a child, was able to get the Lord's personal association when the Lord came to Benares. After the Lord had taken His meal at the house of Tapan Mishra and was resting, Raghunatha used to massage His lotus feet. While staying at Banares, Lord Chaitanya also met Chandrasekhara, who was also a friend of Lord Chaitanya from Navadwipa. While on His return journey from Vrindavana, Lord Chaitanya first went to Prayag where He met Shrila Rupa Goswami, and after instructing him on the science of Krishna consciousness, sent him to Vrindavana. Lord Chaitanya then returned to Benares where He spent a few days staying at the house of Chandrasekhara while taking His meals at the house of Tapan Misra. During His stay at Chandrasekhara's house, Lord Chaitanya met Shrila Sanatana Goswami, who had just been released from prison. At this time Lord Chaitanya personally instructed Sanatana Goswami in the science of Krishna consciousness and asked him to spend the rest of his life in the service of Vrindavana Dhama.

How To Get There: (See map No.48 & 48A).

## 13b Grantha Samadhi

The word 'grantha' means 'sacred books' and this unusual samadhi contains the sacred books of the Six Goswamis. It is believed that these books were of esoteric subjects concerning the very intimate pastimes of Krishna and the gopis and written on palm leaves. It is said that because the subject of these books was beyond the understanding of ordinary devotees, it was decided to place them in samadhi. This is believed to be the only grantha samadhi in existence anywhere in the world.

How To Get There: (See map No.48 & 48A).

End of places of interest at Madana-Mohana Mandira

## 14 Advaita Vata

This is one of Vrindavana's famous banyan trees (vata-vriksa) and the place where Advaita Acharya performed his bhajana during the period of his stay in Vrindavana. It is said that Advaita Acharya had the great opportunity to meet Shrila Madhavendra Puri Goswami who was at the time on pilgrimage to Vraja, and he took initiation from him here in Vrindavana in the year 1482, four years before the appearance of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Beneath this same banyan tree, Advaita Acharya discovered the famous Deity of Madana-Mohana, (also called Madana-Gopala) that had been originally established by Vajranabha Maharaja five thousand years earlier but had been lost during the course of time. According to some, the Deity discovered by Advaita Acharya was called Madana-Gopala, and was a different Deity to Madana-Mohana, but this is not accepted by research scholars, who have concluded that Madana-Gopala was another name of Madana-Mohana. Krishna's great grandson Vajranabha had at least sixteen Deities carved including: four devas, two nathas, and two gopalas (cowherd boys). The two gopalas were named Sakshi-gopala and Madana-Gopala (also called Madana-Mohana). This celebrated spot beneath the banyan tree at Advaita Vata is accepted by all scholars as the actual appearance place of Lord Madana-Mohana. Unfortunately, due to insufficient historical records, there will always be opposing opinions regarding the details of history, not only of this particular Deity, but of many others as well.

When Advaita Acharya left Vrindavana for Navadwipa, it is said that the Deity of Lord Madana-Mohana informed Advaita Acharya in a dream that He was unwilling to leave Vrindavana, and therefore Advaita Acharya kept the Deity with a Mathura brahmana named Choube. It is said that when Advaita Acharya returned to Bengal, he began worshiping a small Deity of Krishna that he also named Madana-Gopala, and this is one of the reasons why the confusion has arisen. Recently, this small Deity of Madana-Gopala was brought to Vrindavana from Bengal amid claims that it was the actual Deity found at Advaita Vata, but this idea has been utterly rejected by Gaudiya Vaishnava scholars. The fact is that all the Krishna Deities carved by Vajranabha are very large and quite distinct, and also carved from black marble. Besides this, there are no historical records that Lord Madana-Mohana (Madana-Gopala) ever left Vrindavana before 1670, prior to Aurangzeb's attack on the holy city. Important evidence is revealed in the Bhakti-ratnakara, which says that both Lord Chaitanya and Lord Nityananda had darshana of Madana-Gopala at Mahavana some years after Advaita Acharya had returned to Bengal, thus proving that Madana-Gopala never left Vrindavana. Madana-Mohana (Madana-Gopala) is accepted to be the original Deity carved by Vajranabha that was discovered at Advaita Vata by Shrila Advaita Acharya and this has been accepted by all the Gaudiya Goswamis and other Gaudiya Vaishnava authorities.

How To Get There: (See map No.48).

## 178 New Madana-Mohana Mandira

In this temple one can see the pratibhu-murti of Lord Madana-Mohana that was originally installed in the year 1748. Later in 1819, this elegant sandstone temple, known locally as the 'New Madana-Mohana Mandira', was established. The term ‘pratibhu' means the 'replica Deity having the same spiritual potency as the original'.

How To Get There: See map no.49).

## 179 Ashtha-sakhi Temple

This temple is dedicated to the ashtha-sakhis, the eight most prominent girlfriends of Radharani, whose Deity forms are worshiped along with the Deities of Radha and Krishna. The temple was established by the king of Hetambur in West Bengal, Raja Ramranjana Chakravarty, who was an initiated disciple of Shrila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Goswami. The kings' devoted wife received a dream in which Lord Krishna appeared before her and requested the queen to build a temple for Radharani's dear-most friends known as the ashtha-sakhis, and thus the king built this temple here in Vrindavana. The word 'ashtha' means 'eight' and 'sakhi' means intimate friend. The names of the ashta-sakhis seen on the altar are (from the left): Sudevi, Tungavidya, Indulekha, Visakha, Lalita, Citra, Champaklata, and Rangadevi. Standing in the center of the ashtha-sakhis are Shri Shri Radha-Rasabihari.

How To Get There: (See map no.49).

## 180 Banke-Bihari Mandira

This is one of Vrindavana's most famous temples and it was built in 1862. The Deity of Banke-Bihari is said to have been discovered at Nidhuvana by Swami Haridas, a famous singer and musician, who belonged to the Nimbharka sampradaya. Swami Haridas was a well-known court musician at the Gwalior royal palace under the patronage of the Tomar Rajput kings, but he later accepted the path of renunciation and moved to Vrindavana. After being found at Nidhuvana, the Deity of Banke-Bihari was moved Tattia-sthan near Pani Ghata where it was worshiped by Swami Haridas. Sometime later after his death, the Deity was moved to this present site in. The Banke-Bihari temple does not follow traditional Vedic practices of Deity worship and there is no mangala-arati offering. The highlight of this temple is the unusual ‘banke-darsana', which means that pilgrims only get a 'fleeting vision of the Deity' as the pujaris repeatedly open and close the Deity's curtain, thus hiding the Deity from the vision of the pilgrims for intervals of ten or twenty minutes. The word 'banke' is a corruption of the word 'jhanki' or 'jhankiya' which means a 'fleeting darshana'.

How To Get There: See map no.49).

## 181 Radha Madhava Mandira

This is the temple where the beloved Deity of the famous bhakti-poet Jayadeva Goswami was being worshiped. In this temple one can see the pratibhu-murti of Radha Madhava because during the attack on Vrindavana by the soldiers of Aurangzeb in 1670, the Deity of Radha Madhava was moved to Jaipur where it is still being worshiped at the Kanak Bhavana Palace.

How To Get There: See map no.49).

## 182 Radha Vallabha Mandira Mandira

This is another of Vrindavana's famous temples popular among the local Vrajavasis. The original temple was established by Hit Harivamsa, the founder of the Radhavallabha-sampradaya. He was a philosopher-poet who composed a number of devotional songs, similar to the songs of Swami Haridasa. The original temple, which can still be seen, was built a number of years after the Govindaji Temple. The Radha-Vallabha temple was also desecrated by the forces of Emperor Aurangzeb in 1670, after which a new temple adjacent to the old one was built where the Deity is now worshiped.

How To Get There: See map no.49).

## 183 Narasinghadeva Mandira Mandira

This is the only temple of Lord Narasingha in Vrindavana. This very large and unique lion-shaped Deity has been carved entirely from wood.

How To Get There: See map no.49).

## 184 Bhattaji Mandira

In this temple one can see the original Srimad-Bhagavatam, read personally by Shrila Raghunatha Bhatta, one of the Six Goswamis of Vrindavana, who was famous for his melodious chanting of Bhagavatam slokas. He would often recite the Shrimad-Bhagavatam before the other Goswamis. Raghunatha would chant each verse of the Bhagavatam in three different ragas or meters. It is said that many who heard Raghunatha chanting the Bhagavatam shlokas would be overcome with transcendental spiritual emotion and some would even swoon in ecstatic trance. Raghunatha himself would often exhibit all the symptoms of spiritual ecstasy. In this temple one can also see the Deities of Madana-Mohanaji.

How To Get There: See map no.49).

End of excursion (Return to Vrindavana Parikrama Route)

## 15 Jugala Ghata

At Jugala Ghata one can see the Jugala-Bihari Mandira which is believed to be around three hundred years old. It is said that Shrila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakura stayed here during his visit to Vrindavana while conducting the Vraja Mandala Parikrama in 1932.

How To Get There: See map no.49).

## Excursion to Other Holy Places 39

Including: \*Vihara Ghata\*Andhera Ghata.

## 185 Vihara Ghata / Bihara Ghata

Although it is difficult to determine one ghata from the next, located just after Yugala Ghata is the famous Vihara Ghata where Radha and Krishna used to bathe and enjoy water sports (jal-krida) in the cooling and refreshing waters of the Yamuna River. The word ‘vihara' means ‘loving pastimes'.

How To Get There: See map no.49).

## 186 Andhera Ghata

This is another unmarked ghata that is glorified as the place where Radha and Krishna and the sakhis used to play a game known as ‘blind man's bluff'. In this particular game, both Radha and Krishna would take turns in blind-folding their eyes. Then with the blind-fold obscuring Their vision, They would try to catch the others. The word ‘andha' means ‘blind'.

How To Get There: See map no.49).

End of excursion (Return to the Parikrama Route)

## 16 Imli-tala / Tentuli-tala / Shri Chaitanya Baithaka

This is the famous tamarind tree where Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu would sit and chant the holy name on His japa beads. The word ‘imli' means ‘tamarind' and ‘tala' means ‘tree'. (Tamarindus-Indicus-amlika). This sacred place is also known as Tentuli-tala and the Sanskrit words ‘tentuli-tala' also mean ‘tamarind tree'. At the present time only the trunk of the original tamarind tree can be seen because the origonal tree died some years ago. Just beneath the tree is a small shrine known as Shri Chaitanya Baithaka, where a Deity of Lord Chaitanya can be seen sitting in meditation. This is the actual spot where Lord Chaitanya used to sit and chant japa.

Imli-tala was formally located on the bank of the Yamuna River but unfortunately the Yamuna has now moved some distance away, however the ancient riverside ghata is still known as Imli-tala Ghata. In ancient times Seva Kunja covered a much larger area than it does today and Imli-tala was not very far from Rasa-sthali where the rasa-dance pastimes took place. Previously the entire area bordered by the River Yamuna from Madana Ter Ghata to Dhira Samira Ghata, was part of Seve Kunja. Imli-tala was Lord Chaitanya's favorite place in Vrindavana and He came here every morning to chant on His beads while admiring the beauty of the river Yamuna. Imli-tala has special significance, as it was a place where both Radha and Krishna had experienced the ecstasies of vipralambha-bhava, on different occasions when They were somehow or other separated from one another.

It is said that after His month-long parikrama of Vraja Mandala, Lord Chaitanya was longing to reach Vrindavana so that He could have darshana of Imli-tala and relish the same mood of vipralambha-bhava, love in separation that Radha had experienced at this same place. To satisfy His innermost transcendental desire, Lord Chaitanya spent over a month staying in Vrindavana, so that He could spend His time at Imli-tala. It is said that Imli-tala was one of Radharani's favorite places in Vrindavana, and whenever She was somehow or other separated from Her beloved Krishna, She would come to this tree by the banks of the Yamuna and experience the emotions of vipralambha-bhava, or love in separation. And this is considered to be the reason why Lord Chaitanya chose Imli-tala as His personal place of bhajana.

While in Vrindavana, Lord Chaitanya stayed at Akrura Ghata and every day He would walk to Vrindavana and spend the morning performing solitary bhajana at Imli-tala. The Chaitanya-charitamrita says. “The next morning Shri Chaitanya returned to Vrindavana and took His bath at Chira Ghata. He then went to Tentuli-tala, where he sat down to rest. The tamarind tree named Tentuli-tala was very old, having been there since the time of Lord Krishna’s pastimes. Beneath the tree was a very shiny platform. Since the Yamuna flowed next to Tentuli-tala, a very cool breeze blew there. While sitting there, Lord Chaitanya happily observed the beauty of Vrindavana and the water of the River Yamuna. Shri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu used to sit beneath this old tamarind tree and chant the holy names of the Lord. At noon He would return to Akrura-tirtha to take His lunch.”

It must be acknowledged that for Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, Imli-tala has more significance than even Radha-kunda. This is because Lord Chaitanya spent only one day at Radha-kunda, whereas He came every day for over one month to sit and chant japa at Imli-tala. Therefore it can be concluded that the inner purpose of Lord Chaitanya’s pilgrimage to Vraja was to have darshana at Imli-tala and perform bhajana at the place where Radha experienced Her most ecstatic emotions of vipralambha-bhava. It should be noted that whereas Radha-kunda is a place of Radha and Krishna’s meeting together (sambhanda), Imli-tala is a place of Their separation (vipralambha), which is the pinnacle of transcendental emotion. During the time that Lord Chaitanya spent at Imli-tala, His own mood of separation from Krishna dramatically increased and by the time He returned to Puri, He became absorbed day and night in the uncontrollable emotions of Radha-bhava, the same as Radha’s own emotions when She is separated from Krishna.

In the book 'Teachings of Lord Chaitanya’, two distinct categories in the relationship of conjugal love are described and they are sambhoga and vipralambha. On the sambhoga platform, the categories are unlimited, but on the vipralambha platform they are just four in number. They are: the ecstasy exhibited before the lover and beloved meet; the ecstasy experienced between them during the meeting; the state of mind experienced by not meeting; and the state of mind experienced after meeting fearing further separation. Furthermore, when the emotions of vipralamba reach the highest point of expression that is called maha-bhava which was manifested by Radharani and the gopis of Vraja.

It is said that on one occasion when Radharani was feeling acute separation from Krishna, She came and sat here beneath this tamarind tree and began chanting Krishna’s names over and over again. As She began remembering Her pastimes with Krishna, tears began to flow incessantly from Her lotus eyes as She entered into the mood of ecstatic separation known as maha-bhava. Radharani was so absorbed in thoughts of Krishna, that Her golden colored complexion began to slowly turn a bluish-black color known as shyama, the same color as Krishna’s own bodily complexion. Such was the emotion experienced by Radharani. It is said that on one occasion when Lord Chaitanya was sitting here at Imli-tala and chanting Krishna’s names, He was also overcome with the mood of separation from Krishna and His golden bodily complexion began turning the same bluish-black color of Krishna’s form, just as Radharani’s complexion had also changed.

Besides Krishna, only the nitya-siddha devotees like the gopis of Vraja exhibit maha-bhava. Radharani is the embodiment; the very epitome of that maha-bhava and in the Chaitanya-charitamrita Radharani is described as being 'maha-bhava-svarupa', or in other words the personification of maha-bhava. Therefore the gopis have said, “The personality of maha-bhava is our Queen, Sri Radha Thakurani. She is the mine of all good, the jewel of Krishna's beloveds." (Adi.4.68-69). Because Radharani is the epitome of maha-bhava or 'maha-bhava-svarupa', Her own ecstasy of maha-bhava exceeds that of all the other gopis and this unique feature is known as Radha-bhava. With regard to maha-bhava, Shrila Prabhupada says, “Therefore the devotees say Krsna is Madana-Mohana, He can captivate Madana. But Radharani is Madana-Mohana-Mohini. She captivates even Madana-Mohana. That is the highest stage of maha-bhava, Radharani's stage.” Shrila Prabhupada also says, “Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is sometimes explained to be radha-bhava-dyuti-suvalita, or characterized by the emotions and bodily luster of Shrimati Radharani.”

In another pastime here at Imli-tala, during the course of the rasa-dance in nearby Seva-kunja, due to being overcome with mana or lovers pique, Radharani suddenly disappeared from the rasa-mandala and noticing Her absence, Krishna began franticly searching for Her everywhere but was unable to find Her. Knowing that this particular tamarind tree was one of Radharani's favorite spots, Krishna came here hoping that She would eventually arrive there. Sitting beneath the tree, Krishna began to experience the symptoms of maha-bhava due to acute separation from Radha and began chanting Her name over and over again. Due to the intensity of Krishna's transcendental emotions in separation from Radha, His complexion began to turn a brilliant golden color, the same as Radha's own divine body. Just at that moment, Radharani arrived there accompanied by some of Her girlfriends and was amazed to see the golden color of Krishna's body. When Krishna became pacified after being reunited with His beloved Radha, She wanted to know the reason behind the wonderful golden form that Krishna had exhibited. Krishna explained that after suddenly losing Her association during the rasa-dance, He came here in a deep mood of separation from Her and began chanting Her name over and over again, at that moment He began to experience Radha's same intense mood of separation and His bodily complexion automatically started to turn a golden color just like Hers. After hearing this explanation Radharani was completely amazed. Krishna then informed Radha that during the Kali-yuga, He would once again appear on earth in order to experience Her unique emotion of separation while exhibiting Her same golden complexion when He would appear as the 'Golden Avatara' Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. The Ananta-samhita says, "The Supreme Person, Shri Krishna Himself, who is the life of Shrimati Radharani; He who is the Lord of the universe in creation, maintenance and annihilation, appears as Gaura, O Maheshvara (Shiva).” As it is said by the Vaishnava acharyas, "Shri krishna caitanya - radha Krishna nahe anya - Both Radha and Krishna have now appeared as Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu”

## 17 Shringara Vata / Shringara Ghata

The word 'shringara' means to 'decorate', or to 'dress', either the Deity or a worshipable person, with various types of jewelry, ornaments, and clothing, and the word 'vata' means a 'banyan tree'. Shringara Vata, like the Radha Damodara Mandira and Imli-tala, is also situated within the area of Seva Kunja. It is said that on one occasion when Krishna left behind the other gopis and took only Radharani with Him, He sometimes came to this place. While sitting under this banyan tree, Krishna combed Radharani's hair into braids and then decorated her long black locks with aromatic forest flowers. Krishna would also decorate Her moonlike face with cosmetics made of natural pigments found in the nearby forests and smear black anjana on Her lotus eyes. He would also carefully decorate Her body with various gem-studded ornaments including a golden girdle, bangles, earrings, and a necklace of shining pearls. While Krishna was decorating Radharani in this way, She would hold up Her mirror and while seeing Her own reflection, gaze in awe at the beauty of Krishna's lotus-like face. In the Vraja-vilasa-stava it says, "While dancing with the radiantly beautiful wives of the cowherd men, Krishna left them and went with Radha to a solitary place to decorate Her with flower ornaments and engage in divine loving play with Her.”

At Shringar Vata Krishna would dress-up in various costumes just to please His cowherd boyfriends. On other occasions the cowherd boys would enjoy decorating Krishna with different dresses, ornaments and fragrant forest flowers. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Look at this wonderful vata tree on the bank of the Yamuna. Everyone calls it Shringara Vata. At this place Lord Krishna would enjoy Himself by dressing in various ways for the pleasure of Subala and the others.” Shringara Vata is also known as Nityananda Vata, because when Lord Nityananda came on pilgrimage to Vrindavana, He stayed at this very place. Lord Nityananda was an avadhuta, which means a sadhu or holy man who does not have any material conception of life, who appears to be almost mad due to intense feelings of love for God. While staying here, Lord Nityananda would often become completely absorbed in the mood of being a cowherd boy, sometimes He would sit down while chanting under this banyan tree and at other times He would roll on the ground in great ecstasy. On other occasions He would decorate Himself with forest flowers and cry out the names of Krishna in a very loud voice while shedding torrents of tears. According to the Bhakti-ratnakara, while Lord Nityananda was absorbed in the mood of Lord Balarama and shedding tears in separation from His younger brother Krishna, He suddenly heard a celestial voice from the sky informing Him that His younger brother Krishna had now taken birth at Navadwipa. After hearing the voice, Lord Nityananda immediately left for Navadwipa to meet Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

## 18 Jaru Mandala / Jamun Tree

This is the site of the famous jamun tree where Krishna once disappeared from Radharani just to intensify Her ecstatic love in the mood of separation. During rasa-lila pastimes at Vamsi Vata, Krishna suddenly left the arena of the rasa-dance and took only Radharani with Him. The gopis became almost mad at losing Krishna and began to search for Him everywhere. Meanwhile, Radha was feeling most fortunate among the gopis as She walked hand in hand with Krishna through Vrindavana forest. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, "As the rasa-dance began, Krishna observed the different grades of gopis and decided to leave them, taking Radharani alone with Him. Hiding at this place, Krishna happily heard the gopis' lamentation. Left alone by Krishna, the gopis inquired from the trees and creepers about His whereabouts. The gopis began imitating Krishna's pastimes, and they glorified Shrimati Radharani's fortunate position.”

While walking through the forest hand in hand with Krishna, in the hope of being embraced closely to Krishna’s chest, Radharani suddenly feigned weariness, hoping that Krishna would pick Her up and carry Her in His powerful arms. Understanding Her mind, Krishna immediately picked Radharani up and gently carried Her while embraced within His arms. Radharani was feeling very proud and especially favored that Krishna had chosen Her above all the other gopis. At that moment Krishna suddenly put Radharani down and disappeared into the bushes, leaving Her alone to lament Her mistake of becoming unnecessarily proud of Her fortunate position. Holding Her face in Her hands, She began weeping piteously and condemned Herself for revealing Her womanly pride in front of Her beloved Krishna, thus causing Him to leave Her. Radharani in great anguish said, “O master! My lover! O the dearest of all, where are You? Where areYou? Please, O mighty-armed one, O dear friend, I am totally helpless (withoutYou). I am Your servant. Please show Yourself to Me!” (SB.10.30.39). After some time, all the other gopis who had been franticly searching for Krishna in the forest, arrived at the jamun tree, and seeing Radharani all alone and in such a forlorn condition, they became very sad and tried to console Her feelings of separation.

The name Jaru Mandala means the area (mandala) swept with a broom (jaru). Some say it received its name as it was part of the area of Seva Kunja that was being swept by Shyamananda Pandita, but this is not correct. In another version, it is said this was a place where ascetics (tyagis) performed bhajana and many such tyagi-babas would gather to hear recitation of the Shrimad-Bhagavatam at this place. The incident in question occurred sometime in the late 18th Century when Vrindavana became more populated. The babas would always sweep the area with a jaru or broom before sitting down to hear the Bhagavatam. And for this reason this place got its name Jaru Mandala. An old blind widow residing nearby used to earn her living by grinding flour with a hand-operated grinding mortar. As she was blind and also half-deaf, she was usually unaware of the time of day. Consequently she would start grinding from the early hours and continue throughout the day and night.

The grinding sound always disturbed the babas who were trying to hear the Bhagavatam and the pastimes of Krishna; however, not wishing to interfere with the old widow whose only means of livelihood was grinding flour, the babas tolerated the grinding noise. Then one day, the old widow said a young boy suddenly arrived there and put his foot on the grindingmortar and stopped it, complaining that the grinding noise was disturbing the babas hearing Krishna-katha. The old widow told him her only income was from grinding flour. The boy then informed the old widow his name was Krishna, and that from now on His lotus foot-print would be indented on the grinding mortar and when local people came there to have darshana of His foot-print, they would leave some small donation, and in this way she could support herself. This foot-print soon became famous amongst local Vrajavasis who came for darshana while offering small donations as is the custom when visiting a holy place.

The Charana-cinha (foot-print) at Jaru Mandala is not included amongst the famous charana-chinhas of Vraja Mandala because it was not manifested during Krishna's pastimes and its antecedents are to some degree unclear. This story of the footprint can never be verified and the real importance of this place is the sacred jamun-vriksha tree connected to Radha and Krishna's pastimes during the rasa-lila in Vrindavana. With regard to the Indian Jambu tree which is also known as jambul, or jamun, it is a variety of damson, also known as black plum, and native to the sub-continent whose small crimson to dark purple colored fruit has a distinctive sweet and sour, as well as astringent taste. The jambu fruit is very popular when it ripens during the summer season as it is rich in vitamins and very good for health.
