Including:\*Bhramara Ghata.

## 195 Bhramara Ghata

Although not so easily recognized, located just after Chira Ghata, is the celebrated Bhramara Ghata. The word ‘bhramara' refers to a large variety of black bumblebee that is native to India. Once, Radha and Krishna were sitting together at this ghata when many black bumblebees suddenly became attracted by the sweet aroma emanating from the garland of forest flowers that Radharani was wearing. The intoxicated bumblebees began buzzing around the flower garland while making a tumultuous humming sound that was very pleasant for all to hear, thus the ghata became known as Bhramara Ghata - the ‘Bumblebee Ghata'.

How To Get There: (See map No.50).

End of excursion (Return to Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 26 Keshi Ghata / Keshi-tirtha

The Adi-varaha Purana says, “Keshi-tirtha, the place where Keshi was killed by Krishna, is a hundred times more sacred than the Ganges. By offering pinda to the forefathers at Keshi-tirtha, one attains the result of offering pinda in Gaya.” This is the ghata where Krishna bathed after slaying the horse-demon Keshi. The powerful demon arrived in the forest of Vrindavana in the form of a gigantic horse with the intention of killing Krishna. The Keshi demon was a servant of Kamsa and had been given the order to find Krishna and kill Him. This demon had been living in the area of Vraja for a long time and had previously terrorized the inhabitants of the Nandagrama area during the period that Parjanya, the father of Nanda Maharaja had lived near there at Tagada Tirtha, consequently Parjanya's family had to move away and establish a new residence at Gokula. The great demons like Keshi, Putana, Trinavarta, Vatsasura, Aghasura, and others, having performed many years of severe penance had achieved various siddhis, or mystical powers, and by the siddhi known as kama-rupa siddhi, they could change their physical form at will. In this regard the word ‘kama' means 'desire' and ‘rupa' means 'form', and simply by their desire they could change their form in an instant.

The Vraja-vilasa-stava says, “With his mad neighing Keshi made the three worlds tremble and with the wild rolling of his eyes he set the entire universe in flames. Krishna killed this demon as easily as one splits a blade of grass and then washed the blood from His hands at a place now known as Keshi-tirtha. I worship that sacred place.”

How To Get There: (See map No.51).

## The Liberation of the Keshi Demon

One day, the Keshi demon heard that Krishna was wandering in the forest of Vrindavana along with His cowherd boyfriends, and immediately went there to kill Him. Being a powerful demon, he possessed the form of a gigantic horse and when he arrived there, he immediately began neighing very loudly to announce his presence. Without wasting any time, Krishna very boldly appeared before the envious demon to accept his challenge. Making a loud whinnying sound, the Keshi demon began charging towards Krishna, kicking up large clumps of earth with his hooves as he galloped. Krishna remained steady and as the horse demon got within reach, Krishna simply picked him up like a child picks up a flower and hurled him at least a hundred meters away. Momentarily stunned due to being thrown over such a long distance, the demon got up and after shaking his head, once again neighing very loudly, started to gallop at even greater speed towards Krishna, hoping this time to trample Him into the ground. Waiting patiently for Keshi to get close enough, Krishna suddenly rammed His fist straight down the demon's throat, which knocked out all his large yellow teeth. Krishna then expanded his fist to such a size that the demon could no longer breathe and suddenly found himself choking to death. As the demon's bloodshot eyes bulged from their sockets, his legs began to shake violently, and streams of sweat poured from his body. As Keshi fell to ground in great pain he passed stool and urine simultaneously, as his life-air burst out from his head and merged with Krishna's lotus feet. Within moments it was all over, Krishna then proceeded to the bank of the Yamuna to wash the blood from His hands and take a purifying bath at this ghata, which then became celebrated as Keshi Ghata. Krishna then went to Chehana Ghata (Chira Ghata) and rested there for some time, surrounded by all His loving cowherd boyfriends.

## 196 Yugala-kishore Mandira

This is one of the early medieval temples built in Vrindavana after Emperor Akbar granted permission for the construction temples dedicated to Lord Krishna. This temple was completed in 1627 and is often referred to as the 'Keshi Ghata' temple due to its location next to the famous riverside ghata. This is not one of the celebrated Goswami temples of Vrindavana and the former presiding Deity is no longer being worshiped here. The temple was desecrated along with the other temples of Vrindavana by the soldiers of the Mughal tyrant Emperor Aurangzeb in 1670 and since then it has been closed.

How To Get There: (See map No.51).

End of excursion (Return to Vraja Mandala Parikrama route)

## 27 Gadadhara Dant Samadhi

This is the place near Keshi Ghata where the tooth (dant) of Gadadhara Pandita was placed in samadhi. Gadadhara Pandita was one of Lord Chaitanya's childhood friends and remained in the association of the Lord throughout his life. He was one of the celebrated members of Lord Chaitanya's inner circle of intimate associates known as the Pancha-tattva. According to Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika Gadadhara Pandita is Shrimati Radharani in Krishna's Vrindavana pastimes. In a purport to Chaitanya-charitamrita (Adi 10.15) it says, “Gadadhara Pandita is simultaneously an incarnation of Shrimati Radharani and Lalita-sakhi.

How To Get There: (See map No.51).

## 28 Vamsi-Gopala Mandira

This is the temple where His Divine Grace A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, the founder-acharya of ISKCON, stayed for four years, prior to moving to the Radha Damodara Mandira. In the year 1954, Shrila Prabhupada retired from family life and adopted the vana-prastha-ashram, he first preached for a year in Jhansi and then spent a few months at the Gaudiya Math in Mathura. Then in 1955 he was invited to stay at the Gaudiya Math in Old Delhi's Karol Bagh area, where he was engaged in editing the Harmonist Magazine and helping to manage the temple. However things did not work out favorably and within months he found himself homeless on the streets of Delhi and without funds. Regardless of these circumstances, Shrila Prabhupada continued to preach the message of Lord Chaitanya. He found free accomodation at various temples in Delhi and with whatever funds he could collect, he began printing his 'Back to Godhead' magazine on a regular basis and distributed the copies himself amongst the citizens of Delhi. Towards the end of 1956, Shrila Prabhupada paid a short visit to the holy city of Vrindavana and by Lord Krishna's mercy, the mahanta of the Vamsi Gopala Mandira, whom Shrila Prabhupada had first met on a previous visit to Vrindavana in 1953, offered Shrila Prabhupada a room on first floor the Mandira. The temple was located near Keshi Ghata, just a few minutes' walk from the Gaudiya Goswami temples of Radha Gokulananda, Radharamana, and Radha Gopinatha. After more than a year of homelessness in Delhi, It was the perfect place for Shrila Prabhupada to find a more permanent refuge.

Shrila Prabhupada had visited Vrindavana on a number of previous occasions, starting in 1925 with his family, and then again in 1932, where he met his spiritual master Shrila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Goswami at Kosi during the Gaudiya Matha's annual Vraja Mandala parikrama. Then again in 1935, he had met Shrila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati for the very last time at Radha-kunda, just one year before his spiritual master disappeared from the world. During that last meeting, his spiritual master advised him that if he ever got sufficient funds, he should print books rather than build temples, as books had a far greater impact on the population and was the most effective way of spreading the teachings of Lord Krishna.

Although Shrila Prabhupada had now found a permanent residence in Vrindavana, nevertheless, he continued to travel by the early morning train to Delhi where he continued with his preaching work, distributing his 'Back to Godhead' magazine and raising funds for printing further editions of the magazine. Shrila Prabhupada would either spend the night in Delhi or return to Vrindavana by the evening train. However, by January 1957, having successfully printed over twelve consecutive editions of his 'Back to Godhead' magazine, Shrila Prabhupada had run out of funds and was unable to find another donor and was forced to stop any further printing.

Being unable to continue 'Back to Godhead' magazine, Shrila Prabhupada decided to remain in Vrindavana and concentrate on his writing. Thus, in order to sustain his simple existence, Shrila Prabhupada performed the age-old tradition amongst mendicants known as madhukari. The performance of madhukari, which literally means 'collecting honey like a bee -from flower to flower', is a spiritual practice undertaken by holy men for maintaining the body and soul. The practice also involves the development of humility, by begging alms from door to door and accepting only a small amount from each house so as not to burden the householder. The householders would usually give chapattis, raw flour, rice, or lentils, which the holy men would either soak in water before eating or otherwise cook the items on a fire. This practice is ordained in the Vedic scriptures for all mendicants including brahmacharis, vanaprastas, and sannyasis. Each morning, Shrila Prabhupada, while carrying his small begging bowl and his umbrella, would first take darshan at the Radha Damodara Mandira, and then after performing madhukari, would go for darshan to the Radharamana Mandira; he would then chant japa while sitting beside the samadhi of Gopala Bhatta Goswami. After some time Shrila Prabhupada would then to Vamsi Gopala Mandira just before noon to honor the prashadam that he had received while performing madhukari.

In July 1959, the mahant of the Radha Damodara Mandira in Vrindavana informed Shrila Prabhupada that he had a number of vacant rooms and invited him to stay there. Shrila Prabhupada considered that the chance to stay at Radha Damodara was most auspicious, because the Radha Damodara Mandira had been established by Shrila Jiva Goswami, and was the place where Shrila Rupa Goswami had written many of his important books including the Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu (Nectar of Devotion). The Radha Damodara Mandira had also been Rupa Goswami's spiritual headquarters for spreading Lord Chaitanya's sankirtana movement, and the place where the Six Goswamis of Vrindavana would regularly meet to discuss transcendental topics. Shrila Prabhupada believed it was the ideal place for him to reside and write his English translation of the Shrimad-Bhagavatam. Without hesitation and looking forward to living in the close association of both Rupa and Jiva Goswamis, Shrila Prabhupada immediately accepted the offer to move his residence from the Vamsi-Gopala Mandira to Radha Damodara. At Radha Damodara Shrila Prabhupada at first occupied two rooms on the first floor and after they had been renovated, He moved into two rooms on the ground floor adjacent to the temple courtyard

How To Get There: (See map No.51).

## 29 Radha Gokulananda Mandira

The temple of Shri Shri Radha Gokulananda is said to have been established by Lokanatha Goswami, who in the later years of his life had performed bhajana in this secluded garden located near the banks of the Yamuna. Although Lokanatha was not directly one of the Six Goswamis of Vrindavana, he was the first Gaudiya Goswami to arrive in Vrindavana Dhama and he was also the eldest and most highly respected amongst the other Goswamis. He became one of the most renowned amongst the Gaudiya Goswamis residing in the holy Dhama and is often referred to as being the 'Seventh Goswami'. The temple of Radha Gokulananda that he founded is included amongst the famous 'Seven Goswami Temples of Vrindavana'. It appears that the temple of Radha Gokulananda may have previously been known as the temple of Radha Vinoda, as this name appears in some historical references. It was around one hundred years later when the Deity named Gokulanandaji, then worshiped by Shrila Vishvanatha Chakravarti, was actually installed in the temple. It is thought that the concept of the 'Seven Goswami Temples of Vrindavana' came into being during the renaissance period ushered in by Shrila Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura and his illustrious disciple Baladeva Vidyabhushana, who became the next Gaudiya Vaishnava acharyas in the Gaudiya Vaishnava sampradaya after Lokanatha Goswami's famous disciple Narottama Dasa Thakura.

Just prior to the attack on Vrindavan by the tyrant Aurangzeb in 1670, the Deity of Radha Vinoda was taken out of Vrindavana along with other Gaudiya Goswami Deities and is now being worshiped in the city of Jaipura. The Deity of Radha Gokulananda in the temple is thought by many to be the original Deity worshiped by Vishvanatha, but some others disagree, saying the original Deity is in Jaipura along with Radha Vinoda. The other Deities that can be seen in this temple are all pratibhu-murtis including: Gauranga Mahaprabhu (Narottama Dasa), Radha Vinoda (Lokanatha Goswami), Radha Vijaya-Govinda (Baladeva Vidyabhushana), and also the pratibhu murti of Mahaprabhu's famous govardhana-shila (Raghunatha Dasa Goswami). This govardhana-shila was worshiped by Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu who gave it as a gift to Raghunatha Dasa Goswami. The original shila which bears the thumb impression of Lord Chaitanya is presently being worshiped at Bhagawata Nivasa in the Ramana Reti area of Vrindavana. Within the compound of the Radha Gokulananda Mandira one can see the samadhis of Lokanatha Goswami, Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura, Narottama Dasa Thakura, and Ganganarayana Chakravarti.

How To Get There: (See map No.51 &51A).

## 29a Lokanatha Goswami Samadhi

According to his biographers, Lokanatha Goswami was born into a Bhatta-brahmana family in Talakhari village of Jessore District, Bengal (now in Bangladesh) in the year 1483. According to a purport in Chaitanya-charitamrta (Adi-lila 12.12.88), Lokanatha Goswami is mentioned as being one of the most important disciples of Gadadhara Pandita. After renouncing householder life, Lokanatha Goswami met Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in Navadwipa just prior to Lord Chaitanya taking sannyasa. It is said Lord Chaitanya ordered him to go to Vrindavana and search out the sacred forests and other important holy places scattered around Vraja Mandala. (Some say that this order was received in a dream). Lokonatha's lifelong friend and companion Bhugarbha Goswami, who was his paternal uncle and also a disciple of Gadadhara Pandita, had received a similar order from Lord Chaitanya and therefore accompanied Lokanath Goswami on his journey to Vrindavana arriving there in the year 1509. It is said that Lokanatha and Bhugarbha were practically inseparable and the extent of their friendship is described in the Bhakti-ratnakara, “Lokanatha’s affection for Bhugarbha was well known everywhere. They had different bodies, but in spirit they were one.” In order to locate the sacred forest the two Goswamis simply wandered here and there around Vraja calling out the names of the twelve forests. It is said that Vrinda Devi revealed the exact location of each forest to the two Goswamis. Due to his natural humility, Lokanatha forbade Krishnadas Kaviraj to write anything about him in the Chaitanya-charitamrita, thus only his name gains mention. Sanatana Goswami had mentioned his name in the mangalacharana to his famous book Hari-bhakti-vilasa, as well as in Vaishnava-toshani, his commentary on the tenth-canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam. Lokanatha Goswami constantly travelled throughout Vraja Mandala while visiting the various holy places where Krishna had performed His pastimes. He also spent some period of time performing bhajana on the banks of Sangama-kunda at Khadiravana, but when he visited Kishori Kund in the village of Umrao near Chatravana, he was so impressed with the transcendental beauty of the place that he stayed there for some years engaged in bhajana. One day, Lokanatha Goswami discovered the Deity of Shri Shri Radha Vinoda, hidden within the depths of Kishori-kunda. After discovering the Deity, Lokanatha Goswami devoutly worshiped the Deity for the rest of his life. It is well known that Lokanatha Goswami was extremely renounced and never accepted a bhajana-kutira. He always kept his Deity in a cloth bag hung around his neck and close to his heart like a necklace. During the rainy season he would keep the Deity in the crevice of a tree while he himself would simply sit on the ground in the pouring rain next to the tree chanting the holy names on his japa beads.

Due to his natural humility, he did not feel qualified to accept any disciples, although many were ready to accept him as their guru. However, Lord Chaitanya appeared to him in a dream and told him that in the future he would have to accept at least one very special devotee as his disciple, whose name would be Narottama Dasa. When eventually Narottama Dasa arrived in Vrindavana, Lokanatha was still not in the mood of initiating any disciples, but once again Lord Chaitanya appeared to him in a dream and asked him to give his mercy to Narottama Dasa, who was certainly the most worthy candidate. After receiving the dream, Lokanatha Goswami relented and accepted Narottama Dasa Thakura as his only disciple. It is believed that Lokanatha Goswami entered samadhi in the year 1585 (others have given the dates 1583 and 1588). His sacred body was entombed next to the temple of Radha Gokulananda that he had founded. According to the Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika (187) in Krishna's Vrndavana pastimes Lokanatha Goswami is the gopi named Lila Manjari, “lokanathakhya-gosvami shri-lila-manjari pura”. (According to some he was Manjulali-manjari)

How To Get There: (See map No.51 &51A).

## 29b Narottama Dasa Thakura Pushpa Samadhi

Shrila Narottama Dasa Thakura disappeared from this world while in Bengal in the year 1611. This samadhi contains a flower garland (pushpa) worn by Narottama Dasa, his outer cloth, a kaupina, and his japa beads. Some say that this was his baithaka or sitting place during the time that he stayed here near where his guru resided on the bank of the Yamuna River. He was the only disciple of Lokanatha Goswami and became famous for the large number of devotional songs that he wrote. Through his singing and expert mridanga playing, he made the Manohar-Shoy style of kirtana, originated by Shrinivasa Acharya, famous throughout the land. He was also a powerful preacher and converted thousands to the bhakti cult of Lord Chaitanya in Bengal and Assam, as well as the state of Manipura, where he was the first to introduce the sankirtana movement.

Some years before Narottama's birth, Lord Chaitanya was on a tour of Bengal where he visited Navadwipa and then Ramakeli, which is now in Bangladesh, where He met the brothers Rupa, Sanatana and Sri Vallabha, who were at that time still engaged in Government service. While there, Lord Chaitanya went to take His bath in the nearby Padma River. On the opposite bank of the river was a village called Kheturi, where in the future Narottama Dasa would be born. While gazing into the water, Lord Chaitanya began to call out in a very ecstatic mood. “O Narottama! O Narottama!” Lord Chaitanya then informed the devotees accompanying Him, that in the future a very great personality would be born at Kheturi, his name would be Narottama and he would become so absorbed in nama-kirtana-rasa, it would be equal to the sankirtana-rasa experienced by Lord Chaitanya Himself. The Lord also told the devotees that He would now bathe in the River Padma, and later when Narottama would come there to, the waters of the river would extend to Narottama the Lord's special mercy and divine love.

In the year 1534, the same year as Lord Chaitanya's disappearance, Narottama Dasa took birth in the village of Kheturi. His father was a kayastha, who are generally accepted as kshatriyas but some consider them to be sudras. Narottama's father however, was revered as a king due to his great wealth and ownership of vast tracts of land. As a boy, Narottama was a brilliant student and loved to hear about the pastimes of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. When he reached his teens, one night he had a dream in which Lord Nityananda appeared before him and told him. “Tomorrow morning you should take your bath in the River Padma, at that time you will receive Krishna-prema, pure love of God.” On waking the next morning, Narottama went immediately to the River Padma and on entering the water, experienced a sudden spiritual transformation. As Narottama became overcome with ecstasy, Lord Chaitanya suddenly appeared before him and embraced him within His arms, and Narottama felt the spirit of the Lord enter his heart. At that moment, Narottama's dark complexion turned a molten gold, the same color as Lord Chaitanya's transcendental body. On coming out of the water, Narottama began to dance in ecstasy up and down the river bank while loudly chanting the holy names of the Lord. As the morning wore on, suddenly realizing that Narottama was missing from home, his anxious parents came to the riverbank in search of their son. When they saw a golden complexioned youth dancing in ecstasy on the river bank, they could not at first recognize him as being their son, because his dark complexion and physical demeanor had so drastically changed. Eventually, they realized that this was in fact their son, and they immediately brought him back to their home. When they got their son home, they noticed that he was a completely changed person, who continually chanted the holy names of Krishna both day and night.

After some months, Narottama had another dream where Lord Chaitanya appeared before him and after tightly embracing him, ordered him to immediately leave for Vrindavana where he should accept Lokanatha Goswami as his spiritual master. Very soon after this dream, Narottama ran away from home and proceeded to Vrindavana, much to the despair of his loving parents. On arrival in Vrindavana, Narottama immediately went to see the Deity of Govindaji, and upon beholding the Deity's beautiful form, fell unconscious on the ground while exhibiting all the eight symptoms of ecstatic love known as ashta-satvika-bhava. The news quickly spread about this most unusual incident and Jiva Goswami immediately came to the Govindaji Mandira to see Narottama. Some of the devotees in Vrindavana had heard about the predictions made by Lord Chaitanya and had been wondering when Narottama would appear. Narottama was immediately placed under the care of Lokanatha Goswami, stayed in a garden near Keshi Ghata where the Gokulananda Mandira now stands. As Narottama had been informed in a dream by Lord Chaitanya to accept Lokanatha Goswami as his guru, he diligently performed all kinds of menial service for Lokanatha, who had also been told in a dream by Lord Chaitanya to accept Narottama as his disciple. Nevertheless, due to his great humility, he did not feel qualified to initiate anyone, and therefore declined. Regardless of Lokanatha Goswamis unwillingness, Narottama continued to offer his menial service to Lokanatha and would even clean the area in the jungle which was used by Lokanatha as a toilet. Lokanatha then had another dream, where Lord Chaitanya again appeared and reminded Lokanatha that it was the Lord's own cherished desire that he should accept Narottama as his disciple and initiate him. After receiving this dream, Lokanatha relented and accepted Narottama as his only disciple and requested Jiva Goswami to accept Narottama as his shikhsa disciple and train him in all the aspects of Vaishnava philosophy. Narottama then became part of Jiva Goswami’s famous troika of shiksa disciples, along with Shrinivasa Acharya and Shyamananda Pandita.

In the year 1582, Jiva Goswami sent these three illustrious and most brilliant disciples on a preaching mission to Bengal and Orissa, by bullock cart with a large trunk of books written by the Six Goswamis that had all been copied by hand and were to be distributed amongst the followers of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. This was the first ever book distribution party in the history of the Gaudiya sampradaya. Before leaving Madhu Pandita Goswami blessed them with flower garlands from Lord Gopinatha. After reached Bengal and having met all the Vaishnavas, Narottama Dasa returned to his home village of Kheturi and organized what was to become the first ever 'Gaura Purnima Festival', celebrating the appearance day of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. All the followers of Lord Chaitanya attended the festival including Jahnava Mata and her son Virabhadra. During the festival, with the help of Shrinivasa Acharya, Narottama installed five sets of Deities for the benefit of the devotees. One of those Deities, Vraja-mohana, is still being worshiped in Vrindavana near Gyana-gudri.

Narottama had one very close and dearly beloved companion named Ramacandra Kaviraja, and one important disciple named Ganganarayana Chakravarti. They both expertly assisted Narottama Dasa in his life's mission of spreading the divine message of Lord Chaitanya, to every town and village. According to the Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika, Narottama dasa is Vilasa-manjari in Krishna's Vrindavana pastimes.

How To Get There: (See map No.51 &51A).

## The Story of Narottama’s Gauranga Deity

It is said that while on a visit to his hometown of Kethuri, Narottam had the desire to install a number of Deities on the auspicious occasion Gaura Purnima, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's appearance day, for the purpose of expanding the preaching of the sankirtan movement. That night in a dream, Narottama saw six Deities, Vallabhi-Kanta, Sri Krishna, Vraja-Mohana, Radha-Kanta, Radha-Ramana and Gauranga Mahaprabhu. After the dream Narottam woke and spent the rest of the night shedding tears of joy. The next day Narottama began arranging for the Deities to be carved. Stone was brought and artisans started carving the six Deities with great devotion. Although the five Deities of Krishna were very beautiful, the Deity of Gauranga had not been carved so nicely and Narottama became disheartened and in an anguished mood began calling out in a loud voice, “Gauranga, Gauranga,” while shedding many tears.

That night in a dream, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu appeared before Narottam saying. “My dear Narottama, with much care you are trying to carve a Deity of Me, but I will never remain in that murti. I will now inform you how to obtain a Deity of Me. Before I accepted sannyasa I had a neem-wood Deity carved of Myself, which I had immersed in the Ganges river. Because you are My most beloved devotee I am telling you this. That Deity is now inside the rice store-room of Vipradas.” After saying this, Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu disappeared. Narottama immediately awoke and saw that morning had arrived so he began making inquiring from the local people about the residence of Vipradas. Narottama was informed that Vipradas was a wealthy merchant who lived nearby and had a business trading in rice and other grains. Hearing this, Narottam went to the house of Vipradas.

On arrival, Vipradas offered his obeisances to Narottama and inquired what had brought him to his home. “I have come on a special mission and want to go to the place where you store your grains.” Vipradas replied that it is not possible because the place had become infested with many kinds of poisonous snakes and as soon as they see anyone they become angry and begin hissing loudly. Out of fear for those snakes no one can go near that store-room. Narottama said, “Don't worry, when I arrive all the snakes will automatically leave.” After saying this, Narottama went to the rice store-room. Immediately on seeing him all the snakes left that place. After searching in the store-room Narottama soon found the Deity of Gauranga. Seeing the Deity, all of the people were surprised and from that time onwards there were no more snakes at that place, Vipradas became very happy and came with his whole family and took shelter at the feet of Narottama. Seeing the beauty of the Gauranga Deity, everyone felt very blissful. All those who had previously seen Chaitanya Mahaprabhu verified that the Deity looked exactly like the Lord Himself. It is said that the pratibhu-murti of Narottama's Gauranga Deity is worshiped on the altar of the Radha Gokulananda Mandira in Vrindavana.

## 29c Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura Samadhi

Shrila Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura entered samadhi in the year 1708, and his sacred body was entombed here in the garden of the Radha Gokulananda Mandira. He was born into a brahmana family of Nadia District in 1638. As a student he became an expert scholar of Sanskrit, philosophy, rhetoric, and poetry, and could easily defeat anyone in an open debate. He was the diksha disciple of the illustrious Vaishnava guru Radharamana Chakravarti and accepted Narottama Dasa Thakura as his shisha-guru. Vishvanatha was married at a very early age by his parents as it was the local custom in Bengal at the time, but had absolutely no interest in family affairs. He immediately left home and went to Vrindavana, where he performed bhajana on the banks of Radha-kunda and stayed in the old bhajana-kutira of Krishnadasa Kaviraja Goswami. After some time, he returned to his home in Nadia, where, at the insistence of his parents, his guru implored him to at least spend one night in the bed of his young wife. He obeyed the order of his guru, but after lying in bed with his very beautiful young wife, he spent the whole night chanting the holy names of the Lord. His parents were disappointed, but his guru was delighted at his sense control realizing he was actually a very advanced Vaishnava.

His guru took him to stay in his own house and engaged him in making a copy of the Shrimad-Bhagavatam, which in those days was done by hand and took a considerable time. While intensely copying the Bhagavatam, Vishvanatha would sometimes enter into trance and exhibit ecstatic symptoms. On another occasion, the sun was beating down, but the spot where Vishvanatha sat appeared to be in the shade. Another time it began raining, but the place where Vishvanatha sat, no rain could be seen falling. A local landowner personally witnessed this event and broadcast the news throughout the village, much to the humble Vishvanatha's embarrassment. After some time, his guru Radharamana Chakravarti, told Vishvanatha to return to Vrindavana and continue with his activities of serving the mission of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Vishvanatha returned and again took shelter at Radha-kunda, where he began writing a number of important books. He also composed many devotional songs of which the most famous is Shri Shri Gurv-ashtaka, the famous prayer to the spiritual master sung in all ISKCON temples during the mangala-arati ceremony each morning.

When he returned to the holy Dhama, he was presented with the Deity of Radha Gokulananda by a brahmachari, who while visiting Mathura, had received a dream in which the Deity informed the brahmachari that He wanted to be worshiped by Vishvanatha. Not knowing who Vishvanatha was, the brahmachari had to search for him. When the brahmachary found Vishvanatha, he was reluctant to accept the Deity because being a mendicant; he lived by begging alms and could not provide the Deity with the requisite standard of worship, therefore feeling disappointed the brahmachari left. That night, Vishvanatha received a dream in which the Lord informed him that he should accept the Deity and worship Him in whatever way he could, as this would make the Lord very happy. The brahmachari also had a dream in which the Lord told him to return again and this time Visvanatha would accept the Deity, which he did. While Vishvanatha was staying at Radha-kunda, he also took over the worship of the famous govardhana-sila given to Raghunatha Dasa Goswami by Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

How To Get There: (See map No.51 &51A).

## 30 Radharamana Mandira

This is one of the 'Seven Goswami Temples' and was established by Gopala Bhatta Goswami, one of the famous Six Goswamis of Vrindavana. The Deity of Radharamana suddenly self-manifested one day from a shalagrama-shila just for the pleasure of Gopala Bhatta. All shalagrama-shilas are considered to be a natural manifestation of Lord Vishnu and are therefore immediately worshipable and do not need to be installed. The shalagrama-shila is a sacred black stone that is worshiped specifically by brahmanas and must be worshiped in all Vedic sacrifices as the yajna-pati, or principle enjoyer of the sacrifice. The shalagram-shila is also an essential part of Deity worship being the principle recipient of the seva-puja, and no worship is considered complete without the shaligrama-shila being worshiped as the seva-pati.

The story regarding the amazing shalagrama-shila of Gopala Bhatta is as follows. After spending a number of years studying and writing in the company of the Goswamis of Vrindavana, Gopala Bhatta decided to make the arduous journey to the holy place known as Muktinatha in the Himalayas, where there is a famous shrine of Lord Vishnu. One day while taking his bath in the sacred Kali Gandaki River that flows in the region of Muktinatha, Gopala Bhatta scooped water with his kamandalu and was about to pour it over his head, when he found that a number of black stones known as shalagrama-shilas had somehow or other entered his kamandalu, perhaps due to the strong currents in the river. After putting them back into the Gandaki, he again scooped water with his kamandalu and found that the shilas had once again entered his kamandalu. Surprised at this, he again put them back into the river, but when this happened for a third time, he realized it was the plan of the Lord and decided to keep all the shilas that had entered his kamandalu, he carefully tied them in a cloth and kept it suspended around his neck for safety. The Kali Gandaki River, which starts high-up in the Himalayan Mountains in what is now Nepal, is the only river in the world where these sacred shalagrama-shilas can be found.

When Gopala Bhatta eventually returned to Vrindavana, he performed his bhajana in a corner of Nidhuvana where he also began worshiping the shalagrama-shilas he had obtained from the Kali Gandaki River. At night, Gopala Bhatta would place all the shalagrama-shilas in a cloth bag and hang them in a nearby tree while he took rest. One day while worshiping the shalagrama-shilas, he began lamenting that he did not have an archa-vigraha or Deity of Lord Krishna like the other Goswamis, which he could dress with beautiful clothing, ornaments, crowns, and other Deity paraphernalia. The following day was Narasingha-chaturdashi, the appearance day of Lord Narasinghadeva, the half-man half-lion incarnation of Vishnu who appeared from a rock pillar. Early the next morning when Gopala Bhatta went to worship his shalagrama-shilas, to his utter amazement he found that one of the shilas had opened up and transformed into a beautiful Deity of Krishna, standing in the tri-bhanga-rupa, or the three-fold bending form and playing a flute. On hearing the news of the miracle, the other Goswamis immediately came to congratulate Gopala Bhatta on his amazingly good fortune and to see for themselves the exquisite beauty of the self-manifested Deity, which stood about ten inches high. The Goswamis gave the Deity the name 'Radharamana' which means 'one who gives pleasure to Radha'. When the Deity is being dressed in the morning, or during abhisheka ceremonies, one can clearly see half of the shalagrama-shila from which the Deity appeared, still attached to Deities back.

It is said that the Deity's lotus face resembles that of Govindaji, His chest is like that of Gopinathaji, and His lotus feet are identical to those of Madana-Mohana, thus it is said that by having darshana of Radharamana one also recieves darshana of the three presiding Deities of Vrindavana, namely: Govindaji, Gopinathaji, and Madana-Mohana. There is no Deity of Radharani in this temple because the Deity of Radharamana is worshiped as a saligram-shila and therefore in accordance with Hari-bhakti-vilasa, a gomati-chakra (sacred stone from the river Gomati) is being worshiped simultaneously. From the Vaishnava perspective Radharani is eternally present with Krishna although She may be in Her unmanifested (aprakata) feature. However, the crown (mukuta) of Radharani is kept on the altar signifying Her presence. The actual spot where the Deity self-manifested from the shaligrama-shila can be seen in a courtyard just next to Gopala Bhatta's Samadhi Mandira. An off-shoot of the original tree where Gopala Bhatta used to hang his shaligrama-shilas in a bag at night can also be seen. According to the historical treatise Seva-prakatya, the abhisheka and installation of the Radharamana took place on Vaishakha-purnima in the year 1543. As the Deity of Radharamana is very small and a temple had not been established at that time, the Deity remained hidden in Vrindavana during the attack on the holy city by the forces of Emperor Aurangzeb in 1690. The present temple of Radharamana that is seen today was opened in 1826.

## 30a Gopala Bhatta Goswami Samadhi

Shrila Gopala Bhatta Goswami entered samadhi in the year 1585, and his sacred body was entombed at this spot where he performed his bhajana and worshiped his Deity named Radharamana. Gopala Bhatta was born in the year 1503 on trayadashi during the lunar month of Pausha (Krishna-paksha). He first met Lord Chaitanya during his childhood at Shrirangam (Rangapatnam) in Tamil Nadu, during the Lord's tour of South India in 1511. When Lord Chaitanya arrived at Shrirangam, He met Gopala Bhatta's father whose name was Venkata Bhatta, in the famous temple of Seshashayi Vishnu, also known as the Ranganatha Mandira. After seeing the transcendental beauty of Lord Ranganatha, Lord Chaitanya chanted the holy names and danced in ecstasy before the Deity. Venkata Bhatta, who was a sevak in the temple, also joined Lord Chaitanya, and chanted and danced along with the Lord in an ecstatic mood. After the kirtana ended, Venkata Bhatta invited Lord Chaitanya to his residence for prashadam, and also requested Him to spend the entire rainy season at his home in Shrirangam. During the four months of the monsoon season, when it rains very heavily, especially in South India, sannyasis and other traveling mendicants generally remain in one place, therefore Lord Chaitanya very happily accepted Venkata Bhatta's proposal.

Venkata Bhatta was a pure Vaishnava of the Shri sampradaya and was a priest at the temple of Rangaji. Every day during Lord Chaitanya's stay at his residence he would discuss the transcendental topics of Krishna-katha with Him. While the Lord was staying at Venkata Bhatta's house, the young Gopala Bhatta had the opportunity to hear all the transcendental topics as well as render service to Lord Chaitanya, including honoring the remnants of Mahaprabhu's prashadam. Lord Chaitanya, who could recognize the devotional qualities of the young Gopala Bhatta, told him not to marry and in the future, and when he was old enough, he should go and stay in Vrindavana. Lord Chaitanya also met Gopala Bhatta's uncle, Prabhodananda Saraswati, who was one of the greatest scholars of the Shri sampradaya, and was also the initiating spiritual master of Gopala Bhatta. Probhodananda was also responsible for the education of Gopala and trained him in Sanskrit grammar, philosophy, rhetoric, poetry, and all the important aspects of Vedic culture. Under the expert guidance of Prabhodananda Saraswati, Gopala Bhatta's scholarship was unparalleled. While Lord Chaitanya stayed at Shrirangam, Prabhodananda Saraswati also had the opportunity to discuss philosophy with Lord Chaitanya and was so impressed with the Lord's precepts and teachings, that he left the Shri sampradaya and became an ardent follower of the Gaudiya Vaishnava sampradaya, and eventually went to live in Vrindavana where he spent the remainder of his life.

After the death of his parents, Gopala Bhatta left for Vrindavana to take shelter of Rupa and Sanatana Goswamis. Lord Caitanya had already informed the two Goswamis that Gopala Bhatta would one day join them, and they immediately accepted him as their younger god-brother. When Lord Chaitanya heard that Gopala Bhatta had arrived in Vrindavan, he was extremely pleased and sent some of His personal belongings to Gopala Bhatta as gifts, including His sitting place (choki), and His loin-cloth (kaupin). There is also a cloth wrapper (chadar) that is also said to have been sent as a gift by Lord Chaitanya.

It is believed that Gopala Bhatta, who was an expert in the subject of Deity worship, made significant contributions to Sanatana Goswami's celebrated book, the Hari-bhakti-vilasa which he also helped to edit. The Hari-bhakti-vilasa delineates the principles of devotional service as well as the authorized Vedic system of Deity worship. Gopala Bhatta is also credited for helping to originate the six theses for Jiva Goswami's famous Sat Sandharbha. Gopala Bhatta's most celebrated disciple was the celebrated Shrinivasa Acharya. In the Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika, Shri Kavi Karnapura Goswami says, "In my opinion, that person who in Vrindavana was Ananga Manjari is now Gopal Bhatta Goswami, some authorities, however, have given their opinion that he was Guna Manjari.”

How To Get There: (See map No.51).

## 31 Radha Gopinatha Mandira

The temple of Radha Gopinatha is one of the 'Seven Goswami Temples of Vrindavana' and was established by Shrila Madhu Pandita Goswami, a prominent disciple of Gadadhara Pandita and an important follower of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Although he was not directly one of the Six Goswamis, he is counted as one of the important Gaudiya Goswamis of Vrindavana. When Madhu Pandita Goswami came to Vrindavana he began searching everywhere for the Deity of Lord Gopinatha that had been lost since many years. Lord Gopinath was one of the three presiding Deities of Vrindavana, along with Govindaji and Madana-Mahana, originally established by Vajranabha Maharaja. However, even after searching for the Deity every day, Madhu Pandita could not find Lord Gopinatha and feeling great sorrow, he eventually gave up eating food altogether and would sit at Vamsi Vata while shedding a constant stream of tears in separation from the Deity. However, Madhu Pandita's ardent desire to serve the Lord Gopinatha would soon be fulfilled.

That year during the monsoon season there was a great flood in Vrindavana and the River Yamuna overflowed her banks. It is said that the great force of the flood waters swept away the famous banyan tree that stood at Vamsi Vata. After the monsoon rains had abated and the flood waters had receded, Paramananda Bhattacharya, a disciple of Gadadhara Pandita and a close companion and god-brother of Madhu Pandita, took a branch from the old banyana tree in order to plant it in the same spot where the old banyana tree had once stood. On his arrival at Vamsi Vata, Paramananda suddenly noticed the Deity of Lord Gopinatha lying half-buried in the ground near the place where the great banyan tree had been uprooted. Paramananda immediately called Madhu Pandita and after retrieving the Deity from the earth, they moved the Deity to the bhajana-kutira of Madhu Pandita near to where the Gopinatha temple now stands. Madhu Pandita then began the worship of Lord Gopinatha, which continued until his dying day.

The Gopinatha Mandira is the only temple where one can see the Deity of Ananga-manjari on the altar. Ananga-manjari is Radharani's younger sister and she can be seen standing on Lord Gopinatha's left-hand side, with Radharani standing on Gopinatha's right-hand side. This arrangement is most unusual because Radharani always stands on the left-hand side of Krishna in all other temples. (if viewed from the darshana mandapa then Ananga Manjari is standing on the right and Radharani is on the left). There is a very interesting story that explains this most unusual occurrence. Soon after the installation of the Deity of Radharani at the Govindaji Mandira, a Deity of Radharani was installed in all the other Gaudiya temples in Vrindavana including Madana-Mohana and Gopinathaji. When Lord Nityananda's wife, Jahnava Mata, visited Vrindavana on pilgrimage in the year 1582, she felt that the Deity of Radharani being worshiped on the altar with Lord Gopinatha was far too small, therefore when she returned to Bengal she asked one of her disciples to carve a new Deity of Radharani especially for the Gopinatha temple. This new Deity was then sent to Vrindavana and immediately installed next to Lord Gopinatha. When all the devotees in Vrindavana saw the new Deity of Radharani, they felt that it looked just like Jahnava Mata. This happened because the devotee who carved the Deity, being a disciple of Jahnava Mata, had modeled it on the beautiful features of Jahnava Mata herself.

After consulting with all the senior Vaishnavas, it was decided that the Deity was actually Ananga-manjari, Radharani's younger sister, who in Chaitanya-lila appeared as Jahnava Mata, Lord Nityananda's consort. Because the Deity resembling Ananga-manjari had already been installed at the left-hand of Lord Gopinatha, it was felt that it must have been prearranged by Lord Gopinatha Himself, and should therefore not be moved. The smaller Deity of Radharani was then placed on Lord Gopinatha's right-hand where She remains even today. All the devotees felt that due to Ananga-manjari's deep desire to serve Lord Gopinatha; out of compassion and love for Her younger sister, Radharani had elevated her to Her own position at the left-hand of Lord Gopinatha. Later in the year 1632, a grand temple was constructed next to Madhu Pandita's bhajana-kutira where he worshiped the Deity of Lord Gopinatha. The temple construction was undertaken by the noted Rajput king named Raja Saganji, one of the Shekawat royal princes of Rajasthana.

In the year 1670, the Deity of Lord Gopinatha was moved to Jaipur due to the attack on Vrindavana by the tyrant Aurangzeb whose soldiers desecrated the important Gaudiya Goswami temples including Govindaji, Gopinathaji and Madana-Mohana. Sometime later a new temple of Gopinatha was constructed next to the original one and the pratibhu-murti of Lord Gopinatha, Radharani and Ananga Manjari were installed there. These pratibhu-murtis are still being worshiped in the new temple and Ananga Manjari can still be seen standing on the left of Lord Gopinatha with Radharani standing on the right. This same arrangement occurs in all the various Gopinatha temples in Vraja including the two Gopinatha temples at Radha-kunda, as well as in Jaipura where the original Deity of Lord Gopinatha is presently being worshiped.

The Deity of Lord Gopinatha along with the Deities of Madana-Mohana and Govindaji, originally established by Vajranabha in Vrindavana, represent the three eternal duties, or in other words the constitutional position of all living entities trapped in the material world under the shackles of maya. The word prayojana refers to the ultimate goal of life, which is to develop love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead and Lord Gopinatha is the Deity who helps us to establish this loving relationship. Lord Gopinatha, who is also known as Gopijanabhallava - the attracter of the gopis, is the Deity who fulfills all our desires and attracts us to return back to Godhead. Therefore, Lord Gopinatha also represents the ultimate goal of devotional service, which is spontaneous attraction in pure love of Godhead.

## 31A Madhu Pandita Goswami Samadhi

The Samadhi Mandira of Shrila Madhu Pandita Goswami can be seen located near to the eastern gate of the old Gopinatha Mandira on the spot where it is believed his bhajana-kutira once stood and where he used to worship the Deity of Lord Gopinatha. Shrila Madhu Pandita Goswami was a prominent disciple of Gadadhara Pandita and one of Lord Chaitanya's important associates. Although Madhu Pandita was not directly one of the Six Goswamis, he was one of the most prominent Gaudiya Goswamis living in Vrindavana during the period. He is credited with discovering the Deity of Lord Gopinatha and establishing His worship as well as being the inspiration behind the construction of the Gopinatha Mandira. Due to the significance of the Gopinatha Deity having been originally established by Vajranabha five thousand years earlier, the Gopinatha Mandira became celebrated as one of the 'Seven Goswami Temples of Vrindavana'. It is said that in Vrindavana-lila Shrila Madhu Pandita Goswami is the gopi named Mandali in the yuta, or group of younger gopis under the leadership of the ashta-sakhi Champakalata.

## 197 Sona Gauranga Mandira

Here are the Gaura-Nitai Deities worshiped by Shrila Jagannatha Dasa Babaji during his first sojourn in Vraja when he stayed at Surya-kunda. These Deities became known as Sona-Gauranga because They always shined brilliantly like gold. Due to Their golden hue, one day, some thieves made an abortive attempt to steal Them, believing that They were made of solid gold. After this incidence, Jagannatha Dasa Babaji brought the Sona-Gauranga Deities to Vrindavana for safety where they were given to a Bengali brahmana to worship.

## 198 Bilvamangala Samadhi

Bilvamangala Thakura was a famous Vaishnava saint who performed solitary bhajana on the banks of Brahma-kunda. There are many legends about him and it is said that he lived in Vrindavana for seven hundred years, but this cannot be confirmed by any historical evidence. The details of his life are somewhat sketchy and the date of his birth is not known, but probobly appeared in the eighth century and originally hailed from the Southern Indian state of Kerala. He is said to have been a disciple of Vishnuswami of the Rudra Vaishnava sampradaya. There were three acharyas in that sampradaya with the same name: Adi Vishnuswami (3rd century BCE) was the first Vaishnava acharya to adopt tridandi-sannyasa, which he brought into practice and initiated over seven hundred sannyasa disciples. It was he who introduced the Astottara-satanami-sannyasa (108 designations of sannyasis), including the dasanami which was later adopted by Sankaracharya in his sect. The second was Raja Gopala Vishnuswami (8th or 9th century CE), and the third was Andhra Vishnuswami (14th century CE). It appears that Bilvamangala lived during the period of Raja Gopala Vishnuswami. However, in the preface to his book Krishna-karnamrita, Bilvamangala mentions Chintamani as his shiksha-guru and Somagiri as his diksha-guru. Therefore it is plausible that Somagiri was a guru in the Vishnuswami sampradaya during the period of Raja Gopala Vishnuswami. It appears that Bilvamangala was a life-long follower of the Vishnuswami sampradaya and some say he became an acharya in that sampradaya. According to some old inscriptions found at Dwarka in Gujarat State, one Bilvamangala established the temple of Lord Dwarkadisha there, but whether it is the same Bilvamangala is unclear.

Bilvamangala Thakura is famous for his devotional songs and he also wrote the celebrated book Krishna-karnamrita, about Radha and Krishna's transcendental pastimes in Vrindavana. This particular book was a favorite of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and Swarupa Damodara would regularly recite the verses of this book for the Lord's pleasure. Because of his expertise in presenting the pastimes of Radha and Krishna, he was given the name Lilasuka (the Sukadeva of Krishna-lila). Sometimes he is confused with another blind saint of Vrindavana named Surdas, who lived at Chandra-sarovara near Govardhana Hill in the late 16th century. Bilvamangala composed many verses, poems and songs about Radha-Krishna prema-rasa but his most famous work is Krishna-karnamrita, which was the first book to reveal the supreme position of Srimati Radharani. In the later writings of Rupa and Sanatana Goswamis, Raghunatha Dasa Goswami, Ramananda Raya, Prabodhananda Saraswati, Krishna Dasa Kaviraja, and Vishvanatha Chakravarti, they expanded on the concept of exclusively serving and worshiping Srimati Radharani, the Queen of Vrindavana and the supreme controller of even Krishna Himself. Krishna-karnamrita is an extremely exalted scripture meant for the most advanced devotees; the word ‘karnamrita' means 'nectar to the ears'. Krishna Dasa Kaviraja Goswami wrote an important commentary on this book entitled Saranga-rangada.

Legend says that one day as Bilvamangala Thakura was singing his bhajanas on the bank of Brahma-kunda, Krishna appeared before him in the guise of an ordinary Vrajavasi cowherd boy and said, "Oh, my dear sir, why are you not eating anything? Why don't you take some milk?" The Thakura replied "Oh, who are you, my dear boy?" Krishna replied "Oh, I am a cowherd boy of this village and if you like I can bring you milk every day." The Thakur was very happy and said "All right." So Krishna supplied Bilvamangala milk every day and they became friends. The cowherd boy would also help Bilvamangala by guiding here and there and make sure he had a comfortable resting place. At first Bilvamangala had no clue about the identity of this wonderful Vrajavasi cowherd boy. But then one day Bilvamangala heard the cowherd boy play his flute and was immediately enraptured by the transcendental sound of the flute. Suddenly, Bilvamangala realized that this cowherd boy was non-other than Krishna Himself, the Lord of his life. He eagerly reached out to touch Krishna, but Krishna instead touched Bilvamangala's hand and while laughing He ran away. Bilvamangala then said, "You can run away from my hand, but You can never run away from my heart."

There is a very famous story about Bilvamangala Thakura during his youth, which says that he fell in love with a very beautiful prostitute named Chintamani. She was a beautiful dancing girl, a musician and also a harlot. He was so overcome and smitten by her charms, that he was prepared to risk even his own life to see her. Bilvamangala had just performed the last rites of his father, but regardless he was overcome with such a blazing passion that he could only think of enjoying sex with Chintamani. As night fell there was a dark and fearful storm, but he was so obsessed that he just had to see Chintamani even though the weather conditions were really bad. In order to reach Chintamani's house Bilvamangala had to face the onslaught of the powerful wind and driving rain. He also had to cross a swollen river and as there were no boats, he latched onto what he thought was a log to paddle across; in fact when he reached the other side, the log turned out to be a dead corpse. It is said that once he reached the house of Chintamani, the gate was locked and due to the howling wind, no one could hear him knocking on the door. He then decided to scale the high compound wall surrounding the house and began to climb the wall with the help of a long vine that was hanging down. When he reached the top of the wall, he realized that the long vine was in fact a very long snake entwined within the vines. Unperturbed, he made his way to Chintamani's bedroom and knocked on the door.

When Chintamani opened the door, she could not believe her eyes, she was simply amazed to see Bilvamangala standing there, soaking wet and having braved such a terrible storm in order just to see her. Although Chintamani was a prostitute, she had great faith in Lord Krishna. On realizing that Bilvamangala had gone through such an incredible endeavor just to meet her she exclaimed, “If you had just one thousandth of the affection for Bhagavan as you have for me, you would be able to become a siddha-purusha and behold the transcendental beauty of Lord Krishna. On hearing these wise words of Chintamani, Bilvamangala was both shocked and embarrassed. Accepting the words of Chintamani as those of his guru, he immediately resolved to renounce the world and devote his life to the service of Lord Krishna. Having taken sannyasa and set out on the path of renunciation, Bilvamangala was once again allured to enjoy sex. While begging alms from a brahmana's house, he became captivated by the beauty of the brahmana's young wife. As it was the religious duty of a brahmana to offer a sannyasi whatever he wished, Bilvamangala was about to ask if he could enjoy the company of the brahmana's wife, but at that moment he suddenly realized what a dastardly thing he was about to do. Instead Bilvamangala asked the brahmana's wife to give him her hair-pin, saying, “Alas, these eyes have become my worst enemy," and he immediately pierced both of his eyes with the pin and was instantly blinded.

## 32 Dhira Samira / Dhira Samira Ghata

After enjoying rasa-lila pastimes with the gopis, Krishna came to this pleasing spot accompanied by all the gopis to relax on the banks of the Yamuna where there was always a very cooling breeze. The words ‘dhira samira' means a 'gentle breeze'. In the Vraja-ritti-cintamani it is said. “One time, when Sri Krishna had gone a little distance from Vamsivata, a gentle breeze sprang up from His flute playing. That place became known as Dhira Samira.” After resting at Dhira Samira for some time, Krishna and the gopis would enter the crystal clear waters of the nearby Yamuna River and refresh themselves by swimming and sporting in the cooling waters. There were formerly two sandy beaches known Rasa-pulina and Yamuna-pulina located in the middle of the Yamuna where Krishna and the gopis enjoyed many wonderful pastimes. The word ‘pulina' means a 'sand bank', or 'small island' located in the middle of a river.

After feasting on various forest fruits, Krishna expanded Himself by His yogamaya potency and simultaneously entered the many flower bedecked bowers (kunjas) to lie down on a bed of flower petals next to each gopi. In this way Krishna fulfilled the desire of each gopi, to spend the night holding Krishna in their arms and embracing Him to their heart's content. Krishna had given a promise to the gopis when He stole their garments during the Katyayani-vrata, that in the near future they would be able to enjoy Him as their husband in the forest groves of Vrindavana, thus Krishna fulfilled His promise to the gopis of Vraja.

The Bhakti-ratnakara says. “O Shrinivasa, at this place, Dhira-samira, Krishna performed endless pastimes in the forest groves. The wonderful meeting of Radha and Krishna at this place is relished by Their dear associates. O Shrinivasa, see here is Manikarnika. In this forest Krishna had many pastimes. At this place Krishna pacified Radharani when She was in an angry mood.” In the area of Dhira Samira, there was a forest grove known as Manikarnika and within that grove was the Mana-bhanjana-sthala where Krishna very expertly dissipated the jealous anger of Shrimati Radharani. The word 'mana' means 'jealous anger' and 'bhanjana' means to 'break' or to 'dissipate'.

How To Get There: (See map no.52)

## 33 Shrinivasa Acharya Kunja

This is where Shrinivasa Acharya, the famous disciple of Gopala Bhatta Goswami performed his bhajana and where he worshiped his famous Deity known as Jula Thakura. The Deity achieved this unusual name because Shrinivas used to keep Him in his bead-bag which is also called a jula (bag). The small Deity of Jhula Thakura is still being worshiped in this temple. It is said that Shrinivasa was the embodiment of Gaura-shakti and was a one-sixteenth part of the full spirit of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. There were two main angas or limbs of Lord Chaitanya: The first were the six Goswamis who were entrusted with the excavation of Vrindavana, compiling books on devotional service and establishing Deity worship. The second anga was the famous troika of Shrinivas Acharya, Narottam das Thakur and Shyamananda Pandita. These three preached the message of Lord Chaitanya throughout Eastern India.

Shrinivasa Acharya appeared on the full-moon day in the lunar month of Vaishakha (April-May) in the year 1517. His parents were Gangadhara Bhattacharya and his wife Lakshmi Priya and they lived in the small village of Chakhandi, on the bank of the Ganges in the Burdwan district of Bengal. The father and mother of Shrinivasa hailed from a brahmana family and were ardent followers of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. They were present at the sannyasa ceremony of the Lord Chaitanya at Katwa. They met Lord Chaitanya again in Puri where He informed them that they would have a son whose name would be Shrinivasa. In his youth Shrinivasa was extremely beautiful and had a golden bodily luster, which reminded everyone who saw him of Lord Chaitanya. After completing his schooling, Shrinivasa left home to join Lord Chaitanya at Puri, but while on the way heard about the Lord's sudden disappearance. On arrival at Puri he met Gadadhara Pandita who informed him that Lord Chaitanya had given specific instructions that Shrinivasa should study Shrimad-Bhagavatam under Gadadhara's personal supervision. After the disappearance of Gadadhara Pandita, Shrinivasa left Puri for Vrindavana where he took shelter of Gopala Bhatta Goswami and later took initiation from him. In turn Gopala Bhatta sent Shrinivasa to study the Gaudiya scriptures under Shrila Jiva Goswami. Shrinivasa excelled in his studies and along with Narottama Dasa Thakura and Shyamananda Pandita, became known as the three most brilliant shiksha disciples of Jiva Goswami.

On the recommendation of Shrila Jiva Goswami, both Shrinivas and Narottama, were taken on the now famous parikrama of Vraja Mandala by Raghava Pandita Goswami, immortalized in the book Bhakti-ratnakara. Once their studies were complete, Jiva Goswami sent these three disciples Shrinivasa Narottama and Shyamananda, to Bengal to distribute the handwritten books of the Six Goswamis among the followers of Lord Chaitanya. During their journey to Bengal the books of the Goswamis were stolen by a gang of thieves working for the dacoit king named Birhambir. After searching for the stolen books, Shrinivasa was able to recover them while at the same time convincing the dacoit king Birhambir to give up his sinful life and become a pure Vaishnava. Shrinivas Acharya went on to become one of the most prominent preachers of Lord Chaitanya's sankirtana movement converting thousands to Vaishnava Dharma. He was also acknowledged as a wonderful kirtan singer and is famous for his brilliant composition entitled Sad-goswami-astaka, the prayers glorifying the Six Goswamis of Vrindavana. Shrinivasa Acharya was the originator the Manohar-Shoy style of kirtana made famous through the songs of Narottama Dasa Thakura. Shrinivasa also helped Narottama organize the first Gaura Purnima Festival at Kheturi, which was attended by Jhanava Mata and her son Balabhadra, along with thousands of other Vaishnavas. Amongst his disciples was Ramachandra Kaviraja, who became a very close friend and confidant of Narottama Dasa Thakura. At the ardent request of his aged mother, Shrinivasa accepted the grihastha-ashrama and became the father of a brilliant daughter named Hemlate Thakurani, who in her own right became a prominent guru and preacher of Lord Chaitanya's teachings and converted thousands to engage in Krishna-bhakti and take part in the sankirtana movement.

How To Get There: (See map no.52).

## 33A Shrinivasa Acharya Samadhi

Located in a room across the courtyard from the temple of Jhula Thakura is the samadhi of Shrinivasa Acharya. According to Gaura-gonaddesha-dipika, Shrinivasa Acharya is the gopi maidservant of Radharani named Mani Manjari in Krishna's Vrindavana pastimes.

How To Get There: (See map no.52).

## 33B Ramachandra Kaviraja Samadhi

The samadhi of Ramachandra Kaviraja is located next to the samadhi of his guru Shrinivasa Acharya. He was given the title kaviraja, or 'king of poets', by the Gaudiya Goswamis for his wonderful poetic compositions about the pastimes of Radha and Krishna. Along with his brother Govinda Kaviraja, he became celebrated as one of the famous 'Eight Kavirajas' of Lord Chaitanya's sankirtana movement. Shrinivasa Acharya also helped his dear friend Narottama Dasa Thakura, to organize the first 'Gaura Purnima Festival' that celebrated the appearance day of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, held in Narottama's hometown of Kheturi.

How To Get There: (See map no.52).

## 33C Hemlata Thakurani Pashpa Samadhi

The samadhi of Hemlata Thakurani, the famous daughter of Shrinivasa Acharya is located just next to the samadhi of her father. She was one of the most prominent female followers of Lord Chaitanya's movement and played an important role in spreading the sankirtana movement in Bengal.

How To Get There: (See map no.52).

## 34 Radha Shyama-Raya Mandira / Dhira Samira Kunja

Gauridasa Pandita was one of the most famous disciple of Lord Nityananda and an important associate of Lord Chaitanya. He performed his bhajana and worshiped the Deities Radha Shyama-Raya at Dhira Samira Kunja during the period that he lived in Vrindavana. It is said that the Deity of Radha Shyama-Raya was discovered by Gauridas whilst he was bathing in the Yamuna River. Gauridasa Pandita hailed from Ambika Kalna in Bengala and on one occasion both Lord Chaitanya and Lord Nityananda visited his house. Both the daughters of Gauridasa's elder brother, whose names were Jahnava and Vasudha, were married to Lord Nityananda. Gauridasa begged Lord Chaitanya and Lord Nityananda to stay for a longer period in his house so that he could serve Their Lordships to his heart's content. In response Lord Chaitanya manifested a set of Gaura-Nitai Deities that were life-like replicas of the two brothers and gave Them to Gauridas Pandita to worship. Even today these same Deities are still being worshiped at Ambika Kalna. Gauridasa Pandita eventually returned to Bengal but his pushpa samadhi can be seen here at Dhira Samira Kunja next to the temple established by his followers and where the Deity of Radha Shyama-Raya is still being worshiped. According to the Gaura-gannoddesha-dipika Gauridasa Pandita is a cowherd boy named Subala in Krishna's Vrindavana Pastimes and was one of the twelve most important cowherd-boy friends of Krishna known as the dwadasha-gopals.

How To Get There: (See map no.52).

## 35 Radha Kanta Mandira / Gopala Guru Pushpa Samadhi

Gopala Guru was born into an Orissan brahmana family and his name was Makaradhvaja Pandita. In his childhood, because of his family's connection with Vakreswara Pandita, he lived with him and remained under his care and guidance. Gopala Guru was fortunate enough to gain the association of Lord Chaitanya and it is said that by the mercy of Lord Chaitanya's servant Govinda, Makaradhvaja was able to render personal service to Lord Chaitanya. Out of affection for the boy, Lord Chaitanya used to jokingly call him Gopala. One day while serving the Lord, Makaradhvaja noticed a devotee holding his tongue between His teeth to stop himself from chanting while going to answer the call of nature. When Gopala asked the devotee about this, the devotee said his tongue could not stop chanting but it was unclean and improper to chant the Lord's name at that time. Gopala replied that as death can occur at any time, therefore one should continue chanting even when answering the call of nature. On hearing the highly intelligent words of Gopala, Lord Chaitanya was very pleased and said that from now onwards he would be known as Gopala Guru. Some say that the devotee in question was in fact the Lord Himself having fun with the young Gopala. In the years that followed Gopala Guru became an initiated disciple of Vakreshwara Pandita and studied under both Swarupa Damodara and Raghunatha Dasa Goswami.

The Deity of Shri Shri Radhakanta worshiped by Vakreshwara Pandita that was installed in a room next to the Gambhira, had been collected from Southern India during one of the military campaigns of Maharaja Purushottam Dev, the father of Prataparudra. The king had gifted these Deities to Kashi Mishra's father who was his family priest. After his father's death the worship passed on to Kashi Mishra. After the disappearance of Lord Chaitanya, Vakreshwar Pandit moved to the Gambhira formerly used by the Lord and took over the worship of Radhakanta from Kashi Mishra. This Deity was later worshiped by Gopala Guru Goswami.

After his education was over, Gopal Guru Goswami had spent some time in Vrindavana performing bhajana near Dhira Samira, where sometime later his followers established a small temple and installed the pratibhu-murti of Shri Shri Radhakanta. Gopala Guru eventually returned to Puri where he spent the remainder of his life. Before leaving this world, Vakreshwar Pandita handed over the service of Radhakanta to his disciple Gopal Guru Goswami. For many years Gopal Guru Goswami served Shri Shri Radhakanta and in his old age he became concerned about who would serve the Deities after his disappearance. In a dream Lord Krishna informed him, “Don't worry. I've arranged for a sevak to continue the service. He will be the first person you meet tomorrow”. After waking and performing his morning duties he went outside. There he found a young and effulgent brahmana who had been waiting outside his room to see him. Gopal Guru Goswami accepted the young brahmana as his disciple giving him the name Dhyanachandra and engaged him in serving the Deities.

When Gopal Guru Goswami passed away, the king of Puri Maharaja Kaluadeva (Ramachandradeva) was somewhat disturbed that he had not been consulted about the appointment of the new mahanta Dhyanachandra at the temple of Radhakanta and consequently, hearing of Gopala Guru's death and that Dhyanachandra was attending the funeral, the king sent his soldiers to take over the temple. Meanwhile Dhyanachandra had arrived at Swargadwar in Puri where the body of Gopala Guru had been placed on the funeral pyre to be cremated, when he heard about the king's sudden action. Dhyanachandra immediately took hold of his guru's feet and began crying piteously while pleading for guidance. All of a sudden Gopal Guru Goswami rose up from the funeral pyre while loudly chanting the holy names of Krishna, much to the astonishment of everyone present and hastily returned to the Gambhira along with Dhyanachandra and all his followers in a large sankirtan procession in order to reclaim the service of Shri Shri Radhakanta. After this, Gopal Guru is said to have remained at the Gambhira until the reign of the next king. Then with the new king's consent he once again appointed Dhyanachandra as the mahanta, after which left his body which was placed in samadhi. When a group of Vaishnavas returned to Vrindavana after attending the Puri Ratha Yatra, they were completely shocked to see Gopal Guru Goswami sitting under a tree near Dhira Samira where he used to perform his bhajana. These devotees immediately sent word to Dhyanachandra in Puri who instantly left for Vrindavana with a group of his guru's followers.

When Dhyanachandra arrived in Vrindavana, he was surprised to see Gopala Guru Goswami sitting under the tree at Dhira Samira chanting on his beads. Gopala Guru Goswami explained that they were now seeing his spiritual body. Dhyanachandra began to weep in simultaneous happiness and distress. He told Gopala Guru Goswami that it was very difficult for him to live as he was unable to tolerate his separation. Gopal Guru told him that when he goes back in Puri, he should go to Siddha Bakul where Haridas Thakur did his bhajan, and from an old neem tree standing nearby, Dhyanachandra should have Gopala Guru's Deity carved and installed in the temple of Radhakanta. In this way Dhyanachandra would continue to have darshana of his guru. Then after meeting all the Vaishnavas that were residing in Vrindavana, Gopala Guru Goswami disappeared while sitting under the same tree. Therefore his disciples established a pushpa-samadhi near the very same tree which is now located in the courtyard of the Shri Shri Radhakanta Temple that can still be seen today. It is said the Gopala Guru Goswami was Tungavidya-sakhi in Krishna's Vrindavana Pastimes. However, in the book Guru-pranai it is said that Gopal Guru Goswami was the gopi Majumedha-sakhi.

How To Get There: (See map no.52).

## 36 Vamsi Vata

The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “Please see the wonderfully beautiful Vamsi Vata on the bank of the Yamuna, the shade of the Vamsi Vata tree removes the distress of the world. Lord Gopinatha eternally enjoys His pastimes here. His attractive dress enchants the world and His movements are flawless as the sound of His flute attracts the gopis.” In the Chaitanya-charitamrita it is said, “Lord Gopinatha, who originated the transcendental mellow of the rasa-dance, stands on the shore at Vamsa Vata and attracts the attention of the cowherd damsels with the sound of His celebrated flute. May they all confer upon us their benediction.” The word 'vamsi' means 'flute, and 'vata' means a ‘banyan tree'. This is the famous banyan tree under which Krishna stood and while playing on His flute, He would call all the gopis of Vraja to join Him for rasa-lila pastimes in the forest of Vrindavana. Upon hearing the enchanting music emanating from Krishna's flute, regardless of what they were doing, the gopis dropped everything and ran to Vamsi Vata, knowing that Krishna wanted to enjoy Himself in their company. So intense was their love for Krishna, that they were ready to abandon their homes, husbands, children, and even their reputation as chaste women, simply to satisfy Krishna's desires. After reaching Vamsi Vata, Krishna and the gopis would spend the entire night enjoying the rasa-dance and various amorous pastimes in the Vrindavana forest. The Bhakti-ratnakara says, “After leaving behind everything, in great agitation from the sound of the flute, the gopis came here to meet Lord Krishna. They swam in the ocean of Krishna's beauty, and Krishna, seeing their love, could not remain steady. Who can understand how Krishna calmly inquired about the gopis' welfare in a happy mood? In this way, Krishna tested the love of the gopis at this place, as He instructed them in various ways to return to their homes.”

At Vamsi Vata one can see the offshoot of the original banyan tree that was growing here during Krishna's pastimes as well as a simhasana where the ‘divine couple' Radha and Krishna would sit in audience with the gopis of Vraja, and also the rasa-mandala platform commemorating the rasa-lila that took place here. The Bhakti-ratnakara mentions that the celebrated banyan tree known as Vamsi Vata disappeared in the waters of the Yamuna during a great flood; however one of the Gaudiya Gosvamis managed to collect a branch from the original tree and replanted that branch at the same place where the original tree grew. According to most Gaudiya commentators, after the uprooting of the banyan tree at Vamsi Vata in the flood, the Deity of Lord Gopinatha was discovered by Paramananda Goswami lying buried in the ground next to the place where the banyan tree formerly stood. After this amazing discovery, Paramananda Goswami called his dear friend and companion Madhu Pandit Goswami and after they retrieved Lord Gopinatha from the mud, Madhu Pandita took the Deity to his bhajana-kutira where he began the worship Lord Gopinatha, which continued for the rest of his life.

How To Get There: (See map no.52).

## 37 Gopishwara Mahadeva Mandira

This temple of Lord Shiva near Vamsi Vata contains one of the famous dig-pala Deities established by Vajranabha that protect the holy Dhama of Vrindavana. The name 'Gopishwara' means the 'protector' as well as 'benefactor' of the gopis. The word 'ishvara' means ‘the protector' or ‘the controller' and is a general term used to denote the Supreme Lord or His incarnations. Because the gopis worshiped this Deity of Lord Shiva so that they could achieve Krishna as their husband, he became known by the name Gopisha. In the Vraja-riti-chintamani it says. “North of Brahma-kunda is Gopisha where, worshiped by them, Lord Siva pleased the gopis hearts by giving them the benediction to enjoy pastimes with Lord Krishna.”

There is a famous story, which has become part of Vrajavasi folklore regarding the name Gopishwara, which is said to have been given to Lord Shiva by Krishna Himself. This pastime occurred during a performance of the rasa-lila at Vamsi Vata. Lord Shiva, who very much desired to witness the rasa-dance between Krishna and the gopis, once arrived at the rasa-mandala where he was stopped by some of the gopis headed by Lalita and Vishakha. The gopis informed Lord Shiva that no male was allowed to enter into the rasa-mandala, and even though he was qualified in every respect to witness the rasa-dance, he would have to change his form to that of a gopi if he wanted to enter. Lalita advised Lord Shiva to first take bath in the Manasarovara Lake and then return to the rasa-mandala. (Some legends say that Shiva took bath in the nearby Brahma-kunda). After bathing in Manasarovara, Lord Siva obtained the form of a gopi and when he returned to the rasa-mandala he was greeted by Krishna, who, upon seeing the new gopi awarded her the name Gopishwara and requested that she should become the protector of the gopis and the rasa-mandala. Some of the gopis then escorted Gopishwara to a corner of the rasa-mandala where she could sit down and witness the rasa-lila pastimes.

How To Get There: (See map no.52).

## 37A Sapta-samudra Kupa

This is one of the famous wells (kupas) of Vrindavana located near the Gopeshwara Mandira. During the course of time this well has become known as Gopa-kupa.

How To Get There: This well is in the compound of the Rasa-Madhava Mandira(See map no.52).
